units.la: ADFERO ad te, nobilissime Domine, Commentarium meum ad voces Hebraicas noui Testamenti, in quibus praeter ea quae ad vocum sensa pertinent, multa obseruata in Theologis antiquis: partim etiam ostensa ratio scripturae veteris, quam diligenter, ac cum cura notaui, duabus potissimum de causis; primum quia ignota haec vulgo. non enim quisquam ante me eam obseruauit (primus hoc iter ingressus sum sine duce, sine comite; quo magis mihi condonandum sicubi aberro) deinde quia argumentum tale, vt si quis illud tractet non obseruata ratione qua vsi prisci in scribendis nominibus Hebraicis, saepenumero fallatur necesse est. Reperies praeter scripturam antiquam, non pauca quae explicant proprietatem linguae Syriacae. Breuiter omnia, quia neq; ipse amaui vnquam in hoc scribendi genere vbertatem: & molestiam lectori consulto obijcere fugi multitudine verborum. Qualiacumq; ea sint (non enim meum ea extollere) grata spero futura tibi, vir nobilissime, partim quia coniuncta cum scientia linguae sacrae, quam intelligis unus eximie & amas: partim quia primitiae quasi laborum studiorumq; meorum, quae certum mihi deinceps prosequi sub tutela ac patrocinio clarissimi per Europam nominis tui. Deus te Ecclesiae ac Reipub. Belgarum diu seruet incolumem. Lugd. Bata. Calend. Sext. M. D. LXXXII.
units.tr: I bring to you, most noble Lord, my Commentary on the Hebrew words of the New Testament, in which, besides those things that pertain to the meanings of the words, I have noted many points found in the ancient theologians, and have in part also set out the method of the Scripture of the Old Testament, which I have observed carefully and with diligence, for two main reasons. First, because these things are generally unknown: no one before me has observed them (I entered upon this path first, without a guide and without a companion, so that all the more ought any error of mine to be forgiven). Second, because a subject of this kind, if anyone treats it without observing the method by which the ancients used to write Hebrew names, will very often necessarily go astray. You will find, besides the ancient Scripture, not a few things that explain the peculiarity of the Syriac language. I have been brief throughout, because I myself have never cared for abundance in this kind of writing, and I deliberately avoided burdening the reader with a multitude of words. Whatever these pages are worth (for it is not my place to praise them), I hope they will be welcome to you, most noble sir, partly because they are connected with the knowledge of the sacred language, which you alone understand outstandingly well and love; and partly because they are, as it were, the first fruits of my labours and studies, which I have resolved to pursue henceforth under the protection and patronage of your name, which is most famous throughout Europe. May God keep you safe for a long time for the Church and the Commonwealth of the Belgians. At Leiden, on the first of June (calends of Sextilis, as the Latin has it), 1582.

units.la: IOHANNIS DRVSI AD VOCES HEBRAICAS NOVI TESTAMENTI COMMENTARIVS.
units.tr: JOHANNES DRUSIUS, COMMENTARY ON THE HEBREW WORDS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: A. Linguam Syrorum antiquitus Hebraicam dictam. B. Lingua vernacula ætate Christi. C. Idioma Ierosolymitanum.
units.tr: A. The Syriac language was anciently called Hebrew. B. The vernacular language in the age of Christ. C. The Jerusalem idiom.

units.la: {A}INSCRIPTIONEM feci huic libro à vocibus Hebraicis, quod latè intelligendum. Nam pleraeque voces merae Syriacæ sunt. tu me magistro disce Hebraicam linguam vocari etiam Syriacam; hoc est eam quæ ætate Christi & Apostolorum in Iudæa vernacula erat. Clarè doceo ex interpretamentis duarum vocum Gabbatha & Golgotha. Iohan. 19, 13. εἰς τόπον λεγόμενον λιθόστρωτον· ἑβραϊστὶ δὲ γαββαθᾶ.
units.tr: I have given this book the title "On Hebrew words," and I mean the term broadly, for most of the words are purely Syriac. Take my word for it that the Hebrew tongue is also called Syriac, that is, the language which in the age of Christ and the Apostles was the vernacular in Judaea. I show this plainly from the explanations of the two words Gabbatha and Golgotha. John 19:13: "to a place called the Pavement, but in Hebrew Gabbatha" [εἰς τόπον λεγόμενον λιθόστρωτον· ἑβραϊστὶ δὲ γαββαθᾶ].

units.la: Ecce ait Hebraicè, cùm sit vox linguæ Syriæ. paulo post vers. 17 εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον κρανίου τόπον, ὃς λέγεται ἑβραϊστὶ γολγοθᾶ.
units.tr: See, he says "in Hebrew," although it is a word of the Syriac language. A little later, verse 17: "to the place called the Skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha" [εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον κρανίου τόπον, ὃς λέγεται ἑβραϊστὶ γολγοθᾶ].

units.la: Calua Hebraicè vocatur גלגלתא, Syriacè גולגולתא, aut verius גלגלתא. Verbum non addam probandæ rei tam claræ.
units.tr: The skull is called in Hebrew גלגלתא, in Syriac גולגולתא, or more correctly גלגלתא [galgalta]. I will not add a word to prove a point so clear.

units.la: Dixi linguam Syriacam olim in Iudæa vernaculam fuisse: cuius rei testem possem laudare Eliam; sed vtar certiore testimonio. Claris verbis hoc significat Nehemias cap. 13 vers. 23. Quod tamen ita accipiendum, vt intelligas linguam non puram putam Syriacam, sed mistam. Nam quamplurimæ voces in ea Hebraicæ.
units.tr: I have said that the Syriac language was once the vernacular in Judaea. I could cite Elias as a witness to this, but I shall use a more reliable testimony. Nehemiah makes this plain in chapter 13, verse 23. This must be understood in such a way that you grasp that the language was not pure Syriac but mixed, for very many Hebrew words occur in it.

units.la: Ab hac paulo diversum erat idioma Vrbis. colligo ex verbis Petri Actò. 1, 19: & ex Targum Ierosolymitano, qua de re dicam aliàs. nunc propero ad ipsas voces, in quibus explicandis non vtar certo ordine, sed vt quæque prior aut posterior occurret, ita ponam.
units.tr: The idiom of the city was somewhat different from this. I gather this from the words of Peter in Acts 1:19, and from the Jerusalem Targum, about which I will speak elsewhere. Now I hasten to the words themselves, and in explaining them I shall not follow a fixed order, but set them down as each one comes up, earlier or later.

units.la: A. Linguam Syrorum antiquitus Hebraicam dictam.
units.tr: A. The language of the Syrians was anciently called Hebrew.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: A. Iannes & Mamres. B. scriptura Græca expensa. C. itémque Latina.
units.tr: A. Jannes and Mambres. B. The Greek Scripture examined. C. And likewise the Latin.

units.la: TANQVAM aurum inter stercora, sic reperio interdum apud Magistros quod facit ad lucem noui Testaméti. De Iohanne & Mamre pridem repperi apud Nathanum autorem Lexici iuris, qui scribit principes eos fuisse magorum Pharaonis, ac Mosi miracula edenti in Aegypto restitisse; qua de re locus insignis est in Gemara capite Col corbanoth hatsibbur, quem locum ibi laudat Nathanus, à quo ego habeo. Verba Lexici.
units.tr: Like gold among dung, I sometimes find among the teachers something that sheds light on the New Testament. Long ago I found, concerning Jannes and Mambres, in Nathan, author of the Lexicon of law, the statement that they were the chief magicians of Pharaoh and that they resisted Moses when he performed miracles in Egypt. There is a notable passage on this in the Gemara, in the chapter Col corbanoth hatsibbur, which Nathan quotes in that place, and from which I have it. These are the words of the Lexicon.

units.la: נזבא משה למצרים באותות שנתן לו הקב״ה אמרו כו יהיו דהני וממרא ראשי החרטומים של פרעוה זו היא מלאכתנו ואנו יכולין לעשות כן בלהטינו ואתתרומה כמי שמביא תבן לעפריים שהיא עיר תנואה וממנרי שבר למקימורי הרבה וגו׳:
units.tr: When Moses went to Egypt with the signs that the Holy One, blessed be he, had given him, they said: "Jannes and Mambres, the chiefs of Pharaoh's magicians, said, 'This is our work, and we too can do the same with our charms, and with the offering, as one who brings straw to the city of ... and ... to make many.'" [נזבא משה למצרים באותות שנתן לו הקב״ה אמרו כו יהיו דהני וממרא ראשי החרטומים של פרעוה זו היא מלאכתנו ואנו יכולין לעשות כן בלהטינו ואתתרומה כמי שמביא תבן לעפריים שהיא עיר תנואה וממנרי שבר למקימורי הרבה וגו׳]

units.la: Verba illa זאת מלאכתנו וגו׳ Philo Græcè extulit ad hunc modum:
units.tr: Philo rendered the words "this is our work, etc." into Greek in this way:

units.la: οὐδ᾽ ἡμεῖς τῷ τοιούτων ἀμελετήτως ἔχομεν, ἀλλὰ χρώμεθα τέχνῃ δημιουργῷ τῶν ὁμοίων. Ex his apparet mendum esse 2 Timoth. 3, 8 in libris Græcis, legendumque μαμβρῆς aut μαμβρῆς: quod tamen nolim pro certo affirmare. Nam potuit διώνυμος esse. certè apud Numenium Philosophum Pythagoricum liquidò scriptum est ἰαννῆς καὶ ἰαμβρῆς, quos dicit fuisse ἱερογραμματεῖς ἄνδρας in libro tertio περὶ τἀγαθοῦ. ita scribens: τὰ δ᾽ ἐξῆς ἰαννῆς καὶ ἰαμβρῆς ἀνυπποι ἱερογραμματεῖς ἄνδρες οὐδενὸς ἤττους μαγείαι κριθέντες εἶναι ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίων ἐξελαυνομένων ἐξ αἰγύπτου.
units.tr: "Nor are we unskilled in such things, but we use a creative art of the same kind." [οὐδ᾽ ἡμεῖς τῷ τοιούτων ἀμελετήτως ἔχομεν, ἀλλὰ χρώμεθα τέχνῃ δημιουργῷ τῶν ὁμοίων.] From this it appears that there is an error in 2 Timothy 3:8 in the Greek books, and it should be read Mambrēs [μαμβρῆς] or Mambrēs, though I would not wish to affirm this as certain. For the man may have had two names (dionymos). Certainly in Numenius the Pythagorean philosopher it is clearly written Iannēs [ἰαννῆς] and Iambrēs [ἰαμβρῆς], whom he says were "sacred scribes, men no less skilled in magic, who were in Egypt when the Jews were driven out" [τὰ δ᾽ ἐξῆς ἰαννῆς καὶ ἰαμβρῆς ἀνυπποι ἱερογραμματεῖς ἄνδρες οὐδενὸς ἤττους μαγείαι κριθέντες εἶναι ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίων ἐξελαυνομένων ἐξ αἰγύπτου.] in the third book On the Good, writing thus.

units.la: Μωυσαῖῳ γὰρ τῷ Ἰουδαίων ἐξηγησαμένου, ἀνδρὶ γενομένῳ θεῷ εὐξαλῆς δυνατωτάτῳ, οἱ παρεσκευασμένοι ἀξιωθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν αἰγυπτίων, οὐδ᾽ ἦσαν τῶν τε συμφορῶν ὡς ὁ μωυσαῖος ἐπῆλθε τῇ αἰγύπτῳ, τὰς χειρικωτάτας αὐτῶν ἐπιλύσεως ὤφθησαν δυνατοί.
units.tr: "For when Moses led the Jews out, a man who had become a god, very mighty and renowned, the men who had been prepared and summoned by the multitude of the Egyptians were not even able to stand against the calamities with which Moses visited Egypt, nor were they shown to be capable of resolving their most hand-wrought (magical) works." [Μωυσαῖῳ γὰρ τῷ Ἰουδαίων ἐξηγησαμένου, ἀνδρὶ γενομένῳ θεῷ εὐξαλῆς δυνατωτάτῳ, οἱ παρεσκευασμένοι ἀξιωθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν αἰγυπτίων, οὐδ᾽ ἦσαν τῶν τε συμφορῶν ὡς ὁ μωυσαῖος ἐπῆλθε τῇ αἰγύπτῳ, τὰς χειρικωτάτας αὐτῶν ἐπιλύσεως ὤφθησαν δυνατοί.]

units.la: Hos intellexit Artabanus cùm scriberet Pharaonem aduocasse, quos Mosi opponeret τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοὺς ὑπὲρ Μέμφιν. sed ad propositum in Syriacis reperio ימברס, id est Iambres ex Græco. In Latina vulgata Mambres: quæ scriptura proximè accedit ad Hebraicam. Interpres ille quisquis tandem fuit; post Græcos inseruit literam b, quod amat facere inter m & r. Exempla Nimbrod Gen. 10: Mambre Gen. 13. 18. & alia pauca, quæ diligens lector facilè per se obseruabit.
units.tr: Artabanus understood this when he wrote that Pharaoh summoned the priests of Memphis to set against Moses. But for our purpose I find in the Syriac the form ימברס, that is, Iambrs (Yimbrs), taken from the Greek. In the Latin Vulgate it is Mambres, which spelling comes closest to the Hebrew. Whoever that translator was, he inserted the letter b after the Greek form, as he was wont to do between m and r. Examples are Nimrod in Genesis 10, Mambre in Genesis 13 and 18, and a few others, which a careful reader will easily observe for himself.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: DE RAKA.
units.tr: CONCERNING RAKA.

units.la: A. Hieronymi expositio confirmata. B. notatus error Caninij. C. Theophylacti locus expositus. D. Locus e Chrysostomo productus. E. error scripturae antiquae.
units.tr: A. Jerome's explanation confirmed. B. An error of Caninius noted. C. A passage of Theophylact explained. D. A passage quoted from Chrysostom. E. An error in an ancient copy of Scripture.

units.la: RAKA, id est ῥακά, vox conuicij Matth. 5, 22. Syrus habet רקא quae scriptura plane firmat expositionem Hieronymi, cui ego, dum meliore edoctus fuero, libenter accedo. Hierony. aduersus Pelagianos lib. 2.
units.tr: RAKA, that is ῥακά [rhaka], a term of abuse in Matt. 5:22. The Syriac has רקא [rqʾ], which plainly confirms Jerome's explanation, and to which I gladly assent until I am better taught. Jerome, against the Pelagians, book 2.

units.la: „ Qui autem dixerit Raka, quod interpretatur vanus & absque cerebro.
units.tr: "But whoever says Raka, which is interpreted as empty and without brains..."

units.la: Idem in comment. Matth. 5 ad hanc vocem: Hoc verbum proprie „ Hebraeorum est. Raka enim dicitur κενός, id est inanis aut vacuus, „ quem nos possumus vulgata iniuria absque cerebro nuncupare.
units.tr: The same, in his commentary on Matthew 5, on this word: "This word is properly Hebrew. For Raka is said to be κενός [kenos], that is, empty or void, which we may call 'without brains', though this is a loose rendering."

units.la: Pro Raka vir doctus posuit רקח quod iubeo illum quaerere apud Hebraeos. Syrum est רקא ad instar טבא nisi fallor. Apud Magistros inuenio ריקה ut opinor substantiue propter he, quae alioqui esset nota generis foeminini. locus est egregius in libro Musar, quem non pigeret adscribere, nisi prolixior esset. Fallitur autem Caninius dum רקה scribit per patach, quod natum putat ex רקח vsitata vocalium mutatione. fallitur inquam, quia thema est ריק. etiam in eo fallitur quod רקה scribat sub resch chirec minus, quae scriptura analogice postulat dagnes, scriptura in hoc ordine nominum plane peregrina. Ex libris Magistrorum paret hanc vocem olim in frequenti visu fuisse, aut potius abusu, quem Seruator ibi merito damnat.
units.tr: Another learned man has put רקח [rqḥ] for Raka, and I bid him look for it among the Hebrews. The Syriac form is רקא, like טבא [ṭbʾ], unless I am mistaken. Among the Masters (the rabbis) I find ריקה [ryqh], which I think is used as a noun because of the final he, which would otherwise mark the feminine gender. There is an excellent passage in the book Musar, which I would gladly transcribe were it not so long. Caninius, however, is wrong when he writes רקה with patach, which he thinks comes from רקח by the usual change of vowels. He is wrong, I say, because the root is ריק. He is also wrong in writing רקה with resh and a short chirek, whereas analogy requires a dagesh, a spelling quite unusual in this class of nouns. From the books of the Masters it appears that this word was once in common use, or rather in abuse, which the Saviour there rightly condemns.

units.la: In Theophylacteis:
units.tr: In the Theophylact passage:

units.la: τῆς δὲ τὸ ῥακὰ συρισί κατάπτυστον φασὶ σημαίνειν. recte συρισί. est enim vox linguae Syrae citata in Lexico iuris ex ea parte Talmud, quae Gemara vocatur; & ex Niddah; עד שהרוק בתוך הפה
units.tr: "They say that ῥακά [rhaka] in the Syriac language means 'to be spat upon' [κατάπτυστον]," rightly, "syrisi" [συρισί]. For it is a word of the Syriac language, cited in the legal lexicon from that part of the Talmud called the Gemara, and from Niddah: "until the spittle is in the mouth" [עד שהרוק בתוך הפה].

units.la: id est donec saliua est in ore. In eodem Lexico רק אותו האיש, id est spuit. Item ראה רוק למעלה בקורה: id est vidit sputum supra in trabe. Igitur à רק spuit in Benoni quod vocant רק siue רקא passiue, ut אובד perditus, ita ῥακὰ sputo dignus conspuedus, καταπτυστος, ut נמאס contemptibilis, contemptibilis. temptibilis, καὶ ἀγνωστος, condemnandus, condemnabilis, & quæ alia Grammatici notarunt. Peccem in Deum meum, si negem hanc declarationem, præ illa altera quam Theophylactus ibi adfert, non vehementer mihi placere. Sed amabo, quænam est illa altera? aiit Theophylactus ex Chrysostomo, τὸ δὲ ῥακὰ σημαίνει εἰτ̀ τοῦ οὐ. Interpres Chrysostomi hom. 16 in Matth.
units.tr: that is, "while the saliva is in the mouth." In the same lexicon: רק אותו האיש, that is, "he spat"; likewise ראה רוק למעלה בקורה, that is, "he saw spittle above on the beam." Therefore, from רק "to spit", the Benoni, which they call רק or רקא in the passive sense, is like אובד "lost" (perditus); so ῥακὰ means "spat upon, to be spat on" [καταπτυστος], like נמאס "contemptible" (contemptibilis), "condemnable" (condemnabilis), and whatever else the grammarians have noted. I would be sinning against my God if I denied this explanation, but I am not greatly pleased with the other one that Theophylact brings forward there. But please, what is that other one? Theophylact says, following Chrysostom, that τὸ δὲ ῥακὰ σημαίνει εἴτ̀ τοῦ οὐ [to de rhaka sēmainei eit' tou ou], the interpreter of Chrysostom's homily 16 on Matthew:

units.la: „ Qui lingua vtuntur Syrorum, Racha, pro eo quod est, tu, dicere „ solent.
units.tr: "Those who use the language of the Syrians are accustomed to say Racha for what is 'you' (tu)."

units.la: Citius inueniam cornua cerui, quàm si quæram apud Syros ῥακὰ pro tu. sed credamus affirmanti hoc Chrysostomo. Pro clausula tollam leuiculum mendum, quod hæret in pleraque Latinorum codicum parte. In libro De nom. Hebr.
units.tr: I would sooner find the horns of a stag than seek among the Syrians ῥακὰ [rhaka] for "tu". But let us believe Chrysostom when he affirms this. For the conclusion, I shall remove a slight blemish that clings to most of the Latin copies.

units.la: Racha vanus.
units.tr: Racha, vain.

units.la: Leg. Raka.nam racha, id est רכא vel ipso Hieronymo teste, quific distinguit inter has literas in eodem libro his verbis:
units.tr: Read Raka. For racha, that is רכא [rkʾ], even by the testimony of Jerome himself, who distinguishes between these letters in the same book, in these words:

units.la: „ Hucusque per simplicem, c, litera scripta sunt nomina, quæ Græci per x efferunt: exin aspiratione addita legendum, quam illi literam Chi vocant.
units.tr: "Up to this point the names that the Greeks render with x have been written with the simple letter c. Afterwards, with an aspirate added, they are to be read, which letter they call Chi."

units.la: Similis error in σαβαχθανί, quem nos suo loco corrigemus.
units.tr: A similar error occurs in σαβαχθανί [sabachthani], which we shall correct in its proper place.

units.la: CAP. IIII. DE NOMINE IESVS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. ON THE NAME JESUS.

units.la: A. Moscopuli commentum. B. etymon. C. Epiphanij locus. D. Lingua Hebraica. E. Scriptura Græca ἰησοῦς. F. Theophylactus expositus. G. Iaoh. H. mendum sublatum è Theodoreto.
units.tr: A. Moscopulus's commentary. B. Etymology. C. Passage from Epiphanius. D. The Hebrew language. E. Greek Scripture, ἰησοῦς [ἰησοῦς]. F. Theophylactus explained. G. Iaoh. H. Error removed from Theodoret.

units.la: NOMEN hoc è Græcis quidam deducunt ab ἰάομαι futuro verbi ἰάω, quod significat sano, sed perperam. Moscopulus τοῦτο χρὴ ὧν. τὸ Ιησοῦς ὄνομα κρείττονως οἶμαι ἀποδίδοσθαι παρὰ τὸ ἰᾶν τὸ θεραπεύω οὗ ὁ μέλλων ἰάσω, καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἰασοῦς· καὶ τεγπὴ ἔσται ἀεὶς ἡ. Ιησοῦς.
units.tr: Some Greeks derive this name from the future ἰάσω of the verb ἰάω, which means "I heal," but wrongly. Moscopulus says: "It must be said: I think the name Iesus is better rendered from ἰᾶν, 'to heal,' whose future is ἰάσω, and from it ἰασοῦς; and so the name would be ..." [τοῦτο χρὴ ὧν. τὸ Ιησοῦς ὄνομα κρείττονως οἶμαι ἀποδίδοσθαι παρὰ τὸ ἰᾶν τὸ θεραπεύω οὗ ὁ μέλλων ἰάσω, καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἰασοῦς· καὶ τεγπὴ ἔσται ἀεὶς ἡ. Ιησοῦς.]

units.la: Consimile errorem errarunt Eusebius & Egesippus in nomine ἐγσολύμων, quanti viri? Verissimè Theophylactus: τὸ ἰησοῦς ὄνομα οὐκ ἑλληνικόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ ἑβραϊκόν.
units.tr: Eusebius and Egesippus made a similar mistake over the name Jerusalem, and they were great men! Theophylactus is most true: "The name Iesus is not Greek but Hebrew." [τὸ ἰησοῦς ὄνομα οὐκ ἑλληνικόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ ἑβραϊκόν.]

units.la: B Quòd Hebraicū nomen sit, liquidò liquet ex etymo quod habet à seruando, Matth. 1, 21.
units.tr: B. That it is a Hebrew name is quite clear from its etymology, which is from saving, Matt. 1:21.

units.la: καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ιησοῦς. αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν. Non latuit hoc Graecos. Origenes Matth.
units.tr: "And you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins." [καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ιησοῦς. αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν.] This did not escape the Greeks. Origen on Matthew.

units.la: 1. Theophylactus ibidem. Damascenus lib. 1 cap. 12 De orthodoxa fide· τὸ Ἰησοῦς ὄνομα σωτὴρ ἑρμηνεύεται.
units.tr: 1. Theophylactus, ibid. Damascene, book 1, ch. 12, On the Orthodox Faith: "The name Jesus is interpreted as Saviour." [τὸ Ἰησοῦς ὄνομα σωτὴρ ἑρμηνεύεται.]

units.la: Iustinus Martyr apologia pro Christianis 2a. Hieronymus in comment. Matth. 1. Iesus Hebraeo sermone salvator dicitur. Etymologiam verò nominis ipsius Euangelista signauit, dicens, Vocabis nomen eius Iesum, quia ipse saluum faciet populum suum.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, Apology for the Christians, 2. Jerome, on Matthew, ch. 1: "Jesus is called Saviour in the Hebrew tongue. The evangelist indicated the etymology of the name itself when he said, 'You shall call his name Jesus, because he shall save his people.'"

units.la: Vnus Epiphanius κατὰ ναζωραίων.
units.tr: Only Epiphanius, Against the Nazarenes.

units.la: Ἰησοῦς γὰρ κατὰ τὴν ἑβραϊκὴν διάλεκτον Σεσωτὴρ καλεῖται ἡ Ἰατρός.
units.tr: "For Jesus, according to the Hebrew language, is called Sesōtēr, that is, the Physician." [Ἰησοῦς γὰρ κατὰ τὴν ἑβραϊκὴν διάλεκτον Σεσωτὴρ καλεῖται ἡ Ἰατρός.]

units.la: Mira interpretatio. Videtur primùm nata non ex iῶ quod Graecum est, sed ex ꞩꞩ verbo Syro, quod sanare significat. Nam scilicet veteres Hebraicam linguam dixisse pro Syra aut Chaldaea. Sic Eusebius ὡς ἀπαρασχ. lib. 3.
units.tr: A remarkable interpretation. It seems that it first arose not from ἰῶ, which is Greek, but from a Syriac verb, which means to heal. For the ancients evidently used "Hebrew" to mean Syriac or Chaldean. So Eusebius, in book 3 of the ... [ὡς ἀπαρασχ.].

units.la: αὐτίκα ἰησοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβῆ τῶν Ἑβραίων φωνὴν, τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἰνᾶ δασυνόμενον ἑρμηνεύεσθαι ὄφις θήλεια.
units.tr: "Hence Iesu, according to the exact speech of the Hebrews, the name ina, with the breathing marked, is interpreted as 'female serpent.'" [αὐτίκα ἰησοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβῆ τῶν Ἑβραίων φωνὴν, τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἰνᾶ δασυνόμενον ἑρμηνεύεσθαι ὄφις θήλεια.]

units.la: Nam ἰνᾶ, id est יְהוּא vox linguae Aramaeae. Haec interpretatio refelli potest ex scriptura ea qua nomen istud scriptum reperitur in nouo testamento Syro: partim etiam in veteri, vt Ezrae 2, 2: vbi Graecè est Ἰησοῦς, in Latina vulgata Iesua, Hebraicè autem יֵשׁוּעַ, quod idem est cum nomine Iosua qui Hebraicè יְהוֹשֻׁעַ. docceo ex eo quia Iosua Iosadaci filius, qui Iesua dicitur Ezrae 3, 2; in Haggaeo passim & Zacharia appellatur Iehosua: argumentum inuictum contra eos, qui volunt Christo diuersum fuisse nomē à nomine ducis Iosuae & Iosuae sacerdotis. Quaeri potest vnde Graecum Ἰησοῦς? nam à ישוע fieret Iesua aut Iesuas, sicut à מָשִׁיחַ. Messias. Credibile est veteres vsitasse ישׁוּ pro ישׁוּעַ consuetudine ea qua vltimam y per apocopen abijciùt. Porrò ישׁוּ id est Ἰησοῦ, & terminatione Graeca Ἰησοῦς. quae appellatio adhuc hodie manet apud Iudaeos. Elias Leuita Tisbite: יש לומר לפי שר־הנרת חעין קשה לכשא לגום לפיכך אינם קורין לו ישוע אך ישו או ושוּ לכך קורין לו היהודים גם כן ישו בלא עין:
units.tr: For ina, that is [יְהוּא], is a word of the Aramaic language. This interpretation can be refuted from the writing in which this name is found in the New Testament in Syriac, and partly also in the Old, as in Ezra 2:2, where the Greek has Iēsous, the Latin Vulgate has Iesua, and the Hebrew has [יֵשׁוּעַ], which is the same as the name Joshua, which in Hebrew is [יְהוֹשֻׁעַ]. I show this from the fact that Joshua, son of Jozadak, who is called Jeshua in Ezra 3:2, is everywhere in Haggai and Zechariah called Jehoshua. This is an unanswerable argument against those who want the name of Christ to be different from the name of the leader Joshua and of the priest Joshua. It may be asked whence the Greek Iēsous comes? For from [ישוע] would come Iesua or Iesuas, as from [מָשִׁיחַ] comes Messias. It is credible that the ancients used [ישׁוּ] for [ישׁוּעַ], by the habit of cutting off the final letter through apocope. Moreover, [ישׁוּ] is Iēsou, and with the Greek ending it is Iēsous. This form of the name still remains today among the Jews. Elias Levita the Tishbite: [יש לומר לפי שר־הנרת חעין קשה לכשא לגום לפיכך אינם קורין לו ישוע אך ישו או ושוּ לכך קורין לו היהודים גם כן ישו בלא עין:]

units.la: id est, Dici potest quòd litera Aijn ardua sit ac difficilis pronuntiatu gētibus. Ideo in lingua sua non dicūt Iesuag, sed Iesu aut Iesus. propterea Iudęi etiam vocant eum Iesu absq. Aijn. Iam perspicuum est ex scriptura errare eos qui derivant à verbo אסא. nec posse aliunde deduci, quàm à יש verbo seruandi, quam nominis origine clarè arguit Euangelista Matthaeus in loco supra citato. errant etiam nuperi interpre-
units.tr: That is: it may be said that the letter ayin is hard and difficult to pronounce for the nations. Therefore in their language they do not say Iesuag, but Iesu or Iesus; for this reason the Jews also call him Iesu without ayin. Now it is clear from Scripture that those err who derive the name from the verb [אסא], and it cannot be derived from anything other than the verb [יש], "to save," as the evangelist Matthew clearly shows in the passage cited above. Recent interpreters also err, who derive it from the name Jehovah by inserting the letter shin. I show that they err from the meaning that Jehovah has from "to exist," not from "to save." But as for what we read in Theophylactus, "For salvation is called Iaō among the Hebrews," I take it as if it were said, "The name Iesus is called among the Hebrews Iaō, salvation."

units.la: C, D, E: marginal reference marks as printed beside the text. interpretes, qui deducunt à nomine Iehoua per interpositionē litere Sin. errare doceo ex significatione quam Iehoua habet ab existendo, non à seruando. Quod autem apud Theophylactum legimus ἰαω γὰρ ἡ σωτηρία παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδαίοις λέγεται: ita accipio, ac si dictū esset τὸ ἰησοῦς ὄνομα παρὰ τοῖς ἑβραίοις λέγεται ἰαὼ σωτηρίᾳ.
units.tr: C, D, E: ... interpreters, who derive it from the name Iehoua by inserting the letter Sin. I show that they err from the meaning Iehoua has from existing, not from saving. [ἰαω γὰρ ἡ σωτηρία παρὰ τοῖς ἑβδαίοις λέγεται]

units.la: Aut est error interpretis, quem eundem reperies apud Moscopulum:
units.tr: Or it is an error of the translator, which you will find the same in Moscopulus:

units.la: καὶ γίνεται παρὰ τὸ ἰαω, ὃ δηλοῖ τὴν σωτηρίαν ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἑβραϊκόν.
units.tr: "And it comes from ἰαω, which signifies salvation, which is Hebrew." [καὶ γίνεται παρὰ τὸ ἰαω, ὃ δηλοῖ τὴν σωτηρίαν ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἑβραϊκόν.]

units.la: Neque enim ab Iaoh derivari potest Iesus. erratum ex hac causa. Interpretamentum vetus Iosua ἰαὼ σωτήριον aut σωτηρία, quasi ψυ nim id est salus Iehouae. Nam ἰαὼ id est Iehoua. Theodoritus Quæst. 15 in Exod. de nomine tetragrammato: καλοῦσιν δὲ αὐτὸ Σαμαρεῖται μὲν ἰαβέ, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ ἰαώ.
units.tr: For Jesus cannot be derived from Iaoh. The error arose from this cause: the old interpretation of Joshua, "Iaō the saving" or "salvation," as if [ψυ] meant the salvation of Jehovah. For ἰαὼ is Jehovah. Theodoret, Question 15 on Exodus, on the tetragrammaton: "The Samaritans call it iabe, but the Jews iao." [καλοῦσιν δὲ αὐτὸ Σαμαρεῖται μὲν ἰαβέ, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ ἰαώ.]

units.la: Vbi perperam ἰὰ scriptum est. Eusebius ἀποδείξ. lib. 4 capite vltimo:
units.tr: Where [ἰὰ] has been wrongly written. Eusebius, Demonstration, book 4, last chapter:

units.la: Σωτήριον θεοῦ εἰς τὴν ἑλλάδα φωνὴν τὸ τοῦ ἰησοῦ μεταλη φθὲν ὄνομα σημαίνει. & mox:
units.tr: "The salvation of God, in the Greek language, is signified by the name Jesus, transferred..." [Σωτήριον θεοῦ εἰς τὴν ἑλλάδα φωνὴν τὸ τοῦ ἰησοῦ μεταλη φθὲν ὄνομα σημαίνει.] And shortly after:

units.la: Ἰωσυὰ δὲ ἑαυτὸν ἰαὼ σωτηρία, τοῦτ' ἐστι θεοῦ σωτήριον, εἰκότως εἶπου θεοῦ σωτήριον ἐν τοῖς ἑλληνικοῖς ἀντηρέφοις ὠνόμασαι, οὐδ' ἄλλο τι ἡ τὸν ἰησοῦν κατὰ τὴν ἑβραίων φωνὴν πεπεισμὸ δηλοῦσας.
units.tr: "Joshua himself is Iaō salvation, that is, the salvation of God; and it was rightly named in the Greek translations 'the salvation of God,' signifying nothing other than Jesus in the Hebrew speech." [Ἰωσυὰ δὲ ἑαυτὸν ἰαὼ σωτηρία, τοῦτ' ἐστι θεοῦ σωτήριον, εἰκότως εἶπου θεοῦ σωτήριον ἐν τοῖς ἑλληνικοῖς ἀντηρέφοις ὠνόμασαι, οὐδ' ἄλλο τι ἡ τὸν ἰησοῦν κατὰ τὴν ἑβραίων φωνὴν πεπεισμὸ δηλοῦσας.]

units.la: Ceterum quòd quidam asserit ex proprietate sermonis Hebraici Iehosua potius Seruandū, quàm Seruatorē denotare, id non possum nō improbare, cùm ea sit potius linguæ proprietas, vt nominum formas propriorum, quæ significationum indices sint, non distinguat.
units.tr: As for what some assert, that from the peculiarity of the Hebrew idiom Jehoshua denotes "to save" rather than "Saviour," I cannot fail to disapprove, since it is rather a feature of that language that it does not distinguish the forms of proper names, which are indicators of meaning.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: Chapter V.

units.la: A. Bar. B. Barrabas. C. Bariona. D. Bartholomæus. E. Bartimæus. F. Bariesus. G. Barchochebas. H. Barporas. I. Quid Giora.
units.tr: A. Bar. B. Barabbas. C. Bariona. D. Bartholomew. E. Bartimaeus. F. Bariesus. G. Barchochebas. H. Barporas. I. What is Giora?

units.la: BAR extra controuersiam Syra vox est, & filium significat, qui Hebraicè Ben dicitur. quanquam & Bar reperitur in textu Hebraeo, vt Psal. 2 & Proverb. 30. nec alibi quod sciam. In nouo Testamento Barrabas, Bariona, Bartholomæus, Bartimæus, Bariesus: apud Eusebium Barchochebas; Xiphilinū Barporas nomina sunt propria composita cum hac voce; de quibus singulatim quæ digna notatu habeo, notabo.
units.tr: Bar is beyond dispute a Syriac word, and it means "son", which in Hebrew is called ben. Yet bar is also found in the Hebrew text, as in Psalm 2 and Proverbs 30, and nowhere else that I know of. In the New Testament there are Barabbas, Bariona, Bartholomew, Bartimaeus and Bariesus; in Eusebius, Barchochebas; in Xiphilinus, Barporas. These are proper names compounded with this word. I will note, one by one, whatever I have that is worth noting about them.

units.la: Barrabas. In Nominibus de Matthæo
units.tr: Barabbas. On the names in Matthew.

units.la: Barrabam filium magistri eorum. Quis credat hanc interpretationem Hieronymi esse? pronomen delendum, vel ex eo quòd Barrabas dicimus in recto casu, non Barrabam, כר רבא filius Magistri. In Syriacis reperio בר אבא filius patris, aut filius patris mei. vide Matth. 27, 16.
units.tr: "Barabbam, the son of their master." Who would believe that this interpretation is Jerome's? The pronoun should be deleted, or else we would say Barrabam rather than Barabbas in the nominative. [כר רבא] means "son of the master". In the Syriac I find [בר אבא], "son of the father", or "son of my father". See Matthew 27:16.

units.la: Bariona. βαειωνᾶ, id est υἱὸς τοῦ ἰωνᾶ. Hebraicè בר יונא. lectio alia βαειωνᾶνου, id est בר יוחנן aut בר יוחנן υἱὸς ἰωάνου. Nonnus poëta: υἱὸς ἰωάνᾳο σὺ μοι πέλεις, ἰασὶ δὲ Σίμων. Priorem lectionem interpretatur Hieronymus in libro De nominibus Hebraicis, & puto germanam esse.
units.tr: Bariona: [βαειωνᾶ], that is, [υἱὸς τοῦ ἰωνᾶ], "son of Jonas". In Hebrew, [בר יונא]. Another reading is [βαειωνᾶνου], that is, [בר יוחנן] or [υἱὸς ἰωάνου], "son of John". The poet Nonnus says: "You are the son of John, but your name is Simon" [υἱὸς ἰωάνᾳο σὺ μοι πέλεις, ἰασὶ δὲ Σίμων]. Jerome explains the former reading in his book On Hebrew Names, and I think it is the genuine one.

units.la: Bartholomæus. In Bartholomæus negat vir doctus Tholomæum esse, qui à nobis Ptolomæus dicitur. Gorionides contra Histor. Iud. lib. 2 cap. 3
units.tr: Bartholomew. A learned man denies that "Tholomaeus" is the one we call Ptolemy. Gorionides, against the Jewish History, book 2, chapter 3.

units.la: אפטולמיוס הוא תלמי
units.tr: [אפטולמיוס הוא תלמי] (Ptolemy is Talmai).

units.la: differèait Ptolomæus & Talmai idem esse. firmandæ rei citabo locum ex Seder Olam Suta, qui Caninium clarè convincit:
units.tr: Gorionides held that Ptolemy and Talmai are the same. To confirm the matter, I will cite a passage from the Seder Olam Suta, which clearly refutes Caninius:

units.la: תלמי כתב את התורה יונית
units.tr: [תלמי כתב את התורה יונית]

units.la: id est ad verbum, Talmai scripsit legem Græcè. Significat autem Ptolomæum Philadelphum regem Aegypti, qui procurauit translationem Græcá Legis per septuaginta duos Interpretes. est autem Talmai à Syris dictus Tulmai, vnde Ptolomæus. fortean Pe additum ex proprietate linguæ Himaeliticæ.
units.tr: That is, word for word: "Talmai wrote the Law in Greek." It refers to Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, who arranged the Greek translation of the Law by the seventy-two interpreters. Talmai is called Tulmai by the Syrians, whence Ptolemy. Perhaps the Pe was added through the idiom of that language.

units.la: Bartimæus. Marci 10, 46. ὁ υἱὸς Τιμαίου βαρτιμαῖος. ex ordine non vanè quis suspicetur ab ipso Euangelista esse τῶ filius Timæi, quæ declaratio indicat nomen patris Bartimæi; eo magis quòd multa nomina propria Syris quorum formatio à Bar voce, quæ apud eam gentè in compositionibus frequens est. In Syriacis Marci שמי בר שמי id est Timæus filius Timæi, lectio alia, filius Timæi Barsemia. eá observat Hieronymus; sed addit corruptá esse in libro De nominibus Hebraicis. Barsemia, id est filius cœcus בר סמיא
units.tr: Bartimaeus. Mark 10:46: [ὁ υἱὸς Τιμαίου Βαρτιμαῖος]. One might not unreasonably suspect, from the order of the words, that the evangelist himself added "son of Timaeus", a clause that names Bartimaeus' father. All the more so because many proper names among the Syrians are formed with the word bar, which is frequent in compounds in that nation. In the Syriac of Mark it is [שמי בר שמי], that is, Timaeus son of Timaeus. Another reading is "son of Timaeus, Barsemia". Jerome notes this, but adds that it is corrupted in the book On Hebrew Names. Barsemia means "the blind man's son" [בר סמיא].

units.la: Bariesus. βαεισοῦς Acto. 13, 6. Admonet Hieronymus de corrupta scriptura, & legit Bericu, in libro De nom. Hebr. ego non capio cur hæc scriptura melior sit præ vulgata. Bariesu, id est בר ישו υἱὸς ἰησοῦ. In schidis meis reperio βαεισοῦ, id est בר יהושע. Apud Syrú בר שומא id est Bar Suma. & paulò post:
units.tr: Bariesus: [βαρισοῦς], Acts 13:6. Jerome warns about the corrupt writing and reads "Bericu" in his book On Hebrew Names. I do not see why this spelling is better than the Vulgate's. Bariesu means [בר ישו], that is, [υἱὸς Ἰησοῦ], "son of Jesus". In my notes I find [βαρισοῦ], that is, [בר יהושע]. Among the Syrians it is [בר שומא], that is, Bar Suma. And a little later:

units.la: B ,, Stetit igitur contra eos magus ille Barsuma; quod interpretatum ,, sonat Elumus.
units.tr: "Therefore that magician Barsuma stood against them, which, translated, means Elumus."

units.la: Pro Elumus in Græco est ἐλύμας, id est אלימא, vt conijcio μάγος ἱπποσοφὸς, quia de re dicam alias.
units.tr: For "Elumus" the Greek has [ἐλύμας], that is, [אלימא]. I conjecture that it is [μάγος], a magician, as I will say elsewhere about this matter.

units.la: Addam aliud, quamquam non repertum in nouo Testamento. Quid refert, si locum faciam paroemiæ Græcæ ἐκτὸς τῶν ἐλαιῶν.
units.tr: I will add another, although it is not found in the New Testament. What does it matter if I make room for the Greek proverb: [ἐκτὸς τῶν ἐλαιῶν], "outside the olive groves"?

units.la: Eusebius eccl. hist. lib. 4 cap. 6 ἱστορεῖ τῶν Ιουδαίων τὴν κώμην βαρχοχέβας ὄνομα· ὃ ἀξίως δηλοῖ. tu à me disce Barchochebas non ἀστήρ, sed υἱὸς τοῦ ἀστέρος. est enim compositio vocis ex βὰρ & χοχὰβ, id est בר כוכב pronuntiatione vetere. χοχαβ sydus siue stella.
units.tr: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 6, records that the name of the Jewish village was [βαρχοχέβας], which fittingly signifies [ὃ ἀξίως δηλοῖ]. Learn from me that Barchochebas is not [ἀστήρ], "star", but [υἱὸς τοῦ ἀστέρος], "son of the star". For the name is compounded of [βὰρ] and [χοχὰβ], that is, [בר כוכב] in the old pronunciation. [χοχαβ] means a star or heavenly body.

units.la: Barporas. Ponam in hac voce emendationem meam, licet enim mihi credo quod alijs multis licuit. si non temere id facio, si receptam scripturam non sollicito, tantum mendum indico, quis reprehendat? Xiphilinus in Vespasiano:
units.tr: Barporas. I will set out my emendation of this word. For if I may believe that what many others have been allowed to do is allowed to me, and if I do this not rashly, and if I do not disturb the received text but only point out a fault, who could rightly find fault with it? Xiphilinus, in the life of Vespasian:

units.la: ,, Capti sunt ab eo multi, præsertim Barporas, qui apud eos princi-
units.tr: "Many were taken by him, especially Barporas, who held the leading place among them,

units.la: ,, patum tenebat, isque solus in triumpho supplicijs affectus est.
units.tr: and he alone was put to death with torture in the triumph."

units.la: Quis iste Barporas? videtur leg. Bargioras, id est filius Giorae. Iosephus captæ Iudææ lib. 4 cap. 30 υἱὸς γιώρα Σίμων τις μεγαπολὺς τὸ γένος νεανίας.
units.tr: Who is this Barporas? He seems to be read as Bargioras, that is, son of Giora. Josephus, The Jewish War, book 4, chapter 30: [υἱὸς Γιώρα Σίμων τις μεγαπολὺς τὸ γένος νεανίας], "Simon, a son of Giora, a young man of a great family."

units.la: υἱὸς γιώρα id est βαργιώρα, & Græca terminatione βαργιώρας. Ne autem putes mendum esse in γιώρα, ecce eadem scriptura apud Ruffinum:
units.tr: [υἱὸς Γιώρα], that is, [βαργιώρα], and with the Greek ending, [βαργιώρας]. Lest you think the error is in [γιώρα], here is the same spelling in Rufinus:

units.la: ,, Erat Simon Giorae filius, patria Gerasenus ætate iuuenis.
units.tr: "Simon was the son of Giora, a native of Gerasa, young in years."

units.la: Fuit tempus cum existimarem legendum Sarporas, quasi שר פריץ pro שר פריים, quod epitheton Iohanni plurimum tribuit Gorionides Historicus Hebræus. nunc muto, & indubitanter de Simone hæc intelligenda esse statuo ex ipsa Historia. solus enim Simon triumpho seruatus est, Iohanne ad perpetuos carceres damnato, Iosep. lib. 7, cap. 46: Σίμων δὲ πολλὰ διαμαχήσας πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγκην ὡς διὰ τῶν ἐξῆς δηλώσομεν ἑαυτὸν παραδιδόντων. ἐφυλάχθη δὲ ὁ μὲν τῷ θεᾷ μβῳ σφάγιον, ὁσὲ ἰωάννης δεσμοῖς αἰωνίοις.
units.tr: There was a time when I thought one should read "Sarporas", as if [שר פריץ] for [שר פריים], which the Hebrew historian Gorionides very often gives as an epithet of John. Now I change my mind, and I hold with confidence that these things are to be understood of Simon, from the history itself. For Simon alone was kept for the triumph, John being condemned to perpetual prison (Josephus, book 7, chapter 46): [Σίμων δὲ πολλὰ διαμαχήσας πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγκην, ὡς διὰ τῶν ἑξῆς δηλώσομεν, ἑαυτὸν παραδιδόντων. ἐφυλάχθη δὲ ὁ μὲν τῷ θεᾷ μβῳ σφάγιον, ὁσὲ Ἰωάννης δεσμοῖς αἰωνίοις.] "Simon, after resisting necessity for a long time, surrendered himself, as we shall show in what follows. He was kept as a victim for the triumph, while John was kept in everlasting chains."

units.la: In Giora hæreo ac dubito proprium nomé sit an pater Simonis ex iis fuerit qui Giorae vocabantur. Eusebius Histor. eccles. lib. 1. cap. 7 τὸ γένος ἀνάγκην ἐπὶ τοὺς πατριάρχας ἢ φωσπλύζους, πύστε καλουμένους μένους γειώρας ζους ἐπιμίκτους.
units.tr: As for Giora, I hesitate and doubt whether it is a proper name, or whether Simon's father was one of those who were called Giorae. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 7: [τὸ γένος ἀνάγκην ἐπὶ τοὺς πατριάρχας ἢ φωσπλύζους, πύστε καλουμένους μένους γειώρας ζους ἐπιμίκτους].

units.la: Iustinus Martyr in disputatione πρὸς Τρύφωνα·
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in the Dialogue with Trypho:

units.la: ταῦτα ὑμεῖς μὲν εἰς τὸν γνόφον καὶ τὺς θεοσπλύζους εἰρηθας νομίζετε.
units.tr: [ταῦτα ὑμεῖς μὲν εἰς τὸν γνόφον καὶ τοὺς θεοσπλύτους εἰρῆσθαι νομίζετε]. "You, however, think these things were said of the darkness and of the God-washed ones."

units.la: In lingua Syrorum אתונא θεοσπλύτος. Theodoritus ad Exod. Quæst. 14.
units.tr: In the Syriac language, "athuna" means [θεοσπλύτος], "God-washed". Theodoret on Exodus, Question 14.

units.la: καὶ γὰρ θεοσπλύτους ματαλαγχάνειν τῶ πάσχα θεοσέταξεν · γοεῶν γὰρ τὸν θεοσπλύτον ἐκάλεσε.
units.tr: [καὶ γὰρ θεοσπλύτους μεταλαγχάνειν τοῦ πάσχα θεὸς ἔταξεν· γόεα γὰρ τὸν θεοσπλύτον ἐκάλεσε]. "For God commanded the God-washed to partake of the Passover; for he called the [γόεα] the God-washed one."

units.la: Non γόεα sed γὴρ. hoc Hebraicum,illud Syrum est, cum pace dixerim Theodoriti. Porrò apud Iosephum vt sit proprium Giora, magis inclinat sententia.
units.tr: It should be read not [γόεα] but [γὴρ]. The latter is Hebrew, and the former is Syriac, and I say this with Theodoret's leave. Moreover, in Josephus, if Giora is a proper name, the opinion inclines more that way.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Sadvcæis.
units.tr: CAP. VI. On the Sadducees.

units.la: A. Vnde dicti. B. correcta scriptura vulgaria. C. Epiphanij locus. D. Hæresis eorum quænam fuerit. E. vnde primùm cæperit.
units.tr: A. Whence they were named. B. The corrected spelling of the common form. C. Epiphanius's passage. D. What their heresy was. E. Where it first began.

units.la: DE Saducæorum nomine ac doctrina, etsi satis plana res est, observabo tamen aliquid, quod ante me nemo obseruauit. ac primùm de nomine Theophylactus: Σαδδουκαῖοι ἑρμηνεύονται δίκαιοι· σιδὶκ γὰρ δικαιοσύνη. δικαίους γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς ὠνόμαζον· ἢ ἀπὸ αἱρετιαρχου Σαδωκ ὀνομάζονται. Duplex sententia: prior dicit quòd appellati sint Saducæi à iustitia. Nam iustitia Hebraicè Sedec dicitur: altera dicit, quòd sic appellati sint ab Hæresiarcho Sadoc. hæc vera est. In Lexico iuiis: וקראו צדוקים על שם צדוק id est, Vocati sunt Saducæi de nomine Sadoc. Hic obiter obseruo, scribendum Saducæi vnica, d, non Sadducæi. id eruo ex scriptura nominis Sadoc; 2 Sam. 8, 17. Nam scilicet idem nomen fuisse & ei, à quo secta appellata est. Porrò à Sadoc qui scribit Sadducæi, peccat bifariam; primùm quia literam consonantem geminat tanquam per daghes: deinde quia legit patach sub tsade cùm sit camets. Hoc posito, quæramus quis fuerit Sadoc iste? Nam ignotum hoc vulgo. Vir doctus in notis ad Augustini libellum De hæresibus ex Epiphanio ita scribit: „ Saducæi tanquam iustitiarij aut iusti dicti sunt, vel à Sadoc summo sacrificatore.
units.tr: Although the name and teaching of the Sadducees are fairly plain, I shall note one point that no one before me has observed. First, on the name, Theophylact says: The Sadducees are interpreted as "righteous," for sidik means righteousness; for they called themselves righteous. Or they are named from the heresiarch Sadoc. There are two views. The first holds that the Sadducees were called after righteousness, since righteousness is called Sedec in Hebrew. The second holds that they were so called from the heresiarch Sadoc, and this is the true view. In the Lexicon of Jais we read: "The Sadducees were called after the name of Sadoc," that is, Vocati sunt Saducæi de nomine Sadoc. Here I note in passing that the name should be written Saducæi with a single d, not Sadducæi. I prove this from the spelling of the name Sadoc in 2 Sam. 8.17, for the heresiarch bore the same name as the sect that took its title from him. Moreover, those who write Sadducæi with a double d go wrong in two ways: first, because they double the consonant as if by a dagesh; second, because they read a patah under the tsade where it should be a qamets. With this settled, let us ask who this Sadoc was, for the common people do not know. A learned man, in his notes to Augustine's book On Heresies, drawing on Epiphanius, writes thus: "The Sadducees were so called as if they were 'justiciaries' or 'the just,' or from Sadoc the high priest."

units.la: Si hoc dicit Epiphanius, frustra est, sed meo animo non videtur hoc dicere. Ponam ipsius verba:
units.tr: If Epiphanius says this, the claim is worthless; but in my judgement he does not say it. I shall give his own words:

units.la: ἦν δὲ καὶ Σαδοὺκ τὶς ᾿Ιουδαῖος τὴν νόμον κατὰ τὸ παλαιὸν τῶν ἱερέων · ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐνέμειναν οὗτοι ἐν τῇ ᾿Ιουδαίων διδασκαλία·
units.tr: There was also a certain Jew named Sadoc, of the priestly line of old; but these men did not abide in the teaching of the Jews. [ἦν δὲ καὶ Σαδοὺκ τὶς ᾿Ιουδαῖος τὴν νόμον κατὰ τὸ παλαιὸν τῶν ἱερέων · ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐνέμειναν οὗτοι ἐν τῇ ᾿Ιουδαίων διδασκαλία·]

units.la: id est, Fuit priscis temporibus sacerdos quidam nomine Sadoc, sed non manserunt isti in præsulis sui doctrina.
units.tr: That is: in earlier times there was a priest named Sadoc, but these men did not remain in the teaching of their leader.

units.la: Quod Epiphanius hic ait, verissimum est: Sadoc autem à quo Saducæi, discipulus fuit Antigoni Sochæi. R. Nathan in vitis patrum. Iehielides in Lexico iuris. Elias Germanus Tisbite. Amplius reperio citatum ex libro Alcosder Iudæ Leuitæ.
units.tr: What Epiphanius says here is most true. Sadoc, from whom the Sadducees took their name, was a disciple of Antigonus of Sokho. So R. Nathan in Vitae patrum, Jehielides in the Lexicon of the Law, and Elias the German of Tishbi. I also find it cited from the book Alcosder of Judah the Levite:

units.la: „ Ezdras Cabalam tradidit Simeoni Iusto: is Antigono, & socijs „ ipsius, è quibus Sadoc & Baithos hæresiarchæ, unde Saducæi & „ Baithusæi.
units.tr: "Ezra handed down the Cabbalah to Simeon the Just; he handed it to Antigonus and his fellows, of whom Sadoc and Baithos were heresiarchs, whence come the Sadducees and the Boethusians."

units.la: Hæc de nomine: in quo falluntur qui à iustitia appellatos censent Saducæos. De doctrina res clarior. Negabant resurrectionem argumentis ab absurdo Matth. 22, 23. à non scripto, ut quod refutat ibidem ὀ σωτὴρ.
units.tr: So much for the name, in which those are mistaken who think the Sadducees were named from righteousness. The teaching is clearer. They denied the resurrection, arguing from absurdity (Matt. 22.23), and from what is not written, which the Saviour refutes there [ὁ σωτὴρ].

units.la: Item dicebant, Si patres nostri sciuissent mortuos resurrecturos, & præmia manere iustos post hanc vitam, non tam sæpe rebellassent. Iehielides in loco memorato: Reijciebant traditiones patrum, adeoq. omnem omnino Legis expositionem. Ioseph Ben Gorion Histor. suæ lib. 4 cap. 29.
units.tr: Likewise they said: "If our fathers had known that the dead would rise and that the righteous would have rewards after this life, they would not so often have rebelled." Jehielides, in the place already cited: they rejected the traditions of the fathers, and therefore every interpretation of the Law whatever. Joseph ben Gorion, Historia, book 4, chapter 29:

units.la: הנרי התרוקים אומרים לא נאמין ולא נשמע לפל מסורת ולכל פירוש כי אם לתורת משה לכר:
units.tr: Behold, the Sadducees said: "We will not believe or listen to any tradition or any interpretation, but only to the Law of Moses." [הנרי התרוקים אומרים לא נאמין ולא נשמע לפל מסורת ולכל פירוש כי אם לתורת משה לכר:]

units.la: id est, Ecce Saducæi dicebant, Ne credamus neque auscultemus vlli traditioni, aut vlli expositioni, sed tantum legi Mosis. Elias Leuita Germanus in Tisbite:
units.tr: That is: "Behold, the Sadducees said: let us not believe nor listen to any tradition, nor to any exposition, but only to the Law of Moses." Elias the Levite, the German, in Tishbi:

units.la: כפרי בתורה שבעל פה ולא האמינו רק מה שכתוב בתורה שבכתב עלכן קורין להם קראים לשון מקרא:
units.tr: He denied the Oral Law and did not believe anything but what stands in the written Law; therefore they were called Qaraim, that is, "scripturalists." [כפרי בתורה שבעל פה ולא האמינו רק מה שכתוב בתורה שבכתב עלכן קורין להם קראים לשון מקרא:]

units.la: id est, Negabant legem oretenus traditam, & non credebant, nisi quod extat in lege scripta: Ideo vocati sunt Caraim. nam μικεῖ scriptura.
units.tr: That is: they denied the law delivered by word of mouth and did not believe it, but only what is in the written law. Therefore they were called Caraim, since they are named from the word for Scripture [mikra].

units.la: De Pharisæis asseuerabant quòd se miserè affligerent in hac vita propter traditiones, neque tamen in altera vita, quod esse credebant, mercedem inde vllam reportarent. Nathan Iustus Iehielides, Nata hæc hæresis ex dicto quodam Antigoni fortasse sequius accepto quàm ipse intellexerat. Meminit Iehielides,& extat in Sententijs patrum.est autem huiusmodi:
units.tr: Of the Pharisees they affirmed that they afflicted themselves wretchedly in this life for the sake of the traditions, yet did not, as they believed, gain any reward from them in the next life. Nathan, Justus, Jehielides: this heresy arose from a saying of Antigonus, perhaps taken in a worse sense than he himself meant it. Jehielides mentions it, and it is found in the Sayings of the Fathers. It runs as follows:

units.la: אל תהיו כעברים המשמשים ארת הרב על מנת לקבל פרס אלא הוי כעברים המשמשים את חרב שלא על מנת לקבל פרס ויהי מירא שמים עליכם:
units.tr: Be not like servants who minister to the master in order to receive a reward; but be like servants who minister to the master without a view to reward, and let the fear of heaven be upon you. [אל תהיו כעברים המשמשים ארת הרב על מנת לקבל פרס אלא הוי כעברים המשמשים את חרב שלא על מנת לקבל פרס ויהי מירא שמים עליכם:]

units.la: id est,Nolite similes esse seruis ijs qui seruiunt domino pro mercede: sed este similes seruis ijs, qui seruiunt quidem domino, non tamen pro mercede. sitque timor cœli super vos.
units.tr: That is: "Do not be like servants who serve their lord for wages, but be like servants who serve their lord without a view to wages; and let the fear of heaven be upon you."

units.la: Sed de his satis superque.
units.tr: But enough and more than enough on these matters.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: IN ACTIS LOCVS ILLVSTRATVS. Elymas quid?
units.tr: A PASSAGE OF THE ACTS ILLUSTRATED. What is Elymas?

units.la: Locus est subobscurus Act. 13, 8: cui lucem dabo hoc capite de coniectura. Nam verba illa:
units.tr: The passage is somewhat obscure, Acts 13:8. I will shed light on it in this chapter by conjecture. For those words:

units.la: ΑΝθίστῶ δ' ἀὐτῇς Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος, ἔτω γὰρ μεθερμηνεύεται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ· mirè torquent quosdam interpretes, & nectunt nodum, quem si quis soluet dicendo quòd μάγος sit interpretatio nominis ἐλύμας, campas loquitur, nisi idem ostendat ἐλύμας magum significare. hic coniectura adfertur non ad meum gustum ἐλύμας יועץ אל id est Dei consiliarius. melior est, quam ponam, nisi fallor: ἐλύμας id est עֲלִימָא magus, sapiens. quæ significatio vocabuli adhuc hodie manet apud Arabes. Nam Arabice אל עלם σοφία, unde אל עלמי φυσικὴ σοφία ars physica,& אל עלם אלהי theologia. Si qua alia coniectura, in qua mihi placeo, ea est hæc, & puto veram esse. Ἐλυμα & ἐλύμας ut ἀνύλα & ἀχύλας. posterior terminatio Græca est, altera Chaldaica.
units.tr: "But Elymas the magician withstood them; for thus his name is interpreted" [ἀνθίστατο δὲ αὐτοῖς Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος· οὕτω γὰρ μεθερμηνεύεται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ] are strangely twisted by some interpreters, and they tie a knot which someone would untie by saying that μάγος is an interpretation of the name ἐλύμας; he talks nonsense, unless he also shows that ἐλύμας means magus. Here a conjecture is offered that does not suit my taste: ἐλύμας, that is, the counsellor of God [יועץ אל]. The one I shall propose is better, unless I am mistaken: ἐλύμας, that is, ʿălîmā [עֲלִימָא], magus, wise man. This meaning of the word still survives today among the Arabs. For in Arabic al-ʿalm means wisdom, whence al-ʿalmī means physical wisdom, the art of nature [φυσικὴ σοφία], and al-ʿalm ilāhī means theology. If there is any other conjecture in which I take pleasure, this is it, and I think it is true. Ἐλυμα and ἐλύμας are like ἀνύλα and ἀχύλας [ἐλυμα, ἐλύμας, ἀνύλα, ἀχύλας]: the latter ending is Greek, the former Chaldaic.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: A. El. B. Iustinus emendatus. C. item Epiphanius. D. locus in euangelio secundum Marcum expositus. E. Emmanuel. F. Theodoriti locus suspectus de mendo. G. Il sive Ilus.
units.tr: A. El. B. Justin, emended. C. Likewise Epiphanius. D. A passage in the Gospel of Mark explained. E. Emmanuel. F. A suspect passage of Theodoret, with a corruption. G. Il, or Ilus.

units.la: EL ad sensum Θεός, vt in verbis Christi· Eli Eli lamma sabachthani,quod ab euangelista interpretatur: „ Deus meus,Deus meus,quare dereliquisti me?' ad verbum δύναμις aut ἰσχύς. In fragmentis veterum Interpretum ad Psal. 22 Aquila:
units.tr: EL, in the sense of God, as in Christ's words, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani," which the evangelist translates, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Literally it corresponds to the Greek word for power or strength. In the fragments of the ancient interpreters on Psalm 22, Aquila has:

units.la: ἰσχυρί μου ἰσχυρέ μου·
units.tr: "ischyri mou, ischyre mou" [ἰσχυρί μου ἰσχυρέ μου]

units.la: post quem Hieronymus Num. 16 pro eo quod in Hebraeo legitur El elohe haruhoth, Latinè transferendo dixit: fortissime Deus spirituum.
units.tr: After him Jerome, on Numbers 16, where the Hebrew reads "El elohe haruhoth," rendered it in Latin: "most mighty God of spirits."

units.la: In Cantico Mariæ ὁ δυνατὸς id est אל Ergo אל fortis. τὸ δὲ ἀκριβέστερον vt Eusebij verbis vtar, quæ est accuratior huius vocis explicatio El, fortitudo aut potentia, quo significatu hoc nomen occurrit Proverb. 3,23 Mich. 2, 1. vide Eusseb. ἀποδ. lib. 10. Idem θεοπαρ-σx. lib. ιγ.
units.tr: In the Song of Mary, "ho dynatos" [ὁ δυνατός] stands for El, that is, "the mighty one" [אל]. Therefore El means mighty. But, to use Eusebius's words, the more exact explanation of this word is El: strength or power. In this sense the name occurs at Proverbs 3:23 and Micah 2:1. See Eusebius, Praeparatio, book 10, and the same author's Theophania, book 13.

units.la: ἐλωΐμ καλοῦσι παρὰ τὸ ἢλ, ὡς ἔοικε. Τοῦτο δὲ ἑρμηνεύουσιν ἰσχύν καὶ δύναμιν·
units.tr: "They call them elohim, apparently from El, and they interpret this as strength and power" [ἐλωΐμ καλοῦσι παρὰ τὸ ἢλ, ὡς ἔοικε. Τοῦτο δὲ ἑρμηνεύουσιν ἰσχύν καὶ δύναμιν].

units.la: Iustinus Martyr dialogo πρὸς τρύφωνα in voce Israël, τὸ γὰρ ἰσρα ἀνθρωπός ἐστι, τὸ δὲ ἢλ δύναμις· locus non caret vitio, ita corrigendus:
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in his dialogue with Trypho, on the word Israel: "for Isra is man, and El is power." The passage is not free from error and should be corrected thus:

units.la: τὸ γὰρ ἰσρα ἀνθρωπός ἐστι νικῶν, τὸ δὲ ἢλ δύναμις·
units.tr: "for Isra is man conquering, and El is power" [τὸ γὰρ ἰσρα ἀνθρωπός ἐστι νικῶν, τὸ δὲ ἢλ δύναμις].

units.la: correctio certa ex illo ipso loco. Nam praecedit:
units.tr: The correction is certain from the passage itself, for it goes before:

units.la: καὶ τὸ οὖν ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα τοῦτο σημαίνει ἀνθρωπος νικῶν δύναμιν·
units.tr: "And so this name Israel signifies man conquering power" [καὶ τὸ οὖν ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα τοῦτο σημαίνει ἄνθρωπος νικῶν δύναμιν].

units.la: sententia Iustini Israël dictus quasi איש שרה אל homo vincens potentiam. Epiphanius κατὰ Οασηνων, quos alij Essaeos vocant:
units.tr: Justin's meaning is that Israel is named as if from the Hebrew ish sarah el [איש שרה אל], a man who prevails against power.

units.la: φανταζονται δὲ δῆθεν καλεῖν τοῦτο δύναμιν ἀποκεκαλυμμένην διὰ τὸ ἢλ καλεῖσθαι δύναμιν, ξαὶ δὲ κεκαλυμμένον·
units.tr: Epiphanius, against the Ossaeans, whom others call Essaeans: "They imagine that they call it 'hidden power' because El is called power, but hidden" [φανταζονται δὲ δῆθεν καλεῖν τοῦτο δύναμιν ἀποκεκαλυμμένην διὰ τὸ ἢλ καλεῖσθαι δύναμιν, ἐαὶ δὲ κεκαλυμμένον].

units.la: Interpretatur nomen ἠλξαὶ. Igitur legendum ἢλ non ἰὴλ. item legendum δύναμιν κεκαλυμμένῳ כסי אל ita postulante sententia. Ex hac nota intelligendus locus qui est Mar. 14, 62.
units.tr: The name is interpreted as hēl [ἠλ]. So one should read ēl, not iēl. Likewise one should read "hidden power" as kesi el [כסי אל], as the sense requires. From this note the passage in Mark 14:62 is to be understood.

units.la: καὶ ὄψεσθε τὸν υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου καθήμενον ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως·
units.tr: "And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power" [καὶ ὄψεσθε τὸν υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου καθήμενον ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως].

units.la: τῆς δυνάμεως הא״ל id est τῦ θεοῦ videbitis filium hominis sedentem ad dexteram potentiæ, id est Dei. Huius loci est ἐμμανουήλ in quo obseruanda pronuntiatio antiqua Emmanuel pro Immanuel. Sic ebri sonabat pro ibri, id est עברי. Theodoritus in Genesin Quæst. 60
units.tr: "Of the power," ha-el [הא״ל], that is, "of God." "You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power," that is, of God. Here belongs Emmanuel, where the old pronunciation is to be noted: Emmanuel for Immanuel. In the same way ebri was pronounced for ibri, that is, Hebrew [עברי]. Theodoret, Questions on Genesis, 60:

units.la: μετὰ γὰρ τὴν τοῦ λὼτ ἀιχμαλωσίαν, ἐλθεῖν τις φησὶ ἀπήγγειλεν Αβραμ τῷ πεφαίτη· τοῦτο δὲ παρὰ τῷ ἑβραίῳ κείμενον εὕρεν ἑβρει·
units.tr: "For after the captivity of Lot, someone came and reported to Abram the one from beyond the river [τῷ περαίτῃ]; the text, he says, is found in the Hebrew as Ebrei [ἑβρει]."

units.la: Hoc verum. sed quod paulò ante ait:
units.tr: This is true. But what he says a little before is not:

units.la: Εβερα γὰρ τῇ Σύρων φωνῇ, ὅπερ ἐυφεάτης ὀνομάζεται·
units.tr: "For Ebera, in the Syriac tongue, is what is called Euphrates" [Εβερα γὰρ τῇ Σύρων φωνῇ, ὅπερ ἐυφεάτης ὀνομάζεται].

units.la: falsum est, nisi legas:
units.tr: This is false, unless you read:

units.la: εβρει γὰρ τῇ Συέων φωνῇ ὅπερ ἐβραῖος ὀνομάζεται·
units.tr: "For Ebrei, in the Syriac tongue, is what is called Hebrew" [εβρει γὰρ τῇ Συέων φωνῇ ὅπερ ἐβραῖος ὀνομάζεται].

units.la: τῷ Συέων φωνὴν intellige, vt cùm ait Adam γὰρ τῷ ἐρυθρὰν γῆν ἔδος ἔθος τῆς Σύρης καλεῖν. τῆς Σύρης ἠρῶν τῆς Ἑβραίας. est enim Adama Hebraeorum proprium verbum. Igitur ἐμμανουὴλ ἀρχαϊκῶς pro ἐμμανουὴλ. Vide sequens caput. Ita scriptum est Matth. 1, 23
units.tr: Understand "the tongue of the Syrians" as when he says that the Syrians customarily call red earth adama. For Adam is the proper Hebrew word. So Emmanouēl archaïkōs [ἐμμανουὴλ ἀρχαϊκῶς] is an archaic form for Emmanouēl [ἐμμανουὴλ]. See the following chapter. It is written thus at Matthew 1:23:

units.la: καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς Ἐμμανουὴλ· ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ Θεός.
units.tr: "And you shall call her name Emmanuel, which means, being interpreted, God with us" [καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς Ἐμμανουὴλ· ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ Θεός].

units.la: Interpretatio clara. ϸy μετὰ ἡμῶν, ἐλ Θεός.
units.tr: A plain interpretation: with us, God [עמנו אל], that is, the Hebrew im-nu, El.

units.la: Pro אל Syriectiam dicunt אל quod reperies in eorum libris Matth. 27, 46: & Mar. 15, 34. recte an secus, nescio. Nam adducor vt putem ibi reponendum אֵלִי transpositis literis, quemadmodum ostendam suo loco. alioqui ʎ pro ℵʎ purum putum Syriacum, à quo ἴλος creditus à Phoenicibus ἰὸς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, qui à Graecis χρόνος, id est Saturnus vocatur. Sanchuniatho vir antiquissimus, aut potius eius interpres Philo Byblius in historia Phoenicum:
units.tr: For the Syriac they say El [אל], which you will find in their books at Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34. Whether this is right or not, I do not know. For I am inclined to think that Eli [אֵלִי] should be restored there by transposing the letters, as I will show in its place. Otherwise ʎ [ʎ] for ℵʎ [ℵʎ] is pure Syriac. From this comes Ilos [ἴλος], believed by the Phoenicians to be the son of heaven and earth [ἰὸς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς], whom the Greeks call Chronos [χρόνος], that is, Saturn. Sanchuniathon, a most ancient man, or rather his interpreter Philo of Byblos, says in his history of the Phoenicians:

units.la: παρελάβων δὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς τὴν τῶν ἀτέρων ἀρχὴν ἄγεται πρὸς γάμον τῆς ἀδελφῆς γῆν, καὶ ποιεῖται ἐξ αὐτῆς παῖδας δ'. Ἥλον, τὸν καὶ χρόνον καὶ ὕπνων &c.
units.tr: "Heaven, having taken over the rule of the others, married his sister Earth, and had four sons by her: El, who is also Chronos, and sleep, etc." [παρελάβων δὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς τὴν τῶν ἀτέρων ἀρχὴν ἄγεται πρὸς γάμον τῆς ἀδελφῆς γῆν, καὶ ποιεῖται ἐξ αὐτῆς παῖδας δ'. Ἥλον, τὸν καὶ χρόνον καὶ ὕπνων, &c.]

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: A. Simon. B. Simeon. C. Theophylacti ἁμαρτημα.
units.tr: A. Simon. B. Simeon. C. Theophylact's error [ἁμάρτημα].

units.la: SIMON. Nomen hoc varie scribitur Graecis σίμων, σιμεὼν & συμεὼν. Hebraeis unica & constans scriptura שִׁמְעוֹן. Scriptura prior non caret exemplo. Nam veteres scilicet aspiratam in medio solitos abscondere. Itaque שׁמעון dicebant pro שִׁמְעוֹן. testis Dauid Grammaticus in Commentariis super Psalmos. Non minus absurdum erit, si quis dicat eosdem usitasse σίμων contracte pro σιμεὼν, licet eius contractionis exemplum apud Hebraeos in hoc nomine mihi nondum observatum sit.
units.tr: SIMON. The Greeks write this name in various ways: σίμων, σιμεὼν and συμεὼν. The Hebrews have one fixed spelling, שִׁמְעוֹן. The first Greek spelling is not without precedent. The ancients were accustomed to suppress an aspirate in the middle of a word, so they wrote שׁמעון for שִׁמְעוֹן, as David the Grammarian attests in his Commentaries on the Psalms. It would be no less absurd for someone to say that the same writers used σίμων as a contracted form of σιμεὼν, although I have not yet found an example of that contraction for this name among the Hebrews.

units.la: SIMEON. σιμεὼν aut σιμεὼν. posterior scriptura melior. In utraq. videtur ε positum loco ψ; quod non dicerem nisi certò scirem veteres vsos fuisse hac litera pro vocali. Sed hoc leue. Addam aliud, nec inane hoc caput.
units.tr: SIMEON. σιμεὼν or συμεὼν. The latter spelling is the better one. In both, ε seems to be put in place of ψ. I would not say this unless I knew for certain that the ancients used that letter for a vowel. But this is a small point. I will add another, and this heading is not empty of substance.

units.la: Locus est Matth. 10 in Theophylacteis, qui nostram hic subibit censuram:
units.tr: There is a passage in Matthew 10 in the commentary of Theophylact, which will now come under our criticism:

units.la: τρεῖς Σίμωνες. ὁ Πέτρος, ὁ Καναναῖος, καὶ ὁ Θαδδαῖος. Σίμων ὁ Ἰούδας Ἰσκαριώτης εἶπεν.
units.tr: τρεῖς Σίμωνες. ὁ Πέτρος, ὁ Καναναῖος, καὶ ὁ Θαδδαῖος. Σίμων ὁ Ἰούδας Ἰσκαριώτης εἶπεν. [There were three Simons: Peter, the Cananaean, and Thaddaeus. Simon Judas Iscariot said.]

units.la: dicit in numero Apostolorum tres Simones fuisse. Nec probat Ioh. 12,
units.tr: He says that there were three Simons among the number of the Apostles. Nor does he prove this from John 12,

units.la: Ioh. 12, 4 lectum:
units.tr: where John 12:4 is read:

units.la: ἰούδας Σίμωνος ἰσκαριώτης. & 6, 71. ἔλεγε δὲ Ἰούδαν Σίμωνος ἰσκαριώτου. ut dubium non sit, quin Iudas habuerit patrem Simonem. Nam Σίμωνος id est Simonis filius: at Ἰούδας Σίμων Ἰσκαριώτης nusquam repertum, quod sciam. Quare frustra est Theophylactus.
units.tr: ἰούδας Σίμωνος ἰσκαριώτης [Judas of Simon Iscariot], and at 6:71, ἔλεγε δὲ Ἰούδαν Σίμωνος ἰσκαριώτου [he was speaking of Judas of Simon Iscariot]. So there can be no doubt that Judas had a father named Simon. For Σίμωνος means "of Simon", that is, the son of Simon. But Ἰούδας Σίμων Ἰσκαριώτης is nowhere found, so far as I know. Therefore Theophylact is wrong to claim otherwise.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAP. X.

units.la: A. Vocis Satan variae interpretationes veterum. B. Quid proprie significet. C. Diabolus. D. vas pro vocas. E. mos abscondendi literas aspiratas in media.
units.tr: A. The varied interpretations of the word Satan by the ancients. B. What it properly means. C. Diabolus. D. "vas" for "vocas". E. The custom of suppressing aspirated letters in the middle.

units.la: Σ Ἀτὰν Hebraicè שָׂטָן. Interpretatur à Graecis ἐχάνπος, ἀντικείμενος, διάβολος, παραβάτης, ἀποστάτης: à Latinis Contrarius, transgressor, adversarius.
units.tr: Satan, in Hebrew שָׂטָן. The Greeks render it ἐχάνπος, ἀντικείμενος, διάβολος, παραβάτης, ἀποστάτης; the Latins render it as contrarius, transgressor, adversarius.

units.la: Ἐχάνπος, id est contrarius. Origenes tract. 1 in Matthaeum, Hieron. in lib. De nom. Hebr. & in Comment. Matth. 16.
units.tr: Ἐχάνπος, that is, contrarius. Origen, Tractate 1 on Matthew; Jerome in his book on Hebrew names and in his Commentary on Matthew 16.

units.la: ἀντικείμενος. id est adversarius. Origenes lib. 10 ad Rom. Hom. 15 in Iesum Naue. Chrysostomus hom. 26 in epist. secundam ad Corinth. Hieron. passim in Collectaneis nominum Hebraicorum.
units.tr: ἀντικείμενος, that is, adversary. Origen, book 10 on Romans, Homily 15 on Joshua; Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; Jerome passim in his Collection of Hebrew Names.

units.la: διάβολος. Num. 22 שָׂטָן LXX εἰς διάβολον. Vide annotationes Erasmi Ioh. 6, 70.
units.tr: διάβολος. Numbers 22: שָׂטָן, the Septuagint εἰς διάβολον. See Erasmus's annotations on John 6:70.

units.la: παραβάτης, id est transgressor. Hieron. in Satan ex epist. ad Romanos: & ex Apocalypsi.
units.tr: παραβάτης, that is, transgressor. Jerome on Satan from the Epistle to the Romans, and from the Apocalypse.

units.la: ἀποστάτης. Irenaeus lib. 5, adversus Haereses: Iustinus Martyr in disputatione cum Tryphone.
units.tr: ἀποστάτης. Irenaeus, book 5, Against Heresies; Justin Martyr in his disputation with Trypho.

units.la: Theophylactus Matth. 12 σαῦ λέγεται ὁ ἀντικείμενος. optima interpretatio vocis. Dauid Grammaticus in libro vbi dictionum sensa collegit: שטן לשון איבה
units.tr: Theophylact on Matthew 12: σαῦ λέγεται ὁ ἀντικείμενος [the adversary is called], an excellent interpretation of the word. David the Grammarian, in the book where he collected the meanings of words: שטן לשון איבה [Satan is a term of enmity].

units.la: Hoc vult, Satan significat ἐχθρὸν καὶ ἀντικείμενον, hostem, inimicum, adversarium. Itaque de Petro legitur ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου σατανᾶ: quod Christo temerè adversaretur. Verissimè Origenes:
units.tr: This means that Satan signifies ἐχθρὸν καὶ ἀντικείμενον [enemy and adversary]: foe, opponent, adversary. Thus of Peter it is written, ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου σατανᾶ [Get behind me, Satan], because he rashly opposed Christ. Origen speaks most truly:

units.la: Omnes, ait, qui adversantur diuinae voluntati, Satanae dicuntur.
units.tr: All, he says, who oppose the divine will are called Satans.

units.la: Igitur Satan Dei ac generis humani hostis. Graeco vocabulo etiam διάβολος vocatur, sed alia ratione: Satan dicitur tanquam adversarius: Diabolus tanquam criminator. Non enim idem est aduersari & criminari. Criminatio sine verbis non fit: aduersari & verbis & factis possumus. Hieronymus Isa. 27.
units.tr: Satan, then, is the enemy of God and of the human race. He is also called by the Greek word διάβολος, but for a different reason: Satan is so called as an adversary, the Devil as an accuser. To oppose and to accuse are not the same thing. Accusation cannot be made without words, but we can oppose both by words and by deeds. Jerome on Isaiah 27:

units.la: „ Tradunt Hebraei diabolum, id est criminatorem, quod Graecum „ nomen est; Hebraicè appellari Satan, hoc est aduersarium. Vnde „ & in Zacharia dicitur, Stabat Satan, id est aduersarius, à dextris eius „ vt aduersaretur ei.
units.tr: "The Hebrews say that the devil, that is the accuser, which is a Greek name, is called in Hebrew Satan, that is, the adversary. Hence also in Zechariah it is said, 'Satan stood, that is the adversary, at his right hand to oppose him.'"

units.la: Qui ἀποςάτω vertunt, vt Irenaeus & Iustinus, videntur deducere à verbo ῦῶ quod deficere significat, vt Nun sit hecmanthicum. sic Grammatici appellant literas, quae extrinsecus accedunt ad thema formandis nominibus. Iustinum induxit terminatio Graeca σατάνας, vt compositum putarit ex ὧν ἀποσάτης & ναὶ τῦτ' ἐπ ὄφις. prorsus inepte. ex quo tamen hoc discimus ῥᾶς ἀρχαϊκῶς pro ναας, id est ὑπ.
units.tr: Those who render it as ἀποστάτης, as Irenaeus and Justin do, seem to derive it from a verb meaning to fall away or to fail. Grammarians call the letters that are added from outside to a stem, in forming nouns, "nun" and similar. Justin was led astray by the Greek ending σατάνας, and so thought it compounded from ὧν ἀποσάτης and ναὶ τῦτ' ἐπ ὄφις, which is quite foolish. Yet from this we learn that the archaic form of ναας is ὑπ.

units.la: Ita solitum antiquis euphoniæ quasi gratia abscondere literam Heth in medio. Sic reperio ꞑnw pro ꞑnnw apud Magistros. Vide, si vacat, Cimhium ad psal. 35.
units.tr: In this way the ancients were accustomed, as it were for the sake of euphony, to suppress the letter heth in the middle of a word. So I find ꞑnw for ꞑnnw among the Masters. See, if you have time, Kimchi on Psalm 35.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: A. Baal. B. Hieronymus correctus. C. Beel sive Bel. D. Beelzebub. E. Vnde dictus? F. Statuae deorum quae forma olim fuerint. G. Beelzebub quid?
units.tr: A. Baal. B. Jerome corrected. C. Beel or Bel. D. Beelzebub. E. Whence so called? F. What the statues of the gods formerly looked like. G. What is Beelzebub?

units.la: BAAL, Iuppiter planeta quasi ϰύριος καὶ δισπότης: Hebraicè ⲬⲬ Epiphanius κατὰ φαεισαίων.
units.tr: BAAL, Jupiter the planet, as it were kyrios and despotes [κύριος καὶ δεσπότης]. In Hebrew [בעל]. Epiphanius, against the ... [κατὰ φαεισαίων].

units.la: ζεὺς χωχ​ε βααλ:
units.tr: Zeus Choche Baal [ζεὺς χωχε βααλ].

units.la: id est בעל. vult dicere, Iouem planetam antiquitus Baal vocatum, quem hodie Sedec indigitant à iustitia. est autem in Baal significatio dominatus. quam expressit Apostolus Corinth. 8, 5. εἰσι θεοὶ πολλοὶ καὶ κύριοι πολλοί. κύριοι id est βααλιμ. In lib. De nom. Hebraicis ex epist. ad Romanos:
units.tr: That is, [בעל]. He means that Jupiter the planet was anciently called Baal, whom today they designate Sedek from justice. Now the meaning in Baal is lordship, which the Apostle expressed in 1 Corinthians 8:5: "there are many gods and many lords" [εἰσι θεοὶ πολλοὶ καὶ κύριοι πολλοί]. "Lords," that is, [βααλιμ]. In the book On Hebrew Names, from the epistle to the Romans:

units.la: Bal habens sive denorans: legendum Baal. posset excusari bal pro baal contracte, vt bel pro beel, nisi in baal consentirent libri omnes Graeci & Latini: Rom. 11 quem locum ibi Hieronymus laudat.
units.tr: "Bal, having or devouring": one should read Baal. Bal might be excused as a contracted form of baal, as bel is for beel, except that all the Greek and Latin books agree on baal, Romans 11. Jerome praises this passage there.

units.la: Baal quod modo exposuimus, Syriac Babylonij efferunt Beel, id est בעל, & contractius Bel ex more antiquo. Suidas in Beelphegor: βηλ ὁ χρόνος.
units.tr: Baal, as we have just explained, the Syrians of Babylon pronounce Beel, that is [בעל], and more contractedly Bel, after the ancient custom. Suidas on Beelphegor: Bel is time [βηλ ὁ χρόνος].

units.la: C Malim ὁ Ζεὺς. quanquam de eo non contenderim. hinc Beelzebub Matth. 10, 25 in Latina vulgata, quomodo legendum monuit iam olim Hieronymus. monuere alij, qua de re dicam sententiā meam in fine huius capitis. Huic nostrae literae tribuunt principatum inter Daemonas, quem Chaldaeus paraphrastes tribuit Asmodaeo Cohel. 1, 12. Dici aiunt ab idolo Acaronitarum, cuius mentio 2 Reg. 1,
units.tr: C. I would prefer "Zeus" [ὁ Ζεὺς], though I would not contend the point. Hence Beelzebub in Matthew 10:25 in the Latin Vulgate, which Jerome long ago advised should be read otherwise. Others have advised too; I will state my opinion on this at the end of this chapter. To this name they give the first place among the demons, which the Chaldee paraphrast assigns to Asmodeus, Ecclesiastes 1:12. They say it is named from the idol of the Accaronites, mentioned in 2 Kings 1.

units.la: 2. Nam beel, id valet baal, & zebub, musca; quasi dicas Ζεὺς μυῖα Iupiter musca. Quaeri potest unde ita appellatus sit? an quia similitudinem habebat muscae? Nam veteribus mos fuit ut statuas deorum sculperent ea forma, quae corpore hominem referebat: capite autem & facie animal aliquod, puta aut aquem aut leonem aut muscam vel contra facie humana referebat caetera parte corporis aliquod animal. Porphyrius περὶ τῶν ἐμψύχων ἀποχῆς claris verbis hoc testatur. quae verba hic subijciam:
units.tr: 2. For beel, that is baal, and zebub, a fly; as if you said Zeus-fly, Jupiter the fly. It may be asked why he was so named. Was it because he had the likeness of a fly? For the ancients customarily sculpted statues of the gods in a form where the body was human, but the head and face were of some animal, say an eagle, a lion or a fly; or conversely, a human face with the rest of the body from some animal. Porphyry bears clear witness to this in On Abstinence from Animals [περὶ τῶν ἐμψύχων ἀποχῆς]. I will append his words here:

units.la: διὸ εἰς τλῶ δαιμονίων παρέλαβον πᾶν ζῷων, καὶ ὁμοίως που ἀνέμιξαν θηρία καὶ ἀνθρώπους, καὶ πάλιν ὁρίσων ζώματα, καὶ ἀνδρώπων. ἑκάστωι γάρ τις παρ' αὐτοῖς μέχει τεχνίλου ἀνθρωποειδὴς. τὸ δὲ ὠεόσωπον ὁρίου ἢ λέοντος, ἢ ἄλλου πιὸς ζῷου πεκτημένον. καὶ πάλιν αὖ κεφαλὴ ἀνθρώπειος, καὶ ἄλλων τινῶν ζῴων μέρη.
units.tr: Therefore they took into the company of demons every kind of animal, and likewise mingled beasts and men, and again the forms of animals and men. For among them each one was in some way man-shaped down to the chest, while the face had the head of a lion or some other animal, and again a human head with parts of other animals. [διὸ εἰς τλῶ δαιμονίων παρέλαβον πᾶν ζῷων, καὶ ὁμοίως που ἀνέμιξαν θηρία καὶ ἀνθρώπους, καὶ πάλιν ὁρίσων ζώματα, καὶ ἀνδρώπων. ἑκάστωι γάρ τις παρ' αὐτοῖς μέχει τεχνίλου ἀνθρωποειδὴς. τὸ δὲ ὠεόσωπον ὁρίου ἢ λέοντος, ἢ ἄλλου πιὸς ζῷου πεκτημένον. καὶ πάλιν αὖ κεφαλὴ ἀνθρώπειος, καὶ ἄλλων τινῶν ζῴων μέρη.]

units.la: Caeterum pro Beelzebub, Graeci scribunt Βεεζεβούλ, quam scripturam ego omnino retinendam censeo, tantisper dum quis probaverit eam à scribis corruptam fuisse, & non ab usu & vulgo. Nam si ab usu est illius temporis, & Euangelistae eam retinuerunt, cur nos mutabimus? Igitur Βεεζεβούλ id valet Ζεὺς κοπρικὸς à stercore, quasi dicas Iupiter stercorarius. ego imbibi medio tempore sic appellatum fuisse nomen Accaronitarum per contemptū, quod in vetere Testamento vocatur Baalzebub. notum ut Idola stercora vocentur à prophetis. Haec mea coniectura est, quam puto veram esse, & ita opto Deum animae meae propitium.
units.tr: Otherwise, for Beelzebub the Greeks write Βεεζεβούλ [Beezebsoul]. I think this spelling should be wholly retained, until someone proves it was corrupted by scribes and not by usage and common custom. For if it comes from the usage of that time, and the Evangelists kept it, why should we change it? So Βεεζεβούλ means Zeus of dung [Ζεὺς κοπρικὸς], from dung, as if you said Jupiter the dunghill god. Meanwhile I have gathered that the name was so called by the Accaronites in contempt, which in the Old Testament is called Baal-zebub. It is well known that the prophets call idols dung. This is my conjecture, which I believe is true, and so I pray that God may be gracious to my soul.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: A. Bethania. B. Beth-esda. C. Bethsaida. D. Bethphage. E. mendum indicatum in exemplaribus Graecis.
units.tr: A. Bethania. B. Beth-esda. C. Bethsaida. D. Bethphage. E. An error noted in the Greek copies.

units.la: A BETH voce quae domum locumue significat, composita recēsebo hoc capite nomina quatuor, Bethania, Beth-esda, Bethsaida, Bethphage, in quibus explicandis siquid dico praeter alios interpretes, debeo ijs, qui nobis primi dederunt editionem Syriacam, quae non parum nos adiuuit in argumento quod tractamus.
units.tr: Beth, the word meaning house or place, in compounds. In this chapter I will go through four names: Bethania, Beth-esda, Bethsaida, Bethphage. If in explaining them I say anything beyond other interpreters, I owe it to those who first gave us the Syriac edition, which helped us not a little in the matter we are treating.

units.la: Βηθανία. Syrus בית עניא. In libro De nominibus Hebraicis.
units.tr: Βηθανία [Bethania]. Syriac [בית עניא]. In the book On Hebrew Names.

units.la: Bethania domus afflictionis eius.
units.tr: Bethania, house of his affliction.

units.la: id est בית עניה. tu expunge pronomen. Ania afflictio, vt in Proverbio Talmudico, Ania batar ania: quod tantundem valet ac si dicas, Mala malis succedunt. malim, Beth-ania, domus ouium. Forte ab ouibus dicta, quòd ibi multæ essent oues. Ioh. 1, 28. in Latina vetere: Hæc in Bethania facta sunt trans Iordanem, quomodo etiam scriptum reperimus in codice Syriaco. Libri Græci variant. Veteres omnes ἐν Ἐνθαναὶα: sed visa quibusdam hæc lectio vitiosa, quòd Bethania fuerit cis Iordanem. Itaque reponunt ἐν Ἐνθαβαρᾷ ex aliis libris. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Suidas. Apud Epiphanium κατὰ ἀνομάτων legimus Ἐνθαμαρᾷ vitio, credo, chalcographiæ pro Ἐνθαβαρᾷ.
units.tr: That is [בית עניה]. You should drop the pronoun. Ania means affliction, as in the Talmudic proverb, "Ania batar ania," which amounts to saying "Misfortunes follow misfortunes." I would rather have Beth-ania, house of sheep, perhaps named from sheep because there were many sheep there. John 1:28 in the old Latin: "These things were done in Bethania beyond the Jordan," as we also find written in the Syriac codex. The Greek books vary. All the ancients have ἐν Ἐνθαναία [en Enthanaia]; but this reading seemed faulty to some, because Bethany was on this side of the Jordan. So they restore ἐν Ἐνθαβαρᾷ [en Enthabara] from other books: Chrysostom, Theophylact, Suidas. In Epiphanius, in the book On Names, we read Ἐνθαμαρᾷ [Enthamara], by an error, I believe, of the printer for Ἐνθαβαρᾷ.

units.la: Ἐνθαδὰ. In Syriacis בית חסדא Ioh. 5, 2 id est Domus gratiæ aut benignitatis. nomen accommodum loco in quo aquæ motu sanabantur ægroti, quod argumentum diuinæ gratiæ ac benignitatis longè maximum. potest etiam reddi Domus misericordiæ. alij scribunt בית אשרא sed fallor, aut prior scriptura vera est.
units.tr: Ἐνθαδὰ [Bethesda]. In the Syriac, [בית חסדא], John 5:2, that is, House of grace or kindness. A name suited to the place where the sick were healed by the moving of the water, which is by far the greatest proof of divine grace and kindness. It can also be rendered House of mercy. Others write [בית אשרא], but I am mistaken, or the former spelling is correct.

units.la: Ἐνθσαϊδὰ. ita scribendum non Ἐνθζαϊδὰ. Syrus בית צידא In lib. De nom. Hebr.
units.tr: Ἐνθσαϊδὰ [Bethsaida]. It should be written so, not Ἐνθζαϊδὰ. Syriac [בית צידא]. In the book On Hebrew Names.

units.la: Beth-zaida domus venatorum.
units.tr: Beth-zaida, house of hunters.

units.la: alij censent dictam à piscatu propter frequentes lacus & stagna. Ioh. 5, 2. vitium est in hoc nomine. Nam scriptum Beth-saida pro Bethesda in Latina vulgata.
units.tr: Others think it was named from fishing, because of the frequent lakes and pools. John 5:2: there is a fault in this name, for Beth-saida is written for Bethesda in the Latin Vulgate.
