units.la: QVINAM fuerint Herodiani quæsitum à doctis, variæ sententiæ. Ego quam repperi apud authores Hebraeos, eam ponam. In Lexico iuris lego Herodianos natione Græcos fuisse, dictos autem ab Herode qui primus eos traduxit ex deserto ad locum habitatum educauitque. ponam verba Hebraica, deinde reddam vt sonant ad verbum.
units.tr: Scholars have disagreed about who the Herodians were. I will set out the view I have found in Hebrew authors. In the Lexicon of the law I read that the Herodians were Greeks by birth, and were so called after Herod, who first brought them out of the desert into an inhabited place and settled them there. I will give the Hebrew words first, and then render them as literally as I can.

units.la: הורדוס המלך הביא אותם מן המדבר וגידל אותם בישוב ונעשו תרבות ונקראו על שמו הורדוסים
units.tr: הורדוס המלך הביא אותם מן המדבר וגידל אותם בישוב ונעשו תרבות ונקראו על שמו הורדוסים

units.la: id est, Herodes rex adduxit secum Græcos ex deserto, & educauit eos in terra habitata, & fecerunt sectam, vocatíque sunt de nomine ipsius Herodiani.
units.tr: That is: King Herod brought the Greeks with him out of the desert and settled them in an inhabited land, and they formed a sect, and they were called Herodians after his name.

units.la: Horum mentio in Gemara capite Silluach haken. Vocabanturalio nomine הורדוסים, id est Dorsiothitae siue Dorsiani, videlicet à loco vnde abducti fuerant. Concludam caput, si addidero, qui huc facere videtur, Iustini Martyris locum disputatione cum Tryphone.
units.tr: They are mentioned in the Gemara, in the chapter Silluach haken. They were also called by another name, הורדוסים (Hordosim), that is, Dorsiothitae or Dorsians, evidently from the place from which they had been led away. I will end the chapter by adding the passage of Justin Martyr in his dispute with Trypho, which seems to bear on this question.

units.la: ἀλλ' Ἰουδαίους ἀπὸ ὀρθῶς ἐξετάσῃ, ὁμολογήσειν εἶναι τοὺς Σαδδου- καίους, ἢ τὰς ὁμοίας αἱρέσεις γενιςῶν, καὶ μεσιςῶν, καὶ γαλιλαίων, καὶ ἑλλησιανῶν, καὶ Φαρισαίων βαπτισῶν.
units.tr: Justin's Greek runs: "But if you examine the Jews rightly, you will find that they confess the Sadducees, or those who produce similar heresies, namely the Genistae and Mesistae, and the Galileans, and the Hellenians, and the Pharisees who baptize." [ἀλλ' Ἰουδαίους ἀπὸ ὀρθῶς ἐξετάσῃ, ὁμολογήσειν εἶναι τοὺς Σαδδουκαίους, ἢ τὰς ὁμοίας αἱρέσεις γενιστῶν, καὶ μεσιστῶν, καὶ γαλιλαίων, καὶ ἑλληνιανῶν, καὶ Φαρισαίων βαπτιστῶν.]

units.la: Quid ἐλληνιαῶν? fallor aut recte expono ηεσθλαιῶν. à me est locus quem supra adduxi. docti expendent: ego affirmare pro certo non ausim.
units.tr: What of the Hellenians [ἐλληνιανῶν]? Either I am mistaken, or I rightly read it as [ηεσθλαιῶν]. The passage I quoted above is my own. Learned men will weigh it; I would not dare to affirm it as certain.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: A. De Gennesar voce, eiusque apud Græcos & Latinos scriptura. B. Hieronymi locus non intellectus ab Erasmo. C. male expositus à viro nupero. D. Plinius correctus. E. Septem maria terræ Israël.
units.tr: A. On the word Gennesar, and how it is written by Greeks and Latins. B. A passage of Jerome not understood by Erasmus. C. Badly expounded by a recent author. D. Pliny corrected. E. The seven seas of the land of Israel.

units.la: GENNESAR, Gennesara, Gennesareth, terra & lacus. Matth. 14, 34. ἦλθον εἰς τὴν γεννησαρὲτ.
units.tr: GENNESAR, Gennesara, Gennesareth: a land and a lake. Matt. 14:34: ἦλθον εἰς τὴν γεννησαρὲτ [they came into the land of Gennesaret].

units.la: libri alij γεννησαρ. In Latina vetere Genesar. apud Hieronymum Gennezareth. Suidas γεννησαρέτ, ὄνομα τόπου.
units.tr: Other books have γεννησαρ. In the old Latin it is Genesar; in Jerome, Gennezareth. Suidas: γεννησαρέτ, the name of a place.

units.la: γεννησαρὲτ siue γεννησαρὲτ. nam anceps scriptura. גנכרת. Malim γεννησαρὲτ גנסרת, quod factum ex גנרת in quo Thau ultima non Teth. sed quoniam mutatio inter has literas, & quia Syri pro Thau fere ponūt Teth, nihil audeo statuere. apud Hebræos neutrum adhuc horum repperi.
units.tr: Whether γεννησαρὲτ or γεννησαρὲτ, the spelling is uncertain [גנכרת]. I would prefer γεννησαρὲτ [גנסרת], which arose from גנרת, with Thau as the final letter, not Teth. But since these letters are interchanged, and since the Syrians often put Teth for Thau, I dare not decide anything. Among the Hebrews I have not yet found either of these forms.

units.la: γεννησαρὲτ גנסרא voce & terminatione Chaldaica. lectio alia γεννησαρ. Sic γεννσαρ & γεννσαρ variantibus libris.
units.tr: γεννησαρὲτ [גנסרא], with a Chaldean word and ending. Another reading is γεννησαρ. Thus γεννσαρ and γεννσαρ appear in different manuscripts.

units.la: Apud Syrum גנסר. In Iure Hebræo גינוסר quomodo scriptam legimus hanc vocem in traductionibus ijs, quas Targumin vocant. Concludam de scriptura ex Hebræo גנרת. non damno γεννσαρ; tamen scripserim præillo γεννσαρ. est autem γεννσαρ, si interpreteris, hortus principum. In Ilmedenu capite Mitte tibi viros. גנוסר גני סריס אלו המלכים שיהוה לחם גנות בתוכה
units.tr: In Syriac it is גנסר. In the Hebrew law we read this word written as גינוסר in those translations which they call Targumim. I shall conclude about the spelling from the Hebrew גנרת. I do not condemn γεννσαρ, but I would write γεννσαρ rather. If you interpret it, γεννσαρ means the garden of princes. In the Ilmedenu, chapter "Mitte tibi viros": גנוסר גני סריס אלו המלכים שיהוה לחם גנות בתוכה [Ginosar, the gardens of eunuchs, these are the kings, which Jehovah made gardens within it].

units.la: Verba clara. גני סריס id est horti principum siue regum. hoc dicit Gennesar; locus vbi regum horti erant. In lib. De nom. Hebr.
units.tr: The words are clear. גני סריס [gardens of eunuchs] means the gardens of princes or kings. This is what Gennesar means: the place where the gardens of the kings were. In the book On Hebrew Names.

units.la: Gennesat, ortus principum.
units.tr: Gennesat, the garden of princes.

units.la: interpolarant bardi, ortus principium, & explicationis causa addiderant, initium natiuitatis. vtinam ego illos vt digni sunt. legendū,
units.tr: The bards interpolated "ortus principium" [the beginning of princes], and, for the sake of explanation, added "initium natiuitatis" [the beginning of birth]. Would that I could treat them as they deserve. It should be read:

units.la: hortus principum. Ex hac nota intelligendus locus Hieronymi, quē Erasmus laudat, & in quo explicando frustra est.
units.tr: "hortus principum" [the garden of princes]. From this note the passage of Jerome, which Erasmus cites and in explaining which he is at a loss, must be understood.

units.la: „ Si sciremus quid in nostra lingua resonaret Gennesareth, intelligeremus quomodo Iesus per typum Apostolorum & nauis, ecclesiam „ clesiam de persecutionum naufragio liberatam, transducat ad „ sittus, & in tranquillissimo portu faciat quiescere.
units.tr: „If we knew what Gennesareth resounds in our language, we would understand how Jesus, through the type of the Apostles and the ship, carries the Church, freed from the shipwreck of persecutions, across the seas, and makes it rest in the most tranquil harbour."

units.la: ad hunc locum nota nupera;
units.tr: On this passage, a recent note:

units.la: „ Gennesareth interpretatur ים נצרת vallis florida: hinc mysticè „ pro tranquillo ecclesiæ portu ponitur.
units.tr: „Gennesareth is interpreted as ים נצרת [sea of Nazareth], a flowering valley; hence mystically it is used for the tranquil harbour of the Church."

units.la: à Mariano est Erasmomaltyge: refelli potest ex scriptura Hebraica, sed magis ex interpretatione ipsius Hieronymi, quam supra posui. In Lexico iuris,
units.tr: This is from Marianus. Erasmus is wrong about it. It can be refuted from the Hebrew Scripture, but more so from Jerome's own interpretation, which I set out above. In the Lexicon of law:

units.la: גינוסר מקים קרוב לנברא יש בו גנות ופרדסים
units.tr: גינוסר מקים קרוב לנברא יש בו גנות ופרדסים [Ginosar, a place near Tiberias, in which there are gardens and orchards]

units.la: id est, γεννησαρ locus est prope Tiberiadem, in quo horti sunt & paradysi. Dignum nota. quia λιμνὴ γεννησαρετ, stagnum Gennesaret, quod legimus Lucæ 5, 1, vocatur Ioh. 21, 1, Θάλασσα τῆς Τιβεριάδος, mare Tiberiadis: & Iohan. 6, 1, mare Galilææ. Iosue 12, 3 ים כנרת id est mare Cinnereth: pro quo Aquila Chaldaicè posuit ים גנוסר id est mare Gennosar. De hoc lacu Plinius hist. nat. lib. 5. cap. 15, vbi describit Iordanem amnem.
units.tr: That is, γεννησαρ is a place near Tiberias, in which there are gardens and orchards. This is worth noting, because the lake of Gennesaret, λιμνὴ γεννησαρετ, which we read in Luke 5:1, is called in John 21:1 "the sea of Tiberias" [Θάλασσα τῆς Τιβεριάδος], and in John 6:1 "the sea of Galilee." Joshua 12:3 has ים כנרת [the sea of Cinnereth], for which Aquila in Chaldean put ים גנוסר [the sea of Gennosar]. Pliny writes of this lake in Natural History, book 5, chapter 15, where he describes the river Jordan:

units.la: „ Ergo, inquit, vbi prima conuallium fuit occasio, in lacum se fundit, quem plures Genesara vocant xvi M. pass. longitudinis, vt „ M. latitudinis, amoenis circumseptu oppidis: ab Oriente Iuliade „ & Hippo, à meridie Tarichea; quo nomine aliqui & lacu appellant, ab occidente Tiberiade, aquis calidis salubri.
units.tr: „Therefore, he says, where the first valleys open, it pours itself into a lake, which many call Genesara, sixteen miles long and six broad, surrounded by pleasant towns: on the east Iulias and Hippo, on the south Tarichea, by which name some also call the lake; on the west Tiberias, with warm and healthful waters."

units.la: Hæc verba dicunt lacum Genesar à Tarichea appellatum. forte ita scripsit Plinius:
units.tr: These words say that the lake Genesar was called from Tarichea. Perhaps Pliny wrote it thus:

units.la: „ à meridie Tarichea, & quo nomine aliqui lacum appellant, ab „ occidente Tiberiade.
units.tr: „on the south Tarichea, by which name some call the lake; on the west Tiberias."

units.la: Vocatur enim passim ab Hebraeis scriptoribus ים רבריא, & memoratur inter septem maria terrae Israël; quae ים קיים vocant, quo nomine etiam lacus intelligunt. mentio horum in Midras Tehillim, & apud Cimhium in commentariis ad Psal. 24.
units.tr: For it is commonly called by the Hebrew writers ים רבריא [the sea of Tiberias], and it is mentioned among the seven seas of the land of Israel, which they call ים קיים [the standing sea], a name by which they also understand the lake. Mention of these is made in the Midrash Tehillim, and in Kimchi's commentary on Psalm 24.

units.la: Septem maria terrae Israël.
units.tr: The seven seas of the land of Israel.

units.la: ים רבא 1 Mare magnum. ים רסיבכי 2 Mare Sibchi.
units.tr: 1 The great sea [ים רבא]. 2 The sea of Sibchi [ים רסיבכי].

units.la: Ita scriptum in Midras Tehillim. In Cimhianis lego רסנני, id est mare Sichni. ים רטבריא 3 Mare Tiberiadis.
units.tr: So it is written in the Midrash Tehillim. In Kimchi I read רסנני, that is, the sea of Sichni. 3 The sea of Tiberias [ים רטבריא].

units.la: In Syriacis noui Testamenti ים רטבריים, quod arguit magnam imperitiam ritiá Interpretis. Non enim à Tiberio dictus lacus, sed à Tiberiade.
units.tr: In the Syriac of the New Testament it is ים רטבריים, which shows great ignorance on the part of the translator. For the lake was named not from Tiberius but from Tiberias.

units.la: יומא רמלחא 4 Mare salsum.
units.tr: 4 The salt sea [יומא רמלחא].

units.la: יומארחילתא 5 Mare chilta.
units.tr: 5 The sea of Chilta [יומארחילתא].

units.la: Apud Cimhium legitur,
units.tr: In Kimchi it is read:

units.la: יומא דיחולתא יומא רת דליתא
units.tr: יומא דיחולתא יומא רת דליתא [the sea of Dihultha, the sea of Rat Dalitha].

units.la: pro his duobus in Dras est רחילתא, quæ lectio verissima est, ita postulante numero.
units.tr: For these two, in Dras it is רחילתא [Rahiltha], which reading is most true, as the number requires.

units.la: יומא רשרייתי 6
units.tr: 6 [יומא רשרייתי].

units.la: יומא דאספמיא 7 Mare Hispanicum.
units.tr: 7 The Spanish sea [יומא דאספמיא].

units.la: In Dras רשריית abest Iod in fine, & ad postremum nomen additum ibidem:
units.tr: In Dras, רשריית lacks the Yod at the end, and at the last name there is added there:

units.la: הוא יומא רחזין יומא רקלטינוס
units.tr: הוא יומא רחזין יומא רקלטינוס [it is the sea of Hazin, the sea of Kaltinos].

units.la: Chilta siue Chulta Latinè arenosum sonat. Nam חול arena.
units.tr: Chilta or Chulta means "sandy" in Latin, for חול means sand.

units.la: Redeo ad lacum Tiberiadis, cuius aquas ferunt soluere aluum. In Lexico iuris,
units.tr: I return to the lake of Tiberias, whose waters they say loosen the bowels. In the Lexicon of law,

units.la: יש נטבריא מים משלשליום אם שתה אותם ארם יוצאין ממנו כמו שיש שם:
units.tr: יש נטבריא מים משלשליום אם שתה אותם ארם יוצאין ממנו כמו שיש שם [There are in Tiberias waters that loosen the bowels; if a man drinks of them, they come out as they went in].

units.la: id est; Sunt in Tiberiade aquæ aluum laxantes: si quis bibat de illis, exeunt quemadmodum intrarunt.
units.tr: That is: there are waters in Tiberias that loosen the bowels; if anyone drinks of them, they come out just as they went in.

units.la: harum aquarum mentio in fine Machschirim in Gemara.
units.tr: Mention of these waters is made at the end of Machschirim in the Gemara.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: A. De Haceldema, eiúsque vera scriptura ac sensu. B. Quid significet ᾿Αςτ. 1, 19. Propria ipsorum dialecto. C. Corinthiam.
units.tr: A. On Haceldema, its true spelling and meaning. B. What ᾿Αςτ. 1, 19 means, in their own dialect. C. Corinthian.

units.la: HIERONYMVS siue quis alius [illegible, ~12 letters] ad Psalmum 108.
units.tr: Jerome, or someone else [illegible, about twelve letters], on Psalm 108.

units.la: Ipsam pecuniam non mittunt in Corbonam, sed emunt ex ipsa agrum, & appellant cum Aceldema, quod interpretatur pretium sanguinis.
units.tr: They do not put the money into the Corbona, but buy a field with it, and call it Aceldema, which is interpreted "the price of blood."

units.la: heu prauam interpretationem! Vel ex hoc loco potest argumentum peti contra eos, qui contendunt commentarios illos Hieronymi esse. Nam Hieronymus rectè interpretatur hanc vocem in libro De nominibus Hebraicis,
units.tr: Alas, what a faulty interpretation! From this passage an argument can even be drawn against those who contend that those commentaries are Jerome's. For Jerome correctly interprets this word in his book on Hebrew names,

units.la: Aceldema, ager sanguinis:
units.tr: Aceldema, the field of blood:

units.la: vbi perperam Acheldema scriptum, & peius in aliis libris Acheldemach. scribendum Aceldema aut haceldema, Græcè ἀκελδαμα.
units.tr: where it is wrongly written Acheldema, and worse in other books Acheldemach. It should be written Aceldema or haceldema, in Greek ἀκελδαμα.

units.la: Acto. 1,19:
units.tr: Acts 1:19:

units.la: ἀκ7π ὥςτε κληθήναι τὸ χωρίον ἐκεῖνο τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν ἀκελδαμα, τουτέστι χωρίον αἵματος.
units.tr: "So that that place was called in their own dialect Akeldama, that is, the field of blood" [ἀκελδαμα, τουτέστι χωρίον αἵματος].

units.la: ἀκελδαμα רמא חקל.clarum est. In lingua Chaldæa חקל ager: דמא אדמא, & sono antiquo דמא, sanguis. Quod autem ait τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν, capiendum vt illud Ioh. 8, 17.
units.tr: Akeldama, חקל דמא, is clear. In the Chaldean language חקל means field, and דמא, in the older sound, means blood. As for what he says, "in their own dialect," this should be taken as in that passage of John 8:17,

units.la: ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ:
units.tr: "in your law" [ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ].

units.la: vel intelligendum de Ierosolymitana. forte in ea vrbe Acel dicebát cum tferi aut fegol,pro Acal: tamen hoc non possumus affirmare. Illud affirmo quòd Ierosolymitana propria olim dialectus fuerit diuersa aliquantum à Syra & Babylonia, in qua lingua Acal dicimus, non Acel. Quod dico diuersam fuisse eam linguam à Babylonia, clarum ex traductione ea, quæ Targum Ierosolymitanum vocatur. Vide Eliam præfatione in Methurgeman. Concludam de Aceldema,si addidero Syri interpretis interpretationem. pro χωρίον ἁιμάτος Syrus habet, רם דמא,id est χωρίῳ ἁμ. quam vocem, si quis dicet Galilæos vsitasse pro Acal, fortasse dicet quod res est. certè χωρίῳ non repertum adhuc mihi apud quenquam interpretem Chaldæum.
units.tr: Or it should be understood of the Jerusalem dialect. Perhaps in that city they said Acel, with tsere or segol, for Acal; yet this we cannot affirm. What I do affirm is that the Jerusalem dialect was formerly its own and somewhat different from the Syriac and Babylonian, in which language we say Acal, not Acel. That this language differed from the Babylonian is clear from that translation which is called the Jerusalem Targum; see Elias in his preface to the Methurgeman. I will conclude on Aceldema if I add the interpretation of the Syriac translator. For "field of blood" [χωρίον αἵματος] the Syrian has רם דמא, that is, χωρίῳ ἁμ. If anyone says that the Galileans used this for Acal, he may perhaps be saying what is true. Certainly I have not yet found χωρίῳ among any Chaldean interpreter.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: A. De Remphan coniectura. B. Græcos codices depravatos esse. C. Resch lectum pro Caph. D. Ciiun Hebraïs & Ceuan apud Arabes quid?
units.tr: A. On the conjecture about Remphan. B. That the Greek manuscripts are corrupted. C. Resch read for Caph. D. What are Kiun among the Hebrews and Keuan among the Arabs?

units.la: LOCVS est Act. 7, 43;quem difficilem faciunt voces aliquot corruptæ, quæ mirandum in modum torquent interpretes .in iis est Remphan.
units.tr: The passage is Acts 7:43, which several corrupted words make difficult, and which interpreters twist in a remarkable way. Among these words is Remphan.

units.la: καὶ τὸ ἄςτρον τῆς θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ρεμφάν.
units.tr: "and the star of your god, Remphan" [καὶ τὸ ἄστρον τῆς θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ρεμφάν].

units.la: Quid Remphan? Non magis chamæleon in colore, quàm hoc nomen variat in scriptura, vt vel inde iure merito quis colligat locum à librariis corruptum esse. Quare frustra se torquent viri docti in eo explicando. Nam constat Græcos ignaros linguæ Hebraicæ multas huiusmodi voces depravasse. Mihi in tam varia scriptura placet ῥεμφάν. ita legunt Iustinus in disputatione cum Tryphone; & Theodoritus in Leuiticum quæst. 15. estque vitium, vt coniicio, à librariis pro καιφάν: nisi potius ipsos interpretes decepit similitudo quæ est inter literas ר & ד,vt legerint רמן absque punctis vocalibus,pro פיון. postremum non caret exemplo. Nam manifeste legunt resch pro caph Nah. 1, 5: videlicet רֹאשׁ quod transtulerunt ἀρχὰς pro כאש, id est ὡς τὸ πῦρ. docti expendent. est autem Ciiun sive Ceuan Saturnus planeta, quem Arabes & Persæ כיון indigitant: quæ appellatio nonnihil adiuuat coniecturam meam: nam argumento mihi est ut credam veteres dixisse Ceuan non Ciiun. Dicam de hac re plura, aut potius iam dixi Amos 5, 26, in Coniectaneis meis ad translationem Græcam.
units.tr: What is Remphan? The name varies no more in its spelling in Scripture than a chameleon changes colour. So one may rightly conclude from this alone that the passage has been corrupted by copyists, and learned men torment themselves in vain in explaining it. For it is established that the Greeks, ignorant of the Hebrew language, corrupted many words of this kind. Among such varied readings I prefer ῥεμφάν. So Justin reads it in his dispute with Trypho, and Theodoret on Leviticus, question 15. The error is, as I conjecture, the copyists' for καιφάν; unless perhaps the translators themselves were deceived by the resemblance between the letters ר and ד, so that they read רמן without vowel points for פיון. The latter has a precedent. For they clearly read resch for caph at Nahum 1:5, namely רֹאשׁ, which they rendered ἀρχάς for כאש, that is ὡς τὸ πῦρ. Learned men will weigh this. Now Kiun or Keuan is the planet Saturn, which the Arabs and Persians designate כיון. This name somewhat supports my conjecture, for I have grounds for believing that the ancients said Keuan, not Kiun. I will say more on this matter, or rather I have already said it at Amos 5:26, in my Coniectanea on the Greek translation.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 27.

units.la: A. De Ephphata, eiusque scriptura apud Syros. B. Patach in sermone Hebræo quid?
units.tr: A. Concerning Ephphatha, and how it is written among the Syrians. B. What does Patach mean in the Hebrew language?

units.la: Ἐφφαθά' Mar. 7, 34. scribo אֶפְתַּח cum daghes in loco Thau: id est Ephphata pronuntiatione vetere. Nam antiqui Phe sonabant ubi nos Pe. docent exempla obuia passim. Syrus אִתְפְּתַח ad Grammaticam non male ad scripturam Græcam, perperam, forte Seruator ita pronuntiauit. nihil affirmo. tamen adducor ut credam scriptum fuisse ἰϑφαθά, & inde postea factum ἐφφαθά. Declaratio Marci διανοίχθητι pertinet tam ad os quam ad aures. Nam agitur non solum de surdo, sed etiam de μογιλάλῳ. Sic vsurpant verbum Patach Hebræi. de muto Psal. 38, 14. כאלם לא יפתח פיו
units.tr: Ephphatha, Mark 7:34. I write אֶפְתַּח with a dagesh in the place of the Tau: that is, Ephphatha, in the old pronunciation. For the ancients sounded Phe where we sound Pe; the examples meet us everywhere. The Syriac form אִתְפְּתַח is not badly suited, grammatically, to the Greek writing, though it is wrong; perhaps the Saviour pronounced it so. I affirm nothing. Still, I am inclined to think that it was written ἰϑφαθά, and that from this later came ἐφφαθά. Mark's explanation, διανοίχθητι, [be opened], applies to the mouth as much as to the ears. For the matter concerns not only a deaf man but also a μογιλάλος, one with an impediment in his speech. The Hebrews use the verb Patach in this sense. Of the mute, Psalm 38:14: כאלם לא יפתח פיו

units.la: id est, tanquam mutus non aperuit os suum. de surdo Isa. 35, 5. ואזני חרשים תפתחנה
units.tr: that is, "like a mute man he did not open his mouth." Of the deaf, Isaiah 35:5: ואזני חרשים תפתחנה

units.la: id est, & aures surdorum aperientur.
units.tr: that is, "and the ears of the deaf shall be opened."

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: A. Abba pater: super que eo Hieron. sententia reiecta. B. mos synagogæ veteris iam primum obseruatus. C. filius Timæi Bartimæus. D. Locus Hieronymi.
units.tr: A. Abba, Father: Jerome's opinion on this is rejected. B. The custom of the old synagogue, observed here for the first time. C. Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus. D. A passage of Jerome.

units.la: אבא id est pater. Syrum est. Grammaticus nuperus mutat אבא ex analogia. sed אבא scriptum in libris Chaldæorum, & ita scribendum argumento mihi ἀββᾶ, quod in novo Testamento. Dictus אבא pater ab affectu quo est in liberos. אב ab אבה. Quod autem ἐκ πατρὸς legimus ἀββᾶ ὁ πατὴρ Rom. 8, 15, Interpreti post Hieronymum & alios placet ex Marci 14, 36, Græcum additum Syriaco vocabulo explicando. Mihi aliud videtur, quod tamen arbitrarium esse volo, nolo sit certum. Coniicio Christum pronuntiasse Abba pater אבא פטיר ex consuetudine veterum Hebraeorum. Nam eos scilicet visitasse voces Graecas, quas addebant vocibus suae linguae. Sic reperio פוטירין פוטירין in Lexico iuris ex Genesi magno cap. 10, & 54, & ex Leuitico maiore. est autem פטיר vocabulum Ierosolymitanum, פטיר Graecum ποτήριον: utrumque significat, quod Hebraicè Chos dicitur, ait author Lexici. Quod si declaratio est ὁ πατὴρ, mirum cur Euangelista non scripsit ἀββᾶ ὁ ἐστι πατὴρ, ut alibi χορτᾶν ὁ ἐστι δῶρον. Neque me turbant exempla Hieronymi. Iam diximus filius Timaei non videri declarationem τῆς Bartimaeus, cum praecedat τὸς Τιμαῖ βαρτιμαῖος. nam par est ut declaratio sequatur. potius patris nomen voluit indicatum Euangelista. Aser, diuitiae, non meminime legere, ut nec Tabitha Dorcas, sed quidem Ταβιθὰ ἡ διερμηνευομένη Δορκὰς, quod parum adiuuat mentem Hieronymi. Pro Melech vernaculus in Genesi est,
units.tr: Abba [אבא], that is, "father." It is Syriac. A recent grammarian changes [אבא] by analogy, but [אבא] is written in the books of the Chaldeans, and so, I argue, it should be written ἀββᾶ, as it is in the New Testament. The word [אב], "father," is so called from the affection a father has for his children; it comes from [אבה]. As for our reading ἀββᾶ ὁ πατὴρ at Romans 8:15, the translator, following Jerome and others, thinks the Greek was added to explain the Syriac word, from Mark 14:36. To me another explanation seems more likely, though I want this to be taken as a conjecture and not as certain. I conjecture that Christ pronounced "Abba, Father" as [אבא פטיר], following the custom of the ancient Hebrews. For they were accustomed to use Greek words and to add them to words of their own language. Thus I find [פוטירין פוטירין] in the Lexicon of Law, from the Great Genesis chapters 10 and 54, and from the Greater Leviticus. [פטיר] is a Jerusalem word, and it is the Greek ποτήριον; both mean what in Hebrew is called [Chos], as the author of the Lexicon says. But if ὁ πατὴρ is an explanation, it is strange that the Evangelist did not write ἀββᾶ ὁ ἐστι πατὴρ, as he elsewhere writes χορτᾶν ὁ ἐστι δῶρον. Nor do Jerome's examples trouble me. We have already said that "son of Timaeus" does not seem to be an explanation of "Bartimaeus," since the words come before it as "Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus"; an explanation ought to follow what it explains. Rather, the Evangelist wished the father's name to be given. "Aser" means riches, and one should not forget to read it so, nor "Tabitha Dorcas," but rather Ταβιθὰ ἡ διερμηνευομένη Δορκὰς, which hardly supports Jerome's view.

units.la: בן משך כיתי
units.tr: The son of the steward of my house [בן משך כיתי].

units.la: Genes. 15, 12, in quo explicando licet varient interpretes, nemo tamen de vernaculo Mesec expositit, neque ipse vulgatus interpres, qui sic reddit:
units.tr: In Genesis 15:12, where the interpreters vary in explaining it, no one has explained the vernacular Mesec, not even the Vulgate translator himself, who renders it thus:

units.la: „ Filius procuratoris domus meae iste Damascus Eliezer.
units.tr: "The son of the steward of my house is this Damascus Eliezer."

units.la: Locus Hieronymi est in commentariis super epistolam ad Galatas:
units.tr: Jerome's passage is in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians:

units.la: „ Abba Hebraicum est, idipsum significans quod & pater. Et hac consuetudinem in pluritus locis Scriptura conseruat, ut Hebraicum verbum cum interpretatione sua ponat. Bartimaeus,

units.tr: APROe,17,g. This must be understood of the schewa, which today sounds like a very short e; but the ancients gave it mostly the sound of patach. Hence Samuel, Chanaan, Manasses, Sabaoth, and many other similar words.

units.tr: But it should be known that the letter g in the middle [illegible] in which the heresy of the Sadducees arose. 6,c. He lived not long after the times of Ezra. In Pirqe Avot: Moses handed down the law he had received to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue, from whose remnants came Simeon the Just, whom Antigonus of Sokho succeeded. Hot water at Tiberias, 24,e. Akiba, teacher of Aquila the proselyte, 20,e. Aquila the translator rendered the canonical books of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek. 20,e. The same man translated the Pentateuch of Moses into Chaldee; this translation is today extant, printed at Venice under the name of Onkelos. 24,c. In this name, after the epenthetic nun, which is conventional among the Arabs, a is changed into o. He was a native of Pontus, and was the brother of the Emperor Hadrian's wife. He is said to have been appointed by him prefect of the works for rebuilding Jerusalem. Artabanus, 2,b. To open is said of the eyes as well as of the ears, 27. Asa, 4,c. They are wrong who derive the name Jesus from this verb, 4,d.

units.la: Mutant Syri Lamed Hebraeorum in Refch. אלמנה vidua ארקמלא; mutatio eadè apud Graecos inter λ & ρ, κείλαvos, κλίλαvos: ἀργαλέος, ἀλγαλέος; & in Latio cùm ex Parma palma deducitur; ex squarore, squalor, ex furuo fuluum. vt mirum nemini videri debeat, si pro belial posteritas dixerit beliar.
units.tr: The Syrians change the Hebrew Lamed into Resh: widow [אלמנה] becomes arkamla; the same change occurs among the Greeks between λ and ρ: keilaros, klilaros [κείλαρος, κλίλαρος]; argaleos, algaleos [ἀργαλέος, ἀλγαλέος]; and in Latin, palma is derived from Parma, squalor from squarore, and fulvum from furuo. So it should seem no wonder to anyone if later generations said beliar for belial.

Chabod: ibidem dele punctum post, Suidas adfert. pag. 37. pone [ו] post לוהט pag. 38 in F, leg. incuria, pro iniuria. pag. 39. alaïn, sine aspiratione. pag. 42 divisim scribe יומא רחילחא; & paulo post leg. mare Iiphamicum per m. & קלטיונים duplici Iod. In eadem pagina scribo Aceldema, sed magis placet Haceldema cum adspiratione, quoniam est het in Hebrao. pag. 45. in C, πεῖτα pro ἐαῖτα. In Indice voce Barrabas, leg. ἐῶ filius divisim. & in C. χ sive Chaph. In, Ezechiel post tragicus, adde 15. a. In Iacobitæ post qui? adde 13, c. In, Eusebij error, ἐελομῶνλος aut ἰσῶν ἐολύμαι. hoc Egesippus, illud Eusebius censet.
units.tr: Page 1 and 5: read Drusl or Drusij. Page 6, in A: אַמְרוּ לוֹ. Likewise in B: ἱερηνεαμίῳ. Put a comma after ὑπάτως and a full stop after propositum; then write manuscula littera, In Syriacis. Page 8, in A: περὶ χιδῶν. Page 13, in A: delete the full stop before Theophylactus. Page 14, in D: read "quam esse credebant" for "quod esse credebant," and put a full stop after Ichielides. Page 16: after the words "id est הָאֵל" a full stop is missing; in D, correct to ἐξῶν. Page 20, in G: read "numen" for "nomen." Page 23: read μαμμαῶ; should it be written μαμαῶ? Page 28, in G: אֵלוֹהַ with a doubled tametsi. Page 29, in B: Benereem without aspiration. Page 34, Chabod: in the same place delete the full stop after "Suidas adfert." Page 37: put [ו] after לוהט. Page 38, in F: read "incuria" for "iniuria." Page 39: alaïn, without aspiration. Page 42: write יומא רחילחא as two separate words; and a little later read "mare Iiphamicum" with one m, and קלטיונים with a double Iod. On the same page I write Aceldema, but Haceldema with aspiration pleases me more, since the Hebrew has a het. Page 45, in C: πεῖτα for ἐαῖτα. In the Index, under the word Barrabas, read ἐῶ as a separate word; and in C, χ or Chaph. In "Ezechiel," after "tragicus," add 15, a. In "Iacobitae," after "qui?" add 13, c. In "Eusebii error," ἐελομῶνλος or ἰσῶν ἐολύμαι: the former is Hegesippus' view, the latter Eusebius'.

units.la: BIsego πετοβύπρΘ', & Annis, & Ordine, Neutri conuenire putaui, quod superest vitæ (si modò quid superesse Deus annuit) alio transigere cursu, quàm qui rectà me deducat eò, quò Christi sacerdoté, qui tanto suo satagat respondere nomini, Sacra solummodo dantem, Sacráque docentem, toto nisu contendere necessum est. Apinas forenses, & Aulicas tricas (Spes, videlicet, magnas, & certamina diuitiarũ) scio grauitati & excellétiæ Presbyterorum non congruere: sed & vetari. Quibus & in Exoticis Ethnicorum disciplinis vitam córerere nefas. Aliud igitur reliqui nihil est, quàm nos exhortationi, lectioni, doctrinæ totos attendere. Doctrinæ (dico) non quæ linguam doctis humanæ sapientiæ verbis exornet, non quæ domos nostras vndiquáque diuitiis amplificet: At ei, quæ fecundum pietatem est,doctrinæ:quæ vitam componat,animum formet, instruat mores, in omni denique Dei iustitia nos erudiat.
units.tr: Since my years and my rank, I have thought, suit neither, and whatever life remains to me (if God grants any to remain), I must spend on a course other than the one that leads me straight to where the priest of Christ, who ought to strive to answer to so great a name, must strive with all his effort to give only sacred things and to teach sacred things. I know that forensic pleadings and courtly intrigues (great hopes, that is, and contests over riches) do not agree with the dignity and excellence of presbyters, and are in fact forbidden. Nor is it right for them to spend their lives on the foreign disciplines of the heathen. So nothing is left to us but to give ourselves wholly to exhortation, reading and teaching. I mean teaching not of the kind that adorns the tongue with the words of human wisdom for the learned, or that enlarges our houses with riches on every side, but teaching that is according to godliness: that shapes life, forms the mind, instructs conduct, and finally trains us in all the justice of God.

units.la: Hoc(vti debeo) dum pro mea tenuitate, próque talentuli mihi crediti negociatiuncula, præstare laboro,de magno Gratiani Decreto nónulla selegi, de quibus, hôc semestri, iuxta demandatum mihi docêdi munus, vobiscum differam. Grande illud,variúmque volumen,quod res tam multas & causas amplectitur, ob vnam dûtaxat, quam nunc instituimus, tædiofum forte foret in scholas quotidie deferre. Quare mihi visum cômodius illinc excerpere, quod ipsi prælecturi sumus. Id autem quale fit, expediam paucis.
units.tr: Doing this, as far as my small ability allows, and labouring at it as a little trade with the small talent entrusted to me, I have chosen some points from the great Decretum of Gratian, about which I shall, this half-year, discuss with you, according to the teaching duty laid upon me. That great and varied volume, which embraces so many subjects and causes, would perhaps be tedious to bring into the lecture hall every day for the one matter we now take up. So I thought it more convenient to pick out from it what we are going to lecture on. What sort of selection it is I shall explain briefly.

units.la: Ecclesiæ Iesu Christi ministrorum tripertita statim fuit ab eius initio,distinctio.videlicet:Epi fcoporum,Presbyterorum, & Diaconorum. Sua singulis erant & officia diuisa, De quibus in noftra(fi Deus hoc mihi voti cócesserit) ad Apoftolicos canonas Ἀναγκαῖα dicemus. Hîc mihi De moribus, ante omnia, sermo futurus est: quamuis obiter de cuiúsque munere multa proponentur: quod etsi non incumbat idem cuique, Mores tamen eosdem, quamuis non eadem munia, videtur ab omnibus exegisse Paulus. Qui tam graphicè Diaconos, Presbyteros, Episcopos Apoftolico suo penicillo deliniauit, vt non melius dignoscere quis valeat hominis amicisimi notisimíque míque sibi facie, quàm veri & Apostolici Diaconi, Presbyteri, vel Episcopi personam. Quam quisquis, vt ille depictam reliquit, non ad viuum referre toto conatu nititur, is mihi certè quidem Apostolicæ minister Ecclesiæ viuus non videtur.
units.tr: From the very beginning of the Church of Jesus Christ there was a threefold distinction of its ministers: namely bishops, presbyters and deacons. Their duties were divided, each to each, and these we will discuss in our own work on the Apostolic canons, the necessary matters [Ἀναγκαῖα], if God grants me this wish. Here my discourse will concern above all morals, although many things about each one's office will be set out in passing. Though the same duties do not fall on everyone, Paul seems to have required the same morals of all, though not the same functions. He drew deacons, presbyters and bishops so vividly with his apostolic pencil that one could no better recognise the face of a most friendly and familiar friend than the person of a true and apostolic deacon, presbyter or bishop. Whoever does not strive with all his effort to represent that portrait from life, as he left it painted, does not seem to me to be a living minister of the Apostolic Church.

units.la: Primò (quod oportuit) in medium protulimus Apostoli verba. Quorum postea declarationem singularem singulis adscripsimus, à Gratiano, diuersis ex authoribus, sanctisque Doctoribus, & veterum Conciliorum, tam Græcorum, quàm Latinorum definitionibus recollectam. Variis quidem suæ Decretorum compilationis hoc agit in locis: at præcipuè, continuis ferè quinque ac viginti Diorismis integris: à vigesima quinta distinctione (scilicet) ad quinquagesimā vsque. Nomina scriptorum prodidit vbique. Locos, raro. Nisi (quod magis opinor. nam sunt in manu scriptis plerique, & citantur à glossographis & commentatoribus) hos omiserit incuria librariorum. quæ, profectò, cófusio, multum certitudinis operi detrahit. Nā, quid ex Hieronymo, vel Augustino, vel Polygraphis aliis proferre, nec indicare descripte locum: perinde est, ac ex hominum turba magna, citare Petrū vel Ioannem, nec electè, quum multi sint ὁμώνυμοι, designare quempiam.
units.tr: First (as was fitting) I have set out the words of the Apostle. To each of these I have added a separate explanation, gathered by Gratian from various authors and holy teachers, and from the definitions of the ancient councils, both Greek and Latin. He does this in various places of his compilation of Decrees, but chiefly in some twenty-five continuous distinctions in full: from the twenty-fifth distinction to the fiftieth. He gives the names of the writers everywhere, but the places only rarely. Unless (as I rather suppose, since most are in manuscripts and are cited by glossators and commentators) the carelessness of copyists has omitted them, which confusion certainly takes much from the reliability of the work. For to bring forward something from Jerome, or Augustine, or other writers, without indicating the passage where it is written, is just like citing Peter or John from a great crowd of men without saying which one, since there are many homonyms.

units.la: Nos, epitomè præterea singulis additā pro scholiis (quæ maiora forte post ædentur) annos & tempus cuiusque fideliter, & vero, quàm potuimus, proximè, obseruauimus: vnde suus antiquus Paulinæ sententiæ, genuinúsque sensus cōstaret, ac intelligeretur.
units.tr: Moreover, I have added to each a brief note as a scholion (larger scholia may perhaps follow later), and have faithfully and truly, as closely as I could, observed the years and the time of each, so that the ancient meaning and genuine sense of Paul's saying might be established and understood.

units.la: Non enim mens ea, vel doctrina Pauli est, quam bene Grammaticus aliquis & Rhetor somniarit: quę Gnosticorum theologia recens est, nihil nisi linguas (magis profecto, quàm linguis) loquentium. Diceres istos apud Infideles declamitare, quibus in signū datæ fuere linguæ. Sensus est ille Pauli solus, quem nos docuit, & qué posteris tradidit Orthodoxorū patrum venerāda cunctis antiquitas. Hæc vera est, hæc unica est discutiendæ cognoscendæque Scripturæ norma: quæ reliquit immesum, intentatúmve nihil. Cæterùm (quod sapiens monet Hebræus) Non litigemus cum hominibus linguatis. In sua nempe civitate terribilis est Ἀνὴρ βλασφήμος. Itaque Sibi loquātur μέγοπς, ac sibi plaudant, atq; suis Bilingues, & Trilingues, & quantum volet ipsi, Linguaces Gnostici: Nos elingues, idiotæ, barbari, nihil intelligentes, non respondebimus Amen.
units.tr: For that is not the mind or teaching of Paul which some grammarian or rhetorician may have dreamed up: that is a recent theology of the Gnostics, of men who speak nothing but tongues (much more than with tongues, indeed). You would think they were declaiming among unbelievers, to whom tongues were given as a sign. That sense of Paul alone is the one that has taught us, and that the venerable antiquity of the orthodox Fathers handed down to posterity. This is the true and only rule for examining and knowing Scripture, which has left nothing unmeasured or untried. Moreover (as the wise Hebrew warns), let us not contend with men of many tongues. In their own city a blasphemer [Ἀνὴρ βλάσφημος] is indeed terrible. So let them talk to themselves and applaud themselves, and let their bilinguals, trilinguals and as many talkative Gnostics as they please do the same. We, tongue-tied, untrained, barbarians understanding nothing, will not answer Amen.

units.la: Sed interim tamen faciamus, quod faciēdum Paulus adhortatur. hoc est, Non istorum, qui sic sunt inflati, sermonem, sed virtutem: non oratione, sed vitæ ratione & institutione cōsideremus: & nemo nos tuc decipiet in multitudine linguarum, vel sublimitate verborum: quia, Non in verbis, sed in factis est regnum Dei. Non bonis nescio quibus literis, at certis moribus bonis cō pervenimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile, however, let us do what Paul urges us to do: that is, we should look not at the speech of those who are so puffed up, but at their virtue; not at their oratory but at the manner and training of their life. No one will deceive us with a multitude of tongues or the loftiness of words, because the kingdom of God is not in words but in deeds. We arrive at good morals not by some good letters I know not what, but by sound good conduct.

units.la: Aliunde verò mores bonos, & Christianas καπλόνης discere non valemus, si non ex Ambrosio, Hieronymo, Augustino, Basilio, Gregorio, Chrysostomo, similísque religionis ac fidei viris, Decretorum doctoribus atque datoribus, addiscamus. A quibus qui dissentit, hic mihi nihil sentit: Procul dubio, si qua fuit in illis (ut in fuit plurima) doctrinæ veritas, atque scientia: iá nulla est in Gnosticis. Sin tale quid his tribuas: illis, oportet, adimas. Apertiùs dicere volo. Catholici patres omnes, quotquot ab Apostolis, cúmque Apostolis vixerunt, aut omnino nihil sciuerút: aut æui præsentis Gnostici nihil omnino sciunt: è diametro cum traditionibus & conciliis illorum pugnantes, omniaque passim redarguentes, & cauillantes. Blasphemum prius illud est, & impiũ. Falsò sunt igitur isti Scientiæ cognomine solo in vulgo clari: moribus alioqui, vitaq; nebulones obscurissimi. De rebus & Politaa loquor Ecclesię. Ná cum Demosthenibus, & Aristotelibus negocij mihi nihil est. De moribus (accipe) Clericorū loquor. quales Apostolus nō solū descripsit, sed etiā cuique nostrū præscripsit: & quales Decretis ac authoritate patrum Gratianus hic explicatos nobis exposuit.
units.tr: We cannot learn good morals and Christian conduct from any other source unless we learn them from Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, and men of similar religion and faith, the teachers and framers of the Decrees. Whoever dissents from them, to me he seems to think nothing. Without doubt, if there was any truth and knowledge of teaching in those men (and there was very much), there is none now among the Gnostics. But if you attribute such things to these men, you must take them away from those. I want to speak more plainly. All the Catholic Fathers, as many as lived from the Apostles and with the Apostles, either knew absolutely nothing, or the Gnostics of the present age know absolutely nothing, since they run directly counter to those traditions and councils, and everywhere refute and carp at everything. The first of these is blasphemous and impious. Therefore those men are falsely famous among the common people by the name of science alone; otherwise they are most obscure rogues in morals and in life. I speak of the affairs and polity of the Church, for I have nothing to do with Demosthenes and Aristotle. I speak of the morals (understand) of the clergy: such as the Apostle not only described but prescribed to each of us, and such as Gratian has here set out and explained for us by the Decrees and the authority of the Fathers.

units.la: In quibus dū pro mea qualicúmq; virili desudo, quæso vos, vt conatus meos orationibus vestris ad iuuetis. Huiusce rei mihi per Euangelij Iesu debitores estis. Qui nos suâ benignitate conseruet.
units.tr: While I toil at these matters with whatever manly strength I have, I ask you to help my efforts with your prayers. You are indebted to me in this matter on account of the Gospel of Jesus. May he keep us by his goodness.

units.la: Apostoli mandatum sic habet.
units.tr: The command of the Apostle runs thus.

units.la: DE PRESBYTERIS, ET EPISCOPIS.
units.tr: ON PRESBYTERS AND BISHOPS.

units.la: Ex Epistola prioris ad Timotheum cap. 3.
units.tr: From the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3.

units.la: IDelis sermo. Si quis Episcopatum desiderat, Bonum opus desiderat. Oportet enim Episcopum, Irreprehensibilem esse, Vnius vxoris virum, Sobrium, Prudentem, Pudicum, Ornatum, Hospitalem, Doctorem, Non vinolentum, Non percussorem, Non litigiosum, Non cupidum. Suae domui bene praepositu: Filios habentem subditos cum omni castitate. si quis autem domui suae bene praeesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiae Dei diligentiam habebit? Non Neophytum: ne in superbiam elatus, in iudicium incidat diaboli. Oportet autem illu & testimoniu habere bonum ab iis, qui foris sunt: ut non in opprobriu incidat, & in laqueum diaboli.
units.tr: This is a faithful saying: if anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. A bishop must therefore be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, chaste, of good behaviour, hospitable, apt to teach, not given to wine, not a striker, not quarrelsome, not covetous. He must rule his own house well, having his children in subjection with all chastity. For if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the Church of God? He must not be a novice, lest he be puffed up with pride and fall into the judgement of the devil. Moreover he must have a good testimony from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.

units.la: Ex Epistola ad Titum capite primo.-
units.tr: From the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1.

units.la: Huius rei gratia, reliqui te Cretae: Ut ea quae desunt, corrigas: & constituas per ciuitates Presbyteros, sicut & ego dispositui tibi. Si quis sine crimine est, Vnius vxoris vir, Filios lios habens fideles, non in accusatione luxuriæ,aut non subditos.
units.tr: For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you. If anyone is without crime, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not accused of riot or disobedience.

units.la: Oportet enim Episcopū sine crimine esse, sicut Dei dispensatorem: Non superbū, Non iracundum, Non vinolentum,Non percussorem, Non turpis lucri cupidū : Sed Hospitalem,Benignum,Sobriū,Iustum, Sanctum, Continentem, Amplectentem eum, qui secundum doctrinam est,Fidelem sermonem: vt potes sit exhortari in doctrina sana:& eos, qui contra dicunt,arguere.
units.tr: For a bishop must be blameless, as God's steward: not proud, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy of base gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who speak against it.

units.la: Hæ sunt virtutes,per quas beatus Paulus, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀρρήτα ἱερέως ἀνυπέρβλητον εἰκόνα, Ineffabilis Sacerdotis absolutam voluit esse Imaginem, ait Chrysostomus lib. 6. de Sacerdo. cap.6.
units.tr: These are the virtues by which blessed Paul wished the bishop, the ineffable priest, to be an absolute image, as Chrysostom says in book 6 of On the Priesthood, chapter 6 [ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀρρήτα ἱερέως ἀνυπέρβλητον εἰκόνα].

units.la: DE DIACONIS.
units.tr: ON DEACONS.

units.la: Ex eodem capite 3.
units.tr: From the same chapter 3.

units.la: Diaconos oportet similiter esse Pudicos, Non bilingues, Non multo vino deditos, Non turpe lucrum sectantes, Habentes mysterium fidei in conscientia pura. Et hi autem probentur primùm:& sic ministrent. Nullum crimen habētes. Diaconi sint vnius vxoris viri:Qui filiis suis bene præsint,& suis domibus.
units.tr: Deacons likewise must be grave, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not pursuing base gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let them first be tested, and then let them minister, being without accusation. Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling well their children and their own households.

units.la: Sacerdotalis hæc est ab Apostolo pietas tabella: quam pro templorum foribus, & nostris in conclavibus vbique suspensam cuperem.
units.tr: This is the priestly picture of piety drawn by the Apostle, which I would wish hung everywhere, at the doors of the churches and in our own rooms.

units.la: Sed ante venit, quàm longiùs progrediamur, cum Chrysostomo quaerendum, λόγῳ in hanc epistolam 10. dum locum de Diaconis interpretatur.
units.tr: But before we proceed further, we must ask, with Chrysostom in his tenth homily on this epistle, where he expounds the passage on deacons.

units.la: Quum Paulus tam diligenter(ait)Episcopos formarit, ostendės quid illos habere conueniat,& à quo debeant abstinere: cur, omisso Presbyterorum ordine, mox ab Episcopis transit ad Diaconos? Respondet. ὅτι οὐ πολὺ τὸ μέσον, quia non est magnum medium. Hoc est, Inter Episcopos & Presbyteros interest modicum. Chirotoniam nempe solam,plus Presbyteris,Episcopi videntur habere:cæteris pares. Ne se Dominos Presbyterorum putent. Sed etiam ne se solutos ac liberos omni publicâ solicitudine credant inferiores Presbyteri, καὶ διδασκαλίας, καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας προστασίας(sic enim Chrysostomus)ipsis quoque demandata est: Et doctrina,& Ecclesiæ cura siue præfectura ipsis est credita. Quare,quæ de Episcopis dixit Apostolus, dixisse de Presbyteris est intelligendus.& exigitur in Presbyteris omnia. Sic Ambrosius hunc explicarat locū. Post Episcopum(ait)Diaconarus ordinationem subiecit. quare? Nisi quia Episcopi,& Presbyteri vna ordinatio est. Vtrque enim sacerdos est,sed Episcopus primus est. Vt omnis Episcopus sit Presbyter:Non tamen omnis Presbyter est Episcopus. Hic enim Episcopus est,qui inter Presbyteros primus est. Sic etiam Theophylactus. Sic est in Occumenio. Tractat hoc & Hieronymus, ad Titum ca.1. To.9.& Epist.Legimus in Esaia. ad Euagriū. To.2.Dicebamus in Apostolico can.1.Et ostendebamus Episcoporū, Presbyterorumq;Tagmata(vt appellamus in canonibus)non eadem esse Ad incœpta, Christo ducente, pergamus.
units.tr: Since Paul, so carefully (he says), has shaped the bishops, showing what they ought to have and what they ought to abstain from, why, passing over the order of presbyters, does he go straight from bishops to deacons? He answers: "because the middle is not great" [ὅτι οὐ πολὺ τὸ μέσον], that is, there is only a small difference between bishops and presbyters. Bishops seem to have only the power of ordination over presbyters, and are otherwise their equals; and lest the presbyters think themselves lords over one another, or believe that as inferiors they are free and released from all public care, the teaching and the oversight [καὶ διδασκαλίας, καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας προστασίας] of the Church have been committed to them as well (for so Chrysostom puts it). Therefore what the Apostle said of bishops must be understood as said of presbyters too, and everything is required of presbyters. Ambrose also explained this passage in this way. After the bishop, he says, the Apostle added the ordination of deacons. Why? Unless because the ordination of bishops and presbyters is one; for both are priests, but the bishop is first. So every bishop is a presbyter, but not every presbyter is a bishop; for he is the bishop who is first among the presbyters. Theophylact too says this, and so does Oecumenius. Jerome treats it as well, in his commentary on Titus, chapter 1 (vol. 9), and in his letter to Evagrius (vol. 2), where we read in Isaiah, and in the commentary on the Apostolic canon 1, where we showed that the ranks of bishops and presbyters (as we call them in the canons) are not the same. With Christ leading us, let us proceed with what we have begun.

units.la: Protritam docendi viam nos hic tenebimus: quæ discentes ab intellectâ verborum vi & significatione ducere solet ad ipsarū rerum cognitionem. Dicemus itaque primò,quid hæ voces,Episcopus, Presbyter, & Diaconus in Ecclesia denotent. quod fecisse videtur hic Apostolus, initiò statim monstrans, quidnam rei sit,Episcopatus:est(ait)bonum opus. & consequenter Episcopum describens,Operis(videlicet)boni procuratorem & executorem.
units.tr: Here we shall keep to the well-worn path of teaching, which usually leads learners from the understood force and meaning of words to knowledge of the things themselves. So first we shall say what the terms bishop, presbyter and deacon signify in the Church. The Apostle seems to have done this too, at once showing at the outset what the office of bishop is: it is (he says) a good work, and then, describing the bishop, he shows him to be the steward and executor of that good work.

units.la: EPISCOPVS.
units.tr: BISHOP.

units.la: In xciij. Distinctione. Can. Legimus.
units.tr: In Distinction 93, Canon "Legimus."

units.la: Hieronymus ad Euagrium. Epist. Legimus in Esaia. To.2. Natus est Hieronymus anno post Christum trecentesimo trigesimo primo: vixit annos, vnum cum nonaginta, obiit anno salutis, 422.
units.tr: Jerome, to Evagrius, Epistle "Legimus in Esaia," vol. 2. Jerome was born in the year 331 after Christ; he lived ninety-one years and died in the year of salvation 422.

units.la: Episcopus est author ecclesiasticarum rerum prouidus, aut(si mauis) prouisor magnus.
units.tr: A bishop is a provident author of ecclesiastical affairs, or (if you prefer) a great provider.

units.la: REgite gregem Christi: & inspicite, non ex necessitate, sed voluntarie, iuxta Deum. Quod quidem Græcè significantius dicitur, ἐπισκοποῦντες. id est, superintendentes. Vnde & nomen Episcopi tractum est.
units.tr: Rule the flock of Christ, and oversee it, not from necessity but willingly, according to God. The Greek expresses this more forcefully as ἐπισκοποῦντες [episkopountes], that is, "superintending." Hence the name bishop is also derived.

units.la: Eadem rursus in Epistola.
units.tr: The same again, in the Epistle.

units.la: ALexandriæ, à Marco Euangelista vsque ad Heraclan & Dionysiū Episcopos, Presbyteri semper vnum exse delectum, & in excelsiori gradu collocatum, Episcopum nominabant.
units.tr: At Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one man from among themselves, set him in a higher rank, and called him bishop.

units.la: Viij. q. i. Can. Qui Episcopatum.
units.tr: Causa VIII, question 1, Canon "Qui Episcopatum."

units.la: Augustinus cap.19.lib.19.De ciuitate Dei. To.5. Annos quadraginta, aut eò amplius, Episcopi munere functus est Augustinus: obiit aetatis anno septuagesimo sexto. Salutis anno 430.
units.tr: Augustine, chapter 19 of book 19 of The City of God, vol. 5. For forty years or more he discharged the office of bishop, says Augustine. He died in the seventy-sixth year of his age, in the year of salvation 430.

units.la: Ἐπισκοπὴν (qui dici solet Episcopatus) non honorem, non gloriam, sed opus esse definiit Apostolus.
units.tr: The Apostle defined episcopacy (which is commonly called the episcopate) not as an honour, not as glory, but as a work: ἐπισκοπὴν [episkopēn] is a work.

units.la: QVi Episcopatum desiderat, Bonum opus desiderat. Exponere voluit quid sit Episcopatus: quia nomen est operis, non honoris: Graecum est enim, atque inde ductum vocabulum, quòd ille qui praeficitur, eis, quibus praeficitur, superintendit, curam eorum, scilicet, gerens. ἐπὶ quippe, Super, σκοπός vero, Intentio est: ergo ἐπισκοπεῖν Graecè, si velimus, Latinè, Superintendere, possumus dicere: Ut intelligat non se esse Episcopum, qui praeesse dilexerit, non prodesse.
units.tr: Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work. He wished to explain what the episcopate is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour. The word is Greek and derived from this: the one who is set over those over whom he is set oversees them, that is, bearing their care. For ἐπί [epi] means "over," and σκοπός [skopos] means "intention"; so if we wish, we may say in Latin ἐπισκοπεῖν [episkopein], "to superintend." So that he may understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to be in charge rather than to be of service.

units.la: In xxj. Distinctione. Can. Cleros. §. Episcopatus.
units.tr: In Distinction 21, Canon "Cleros," §. "Episcopatus."

units.la: Isidorus cap.xij.lib.vii. Etymologiarum. Isidorus Ispalensis Episcopus (Ispalis Hispanorum vulgo nunc est Scuilla) salutis anno 630. scribebat.
units.tr: Isidore, chapter 12 of book 7 of the Etymologies. Isidore, bishop of Seville (Ispalis, which is now commonly called Seville by the Spanish), was writing in the year of salvation 630.

units.la: EPiscopatus vocabulum inde dictum, quòd ille qui super efficitur, etiam superintendat: curam (scilicet) gerens subditorum. ἐπισκοπεῖν enim Graecè, Latinè intendere dicitur: Et Episcopi Graecè, Latinè Speculatores interpretantur: Nam Speculator est Episcopus praepositus in Ecclesia: dictus eò, quòd speculetur, atque perspiciat populorum infra se positorum mores & vitam. Cognoscere licet ex his, quid nominis est, Episcopus. Iam, qui sint Presbyteri, nobis ostendit Anacletus, à Petro tertius Romę Pontifex. Anno Christi centesimo. In Epistola sua secunda, ad Episcopos Italiae scripta.
units.tr: The word episcopate is derived from this: the one who is made to be over others also oversees them, bearing (that is) the care of his subjects. For ἐπισκοπεῖν [episkopein] in Greek is said in Latin to be "to intend." And bishops (ἐπίσκοποι [episkopoi]) are translated in Greek as "watchmen" [speculatores]: for a bishop is a watchman set over the Church, so called because he watches and observes the morals and life of the people placed under him. From these things it can be known what the name bishop means. Now, who the presbyters are, Anacletus, the third Roman pontiff from Peter, shows us, in the year of Christ 100, in his second epistle, written to the bishops of Italy.

units.la: PRESBYTER.
units.tr: PRESBYTER.

units.la: In lxxxiiij.Distinctione.Can.vltimo.
units.tr: In Distinction 84, final canon.

units.la: Non aetas longa, sed rerum prudentia magna, verum πρεσβύτερον facit in Ecclesia.
units.tr: It is not long age but great prudence in affairs that truly makes a πρεσβύτερον [presbyteron, elder] in the Church.

units.la: MOysi praecipitur, vt eligat πρεσβυτέρους, id est, Seniores. In prouerbiis autem dicitur, Gloria senum, Canicies. Hæc vero canicies, Sapientiam designat: de qua scriptum est: Canicies hominum, Prudentia est. Nongentos, & amplius, annos, ab Adam vsque ad Abraham, homines vixisse legimus. Nullus tamen alius priùs appellatus est πρεσβύτερος, id est, Senior, nisi Abraham, qui multo paucioribus annis vixisse cognoscitur: Non ergo propter decrepitam senectutem, sed propter sapientiam, Presbyteri nominantur.
units.tr: Moses was commanded to choose πρεσβυτέρους [presbyterous], that is, elders. In the Proverbs it is said, "The glory of old men is their grey hair." But this grey hair signifies wisdom, of which it is written: "The grey hair of men is prudence." We read that men lived nine hundred years and more, from Adam to Abraham. Yet no one before Abraham was called πρεσβύτερος [presbyteros], that is, elder, although he is known to have lived for far fewer years. Therefore they are called presbyters not because of decrepit old age, but because of wisdom.

units.la: Isidorus in cap.iam citato xij.dictóque Can.Cleros.
units.tr: Isidore, in the chapter already cited, number 12, and in the cited canon "Cleros."

units.la: Πρεσβύτερος Græcè, Latinè Senior interpretatur. Non pro ætate, vel decrepita senectute: sed propter honorem & dignitatem, quam acceperunt, Presbyteri nominantur. Vnde & apud veteres, iidem Episcopi, & iidem Presbyteri fuerunt, quia nomen illud est dignitatis, non ætatis. Ideo autem & Presbyteri vocantur Sacerdotes, quia Sacrum dant. Presbyteri nomen, nominisque rationem satis ista demonstrant. In sacris verò quis appelletur Diaconus, ostendit author ipse sacer atque sanctus, Cyprianus.
units.tr: Πρεσβύτερος [presbyteros] in Greek is translated in Latin as "senior." They are called presbyters not on account of age or decrepit old age, but on account of the honour and dignity they have received. Hence among the ancients the same men were both bishops and presbyters, because that name belongs to dignity, not to age. Presbyters are also called priests for this reason, because they give the sacred things. These points sufficiently demonstrate the name presbyter and the reason for the name. As to who is called deacon in sacred matters, the holy and sacred author Cyprian himself shows it.

units.la: DIACONVS.
units.tr: DEACON.

units.la: In dicta xciij.Distinctione, Can.Dominus noster Iesus. §.Meminisse.& Can. Diaconi.
units.tr: In the aforesaid ninety-third Distinction, Canon "Dominus noster Iesus," §. "Meminisse," and Canon "Diaconi."

units.la: Cyprianus Epist xi. lib.3. Hic Episcopus, Carthaginensis sub Decio, deinde sub Volusiano, carcere & exilium passus: Martyrio demum coronatus sub Valeriano & Gallieno, circiter annum Do.255.
units.tr: Cyprian, Epistle 11, book 3. He was bishop of Carthage under Decius and then under Volusian, suffered imprisonment and exile, and was at last crowned with martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus, about the year of the Lord 255.

units.la: Diaconi est obsequiosum se praebere iuniis Episcoporum atque Presbyterorum.
units.tr: It is the duty of a deacon to show himself obedient to the younger men among bishops and presbyters.

units.la: MEminisse Diaconi debent, quoniam Apostolos (id est, Episcopos) & Presbyteros Dominus elegit: Diaconos autem, post ascensum Domini in coelos, Apostoli sibi constituerunt: Episcopatus sui, & Ecclesiae ministros. Item. Ex quarto concilio Carthaginensi. cap. concilij 37. In Graecis Carthaginensibus conciliis, hoc desideratur concilium, praeter eius inscriptionem, quae sic habet, o'ωφιου Αυγυςτε Τετάρτω, και Ευτυχιάνε, τῶ λαμπροτάτε, id est, Honorio Augusto, quartum, & Eutychiano clarissimo, Cos. hoc est, Anno Christi 400.
units.tr: Deacons ought to remember that the Lord chose the apostles (that is, the bishops) and the presbyters, but that the apostles, after the Lord's ascension into heaven, appointed deacons for themselves as ministers of their episcopate and of the Church. Likewise, from the fourth Council of Carthage, canon 37 of the council. In the Greek copies of the Carthaginian councils this council is wanting, apart from its inscription, which reads thus: [Ὀνωρίου Αὐγούστου τὸ τέταρτον καὶ Εὐτυχιανοῦ τοῦ λαμπροτάτου], that is, "in the fourth consulship of Honorius Augustus and of the most illustrious Eutychianus," which is the year of Christ 400.

units.la: DIaconi, ita se Presbyteri, sicut & Episcopi, ministros esse cognoscant. Item. Hieronymus in ea Epistola, Legimus. adversus Presbyteros inferiores, Diaconorum supercilium retundens, ait.
units.tr: Deacons, just as presbyters as well as bishops, should recognise that they are ministers. Likewise Jerome, in that letter which begins "We read," rebuking the arrogance of deacons against the lesser presbyters, says:

units.la: QVid patitur mensarum & viduarum minister, ut supra eos tumidus se efferat, ad quorum preces, Christi corpus, sanguisque conficitur? Item. Isidorus in eo cap. xij. bis paulo ante citato. Can. Cleros.
units.tr: What does the minister of tables and of widows suffer, that he should puff himself up proudly above those at whose prayers the body and blood of Christ are made? Likewise Isidore, in the twelfth chapter cited twice a little above, Canon "Clerus."

units.la: LEuitae sunt ex authoris sui nomine vocati. De Levi enim Levitae exorti sunt: a quibus in Dei templo, mystici sacramenti ministeria explebatur. Hi Graece Διάκονοι, Latine, Ministri dicuntur: quia sicut in Sacerdote Consecratio, ita & in Diacono Ministerij dispensatio habetur.
units.tr: The Levites are named from the name of their author. For Levites arose from Levi, and by them the ministries of the mystical sacrament were performed in God's temple. These are called in Greek Diakonoi, in Latin ministers, because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the dispensing of the ministry belongs to the deacon.

units.la: Hinc apparere potest, quae sit ea res, de qua sumus disserturi: de qua quidem aliunde potuissem dissertiora sumere: sed hic ab Eucriniis Gratiani diuertere nolo. Quod autem desideratur, Apostolicorum canonum dabit additio nostra, si Christus adiuuerit. Hieronymi verbum duntaxat subiungam, mire congruens antedictis, & omnia confirmans. Id inuenies in libro contra Iouinianum primo, To.1. sic habens.
units.tr: From this it can be seen what matter we are about to discuss. I could indeed have drawn fuller discussion of it from elsewhere, but I do not wish to turn aside here from the Eucrinias of Gratian. What is lacking, our own addition will supply from the Apostolic canons, if Christ helps. I shall add only the word of Jerome, which agrees wonderfully with what was said above and confirms everything. You will find it in the first book against Jovinian, volume 1, where it reads thus:

units.la: Episcopus, & Presbyter, & Diaconus non sunt meritorum nomina, sed officiorum: nec Episcopus, Presbyter, & Diaconus ideo sunt beati, quia Episcopi, vel Presbyteri sint, aut Diaconi: sed si virtutes habuerint nominum suorum & officiorum. Hac ille.
units.tr: Bishop, presbyter and deacon are not names of merits but of offices; nor are bishops, presbyters or deacons blessed for being bishops, presbyters or deacons, but only if they have the virtues of their names and offices. Thus he.

units.la: Post hanc autem verborum significationem sic explanatam, iam res ipsas aggrediamur. Cœterùm (quæ nostri est infœlicitas æui) quia moribus tam diuersis hodie viuitur, ut hæc omnia iure πλαλὰ videri queat, ne me forte (quod lex prohibet) πῶς πρὸσβυτέρους κακολογῶν velle suspicetur aliquis, Hic ego præfabor, quod & Hieronymus hæc ipsa interpretaturus ad Oceanum scribit; inquiens.
units.tr: Now that the meaning of these words has been explained in this way, let us turn to the matters themselves. But (such is the misfortune of our age) people live today by customs so different that all of this could rightly seem idle talk. Lest anyone perhaps suspect that I wish, which the law forbids, to speak ill of presbyters [πῶς πρεσβυτέρους κακολογῶν], I shall preface here what Jerome himself also writes to Oceanus when he is about to explain these very things, saying:

units.la: Obsecro, ne quis me in suggillatione istius temporis sacerdotum scripsisse, quæ scripsi, existimer: sed in Ecclesiæ utilitate. Vt enim Oratores & Philosophi, describentes qualem velint esse perfectum Oratorem & Philosophum, non faciunt iniuriam Demostheni & Platoni, sed res ipsas absque personis definiunt: Sic in descriptione Episcopi, & in eorum expositione, quæ scripta sunt, quasi S P ECVLVM SACERDOTII proponitur. Iam in potestate & conscientia singulorum est, quales se ipsi aspiciant: ut vel dolere ad deformitate, vel gaudere ad pulchritudinem possint. Hàc ego, nec alia mente, suscepi modo tractandas istas Gratiani iuxpiveas, exordiens à tertia vigesima quinte Distinctionis parte. Can. Vnum oratorium, §. Ac primùm.
units.tr: I beg you, let no one think that I have written what I have written as a censure of the clergy of this time, but for the good of the Church. For just as orators and philosophers, describing the sort of perfect orator and philosopher they wish for, do no wrong to Demosthenes and Plato, but define the things themselves without naming persons, so in the description of a bishop, and in their exposition, what is written is set forth as a MIRROR OF THE PRIESTHOOD. Now it lies in the power and conscience of each to see what sort of person he is, so that he may either grieve at the deformity or rejoice at the beauty. It is with this and no other intention that I have undertaken to treat these matters of Gratian now, beginning from the third part of the twenty-fifth Distinction, Canon "Unum oratorium," §. "Ac primum."

units.la: Auditor Christiane, Non est vana, nec ociosa res, Esse Sacerdotem: Rasum non satis est habere verticem: Pileolo caput, orbiculato quondam, nunc autem cornuto & cristato velare: vestem ad talos demittere: linea superinduere: & alia Sacerdotis externa signa gerere non sufficit: Nisi tu quóque fis internis illis vestitus ornamentis, quæ Sacerdotibus per Apostolū suum Christus ipse confuit & concinnauit. Ea modò vobis ipsius Apostoli verbis singula referam: quæ sunt huius initio libelli proposita. Deinde cū Gratiano singulorum aggrediemur interpretationem.
units.tr: Christian listener, it is no empty or idle thing to be a priest. It is not enough to have a shaven crown, to cover the head with a little cap, once round but now horned and crested, to let the robe reach to the ankles, to put on a linen garment, and to bear the other outward signs of a priest, unless you too are clothed with those inner ornaments of dress which Christ himself has arranged and fitted for priests through his Apostle. I shall set out each of these for you in the Apostle's own words, which are placed at the beginning of this little book. Then, with Gratian, I shall approach the interpretation of each one.

units.la: ΔΕΙ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ (ut ait Apostolus) Oportet Presbyterum esse.
units.tr: It behoves the presbyter to be (as the Apostle says) [ΔΕΙ ΤΟΝ ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΕΡΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ].

units.la: ΑΝΕΠΙΛΗΠΤΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΓΚΛΗΤΟΝ, Id est, Irreprehensibilem & Inaccusabilem.
units.tr: Blameless and unaccused [ΑΝΕΠΙΛΗΠΤΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΑΝΕΓΚΛΗΤΟΝ], that is, irreprehensible and unaccusable.

units.la: ΜΙΑΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΟΣ ΑΝΔΡΑ. Id est, Vnius uxoris virum, seu maritum.
units.tr: A man of one wife [ΜΙΑΣ ΓΥΝΑΙΚΟΣ ΑΝΔΡΑ], that is, the husband of one wife, or a married man of one wife.

units.la: ΝΙΦΑΛΙΟΝ, Id est, Vigilem, Intentu & Sobrium.
units.tr: Vigilant [ΝΗΦΑΛΙΟΝ], that is, watchful, attentive and sober.

units.la: ΣΩΦΡΟΝΑ. Id est, Prudentem, Prouidum, Pudicum.
units.tr: Prudent [ΣΩΦΡΟΝΑ], that is, prudent, provident, chaste.

units.la: ΚΟΣΜΙΟΝ, Id est, Ornatum, Modestum, Benéque moratum.
units.tr: Orderly [ΚΟΣΜΙΟΝ], that is, well-ordered, modest and of good conduct.

units.la: ΦΙΛΟΞΕΝΟΝ Id est, Hospitalem, Peregrinos, & absentes à patria benigne suscipientem.
units.tr: Hospitable [ΦΙΛΟΞΕΝΟΝ], that is, hospitable, kindly receiving strangers and those away from their homeland.

units.la: dist. 42.
units.tr: Distinction 42.

units.la: ΔΙΔΑΚΤΙΚΟΝ, Id est, Qui sic doctrinâ polleat, ut alios docere possit.
units.tr: Apt to teach [ΔΙΔΑΚΤΙΚΟΝ], that is, one who is so strong in doctrine that he can teach others.

units.la: ΜΗ ΠΑΡΟΙΝΟΝ, Id est, Non vinolentum, nec ebriosum. Quale sit hoc ornamentum videbimus in dist. 44.
units.tr: Not given to wine [ΜΗ ΠΑΡΟΙΝΟΝ], that is, not addicted to wine, nor a drunkard. What sort of ornament this is we shall see in Distinction 44.

units.la: MH ΓΛΗΚΤΗΝ, id est, Non percussorem, nec violentum hominem. Comperies hoc enodatum in dist. 45.
units.tr: μὴ πλήκτην [MH ΓΛΗΚΤΗΝ], that is, not a striker, nor a violent man. You will find this explained in dist. 45.

units.la: ἈMAXON, id est, A rixis, & altercationibus, & pugnis quibuslibet alienum. Vt ostendetur in dist. 46.
units.tr: ἄμαχον [ἈMAXON], that is, free from brawls, quarrels and fights of any kind. This will be shown in dist. 46.

units.la: MH ΑΙΣΚΡΟΚΕΡΔΗ. ΑΦΙΛΑΡΓΥΡΟΝ. ΤΟΝ ΙΔΙΟΝ ΟΙΚΟΝ ΚΑΛΩΣ ΠΡΟΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΝ. id est, Non turpium lucrorum sectatorem. Non cupidum, nec amantem pecuniae. Familiae suae bene praesidentem. Quae tria declarabuntur in dist. 46.
units.tr: μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ, ἀφίλαργυρον, τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον καλῶς προϊστάμενον [MH ΑΙΣΚΡΟΚΕΡΔΗ. ΑΦΙΛΑΡΓΥΡΟΝ. ΤΟΝ ΙΔΙΟΝ ΟΙΚΟΝ ΚΑΛΩΣ ΠΡΟΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΝ], that is, not a pursuer of shameful gain; not covetous, nor a lover of money; ruling his own household well. These three points will be explained in dist. 46.

units.la: MH ΝΕΟΦΥΤΟΝ. ΚΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΝ ΚΑΛΗΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΩΝ ΕΞΩΘΕΝ. id est, Non Neophytum. & ab extraneis etiam probatum, & laudatum. De Nouitiis non ordinandis, & de bona fama necessaria presbyteris agetur, in dist. 48.
units.tr: μὴ νεόφυτον, καὶ μαρτυρίαν καλὴν ἔχειν ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν [MH ΝΕΟΦΥΤΟΝ. ΚΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΝ ΚΑΛΗΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΩΝ ΕΞΩΘΕΝ], that is, not a neophyte, and to have a good testimony even from outsiders. The rule against ordaining novices, and the good reputation required of elders, will be discussed in dist. 48.

units.la: Sacerdotales quindecim vestes, nec vnius illas generis, formae, vel coloris, videtis, Auditores Christiani. Quibus quidem, sicut oportet, si nos ornauerimus, si nobis illas adaptauerimus, A frigoribus niuis nihil est, quod timeamus, vestiti duplicibus: vt vestiri monemur, prouerb. 31. cap. Nos haec habetes (inquam) vestimenta nuptialia possumus ad Regis nuptias intrepidi accedere. Non eiiciemur. Alioqui, extremo cum probro sumus audituri, Amice, Quomodo huc intrasti non habens vestem nuptialem? Id est, Tu qui Sacerdos & amicus meus dici vis, quo te potes ore Sacerdotem vocare? qua tu fronte nunc audes ad filij mei conuiuium venire, licet inuitatus fueris, non habens eius ordinis insigne gestamen? Suis tandem ministris dicturus est ille magnus Regu rex, Ligatis manibus & pedibus eius, mittite eum in tenebras exteriores. Ibi fletus erit, & stridor dentium. Matthei cap. 22. A nobis Deus auertat iram suam tantam.
units.tr: Christian hearers, you see fifteen priestly garments, and they are not all of one kind, shape or colour. If we adorn ourselves with them as we ought, if we fit them to ourselves, we have nothing to fear from the cold of snow, being clothed doubly, as we are urged to be clothed (Prov. 31). Having these wedding garments (I say), we can approach the king's wedding fearlessly, and we will not be cast out. Otherwise we shall hear, to our utmost shame, "Friend, how did you come in here not having a wedding garment?" That is: you who wish to be called a priest and my friend, with what mouth can you call yourself a priest? With what brow do you now dare to come to my son's banquet, though invited, not having the badge of that order? Finally that great King will say to his ministers: "Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matt. 22). May God turn his great wrath away from us.

units.la: Iam rerum series hoc in Speculo visendarum singulatim proponatur. Dominus iesus oculos nobis aperiat, vt omnia penitissime contemplari valeamus. prima sequitur.
units.tr: Now let the order of the things to be seen in this Mirror be set out one by one. May the Lord Jesus open our eyes, so that we may be able to contemplate all things most thoroughly. The first follows.

units.la: DISTIN-
units.tr: DISTINCTION

units.la: DISTINCTIO. XXV.
units.tr: DISTINCTION 25.

units.la: ἘΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΣ ἈΝΕΠΙΛΗΠΤΟΣ, ΚΑῚ ἈΝΕΓΚΛΗΤΟΣ.
units.tr: A bishop must be irreproachable and unaccused [ἘΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΣ ἈΝΕΠΙΛΗΠΤΟΣ, ΚΑῚ ἈΝΕΓΚΛΗΤΟΣ].

units.la: In Episcopo quod inesse primum Paulus præcipit, id est, ἐὰν ἦν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι. Et, ἐὰν ἦν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνέγκλητον εἶναι. Sic vertit: Oportet Episcopum irreprehensibilem esse. Et, Oportet Episcopum sine crimine esse, quod idem est, authore Hieronymo. Quum vero Diaconos ipse iubet, in bona conscientia habere mysterium fidei: His verbis (ait Chrysostomus) irreprehensibiles esse debere significat, & sine crimine, siue, nullum crimen habentes. Criminis autem nomine, quodlibet peccatum intelligitur. Hieronymus ad Oceanum, circa finem Epistolæ: Nunquam, fili Oceane. To.1.
units.tr: What Paul first commands to be in a bishop is, that is, "if anyone is to be a bishop, he must be irreproachable" [ἐὰν ἦν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι]. And, "if anyone is to be a bishop, he must be unaccused" [ἐὰν ἦν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνέγκλητον εἶναι]. Thus Jerome translates: "A bishop must be irreproachable," and "A bishop must be without crime," which is the same thing. When he orders deacons to hold the mystery of the faith in a good conscience, by these words (says Chrysostom) he signifies that they must be irreproachable, and without crime, or having no crime. By the name of crime, any sin is understood. Jerome to Oceanus, near the end of the letter: "Never, son Oceanus." Tom. 1.

units.la: Episcopus talis esse debet, ut subditis collatus, reprehensioni non sit obnoxius.
units.tr: A bishop ought to be such that, set over his subjects, he is not liable to reproach.

units.la: Omnes virtutes uno sermone comprehendit: & penè rem contra naturam exigit. Si enim omne peccatum, etiam in otioso verbo, reprehensione dignum est, quis est ille, qui absque peccato, id est, sine reprehensione versetur in hoc mundo? Sed futurus pastor Ecclesiæ talis eligitur, ad cuius comparationē rectè Grex, cæteri nominētur.
units.tr: He comprehends all virtues in one word, and demands something almost contrary to nature. For if every sin, even an idle word, deserves reproof, who is that man who lives in this world without sin, that is, without reproach? But the future minister of the Church is chosen so that, in comparison with him, the rest are rightly called the flock.

units.la: Idem Hieronymus in primum caput Epistolæ ad Titum. To. 9.
units.tr: The same Jerome on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus. Tom. 9.

units.la: Nullius debet infamia peccati laborare, quisquis ad ministerium capitur Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Whoever is taken up into the ministry of the Church ought not to labour under the infamy of any sin.

units.la: Primùm quidem, sine crimine sit Episcopus. quod alio puto verbo ad Timotheum nominari, Irreprehensibilem. Non intelligas, quòd eo tantùm tempore, quo ordinandus est, sine vllo sit crimine, quódque præteritas maculas nouâ conuersatione diluerit: sed ex eo tempore, quo in Christo renatus est, nullâ peccati conscientiâ remordeatur: Quomodo enim potest Præses Ecclesiæ auferre malum de medio eius, qui in delictum simile corruit? Aut quâ libertate peccantem corripere potest, quum tacitus ipse sibi respondeat, eadem se admisisse, quæ corripit?
units.tr: First of all, a bishop must be without crime; this is what, in the letter to Timothy, is called "irreproachable." Do not understand this to mean only that he is free of any fault at the time he is ordained, and that he has washed away his past stains by a new way of life; rather, from the time he was reborn in Christ, his conscience must not be troubled by any sin. For how can the president of the Church remove evil from its midst if he has fallen into a similar offence? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner, when he silently answers himself that he has committed the very things he rebukes?

units.la: C publicáque tantùm, quæ pro tribunali digna sint accusatione, atque damnatione, quorúmque perpetua est infamia.
units.tr: Only public crimes, which deserve accusation and condemnation before a tribunal, and whose infamy is lasting, are meant.

units.la: LXXXJ. Distinctione. Can. I.
units.tr: LXXXI. Distinction. Canon I.

units.la: Augustinus Tractatu 41. in Euangelium Ioannis. To.9.
units.tr: Augustine, Tractate 41 on the Gospel of John, Tom. 9.

units.la: Omne crimen est peccatum: sed non omne Peccatum est crimen. Ipse idem Augustinus hoc habet in cap.64. Enchiridij. To 3.
units.tr: Every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. The same Augustine has this in chapter 64 of the Enchiridion, Tom. 3.

units.la: A Postolus Paulus (quando elegit ordinandos vel Presbyteros, vel Diaconos, & quicunque ordinandus est ad Præposituram Ecclesiæ) non ait: Si quis sine peccato est (Hoc enim si diceret, omnis homo reprobaretur, nullus ordinaretur) Sed ait, Si quis sine crimine est: sicut est homicidium, adulterium, aliqua immunditia, fornicationes, furtum, fraus, sacrilegium, & cætera huiusmodi. Crimen enim est peccatum graue, accusatione & damnatione dignissimum. Ecce. Quisquis ordinandus est in Episcopū, non solùm suæ ordinationis tempore, sed etiam omni tempore post Baptisma, debet à crimine immunis esse.
