units.tr: Where there is drunkenness, there is lust, and fury, and at last death rules.

units.la: VEnter mero æstuans citò desþumat in libidines. In vino enim, Luxuria est. In Luxuria, Voluptas. In Voluptate, Impudicitia. Qui Luxuriatur, Viuens mortuus est: Ergo, Qui inebriatur, & mortuus, & sepultus est. Idem, Scribens ad Nepotianum De vita Clericorum. Tom.1.
units.tr: Wine heated by the belly soon foams over into lusts. For in wine there is luxury; in luxury, pleasure; in pleasure, impurity. He who revels is a living dead man; therefore, he who is drunk is both dead and buried. The same, writing to Nepotian, On the Life of Clerics, vol. 1.

units.la: VInolentos Sacerdotes & Apostolus damnat, & Lex vetus prohibet. Qui altario seruiunt, Vinum & Siceram non bibant. Sicera, Hebraeo sermone, omnis potio nuncupantur, quae inebriare potest. Quicquid inebriat, & statum mentis euertit, fuge similiter, Vt vinum.
units.tr: The Apostle condemns priests who are given to wine, and the Old Law forbids it. Those who serve at the altar should not drink wine or strong drink. In the Hebrew language, every drink that can make one drunk is called sicera. Whatever makes one drunk and overturns the state of the mind, flee it likewise, as you would wine.

units.la: Christi quoque virginibus, & Nonnis interdictum vini. Ad Eustochium. De custod. virgi.
units.tr: Wine is also forbidden to the virgins of Christ and to nuns. To Eustochium, On Keeping Virginity.

units.la: § Si quid in me potest esse consilij, Si experto creditur, Hoc primum moneo, Hoc obtestor: Vt sponsa Christi Vinum fugiat pro veneno. Vinum, & Adolescentia, duplex incendium voluptatis. Hæc Palea annumerant.
units.tr: § If there is any counsel in me, if I am to be believed on the basis of experience, I first advise this and beg it: that the bride of Christ should flee wine as poison. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. The Palea counts these among the things to be noted.

units.la: Item. Prosper. lib. 2. De vita contemplativa. cap. 22. Hic fuit Aquitanus a secretis Leonis Papæ. 1. circiter an. Do. 450. Augustini studiosissimus. Interfuit Concilio Calchedonensi. Et vitâ sanctissimus, & doctrinâ.
units.tr: Likewise Prosper, book 2, On the Contemplative Life, chapter 22. He was an Aquitanian, secretary to Pope Leo I, around the year of the Lord 450, a most devoted student of Augustine. He was present at the Council of Chalcedon, and most holy in life and learning.

units.la: DE vino percipiendo sanctus Apostolus certam fixit regulam, dicens: Nolite inebriari vino, in quo est Luxuria. quasi diceret: Luxuriam facit, & nutrit Vini perceptio nimia, non natura. Item. Ambrosius in sermone de Helia, & Ieiunio: qui ita incipit, Diuinum ad patrem resultat oraculum. ca. 4. & 5. Multa hic intersecta sunt, quae melius fuisset continuasse.
units.tr: Concerning the taking of wine, the holy Apostle laid down a certain rule, saying: "Do not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury." As if to say: excessive drinking of wine, not its nature, produces and nourishes luxury. Likewise Ambrose, in his sermon on Elijah and Fasting, which begins, "The divine oracle resounds to the father," chapters 4 and 5. Many things are cut short here, which would have been better continued.

units.la: In Paradiso, Abstinentia: post Paradisum, Edendi lasciuia incæpit.
units.tr: In Paradise, abstinence; after Paradise, the wantonness of eating began.

units.la: SExto die bestiæ sunt creatæ: & cum bestiis orta est edendi potestas, & usus escarum: ubi cibus cœpit, ibi finis factus est mundi. Vbi cœpit sua incrementa nescire, ibi cœperunt diuina opera circa eum feriari : quo indicio declaratum est, quòd per cibos mundus habetet imminui, per quos desiit augeri.
units.tr: On the sixth day the beasts were created; and with the beasts the power of eating and the use of foods arose. Where food began, there the end of the world was made. Where it began not to know its increase, there the divine works began to cease about it; by this sign it was declared that through foods the world was to be diminished, by which it ceased to be increased.

units.la: § Vt sciamus nouum non esse Ieiunium, Primam illic legem constituit de Ieiunio.
units.tr: § So that we may know that fasting is not new, there the first law about fasting was laid down.

units.la: § Eousque nemo prœuaricari nouerat : quum adhuc orta non esset, quæ prima est Prœuaricatio. Indictum est Ieiunium : Abstinentiæ Lex, à Domino Deo : Prœuaricatio Legis à Diabolo: Culpa per cibum : Latebra post cibum : Cognitio infirmatis in cibo : Firmitatis virtus in Ieiunio: Serpens gulæ persuadet, Dominus Ieiunare decernit. Itaque, gula à Paradiso regnantem expulit: Abstinentia ad Paradisum reuocauit errantem.
units.tr: § Until then no one had known how to transgress, since that first transgression, which is the first, had not yet arisen. Fasting was enjoined: the law of abstinence, from the Lord God; the transgression of the law, from the Devil. Fault through food; hiding after food; knowledge of weakness in food; the strength of firmness in fasting. The serpent of gluttony persuades; the Lord decrees fasting. Thus gluttony drove out the man who reigned in Paradise; abstinence called back to Paradise the one who had wandered.

units.la: Quid non Ebrietas designat?
units.tr: What does drunkenness not signify?

units.la: § In principio generis humani ignorabatur Ebrietas: primus Noé vineam plantauit, dedit naturam, sed ignorauit potentiam. Itaque, Vinum nec suo pepercit authori: Sed illius Ebrietas nobis suadet sobrietatem. Semel enim inebriatus est Noé. Vbi autem malú Ebrietatis agnouit, inuentum suum ad remedium temperauit, non effudit ad vitium. Manebat, antequam vinum inueniretur, omnibus inconcussa libertas : nemo sciebat à consorte naturæ suæ obsequia seruitutis exigere. Non esset hodie seruitus, si Ebrietas non fuisset. Obrepserat quidem iam fraternæ prælationis inuidia, manebat tamen adhuc paternæ pietatis reuerentia. Læsa est pietas, dum irridetur Ebrietas. Non illis itáque solis nocent vina, quos tentant, sed & illis amplius, quorum oculis temulenta Ebriorum membra nudantur.
units.tr: § In the beginning of the human race drunkenness was unknown: Noah was the first to plant a vineyard. He gave the nature of wine, but did not know its power. Thus wine did not spare even its own author; but Noah's drunkenness persuades us to sobriety. For Noah was made drunk only once. But when he recognised the evil of drunkenness, he tempered his discovery as a remedy and did not pour it out into vice. Before wine was discovered, unshaken freedom remained for all; no one knew how to exact the services of slavery from a companion of his own nature. There would be no slavery today if drunkenness had not existed. Indeed, envy of the brother's precedence had already crept in, yet the reverence of paternal piety still remained. Piety was harmed when drunkenness was mocked. Therefore wine harms not only those whom it tempts, but also those more, before whose eyes the drunken limbs of the intoxicated are laid bare.

units.la: § Legimus etiam quòd Patrem Loth inebriauerunt filiæ in monte, ad quem timentes incendium Sodomitarum confugerant: & habitabant in spelunca. Fuit itaque Ebrietas origo incesti: Pessimæ regeneratricis partus deterior. At, non Abraham vina in suo conuiuio ministrabat: sed immolabat Vitulum: Butyrum, & Lac etiam angelis hospitibus exhibebat. Rectè enim illic deerat materia peccati, vbi erat remissio peccatorum. Denique, annuntiauit Dominum Ioannes neque manducans panem, neque bibens vinum. Qui enim Christum annuntiat, ab omni vitiorum incentiuo præstare se debet alienum.
units.tr: We also read that the daughters made their father Lot drunk on the mountain, where they had fled for fear of the fire of the Sodomites, and that they lived in a cave. Drunkenness was therefore the origin of incest, a worse offspring than that of the most wicked mother. But Abraham did not serve wine at his table; he slaughtered a calf, and offered butter and milk to the angels who were his guests. For there was rightly no matter of sin where there was forgiveness of sins. Finally, John announced the Lord neither eating bread nor drinking wine. For whoever announces Christ ought to show himself free from every incitement to vice.

units.la: Item. Ex Concilio Agathensi, cap.41. Tum Sixtus 3. Romæ Pontificatum gerebat.
units.tr: Likewise. From the Council of Agde, chapter 41. At that time Sixtus III was presiding as pope at Rome.

units.la: Triginta diebus à communione abstinet Clericus, quem constiterit Ebrium fuisse.
units.tr: A clergyman who is shown to have been drunk abstains from communion for thirty days.

units.la: ANte omnia, Clericis vetatur Ebrietas, quæ omnium vitiorum fomes ac nutrix est. Itaque, eum quem Ebrium fuisse constiterit (vt ordo patitur) Aut triginta dierum spatio à communione submoueatur: Aut corporali subdatur supplicio. Intelligimus hinc, quàm sit turpe Clericis diffluere Luxuriâ, & delicatè ac molliter viuere: quámque sit his honestum, imò necessarium, parce, continenter, seuerè, sobriè: sed & prudenter omnibus in rebus sese gerere: prout sequitur (quod Quartum est) in Apostolico Speculo.
units.tr: First of all, drunkenness is forbidden to clergy, since it is the kindling and nurse of all vices. Therefore, the one who is shown to have been drunk (as the rule requires) is either removed from communion for a space of thirty days, or made subject to bodily punishment. From this we understand how shameful it is for clergy to dissolve in luxury and live delicately and softly, and how honourable, indeed necessary, it is for them to be sparing, continent, strict and sober, and also to conduct themselves prudently in all matters; as follows (which is the fourth point) in the Apostolic Mirror.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XXXVI.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XXXVI.

units.la: ΔΕΙ ΣΩΦΡΟΝΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ. - Idest.
units.tr: That he must be prudent [δεῖ σώφρονα εἶναι]. - That is.

units.la: Ecclesiastici, Sophronesfunto. Vox hæc vna Græca duabus illis respondet Latinis, quas interpres noster posuit, Prudentem, pudicum. Gratianus. OPORTET Ordinandum esse Prudentem.
units.tr: Ecclesiastics, let them be prudent [σώφρονες ἔστωσαν]. This one Greek word corresponds to the two Latin words that our translator used, prudentem and pudicum (prudent, modest). Gratian: It is fitting that the man to be ordained be prudent.

units.la: HOc excludit eos, qui sub nomine simplicitatis excusant stultitiam Sacerdotum: Nisi enim cerebrum sanum fuerit, omnia membra in vitio erunt.
units.tr: This excludes those who, under the name of simplicity, excuse the foolishness of priests. For, "unless the brain is sound, all the members will be diseased."

units.la: Prudens est, qui suâ intelligentiâ aliquid cognoscit, id est, Sciens & doctus. Prudens est etiam, qui res bonas atque malas, fugiendas & expetendas, agendas & omittendas intelligit. Utrumque prudentiæ genus ab Ecclesiasticis exigit Gratianus inquiens. PRVDENTEM autem Episcopum oportet intelligi, Non solùm literarum peritiâ, Verumetiam, Secularium negotiorum dispensatione. Unde in Epistola Gelasii Papæ legitur: quam superius annotauimus, distinct. 33. Est in cap. 18. illius Epistolæ.
units.tr: A prudent man is one who knows something by his own understanding, that is, one who is knowing and learned. A prudent man is also one who understands good and bad things, those to be avoided and those to be sought, those to be done and those to be left undone. Gratian demands both kinds of prudence from churchmen when he says: "A bishop must be understood to be prudent not only in his skill with letters but also in managing secular affairs." Hence it is read in the letter of Pope Gelasius, which we noted above in distinction 33, in chapter 18 of that letter.

units.la: Illiterati, & corpore vitiati non promoueantur ad Clerum.
units.tr: Those who are illiterate, and whose bodies are impaired, are not to be promoted to the clergy.

units.la: Lliteratos, aut aliquâ parte corporis imminutos nullus præsumat ad Clericatus Ordinem promouere: quia literis caret, Sacris non potest esse aptus officiis. Et vitiosum nihil prorsus offerri Deo Legalia præcepta sanxerunt.
units.tr: No one shall presume to promote to the order of the clergy anyone who is illiterate or lacking in some part of his body, because one without letters cannot be fit for sacred offices. The laws of Leviticus also decreed that nothing blemished at all should be offered to God.

units.la: Item. Sozimus Papa. Sedit unum duntaxat annum, duosque menses. A Gallis, & Hispanis, & Aphris Patribus interrogatus antea respondERAT id, quod Hesychio Salonitano Episcopo (Dalmatiæ ciuitas est) se pariter consulenti oblatos rescripsit. Inter alia, De non Ordinandis ineruditis & indoctis. Habes Epistolam, Tomo Conciliorum primo, scriptam, Honorio.12. & Theodosio Iuniore. 8. Augustis Coss. hoc est, Anno Do. 411.
units.tr: Likewise, Pope Zosimus. He sat for one year and two months only. Asked by the Gallic, Spanish and African Fathers, he had earlier answered what he wrote in reply to Hesychius, bishop of Salona (a city of Dalmatia), who consulted him in the same way. Among other things, about not ordaining the unlearned and untaught. You have the letter, in the first volume of the Councils, written in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius (for the twelfth time) and Theodosius the Younger (for the eighth), that is, in the year of the Lord 411.

units.la: Sacerdos assumatur nemo, qui non & Literis, & Ecclesiæ stipendiis antè meruerit.
units.tr: No one is to be taken up as a priest who has not first earned his place both by learning and by support from the Church.

units.la: Qui disciplinis Ecclesiasticis per ordinem non est imbutus: & tèporis approbatione, diuinis stipendiis non est eruditus: nequaquam ad summum Ecclesiæ Sacerdotium aspirare præsumat. Et non solùm in eo Ambitio inefficax habeatur, verumetiam Ordinatores eius careant eo ordine, quem contra præcepta Patrum crediderunt præsumendum. Ecce (inquit Gratianus) quòd Sacrarum literarum oportet Episcopum habere peritiam. Unde
units.tr: Whoever has not been instructed in the church disciplines in due order, and has not been trained by the approval of time and by divine provision, must not presume to aspire to the highest priesthood of the Church. Not only is ambition in that matter held to be ineffective, but also those who ordain him are deprived of that order, which they believed they could presume to confer contrary to the precepts of the Fathers. Behold (says Gratian) that a bishop ought to have skill in the sacred letters. Hence

units.la: Antè discas, quàm doceas.
units.tr: Learn before you teach.

units.la: N veteri testamento, inter cætera ornamenta, Pontifex Rationale ferebat in pectore, in quo scribebatur† Manifestatio & Veritas: quia in pectore Pontificis manifesta debet esse cognitio veritatis. Hinc etiam Vectes, quibus Arca portabatur, iugiter annulis erant inserti: vt quum Arca esset portanda, nulla esset, vel fieret mora de intromittendis vectibus: quia Prædicatores, per quos Ecclesia circumfertur, Sacris literis semper debent insistere: ne tunc quærant discere, quum ex officio alios debeant docere. Hinc etiam, Dauid prius ex gratia Spiritus Sancti, donū Scientiæ percepit:& postea administrationem regni assecutus est. Salomon quoque non diuitias, non longa tempora huius vitæ, sed Sapientiam à Deo expetiit, & impetrauit. Hinc etiam Dominus prius posuit verba sua in ore Prophetæ: & postea constituit eum super gentes & regna, dicens ad Hieremiā: Ecce dedi verba mea in ore tuo: ecce constitui te super gentes & regna. Hinc etiam, Malachias: Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt Scientiam, & Legem exquirunt de ore eius: quia angelus Domini exercituum est. Hinc etiam, Idem Saluator noster prius in medio Doctorum sedit audiens illos & interrogans: & postea prædicare cœpit. quia prius quisque discere,& postea prædicandi officium vsurpare debet. Hinc etiam, Salomon ait prius, Tempus tacendi: & postea, Tempus loquendi. quia Veritas, prius tacendo, discitur, & postea loquendo, prædicatur. Hinc idē Dominus ait: Qui audit, dicat, Veni. Hinc etiam, Prius Apostolos docuit: deinde eos ad prædicandum misit, dicens: Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices sicut columbæ. Sic etiam post resurrectionem, Prius illis sensum aperuit, & scripturas explanauit, & postea dixit eis_ Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate.
units.tr: In the Old Testament, among other adornments, the high priest bore a breastplate on his chest, on which was written "Manifestation and Truth", because the knowledge of truth ought to be manifest in the breast of the high priest. Hence also the poles by which the ark was carried were always inserted in its rings, so that when the ark was to be carried there would be no delay in putting the poles in place; for preachers, through whom the Church is carried about, must always devote themselves to the sacred letters, so that they do not then seek to learn when they ought, by their office, to be teaching others. Hence also David first received, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the gift of knowledge, and afterwards obtained the government of the kingdom. Solomon too did not ask God for riches or a long span of this life, but for wisdom, and obtained it. Hence also the Lord first put his words into the mouth of the prophet, and afterwards set him over nations and kingdoms, saying to Jeremiah: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms." Hence also Malachi: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts." Hence also our Saviour himself first sat in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them, and afterwards began to preach, because each man ought first to learn and afterwards take up the office of preaching. Hence also Solomon says first, "A time to keep silence," and afterwards, "A time to speak," because truth is first learned by keeping silent and afterwards is proclaimed by speaking. Hence the same Lord says, "Let him who hears say, Come." Hence also he first taught the apostles and then sent them to preach, saying: "Be wise as serpents, and simple as doves." So also after the resurrection he first opened their understanding and explained the Scriptures, and afterwards said to them, "Go into all the world and preach."

units.la: Unde, Quum de quinque panibus quinque milia hominum vellet reficere, Prius panes accipiens fregit: & postea, Discipulis dedit: & per eos demum turbis appossuit: quia Sacramenta legis & Prophetarum prius differendo exposuit, & postea eorum Scientia discipulis dedit: & per eos tandem illa fidelibus dispensauit. Hinc Petrus etiam cum rectoribus Ecclesiæ scriberet, ait: Parati esse debetis reddere rationem omni poscenti vos satisfactionem de ea fide & spe, quæ in vobis est. Hinc etiam Paulus scribens ad Timotheum, ait: Attende lectioni, & exhortationi, & doctrinæ. E X quibus omnibus liquidò colligitur, quòd non sufficit prælatis bona conuersatio, & morum honestas, nisi addatur Scientia doctrinæ.
units.tr: Hence also, when he wanted to feed five thousand men with five loaves, he first took the loaves and broke them, and afterwards gave them to the disciples, and through them at last set them before the crowds; because he first set forth the sacraments of the law and the prophets by delaying, and afterwards gave their meaning to the disciples, and through them at last dispensed those things to the faithful. Hence also Peter, writing to the rulers of the Church, says: "You must be ready always to give an account to everyone who asks you for a reason for the faith and hope that is in you." Hence also Paul, writing to Timothy, says: "Give attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching." From all these things it is clearly gathered that good conduct and moral integrity are not enough for prelates, unless knowledge of doctrine is added.

units.la: Gratianus. E X quibus omnibus liquidò colligitur, quòd non sufficit prælatis bona conuersatio, & morum honestas, nisi addatur Scientia doctrinæ.
units.tr: Gratian: From all these things it is clearly gathered that good conduct and moral integrity are not enough for prelates, unless knowledge of doctrine is added.

units.la: § Unde, Sacerdotes ingressuri templum tabernaculi, Prius lauabantur in labio æneo, quod fecerat Moyses ex speculis mulierum. Hinc etiam, In Canticis Canticorum, Oculi (per quos Prælati Ecclesiæ intelliguntur) assimilantur columbis, quæ residet iuxta fluenta plenissima.
units.tr: § Hence also, the priests about to enter the tabernacle first washed in the bronze laver which Moses had made from the mirrors of women. Hence also, in the Song of Songs, the eyes (by which the prelates of the Church are understood) are compared to doves, which sit beside the most full streams.

units.la: Hinc etiam, Hieronymus in Leuiticum. Origenis in Genesin, in Exodum, in Leuiticum, in Numeros, homilias quas Latinè versas, Gennadius Ruffino tribuit, Hieronymo, Gratianus, & alij multi perperam tribuerunt: Hieronymíque nomine citárunt, vt hic videmus, quod habetur in homilia sexta fine. Leuiti. octauo cap. Clarus erat Origenes anno Do. 200. Si cui vacaret Apostoporum regiorum, canibus & Damis auferre, quod edendo Græcè (quando non vacant intelligendo) conferret Origeni, nomen hic apud studiosos iam fortasse mererétur Episcopi.
units.tr: Hence also Jerome on Leviticus. The homilies of Origen on Genesis, on Exodus, on Leviticus, and on Numbers, which were translated into Latin, Gennadius attributes to Rufinus; Gratian and many others wrongly attribute them to Jerome, and cite them under Jerome's name, as we see here, in the sixth homily at the end of Leviticus, chapter 8. Origen was famous in the year of the Lord 200. If anyone had leisure, he might take from the dogs and the deer of the royal hunt what he could read in Greek (when they are not busy with understanding), and compare it with Origen; perhaps he would already earn, here among scholars, the name of bishop.

units.la: Sacerdotis est scientiam Legis habere: neque Bellis, sed Orationibus vacare.
units.tr: It is the duty of a priest to have knowledge of the law, and to be occupied not with wars but with prayers.

units.la: S I quis vult Pontifex esse, non tam vocabulo, quàm merito, imitetur Moysen, imitetur Aaron. quid enim dicitur de eis? quòd non discedüt de tabernaculo Domini: erat ergo Moyses indesinenter in tabernaculo Domini. Quid autem ei opus erat? Vt, aut à Deo aliquid disceret: L aut ipse populum doceret. Hæc duo sunt Pontificis opera, ut, aut à Deo discat (legêdo scripturas diuinas, & sæpiùs meditando). Aut populum doceat. Sed illa doceat, quæ à Deo ipse didicerit, non ex proprio corde, vel humano sensu, sed quæ Spiritus sanctus docet. Est & aliud opus quod fecit Moyses: ad bella non vadit, non pugnat contra inimicos. Sed quid facit? Orat: & donec orat, vincit populus eius: si relaxauerit & demiserit manus, Populus eius vincitur & fugatur. Oret ergo Sacerdos Ecclesiæ indefinenter, ut vincat populus, qui sub ipso est, hostes invisibiles Amalechitas: qui sunt Dæmones impugnantes eos, qui volunt piè viuere in Christo. Episcopus igitur, & omnis Sacerdos Sacri diuinique Iuris esse debet, ac esse iubetur, prudens. Hoc indubitatum relinquitur. Atqui, Fas ne est? Licet ne disciplinas alias (quæ tam multæ sunt, & viles pleræque proximis) addiscere? Supervacanea nostris Apostolis disputatio: quæ tamen hic proponitur. Neoptolemi nescio cuius Ennliani responsio mihi perplacet hac in re.
units.tr: If anyone wishes to be a high priest, let him imitate Moses and Aaron, not so much in name as in merit. For what is said of them? That they did not depart from the tabernacle of the Lord; Moses was therefore continually in the tabernacle of the Lord. But what need had he of it? That either he might learn something from God, or he himself might teach the people. These two are the works of a high priest: that he either learn from God (by reading the divine Scriptures and meditating on them more often), or teach the people. But let him teach those things which he himself has learned from God, not from his own heart or human sense, but what the Holy Spirit teaches. There is also another work that Moses did: he did not go out to war, he did not fight against enemies. But what did he do? He prayed; and as long as he prayed, his people conquered; if he relaxed and let down his hands, his people were conquered and put to flight. Therefore let the priest of the Church pray without ceasing, that the people who are under him may conquer the invisible enemies, the Amalekites, who are the demons attacking those who wish to live piously in Christ. Therefore a bishop, and every priest of sacred and divine law, ought to be, and is commanded to be, prudent. This is left as beyond doubt. But is it lawful? Is it permitted to learn other disciplines as well (which are many, and for the most part worthless to our apostles)? The discussion is superfluous for us, yet it is put forward here. The reply of a certain Neoptolemus of Ennius pleases me greatly on this point.

units.la: Philosophandum est paucis. Nam, Omnino: haud placet. Sic etiam Grammaticandum, Dialecticaudum, Rhetoricandum puto. Sed in hanc, & in illam modò partem, prius more suo esse volentem Gratianum videamus.
units.tr: One should philosophize only a little. For to do so altogether is not pleasing. So too, I think, one should practise grammar, dialectic and rhetoric. But let us see how Gratian, who wishes to proceed in his own manner first, goes this way or that.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XXXVII.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XXXVII.

units.la: Gratianus. SED quæritur, An secularibus literis oporteat eos esse eruditos. De his ita scribitur in Concilio Carthaginensi quarto. cap. 16. Quum supra de Diaconis loqueremur, huius e Concilij nequaquam Græcè versi meminimus.
units.tr: Gratian. But it is asked whether they ought to be learned in secular letters. Concerning these things it is written thus in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chap. 16: "Since we spoke above of deacons, we have recalled this council, which was in no way translated from Greek."

units.la: Hæreticos diligenter, Ethnicos verò libros non legat Episcopus.
units.tr: A bishop should read heretical books carefully, but should not read pagan books.

units.la: E Piscopus gentilium libros non legat: Hæreticorum autem perlegat, pro necessitate, aut tempore. Item. Hieronymus ad Damasum Papam, De filio Prodigo, & frugi. Epist. Beauturdinis tuæ. In Lucæ cap. 17. To.3.
units.tr: A bishop should not read pagan books, but he may read through heretical books as necessity or time requires. Likewise Jerome to Pope Damasus, on the Prodigal Son and the thrifty one, the letter Beatitudini tuae, on Luke chap. 17, vol. 3.

units.la: Reprehenduntur Sacerdotes qui omissis Euangeliis comœdias legunt.
units.tr: Priests are rebuked who, leaving aside the Gospels, read comedies.

units.la: S Acerdotes Dei, omissis Euangeliis & Prophetis, videmus Comœdias legere: amatoria Bucolicorum versuum verba cātare: tenere Virgiliū: Et, quod in pueris necessitatis est, crimen in se facere voluptatis.
units.tr: Priests of God, leaving aside the Gospels and the Prophets, we see reading comedies; singing the words of the amatory verses of the Bucolics, keeping Virgil, and making a crime of pleasure out of what is only a necessity in boys.

units.la: Vani sensu, obscuri mente sunt, qui secularibus, aut disciplinis, aut negociis occupantur.
units.tr: They are vain in sense and obscure in mind who are occupied with secular things, or with disciplines, or with business.

units.la: NOnne vobis videtur in vanitate sensus, & obscuritate mentis ingredi, qui diebus ac noctibus in Dialectica arte torquetur? qui Physicus perscrutator oculos trans cœlum leuat? & ultra profundum terrarum, & abyssi, quoddam inane demergit? qui lambum struit? qui tantam metrorum syluā in suo studiosus corde distinguit & cogerit?
units.tr: Does it not seem to you that they enter into vanity of sense and darkness of mind, who are racked day and night in the art of dialectic? who, as natural philosophers, lift their eyes beyond the heavens, and plunge down beyond the depths of the earth and of the abyss into some empty void? who construct the lambda? who, eager in heart, distinguish and gather such a forest of metres?

units.la: Hieronymus haec explicans Apostoli verba d. cap. 4. Contestor in Domino, Vt non ampliùs ambuletis, sicut & gentes ambulant, in vanitate sensus sui obscurati mente, sic, ait.
units.tr: Jerome, explaining the words of the Apostle in chap. 4: "I testify in the Lord that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their sense, with their mind darkened," thus he says.

units.la: VAnitas sensus, & mentis obscuritas bifariam diuiditur: In Seculi huius negocia, & in Sapientiam seculare: quando, aut in his, quae mūdi huius sunt, & citò transeunt detinemur: Aut non profutura cognoscimus.
units.tr: The vanity of sense and the darkness of mind are divided in two ways: into the affairs of this age, and into secular wisdom; that is, when we are held by those things which belong to this world and pass quickly away, or when we learn things that will not profit us.

units.la: § Et (vt ad alteram partem transeam) Qui diuitias per fas & nefas quærit? qui adulatur Regibus? hæreditates captat alienas? & opes cögregat, quas in momento, cui sit relicturus, ignorat?
units.tr: § And (to pass to the other part): who seeks riches by fair means and foul? who flatters kings? who hunts after other men's inheritances? and gathers wealth which, in a moment, he does not know to whom he will leave?

units.la: Sacerdos & Propheta nescierunt: Præ Ebrietate absorpti sunt à Vino: Erraverunt in Ebrietate. To. 5.
units.tr: The priest and the prophet have not known; they were swallowed up by wine, they erred in drink. Vol. 5.

units.la: Sacra scriptura nominatur Vinum. Reliquæ disciplinæ sunt, vt Sicera. Quibus quisquis abutitur, vt Ebrius Vino, vel Sicerā damnatur.
units.tr: Holy Scripture is called wine. The other disciplines are like sicera (strong drink). Whoever abuses them, like a drunkard with wine or with sicera, is condemned.

units.la: VIno inebriantur, quando scripturas Sacras male intelligunt, atque peruertūt: Sicerā quando abutuntur seculari Sapientiā; & Dialecticorum tendiculis: Quæ non tam vincula sunt appellanda, quàm φάσματα, id est vmbræ quædam & imagines, quæ cito petunt & soluuntur.
units.tr: They are made drunk with wine when they misunderstand and pervert the Holy Scriptures; they abuse sicera when they abuse secular wisdom and the snares of the dialecticians. These are to be called not so much chains as phantasms [φάσματα], that is, certain shadows and images, which quickly vanish and dissolve.

units.la: Idem In illud Hieremiæ, Non vos seducant Prophetæ vestri, & diuini vestri.cap.29.eodem To.
units.tr: The same, on that passage of Jeremiah, "Let not your prophets and your diviners deceive you," chap. 29, in the same volume.

units.la: Scripturæ falsus interpres, ψευδοπροφήτης est. Ac μάρτυς est, qui non ex eadem, prædicit futura.
units.tr: A false interpreter of Scripture is a false prophet [ψευδοπροφήτης]. And he is a diviner [μάντις] who foretells the future not from the same source.

units.la: § Secundum Tropologiam: Pseudoprophetas, eos debemus accipere, qui aliter scripturarum verba accipiunt, quàm Spiritus Sanctus sonat: & Diuinos, eos qui coniecturam mentis suæ, & incerta futurorum, quasi vera, pronuntiant, absque diuinorum authoritate verborum.
units.tr: § According to the tropological sense: we ought to understand by false prophets those who take the words of Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit sounds them; and by diviners those who pronounce the guesses of their own minds and uncertain matters of the future as if they were true, without the authority of the divine words.

units.la: Idem. Hieremiæ vaticinium interpretans—
units.tr: The same, interpreting the prophecy of Jeremiah:

units.la: Vuæ comestores acerbæ sunt Hæretici.
units.tr: The eaters of sour grapes are heretics.

units.la: QVicunque scripturas non ita intelligit, vt rei veritas habet, Vuam acerbam comedit. Vnde, Omnes Hæretici peruersa credentes, Panem de cælo descendentem comedere non possunt: sed obstupescüt dentes eorum: Non ciborum austeritate, sed vitio dentium. Idem. De Paulina illa Patribus erga filios mandata ʋʋʋʋ loquens, vbi iubet Apostolus: Patres, Educate filios vestros in disciplina, & conuersatione Domini.ad Ephes.cap.6.rursus ait.
units.tr: Whoever does not understand the Scriptures as the truth of the matter has them, eats sour grapes. Hence, all heretics, believing perverse things, cannot eat the bread that comes down from heaven; but their teeth are set on edge, not by the harshness of the food, but by the defect of their teeth. The same, speaking of the command given by Paul to fathers concerning their children, where the Apostle orders: "Fathers, bring up your children in the discipline and admonition of the Lord," Eph. chap. 6, he says again.

units.la: Ecclesiasticæ pecuniæ non sunt in poëtarum studiis impendendæ.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical money is not to be spent on the studies of poets.

units.la: LEgant Episcopi, atque Presbyteri, qui filios suos secularibus eruditunt literis, & faciunt Comœdias legere, & Mimorum turpia scripta cantare, de Ecclesiasticis sumptibus forsitan eruditos. Et quod in Corbonam pro peccato virgo vel vidua, vel substantiam suam totam effundens quilibet pauper obtulerat: hoc Orator & Grammaticus in Calendarum strenam, & Saturnalium sportulam, & Minerualemunus, aut in sumptus domesticos, sticos, aut in templi stipes, aut in sordida scorta conuertit. Heli Sacerdos ipse sanctus fuit: sed quia filios suos non erudiuit in omni disciplina & correctione, supinus cecidit, & mortuus est. Item. Ex responsalibus Adriani Papæ, ad Carolum. cap. 4. Baisius ita lectum notat. & nō, ex responsalibus Vibani. Verámque puto Baisii lectionem. Fuit u Adrianus primus, anno Christi 780 qui Carolo Magno, quem sacrarat Imperatorem, talia rescripsit. Hoc inquā, mihi verisimile est. Nam videri voluit ille Rex argutator sciolus: Cuius etiam de Rhetorica disceptationes cum suo magistro Alcuino leguntur. Prouidus autem Pontifex nolebat Academias, quas tunc Rex instituebat, nimium Dialecticari. Sed παλαια. Sunt Adriani ad Carolum alia quædam scripta in Ionus Pannomis.
units.tr: Let bishops and presbyters read this, who educate their sons in secular letters and make them read comedies and sing the shameful writings of the mimes, perhaps educated at the expense of the Church. And what any poor man, a virgin or a widow, or anyone pouring out their whole substance, had offered into the Corbona for sin, this orator and grammarian turns into New Year's gifts, Saturnalia baskets and gifts for Minerva, or into domestic expenses, or into the offerings of the temple, or into filthy prostitutes. Eli the priest himself was holy, but because he did not train his sons in all discipline and correction, he fell backwards and died. Likewise, from the responses of Pope Hadrian to Charles, chap. 4. Baisius notes that it is read thus, and not "from the responses of Vibanus." I think Baisius's reading is the true one. Hadrian I, in the year of Christ 780, wrote such things in reply to Charles the Great, whom he had consecrated emperor. Yes, I say this seems probable, for that king wished to be seen as a quibbling smatterer, whose disputations on rhetoric with his master Alcuin are also read. The prudent pontiff, however, did not want the academies which the king was then founding to dialecticise too much. But these are old things [παλαια]. There are certain other writings of Hadrian to Charles in Ivo's Panormia.

units.la: Non bene dialecticis argutiis conuenit cum fidei simplicitate.
units.tr: Dialectical subtleties do not well agree with the simplicity of faith.

units.la: OMnem vim inuentorum suorum in Dialectica disputatione ponunt Hæretici: Quæ, Philosophorum sententiâ, diffinitur, Non astruendi vim habere, sed studium destruendi: sed non in Dialectica placuit Deo salvare populum suum: Regnum enim Dei in simplicitate fidei est, non in contentione sermonis.
units.tr: Heretics put all the force of their inventions into dialectical disputation, which, by the opinion of the philosophers, is defined as having not the power of establishing but the zeal of destroying. But it did not please God to save his people by dialectic; for the kingdom of God is in the simplicity of faith, not in contention of words.

units.la: Item Rabanus, De præsutis Ecclesiasticis. Rabanus, cognomento Maurus, natione Teutonicus, Episcopus Moguntinus, Caroli Magni, eiúsque filij Ludouici tempore vixit, anno Do. 800. Multa scripsit, ex Augustino ferè compilans & transcribens omnia, ne immutatis quidem verbis. Inter hominis y lurima scripta, Trithemius non recenset opus, De præsuris Ecclesiasticis, à Gratiano post Ionem, ut. Qui libri sint ab Ecclesia recepti, Pannomiæ libro 1. nunc adductum. Quod hic tamen refertur, Hieronymus sibi conuigisse narrat in Epistola ad Eustochium. De custodia virginitatis. To.1.
units.tr: Also Rabanus, On the Ecclesiastical Prelates. Rabanus, surnamed Maurus, a German by birth, bishop of Mainz, lived in the time of Charles the Great and of his son Louis, in the year 800. He wrote many things, compiling and copying almost everything from Augustine, without even changing the words. Among this man's very many writings, Trithemius does not list the work On the Ecclesiastical Prelates, which Gratian cites after Ivo, as received by the Church, in book 1 of the Panormia, now brought forward. What is referred to here, however, Jerome relates as having happened to himself, in his letter to Eustochium, On the Keeping of Virginity, vol. 1.

units.la: Senex est virgâ dignus, qui Rhetorum floículis legendis repuerascit.
units.tr: An old man is worthy of the rod who, by reading the little flowers of the rhetoricians, becomes a boy again.

units.la: LEgimus de beato Hieronymo, quòd quum libros lege- ret Ciceronis, ab angelo est correptus: eò quòd vir Chri- stianus Paganorum figmentis intenderet. Gratianus adhuc in pr- ædictorum confirmationem duo profert. Ex Hieronymo, prius. de quo nos in Can. 1. superius. Ex Origene, secundum.
units.tr: We read of blessed Jerome that, while he was reading the books of Cicero, he was rebuked by an angel, because a Christian man was giving his attention to the fictions of the pagans. Gratian adds two further authorities in confirmation of the above. The first is from Jerome, whom we mentioned above in Can. 1. The second is from Origen.

units.la: Siliquæ sunt, Carmina Poëtarum, Secularis Sapientia, & Rhetoricorum Pompa verborum.
units.tr: Siliquae are the songs of the poets, secular wisdom, and the show of rhetorical words.

units.la: HInc Filius ille prodigus in Euangelio reprehenditur, qui de siliquis, quas porci manducabant, ventrem
units.tr: Hence that prodigal son in the Gospel is rebuked, who wished to fill his belly with the husks that the swine were eating.

units.la: suum replere cupiebat. Hinc etiam, Origenes, Ciniphes & Ranas, quibus Ægyptü sunt percusi, vanam Dialecticorum garrulitatem, & sophistica argumeta intelligit.
units.tr: Hence also Origen understands the gnats and frogs, with which the Egyptians were struck, to be the empty chatter of the dialecticians and sophistical arguments.

units.la: Sed hic præstat ipsius Origenis verba, prout à Ruffino versa sunt, adscribere, ex Homilia quarta in Exodum.
units.tr: But here it is worth setting out Origen's own words, as Rufinus translated them, from his fourth homily on Exodus.

units.la: Poëtæ sunt Ranæ: Dialectici verò Scnipes. Deus nos conseruet à plagis istis.
units.tr: The poets are the frogs; the dialecticians are the gnats. May God preserve us from these plagues.

units.la: PEr secundam plagam, in qua Ranæ producuntur, indicari figuraliter arbitror, Carmina Poëtarum: qui inani quadam & inflatâ modulatione, velut Ranarum sonis & cantibus, huic mundo deceptionis fabulas intulerunt. Ad nihil enim aliud, Animal vtile est, nisi quòd sonum vocis improbis & importunis clamoribus reddit.
units.tr: In the second plague, in which frogs are brought forth, I think the songs of the poets are figuratively indicated: who, with a certain empty and inflated modulation, as with the sounds and croaking of frogs, have brought deceptive fables into this world. For that animal is useful for nothing else except that it makes a sound with wicked and troublesome clamours.

units.la: Post hoc, σκνίφες producûtur. Hoc animal pennis quidem suspenditur, per aëra volitans: sed ita subtile & minutum, vt oculi visum, nisi acutè cernentis, effugiat: corpus tamen quum insederit, acerrimo terebrat stimulo: Ita, vt quem volitantem videre quis non valeat, stimulantem sentiat. Hoc ergo animalis genus dignissimè puto arti Dialecticæ comparari: quæ minutis & subtilibus verborum stimulis animas terebrat, ac tantâ calliditate circunuenit: vt deceptus nec videat, nec intelligat, vnde decipitur. Hæc Origenes. De duabus illis plagis habet Exo. cap. 8. Post hæc, Gratianus ait.
units.tr: After this, the gnats [σκνίφες] are brought forth. This creature hangs in the air on wings, flying about, but it is so fine and small that it escapes the eye unless one looks very sharply; yet when it has settled on the body, it pierces with a very sharp sting, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging. I think therefore this kind of creature is most fittingly compared to the art of dialectic, which pierces souls with minute and subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such cunning that the one deceived neither sees nor understands by what he is deceived. Thus Origen. He has these two plagues in Exodus, chapter 8. After this, Gratian says.

units.la: Gratianus. E X his omnibus colligitur, Quòd non est ab Ecclesiasticis Secularium literarum quærenda peritia. Iam sequitur pars oppositum firmans. Sed(ait Gratianus) econtrario legitur.
units.tr: Gratian. From all these things it is gathered that the knowledge of secular letters is not to be sought from churchmen. Now he follows with the part that confirms the opposite. But (says Gratian) on the contrary it is read

units.la: NEC ab Ethnicorum libris Christiani, nec à Prophanis literis homines Sacri sunt omnino prohibendi.
units.tr: Neither are Christians to be entirely forbidden the books of the heathens, nor holy men the profane letters.

units.la: MOyses, & Daniel omni Scientia Ægyptiorum & Chaldæorum eruditi fuerunt. Legitur etiam, Quod
units.tr: Moses and Daniel were learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and Chaldeans. It is also read that

units.la: Quòd præcepit Dominus filiis Israël, ut expoliarẽt Ægyptios auro & argento: moraliter instruens, ut sive aurum sapientiæ, sive argentum eloquentiæ apud Poëtas inveniremus: in usum salutiferæ eruditionis vertamus. In Leuitico etiam, Primitias mellis, id est, dulcedinem humanæ eloquentiæ, Domino iubemur offerre. Magi quoque tria munera obtulerunt: In quibus nonnulli tres partes Philosophiæ volunt intelligi. Denique, In expositione Psalterij Cassiodorus. cap. 15. prologi in Psalterium testatur.
units.tr: The Lord commanded the sons of Israel to despoil the Egyptians of gold and silver, teaching morally that, whether we find gold of wisdom or silver of eloquence among the poets, we should turn it to the use of saving learning. In Leviticus too we are commanded to offer to the Lord the firstfruits of honey, that is, the sweetness of human eloquence. The Magi also offered three gifts, in which some want three parts of philosophy to be understood. Finally, Cassiodorus testifies in his exposition of the Psalter, in the prologue to the Psalms, chapter 15.

units.la: OMnis splendor Rhetoricæ eloquentiæ, omnis modus Poëticæ locutionis, qualibet varietas decoræ pronunciationis, à divinis scripturis sumpsit exordium. Hinc etiam Ambrosius, ait, super Epistolam Colossensiū, cap. 2. Exponens illud In Christo sunt omnes thesauri Sapientiæ, & Scientiæ absconditi.
units.tr: Every splendour of rhetorical eloquence, every mode of poetic speech, every variety of graceful expression, took its beginning from the divine Scriptures. Hence also Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2, expounding that "In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," says:

units.la: Deus omnium Scientiarum, Dominus est. 1 Reg. cap. 2.
units.tr: The Lord is the God of all knowledge. 1 Reg. chapter 2.

units.la: OMnis ratio superna Scientia, Vel terrena creaturæ, in eo est, qui est caput earum & author: ut qui hunc novit, nihil ultra quærat: quia hic est perfecta virtus, & Sapientia: quicquid alibi quæritur, hic perfectè inuenitur. In Daniele, & in Salomone ostendit infidelibus se esse authorem totius eloquentiæ, & Sapientiæ: Quod infideles non putant, quia non legunt in Euangeliis & Prophetiis Astrologiam, vel Geometriam, & alia huiusmodi: quæ despecta sunt à nostris, quia non pertinent ad salutem, sed magis in errorem mittunt, & avocant à Deo: Dúmque his studen disputationibus, animæ suæ curam non habent. Qui verò Christum novit, thesaurum Sapientiæ & Scientiæ invenit: quia id novit, quod utile est. Hinc etiam ait Beda in lib.2. Regum, Sumpsit & hoc ex Pannomia Gratianus. In Tit.nunc allegato. Nec enim talès Bedæ libros habe nus.
units.tr: Every higher reason of knowledge, and every earthly knowledge of creatures, lies in him who is their head and author, so that whoever knows him seeks nothing further; for he is perfect virtue and wisdom; whatever is sought elsewhere is perfectly found here. In Daniel and in Solomon he shows unbelievers that he is the author of all eloquence and wisdom. Unbelievers do not think so, because they do not read in the Gospels and Prophets about astrology, or geometry, and other things of this kind, which are despised by our people because they do not pertain to salvation, but rather lead into error and call away from God; and while they devote themselves to these disputations they have no care for their souls. But he who knows Christ finds the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, because he knows what is useful. Hence also Bede says in the second book of Kings, Gratian took this too from the Pannormia, in the title just cited. For we do not have such books of Bede.

units.la: TVrbat acumen legentium, & deficere cogit, qui eos à legendis Secularibus libris, omnibus modis, existimat prohibendos: in quibus si qua inventa sunt utilia, quasi sua sumere licet. Alioquin Moyses & Daniel Sapientiâ & literis Ægyptiorum, Chaldæorúmque non paterentur se erudiri: quorum tamen superstitiones simul & delicias horrebant. Nec etiam ipse magister Gentium aliquot versus Poëtarum, suis vel scripturis vel dictus indidisset. Gratianus discordantes istos Canones ad concordiam sic redigit. Interrogans primo. Cur ergo legi prohibentur, quæ tam rationabiliter legêda probantur? Idem respondet.
units.tr: It disturbs the keenness of readers and compels them to faint, when someone thinks they should be forbidden by every means to read secular books; in which, if anything useful is found, it is permitted to take it as one's own. Otherwise Moses and Daniel would not have allowed themselves to be instructed in the wisdom and letters of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, though they abhorred their superstitions and delights alike. Nor would the teacher of the Gentiles himself have inserted some verses of the poets, either in his writings or in his speech. Gratian brings these discordant canons back to concord thus, first asking: Why then are those things forbidden to be read which are proved to be rightly readable? He answers the same.

units.la: Seculares literas, quidam legunt ad voluptatem, Poëtarum figmentis, verborúmque ornatu delectati: quidam vero, ad eruditionem eas addiscunt, ut errores Gentilium legendo detestentur: & vtilia quæ in eis inveniunt, ad vsum Sacræ eruditionis devoti vertant. tales laudabiliter Seculares literas addiscūt. Vnde beatus Gregorius quendam Episcopum non reprehendit, quia eas didicerat: sed quia, contra Episcopale officium, pro lectione Euangelica, Grammaticam populo exponebat. Gregorius Desiderio Episcopo Galliæ. Epist. 48. lib. 9.
units.tr: Some read secular letters for pleasure, delighted by the fictions of the poets and the ornament of words; but some learn them for instruction, so that by reading them they may detest the errors of the Gentiles, and devoutly turn whatever useful things they find in them to the use of sacred learning. Such people learn secular letters commendably. Hence blessed Gregory did not rebuke a certain bishop because he had learned them, but because, contrary to the episcopal office, he was expounding grammar to the people in place of the Gospel reading. Gregory to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, Ep. 48, book 9.

units.la: Execrabile est Sacerdoti, nugis ac sæcularibus literis detineri, blasphemisque nephandorum laudibus maculari.
units.tr: It is abominable for a priest to be occupied with trifles and secular letters, and to be defiled by the blasphemous praises of wicked men.

units.la: QVum multa nobis bona de vestris fuissent studiis nuntiata, ita cordi nostro nata est lætitia, ut negare ea, quæ sibi fraternitas vestra concedenda popposcerat, minimè valeremus. Sed post hoc, pervenit ad nos (quod sine verecundia memorare non possumus) fraternitatem tuam, Grammaticam quibusdam exponere. Quam rem ita molestè suscepimus, ac sumus vehementius aspernati, ut ea, quæ prius dicta fuerunt, in gemitum & tristitiam vertemus: quia, in uno se ore, cum Iouis laudibus, Christi laudes non capiunt. Et quàm graue nefandùmq; sit Episcopis canere, quod nec Laico religioso conueniat, ipse consídera. Hinc etiam Ambrosius scribit super Lucam, Explanans proœmium: In principio proœmij.
units.tr: When many good things had been reported to us about your studies, such joy was born in our heart that we could by no means refuse those things which your brotherhood had asked to be granted. But afterwards there came to us (and we cannot mention it without shame) that your brotherhood was expounding grammar to certain people. We took this matter so badly, and spurned it so vehemently, that what was said before has turned into groaning and sadness, because the praises of Christ cannot be held together with the praises of Jupiter in one mouth. And consider for yourself how grave and wicked it is for bishops to sing what does not even suit a religious layman. Hence also Ambrose writes on Luke, expounding the proem: In the beginning of the proem.

units.la: Scculares litera legenda sic sunt, ne releg entur.
units.tr: Secular letters are to be read in such a way that they are not reread.

units.la: LEgimus aliqua, † ne legantur. Legimus, ne ignoremus. Legimus, non vt teneamus, sed vt repudiemus. Item. Hieronymus super primum cap. Epistolæ ad Titum. In salutationis exordio. Gratianus Hieronymo non debuit addere quicquam: sed integram transscribere sententiam Doctoris, qui sequentia declarans Apostoli verba——Secundum cognitionem veritatis, quæ est iuxta pietatem. quærit, Vtrum nam sit aliqua veritas, quæ non sit in pietate posita? Et ait——
units.tr: We read some things, yet they are not to be read. We read so that we may not be ignorant. We read not that we may hold, but that we may reject. Likewise, Jerome on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus, at the opening of the salutation. Gratian ought not to have added anything to Jerome, but to have transcribed the whole sentence of the Doctor, who, explaining what follows the Apostle's words, "according to the knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness," asks whether there is any truth that is not set in godliness, and says:

units.la: EST planè veritas, quæ non habet pietatem. Veluti, si quis artem nouerit Grammaticam, vel Dialecticam, vt rectè loquendi rationem habeat: & inter falsa & vera diiudicet. Geometria, & Arithmetica, & Musica habent in sua Scientia veritatem: sed non est Scietia illa, Scientia pietatis. Scientia pietatis est nosse Legem, intelligere Prophetas, Euangelio credere, Apostolos non ignorare.
units.tr: There is indeed a truth that does not have godliness, for example, if someone knows the art of grammar or dialectic, so as to have the reasoned method of speaking correctly and to distinguish false from true. Geometry, arithmetic and music have truth in their knowledge, but that knowledge is not the knowledge of godliness. The knowledge of godliness is to know the Law, to understand the Prophets, to believe the Gospel, and not to be ignorant of the Apostles.

units.la: Hæc non improbant quidem, sed etiam non confirmant istarum disciplinarum studia. Deinde Gratianus hic Isidori verbum subiungit. ex fine cap. 13 libri tertij De summo bono. Non erat abscindendum quicquam. Nam tota sententia themati nostro conuenientissima est. sic habet.
units.tr: These indeed do not condemn the study of these disciplines, but neither do they confirm it. Then Gratian here adds a word of Isidore, from the end of chapter 13 of book 3 On the Supreme Good. Nothing was to be cut out, for the whole sentence is most suited to our theme. It reads thus:

units.la: Minus male sunt Gentilium litera, quam sint Hæreticorum.
units.tr: The letters of the Gentiles are less bad than those of the heretics.

units.la: MEliores scias esse Grammaticos, quàm Hæreticos. Hæretici enim haustu letiferi succi hominibus persuadendo propinant. Grammaticorum autem doctrina etiam potest proficere ad vitam, dum fuerit in meliores vsus assumpta. Retulit hanc duntaxat vltimam clausulam, quam falsus quoque tribuit Hieronymo. Item. Hieronymus in primum cap. Danielis. To. 5.
units.tr: You should know that grammarians are better than heretics, for heretics, by persuading, offer men a draught of deadly juice. But the teaching of grammarians can also profit for life, provided it is taken up for better uses. He reported only this last clause, which the false one also attributes to Jerome. Likewise, Jerome on the first chapter of Daniel, tom. 5.

units.la: Ecclesiastici secularia discant, vt conuincant.
units.tr: Let churchmen learn secular subjects so that they may refute them.

units.la: QVi de mensa & vino Regis nolunt comedere, ne polluantur: Vtique, si Sapientiam atque doctrinam BaM babyloniorum scirent esse peccatum, nunquam acquiescerent discere, quod non licebat. Discunt autem, non ut sequantur, sed ut iudicent atque convincant: quomodo si quispiam aduersus Mathematicos velit scribere, imperitus Matheseos, risui patebit: & aduersus Philosophos disputans, si ignoret dogmata Philosophorum. Discant ergo eâ mente doctrinam Chaldaicam, quâ & Moyses omnem Sapientiam Ægyptiorum didicerat.
units.tr: Those who were unwilling to eat from the king's table and drink his wine, lest they be defiled, would certainly never have agreed to learn the wisdom and learning of the Babylonians if they had known it to be sinful, and so forbidden to them. They learned it, however, not so that they might follow it but so that they might judge it and refute it. It is like someone who wishes to write against the mathematicians: if he is ignorant of mathematics, he will be laughed at; and so too with one who argues against the philosophers without knowing their doctrines. Let them therefore learn Chaldean doctrine with the same purpose with which Moses also learned all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

units.la: Theologum, Necessitas, non Voluntas ad Gentilium disciplinas trahat.
units.tr: Let necessity, not desire, draw the theologian to the disciplines of the Gentiles.

units.la: SI quando cogimur literarum secularium recordari, & aliqua ex his dicere, quae olim omisimus: non nostrae est voluntatis, sed (sed ut ita dicam) gravissimae necessitatis: ut probemus ea quae à sanctis Prophetis ante secula multa praedicta sunt, tam Graecorum, quàm Latinorum, & aliorum Gentilium literis contineri.
units.tr: If at any time we are forced to recall secular literature and to say something from it that we once left aside, it is not from our own will but from (so to speak) the most pressing necessity. We do this so as to prove that the things which the holy prophets foretold many ages ago are also contained in the writings of the Greeks, the Latins, and other Gentiles.

units.la: Hic fuit Eugenius 3. anno salutis 1145. quem prius D. Bernardus elegerat in Monachum. Papa creatus in Galliam se recepit: ubi Lutetiae, ac Remis, habuit Concilium, unde Gratianus hoc decretum collegit, qui tum quoque Bononiae vivebat.
units.tr: This was Eugenius III, in the year of salvation 1145, whom St Bernard had earlier chosen as a monk. Created pope, he withdrew into France, where he held councils at Paris and at Reims. From these Gratian gathered this decree, and Gratian was still living at Bologna at that time.

units.la: Magistros & Doctores Episcopi congruis in locis instituant, & alant.
units.tr: Bishops should establish masters and teachers in suitable places and support them.

units.la: DE quibusdam locis ad nos refertur, Neque Magistros, Neque curam inueniri pro studio literarum. Idcirco ab vniuersis Episcopis, subiectis plebibus, & aliis locis, in quibus necessitas occurrerit, omnino cura & diligentia habeatur, Ut Magistri & Doctores constituantur, qui studia literarum, liberaliumque artium dogmata assiduè doceant: quia in his maximè Diuina manifestantur atque declaratur mandata.
units.tr: We are told of certain places where neither masters nor provision for the study of letters is to be found. Therefore, by all the bishops, in the districts subject to them and in other places where need arises, all care and diligence must be taken that masters and teachers be appointed who will constantly teach the study of letters and the doctrines of the liberal arts, because in these above all the divine commands are made manifest and declared.

units.la: Sua Gentilium vanitas, suis conuincitur authoritatibus & libris.
units.tr: The vanity of the Gentiles is refuted by their own authorities and books.

units.la: SI quid veri de Deo, Sibylla, vel Orpheus, aliive Gentilium Vates, aut Philosophi dixisse, vel praedixisse perhibentur: valet quidem ad reuincendam Paganorum vanitatem, non tamen ad istorum authoritatem complectendam. Quantum enim distat de Christi aduentu inter praedicationem Angelorum, & confessione Daemoniorum, tantum inter authoritatem Prophetarum, & curiositatem Sacrilegorum.
units.tr: If the Sibyl, Orpheus, or any other of the Gentile seers or philosophers is reported to have said or foretold something true about God, this is indeed useful for refuting the vanity of the pagans, but it is not useful for embracing their authority. For as much as the proclamation of the angels about the coming of Christ differs from the confession of the demons, so much does the authority of the prophets differ from the curiosity of the sacrilegious.

units.la: Item. Clemens Papa, Epistola quinta ad condiscipulos. Clemens (cuius Paulus meminit) Apostolorum sectator ac discipulus, praecipuus Petri comes primusque successor, Anno Christi circiter 71 quinque scripsisse fertur Epistolas ad Fratres & Condiscipulos Hierosolymis habitantes cum Iacobo Fratre Domini. De postrema sumpsit Gratianus praesentem Canonem.
units.tr: Likewise: Pope Clement, fifth epistle to his fellow disciples. Clement, whom Paul mentions, a follower and disciple of the apostles, the chief companion and first successor of Peter, is said to have written five epistles around the year of Christ 71 to the brethren and fellow disciples living at Jerusalem with James, the brother of the Lord. From the last of these Gratian took the present canon.

units.la: In interpretatione scripturae, quae sine doctore satis intelligi nequit, nemo sibi soli credat: d maioribus tradita sequatur. hanc enim ad suum sensum trahere, vitiosissimum est, ait Clemens.
units.tr: In interpreting Scripture, which cannot be sufficiently understood without a teacher, no one should trust himself alone; he should follow what has been handed down by our forebears. For to bend it to one's own sense is most faulty, says Clement.

units.la: RElatum nobis est, quod quidam in vestris partibus commorantes, aduersantur sanis doctrinis: & prout eis videtur, non secundum traditionem patrum, sed iuxta suum sensum, docere videntur. Multas enim quidam (ut audiuimus) vestrarum partium ingeniosi homines, ex his quae legunt, verisimilitudines capiunt: Et ideo diligenter obseruandum est, ut Lex Dei quum legitur, non secundum propriam ingenii virtutem vel intelligentiam legatur, aut doccatur. Sunt enim multa verba in scripturis Diuinis, quae possunt trahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi unusquisque sponte praesumpserit: sed fieri non oportet: non enim sensum extrinsecus alienum & extraneum debetis quaerere, ut quoquo modo ipsum ex scripturarum authoritate confirmetis: sed ex ipsis scripturis sensum capere veritatis oportet. Et ideo oportet intelligetiam ab eo discere scripturarum, qui eam à maioribus secundum veritatem sibi traditam seruat: ut & ipse possit ea quae rectè susceperit, competenter asserere.
units.tr: It has been reported to us that certain men living in your parts oppose sound doctrines, and teach not according to the tradition of the fathers but, as seems good to them, according to their own sense. For certain clever men of your parts (as we have heard) draw plausible notions from what they read. And so it must be carefully observed that when the Law of God is read, it is not read or taught according to one's own cleverness or understanding. For there are many words in the divine Scriptures that can be twisted to whatever sense each person rashly assumes for himself; but this must not be done. For you ought not to seek a sense foreign and alien from outside, so that you may somehow confirm it by the authority of Scripture; rather, one ought to draw the sense of truth from the Scriptures themselves. Therefore one must learn the understanding of the Scriptures from the one who keeps it as it has been truly handed down to him by his forebears, so that he may himself competently assert what he has rightly received.

units.la: Ad Sacram scripturam sunt omnes humanæ disciplinæ reducendæ: sed ad nullas illa. Si quæ nequeunt, aut repugnant, omnes sunt abiiciendæ.
units.tr: All human disciplines are to be brought back to Sacred Scripture, but Scripture is not to be brought back to any of them. Whatever cannot agree with it, or contradicts it, must all be rejected.

units.la: §. Quum verò ex Diuinis scripturis integram quisque & firmam regulam veritatis susceperit, absurdum non erit, si aliquid etiam ex eruditione communi, ac liberalibus studiis, quæ forte etiam in pueritia attigit, ad assertionem veri dogmatis conferat: ita tamen, ut ubi vera didicit, salsa & simulata declinet. Item. Isidorus cap.13.lib.3. De summo bono. Gratianus hos libros appellat, Sententiarum.
units.tr: §. But when someone has received from the divine Scriptures a complete and firm rule of truth, it will not be absurd if he also brings something from general learning and the liberal studies, which perhaps he touched on even in boyhood, to the assertion of the true doctrine; yet only in such a way that, where he has learned true things, he turns aside from false and feigned ones. Likewise Isidore, chapter 13, book 3, On the Highest Good. Gratian calls these books the Sentences.

units.la: Diis gentilium sacrificat, qui de Diis scripta lubens lectitat.
units.tr: He sacrifices to the gods of the Gentiles who gladly reads writings about those gods.

units.la: Deo prohibetur Christianis figmenta legere Poëtarum: quia per oblectamenta inanium fabularum, mentè excitant ad incitiua libidinum. Nō enim thura solùm osserendo, Dæmonibus immolatur, sed etiam eorum dicta li-bentius capiendo.
units.tr: Christians are forbidden to read the fictions of the poets, because through the delights of empty fables the mind is stirred to incitements of lust. For a sacrifice is made to demons not only by offering incense but also by taking up their sayings more readily.

units.la: Vt itaque ex præmissis authoritatibus apparet.
units.tr: So, as appears from the authorities set out above.

units.la: Imperitia sacerdotibus semper est fugienda: quoniam si per ignorantiam cæcitatis aliis ducatum præstare cœperint, ambo in foveam cadunt. unde dicitur in Psalmo: Obscurentur oculi eorum ne videant: & dorsum eorum semper incurua. Quum enim obscurantur illi qui præeunt, ad ferenda onera peccatorum, facilè sequentes inclinantur. ELABORANDVM est itaque Sacerdotibus, ut ignorantiam à se, quasi quandam pestem, abiciant.
units.tr: Ignorance must always be avoided by priests, since if through the blindness of ignorance they begin to lead others, both fall into the pit. Hence it is said in the Psalm: "Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and let their back be always bent." For when those who go before are blinded, those who follow them easily bend down to bear the burdens of sins. Priests must therefore take pains to cast off ignorance from themselves as if it were a kind of plague.

units.la: Licet enim Servus nescius voluntatem Domini sui, & non faciens dicatur vapulare paucis: non tamen hoc de omnibus generaliter intelligitur. Ait enim Apostolus: Qui ignorat, ignorabitur quod de eo intelligendum est, qui noluit intelligere, ut bene ageret. Unde Augustinus ait in lib. quaestionum veteris ac novi testamenti. quaest.67. Tomo 4.
units.tr: For although it is said that a servant who does not know the will of his lord and does not act on it is beaten with few stripes, this is not understood generally of everyone. For the Apostle says: "He who is ignorant, let him be ignorant," which must be understood of the one who was unwilling to understand, so that he might act well. Hence Augustine says in the book of questions on the Old and New Testaments, question 67, Tome 4.

units.la: Spontaneus ignorans non habet excusationem
units.tr: A wilfully ignorant person has no excuse

units.la: NON omnis qui ignorat, immunis est à poena. Ille enim ignorans potest excusari à poena, qui à quo disceret, non invenit. Illis autem ignosci non poterit, qui habentes à quo discerent, operam non dederunt. In summam colligas ante dicta. Et eruditum, & doctum decet esse Sacerdotem. Sed quibus artibus atque disciplinis, inquirit Gratianus adhuc.
units.tr: NOT everyone who is ignorant is immune from punishment. For one who is ignorant can be excused from punishment if he did not find anyone from whom he could learn. But those who had someone from whom they might learn, and did not make the effort, cannot be pardoned. Gather up the foregoing in summary. A priest ought to be learned and instructed. But by what arts and disciplines does Gratian next inquire?

units.la: DISTINCTIO XXXVIII.
units.tr: DISTINCTIO XXXVIII.

units.la: QVVM itaque (ait Gratianus) voluntaria ignorantia sit omnibus noxia, Sacerdotibus est periculosa.
units.tr: Since, therefore (says Gratian), voluntary ignorance is harmful to all, it is dangerous for priests.

units.la: Unde. In Concilio Toletano 4. cap. 24. Tum Sisebutus, sive Sisenandus cum suis Gothis occupabat Hispanias, sub annos Do. 630.
units.tr: Whence. In the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 24. Then Sisebut, or Sisenand, with his Goths was occupying Spain, around the year of the Lord 630.

units.la: Sac- erdotis opus, est Prædicatio in omni doctrina. Huic repugnat Imperitia.
units.tr: The work of a priest is preaching in every kind of teaching. Ignorance opposes this.

units.la: IGnorantia, mater cunctorum errorum, maximè Sacerdotibus Dei evitanda est: qui docendi officium in populo Dei susceperunt. Sacerdotes enim legere sanctas admonentur scripturas, Paulo Apostolo dicente ad Timotheum: Attende lectioni, & exhortationi doctrinæ: & semper permane in his. Sciant ergo Sacerdotes Sanctas scripturas, & Canones: & omne opus eorum in Prædicatione & Doctrina consistat: atque ædificent cunctos tam fidei scientiâ, quàm operum disciplinâ. Item. Ex eodem.ca.25.
units.tr: Ignorance, the mother of all errors, is above all to be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the office of teaching the people of God. For priests are urged to read the holy Scriptures, the Apostle Paul saying to Timothy: "Give attention to reading, to exhortation and to doctrine, and continue in these things." Let priests therefore know the holy Scriptures and the canons, and let all their work consist in preaching and teaching, and let them build up everyone both with the knowledge of faith and with the discipline of works. Likewise. From the same, chapter 25.

units.la: Qui Parochias regunt, unà cum Sanctis Bibliis, & Canonibus, Officialem quoque debent habere librum: Reddereque poscenti Episcopo muneris iniuncti rationem.
units.tr: Those who govern parishes should have, along with the holy Bibles and the canons, also an official book, and they must give an account of their office when the bishop demands it.

units.la: QVando Presbyteri in parœciis ordinantur, Libellum officialem à Sacerdote suo accipiant, ut ad Ecclestabit: quia valde periculosæ Euangelicæ minæ sunt, quibus dicitur: Si Cæcus Cæco ducatum præstet, ambo in foveam cadunt. Item. Ex 7. Synodo. Œcumenica & sancta hæc Synodus habita fuit Nicææ (propterea, secunda Nicæna vocatur) anno salutis octingentesimo. In quam trecenti tres & sexaginta Patres convenerunt aduersus Iconomachos, quorum sub impio quodā Isaurico Leone 3. Imperato. Constantinopoli cœperat Hæresis, quæ duraverat annos plures sexaginta: demum fuit hoc in Concilio damnata. Cui per suos vicarios præfuit Adrianus Papa 1. Constantinopolitanis præerat insignis Tharasius. Occidentale tum regere cœperat Imperium Carolus Magnus, Galliæ Rex. Sic habet illius Synodi Canon 2. ex interpretatione quidem vetere.
units.tr: When presbyters are ordained in parishes, they should receive an official little book from their bishop, so that they may stand fast in the Church, because the threats of the Gospel are very dangerous, in which it is said: "If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the pit." Likewise. From the Seventh Synod. This holy and ecumenical synod was held at Nicaea (for which reason it is called the Second Council of Nicaea) in the year of salvation 787. Three hundred and sixty-three Fathers met there against the Iconoclasts, whose heresy had begun at Constantinople under the impious Leo the Isaurian, the third emperor of that name, and had lasted more than sixty years; at last it was condemned in this council. Pope Hadrian I presided over it through his legates, and the renowned Tarasius presided over the Constantinopolitans. Charles the Great, King of the Gauls, had then begun to rule the Western empire. So reads canon 2 of that synod, in the older translation.

units.la: psalterium, Canones, & Euangelium, & Apostoli librum, & omnem Sacram scripturam sciant, Sèque observaturos, atque Prædicaturos spondeant Episcopi futuri.
units.tr: They should know the Psalter, the canons, the Gospel, the book of the Apostle, and all Holy Scripture, and promise, as future bishops, that they will observe and preach them.

units.la: OMnes psallentes † repromittimus Deo, In tuis iustificationibus meditabor: Non obliuiscar sermones tuos. Quod omnes quidem Christianos obseruare † saluberrimum est, sed præcipuè hos qui Ecclesiasticam consecuti sunt dignitatem. Vnde definimus, Omnem, qui ad Episcopatus est prouehendus gradum, modis omnibus Psalterium nosse: vt ex hoc etiam omnis Clerus, qui sub eo fuerit, tita moneatur & imbuatur. Inquiratur autem diligenter à Metropolitano, Si in promptu habeat Lege scrutabiliter, & non transitorie, Tam Sacros Canones & sanctum Euangelium, quàm Diuini Apostoli librum, & omnem Diuinam scripturam: atque secundum mandata conseruare, & docere sibi populum commissum. Substantia enim † summi Sacerdotij nostri sunt eloquia Diuinitus tradita, id est, vera Diuinarum scripturarum disciplina, quemadmodum magnus perhibet Dionysius † Quòd si disceptauerit, & ita libenter facere & docere minimè spoponderit, nullatenus cōsecretur: ait enim Prophetæ Deus: Tu scientiam repulisti, & ego repellam te, ne Sacerdotio fungaris mihi.
units.tr: We, all who sing psalms, promise God: "I will meditate on your justifications; I will not forget your words." Although it is most wholesome for all Christians to observe this, it is especially so for those who have attained ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore we decree that everyone who is to be advanced to the rank of bishop must in every way know the Psalter, so that through this the whole clergy under him may also be admonished and imbued with it at all times. Let the metropolitan carefully inquire whether he has at hand, and reads attentively and not superficially, the sacred canons and the holy Gospel, as well as the book of the divine Apostle and all divine Scripture, and whether he keeps and teaches the people committed to him according to the commandments. For the substance of our high priesthood is the words divinely handed down, that is, the true discipline of the divine Scriptures, as the great Dionysius declares. But if he disputes, and does not promise that he will gladly do and teach these things, he must by no means be consecrated; for God says to the prophet: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me."

units.la: Inquiratur autem diligenter, &c.
units.tr: But let it be inquired diligently, etc.

units.la: Huiusce commatis Graeca mihi visum fuit hic annectere, quo sensus appareret clarior: quem vetus interpres nonnihil inuoluit. Alia sunt in margine annotata.
units.tr: It seemed good to me to add here the Greek of this clause, so that the sense may appear clearer, since the old translator somewhat obscured it. Other matters are noted in the margin.

units.la: Ἀ Νακρίνεσθαι δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ἐπὶ τῷ μητροπολίτῃ, εἰ πεπιθύμως, ἔχει ἀναγινώσκειν, ἐξουνιλικῶς καὶ οὐ παροδοντικῶς, τοὺς πε ἱερ-ὸυς κανόνας, τὸ ἅγιον εὐαγγέλιον, τῶν π τοῦ θείου ἀποστόλου βί-βλον, καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν θείαν γραφὴν. καὶ κατὰ τὰ θεῖα ἐντάλματα ἀναγρέφεσθαι, καὶ διδάσκειν τὸν κατὰ αὐτὸν λαόν.
units.tr: It is safe for the metropolitan to examine, if he is eager, that he should read the sacred canons, the holy Gospel, the book of the divine Apostle, and all divine Scripture carefully and thoroughly, not cursorily, and should conduct himself according to the divine commands and teach the people under him. [ἀνακρίνεσθαι δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ἐπὶ τοῦ μητροπολίτου, εἰ προθύμως ἔχει, ἀναγινώσκειν ἐξακριβωτικῶς καὶ οὐ παροδικῶς τοὺς ἱεροὺς κανόνας, τὸ ἅγιον εὐαγγέλιον, τὴν βίβλον τοῦ θείου ἀποστόλου, καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν θείαν γραφήν, καὶ κατὰ τὰ θεῖα ἐντάλματα ἀναστρέφεσθαι καὶ διδάσκειν τὸν ὑπ᾽ αὐτὸν λαόν]

units.la: Id est.
units.tr: That is.

units.la: INterrogetur autem diligeter à Metropolita, Si studioso velit animo legere, noscereque diligenti cum scrutatione atque discutione, & non velut in transitu ac perfunctorie, Sacros Canones. sanctum Euangelium, Diuinique Apostoli librum, & omnem Diuinam Scripturam, Secundúmque Diuina mandata conuersari, & docere subditum sibi populum. Item. Ex Concilio Carthaginensi 4.
units.tr: The metropolitan shall be asked diligently whether he is willing to read with an eager mind, and to know through careful scrutiny and examination, and not in passing or perfunctorily, the sacred canons, the holy Gospel, the book of the divine Apostle, and all divine Scripture; and to live according to the divine commands and to teach the people subject to him. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage.

units.la: PLacuit, Vt ordinandis Episcopis, vel Clericis, prius ab ordinatoribus suis Decreta Conciliorum auribus eorum inculcentur: ne se aliquid contra statuta Concilij fecisse pæniteant. Item. Zepherinus Papa, Epist. 1. Ad Episcopos Sicilienses. Hic fuit à Petro Papa decimus tertius. Hanc Epistolam scripsit, Saturnino & Gallo Consulibus. Hoc est, anno salutis 199. Gratianus omisit, quæ fuit apponenda, ex assumpto conclusionem, quam nos attexuimus. ex To. 1. Concil.
units.tr: It was decided that before bishops or clerics are ordained, the decrees of the councils should be impressed upon their ears by those who ordain them, so that they do not regret having done anything contrary to the statutes of the council. Likewise, Pope Zephyrinus, Epistle 1, to the Bishops of Sicily. This was the thirteenth pope from Peter. He wrote this letter in the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus, that is, in the year of salvation 199. Gratian omitted what ought to have been appended from the assumed conclusion, which we have added. From volume 1 of the Councils.

units.la: Episcopi semper in scripturarum lucem fixos debent oculos habere: quæ nullis vnquam mundi tenebris obfuscari potest.
units.tr: Bishops should always keep their eyes fixed on the light of the Scriptures, which can never be obscured by any darkness of the world.

units.la: SIcut stellas cœli non extinguit nox: sic mentes fidelium, inhærentes firmamento sanctæ scripturæ, non obscurat mundana iniquitas.
units.tr: As night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not darken the minds of the faithful, who cling to the firmament of holy Scripture.

units.la: Idcirco, meditari vos oportet scripturas: & præcepta Diuina, quæ in scripturis continentur, diligenter attendere: Ne transgressores Legis Dei, sed impletores apparetis.
units.tr: Therefore you ought to meditate on the Scriptures and to attend diligently to the divine precepts contained in the Scriptures, so that you may appear not transgressors of the Law of God, but its fulfillers.

units.la: Ignorantia scripturarum est ignorantia Christi.
units.tr: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

units.la: I iuxta Apostolum Paulum, Christus, Dei virtus est, Deíque Sapientia: & qui nescit scripturas, nescit Dei virtutem, eiúsque Sapientiam: Ignoratio ergo scripturarum, Ignoratio Christi est.
units.tr: According to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; and whoever does not know the Scriptures does not know the power of God and his wisdom. Ignorance of the Scriptures is therefore ignorance of Christ.

units.la: Non sapiunt Christo, qui Christum non sapiunt.
units.tr: They have no savour of Christ who have no understanding of Christ.

units.la: Qui ea, quæ sunt Domini, nesciunt, à Domino nesciuntur: Paulo attestante, qui ait: Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur. Item Augustinus,cap.17. Enchiridij ad Laurentiū. To.3.
units.tr: Those who do not know the things of the Lord are not known by the Lord, Paul bearing witness, who says: "If anyone does not know, he will not be known." Likewise Augustine, chapter 17 of the Enchiridion to Laurentius, volume 3.

units.la: Errare nihil est aliud, quàm verum putare, quod falsum est: falsúmque, quod verum est. Vel certum habere pro incerto, incertúmve pro certo.
units.tr: To err is nothing other than to think true what is false, and false what is true; or to hold as certain what is uncertain, or uncertain what is certain.

units.la: Quanuis error, quantâ possumus cura, cauendus sit, non solùm in maioribus, verumetiam in minoribus rebus: nec nisi rerum ignorantiâ possit errari: non est tamen consequens, ut continuò erret, quisquis aliquid nescit: sed si quis existimet se scire, quod nescit. pro vero quippe approbat falsum: quod erroris est proprium. Verumtamen, in qua re quisquis erret, interest plurimùm. nam in una eademque re, & nescienti, sciens, & erranti, non errans, rectâ ratione præponitur. In diuersis autem rebus, id est, quum iste scit alia, ille alia, & iste utiliora, ille minùs utilia, vel etiam noxia: quis non in cis, quæ ille scit, ei præferat nescientem? Sunt enim quædam, quæ nescire melius est, quàm scire.
