Gratianus proximis totis tribus Eucriniis docuit Ecclesiasticos Ecclesiasticarum, Diuinarúmque literarum peritos esse, nec humanas ignorare debere. Non est illarum tolerabilis insciatia. Caterùm, Quid si seculares istas literas non probè satis calleant, ignari forte Poëtices, Dialecticæ, aut Rhetorices? ille respondet, vt sequitur.
units.tr: Although error must be guarded against with all the care we can, not only in greater matters but also in lesser ones, and although one can err only through ignorance of things, it does not follow that whoever does not know something errs at once. But if someone thinks he knows what he does not know, he approves the false as true, and that is the mark of error. However, it matters greatly in which matter someone errs. For in one and the same matter, by right reason, the one who knows is preferred to the one who does not know, and the one who does not err to the one who errs. But in different matters, when this man knows one thing and that man another, and this one knows more useful things and that one less useful or even harmful, who would not, in those things that the one knows, prefer the one who does not know? For there are some things it is better not to know than to know. Gratian, in the next three whole distinctions, taught that ecclesiastics should be skilled in ecclesiastical and divine letters, and should not be ignorant of human letters. Ignorance of those is not tolerable. But what if they do not know well enough those secular letters, perhaps being ignorant of poetry, dialectic, or rhetoric? He answers as follows.

units.la: Gratianus. SED licet per ignorantiam Grammaticæ artis aliquid vitiosum proferant Episcopi, vel Presbyteri, non tamen ideo à Scholasticis sunt despiciendi: quia morum vitia, magis quàm verborum sunt præcauenda. Vnde Augustinus in lib. De Catechizandis rudibus. cap.9. To.4. Augustinus in eo cap.docet, quomodo Grammatici, & Rhetores sint catechizandi, id est, instituendi, erudiendi, initiandi.
units.tr: Gratian. But although bishops or presbyters may utter something faulty through ignorance of the art of grammar, they must not for that reason be despised by the scholastics, because the vices of morals must be guarded against more than those of words. Hence Augustine, in his book On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 9, volume 4. In that chapter Augustine teaches how grammarians and rhetoricians are to be catechized, that is, instructed, educated, and initiated.

units.la: Ecclesiasticarum loquutionum simplicitas, à nihil sibi non arrogantibus Grammaticis, seu quibusdam Criticis, reprehendenda non est.
units.tr: The simplicity of ecclesiastical speech must not be censured by grammarians, or by certain critics, who arrogate everything to themselves.

units.la: SEdulò monendi sunt à Grammaticorum, Oratorúmque Scholis venientes, Vt humilitate induti Christianâ, discant non contemnere, quos cognouerint morum vitia magis, quàm verborum, deuitate: sed cordi casto linguam exercitatam nec conferre audeant, quam etiam praferre consueuerunt. His enim maximè utile est, nosse ita esse præponendas verbis sententias, vt præponitur animus corpori: ex quo fit, vt ita malle debeat veriores, quàm disertiores audire sermones: sicut malle debent prudentiores, quàm formosiores habere amicos. Nouerint etiam non esse voces ad aures Dei, nisi animi affectum. Ita enim non irridebunt, si aliquos antistites, & ministros Ecclesiæ forte animaduerterint, vel cum barbarismis, & solœcismis Deum invocare, vel eadem verba, quæ pronuntiant, non intelligere, perturbatéque distinguere. Non quia ista minimè corrigenda sunt, vt populus, ad id, quod plane intelligit, dicat Amen: sed tamen piè toleranda sunt ab eis, qui didicerint, vt sono in foro, sic voto in Ecclesia benedici. Itaque, Forensis illa nonnunquam forte Bona dictio, nunquam tamen Benedictio dici potest.
units.tr: Those coming from the schools of grammarians and orators must be diligently warned that, clothed in Christian humility, they should learn not to despise those whom they see avoiding the vices of morals more than those of words; and they should not dare to compare with a pure heart the tongue they are accustomed to practise and even to prefer. For it is especially useful for them to know that sentences should be placed before words just as the mind is placed before the body; hence they ought to prefer hearing truer speech rather than more eloquent, just as they ought to prefer wiser friends rather than more handsome ones. Let them know also that words do not reach the ears of God unless there is affection of mind. Thus they will not mock if they notice some bishops and ministers of the Church perhaps invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, or not understanding the very words they pronounce and punctuating them confusedly. Not that these things must not be corrected, so that the people may say Amen to what they plainly understand; but they must nevertheless be piously tolerated by those who have learned that one is blessed in the church by vow, just as one is greeted in the forum by sound. Therefore that forensic good-saying may sometimes be called good, but never a blessing.

units.la: Ecclesia Christi intenta tota norma benefaciendi, benèque docendi, de bene loquendo non semper intendit regulis Donati.
units.tr: The Church of Christ, wholly intent on the rule of doing good and teaching well, does not always concern itself with the rules of Donatus in speaking well.

units.la: INdignum vehementer existimo, Ut verba cælestis oraculi restringam sub regulis Donati. Augustinus cap. 50. De vera Religione. To. 1.
units.tr: I think it deeply unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus. Augustine, chapter 50, On True Religion, volume 1.

units.la: Sua cuique linguæ proprietas est, & Idiotismus. Gnosticis & Grammaticis τιλαία.
units.tr: Each tongue has its own peculiarity and idiom, for the Gnostics and the grammarians alike.

units.la: LOcutio Diuinarum scripturarum secundùm cuiusque linguæ proprietatem accipienda est. Habet enim omnis lingua quædam propria locutionum genera: quæ quum in aliam transferuntur, videntur absurda. Item. Hieronymus ad Pammachium, pro libris suis aduersus Iouinianum. Epist. Christiani. To. 2.
units.tr: The language of the divine Scriptures must be understood according to the peculiarity of each language. For every language has certain proper modes of expression, which, when transferred into another, seem absurd. Likewise Jerome, to Pammachius, in his books against Jovinian. Epistle "Christiani," volume 2.

units.la: In Ecclesiasticis tractandis, Eloquentia, si qua est, dissimulanda est, non ostentanda.
units.tr: In treating ecclesiastical matters, any eloquence there is ought to be concealed, not displayed.

units.la: ECclesiastica interpretatio, etiamsi habeat eloquentiæ venustatem, dissimulare eam debet, & fugere: ut non in otiosis Philosophorum scholis, paucis discipulis, sed uniuerso loquatur hominum generi. Item. Clemens Papa. Epist. 3. ad omnes Christianos. quæ est, De officio Sacerdotis, & Clericorum.
units.tr: An ecclesiastical interpretation, even if it has the charm of eloquence, ought to hide it and avoid it, so that it speaks not in the idle schools of philosophers to a few pupils, but to the whole human race. Likewise Pope Clement, Epistle 3, to all Christians, which concerns the office of the priest and of the clergy.

units.la: Clericus, & quiuis alius, à quouis edoceri, & discere paratus esto.
units.tr: Let a cleric, and anyone else, be ready to be taught by anyone and to learn.

units.la: NVllus propter opprobrium Senectutis, aut Iuuentutis, vel nobilitatem generis, à paruulis & minus eruditis, si quid forte est utilitatis, aut salutis, inquirere negligat. Qui enim rebelliter viuit, & discere atque agere bona recusat: magis Diaboli, quàm Christi membrum esse ostenditur: & potiùs infidelis quàm fidelis esse monstratur.
units.tr: Let no one, on account of the disgrace of old age or youth, or the nobility of his birth, neglect to seek from little ones and the less learned whatever usefulness or salvation there may be. For he who lives rebelliously and refuses to learn and to do good is shown to be a member of the devil rather than of Christ, and is shown to be unbeliever rather than believer.

units.la: Duo Prudentiæ genera fecimus in distinct. 36. Requiruntur in Clericis vtrunque. De priore, quod in literarum peritia consistit, satis iam tractatum. Posterius est in rerum cognitione & administratione situm. Necessarium pariter & Ecclesiasticis viris. De quo nunc
units.tr: We have made two kinds of prudence in distinction 36, and both are required in clerics. Of the former, which consists in skill in letters, enough has already been said. The latter lies in the knowledge and management of affairs, equally necessary for churchmen. Concerning this, now

units.la: DISTINCTIO XXXIX.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XXXIX.

units.la: Gratianus. ECCE, plenarie monstratum est, quòd Sacerdotes oportet literarum tam Sacrarum, quàm Secularium esse peritos. Nunc autem quaeritur, An secularium negociorum oporteat eos habere peritiam. Hanc esse Praelatis Ecclesiae necessariam multis rationibus probatur. Debent Praelati subditis non solùm Spiritualia, sed etiã Carnalia subsidia ministrare, exemplo Christi, qui turbas sequentes non solùm verbo docebat, sed etiam virtute sanabat, & corporalibus alimentis reficiebat. Vt autem Praelati haec omnia plenè perficere possint, Secularium negociorum oportet eos habere solertiam: ut eorum cautelâ, & Ecclesiae seruetur indemnes: & cuique necessaria pro suo modo ministrentur. Unde quidam in Episcopum electus, à beato Gregorio pro sua simplicitate repellitur, ne eius occasione res Ecclesiae dilapidarentur. Gregorius Epistol.40.lib.8. scribit nobilibus civibus Neapolitanis.
units.tr: Gratian. Behold, it has been fully shown that priests ought to be learned both in sacred and in secular letters. Now the question is whether they ought to have skill in secular affairs. That this skill is necessary for the prelates of the Church is proved by many arguments. Prelates owe their subjects not only spiritual but also material help, following the example of Christ, who, when crowds followed him, not only taught them by word but also healed them by his power and fed them with bodily food. In order that prelates may be able to perform all these duties fully, they must have skill in secular affairs, so that the Church is kept safe under their watch and each person is supplied with what he needs according to his station. Hence blessed Gregory rejected a certain man who had been elected bishop, on account of his simplicity, lest through him the property of the Church be squandered. Gregory, in Letter 40 of Book 8, writes to the noble citizens of Naples.

units.la: Secularium negociorum imperitii non sunt in Episcopos ordinandi. Id est, Qui suae Domui bene praeesse non possunt.
units.tr: Those inexperienced in secular affairs are not to be ordained as bishops. That is, those who cannot rule their own household well.

units.la: PEtrus Diaconus, quem à vobis electum asseritis, omnino (ut dicitur) simplex est: & nostis, quia hoc tempore, Talis in regiminis arce debet constitui, qui non solùm de salute animarum, verumetiam de extrinseca utilitate & cautela sciat esse solicitus. De ministrorum Prudentia, videlicet, De disciplinis & doctrina, de sagacitate & providentia in actibus rerum, dictum sufficienter. Ad aliud transit Gratianus. Est in Apostoli speculo videndum Quintum.
units.tr: Peter the deacon, whom you assert was chosen by you, is altogether simple (as it is said), and you know that in these times one ought to be placed at the helm of government who knows how to be concerned not only for the salvation of souls but also for external usefulness and prudent management. Concerning the prudence of ministers, namely their discipline and teaching, and their shrewdness and foresight in handling affairs, enough has been said. Gratian passes on to another matter. In the mirror of the Apostle the fifth point is to be seen.

units.la: ΔEÎ KOΣMION EINAI.
units.tr: It must be orderly [δεῖ κόσμιον εἶναι].

units.la: Quid hoc est mandati? Referibit Oceano Hieronymus. ἐπίτασις est prioris illius veruï, hoc est, Irreprehensibilis. Qui vitia non habet, irreprehensibilis appellatur. Qui virtutibus pollet, Ornatus est. Haec ex Hieronymo. Sed audiamus Gratianum.
units.tr: What is the meaning of this command? Jerome discusses it in his letter to Oceanus. The word [ἐπίτασις] belongs to that former word, that is, blameless. He who has no faults is called blameless; he who excels in virtues is called adorned. These are the words of Jerome. But let us hear Gratian.

units.la: DISTINCTIO. XL.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XL.

units.la: Gratianus. OPORTET quoque esse Episcopum ornatum. Per ornamenta Episcopalia, Virtutes debent intelligi: quae à Domino eis repromittuntur, dum dicitur: Sacerdotes eius induentur salutari. Unde in veteri testamento, Variis vestibus, ex praecepto Domini, Sacerdotes ornati leguntur: quia multimodis virtutibus debet splendere vita Pontificis: ut gradui conferat decorem, quem ab eo non accepit: Non enim loca, sed vita & mores sanctum faciùt Sacerdotem. Unde ex officio suscepto non licentiam peccandi, sed necessitatem bene viuendi se nouerint assecutos. Unde Symmachus Papa ait.Symmachus Papa, salutis anno quingentesimo, dum per ignauiam Graecorum, Gothicus Rex Theodoricus Italiae dominaretur, ab aemulis per annos fere 15. quibus praefuit, saepiùs est impetitus quater in Concilio cum suam dixit. Scribens tum periculosissimum fuit. Sex habuit ille Romae Synodos, quarta fuit absolutus, anno 504. quae propterea, Palmaris, nuncupata tunc est. Hanc tamen Clericorum pars aduersa Symmacho, tanquam minùs Canonicè factam, calumniabatur. Ennodius quidam Symmachi Diaconus, tunc ad illius defensionem non melegantem. gantem libellum composuit: quem postea quintâ Synodo confirmatum, vim quoque Synodalium Decretorum iusserût habere. Sumptus est ex eo Canon praesens, aliique non pauci quos tamen in opere suo Gratianus ipsi Symmacho tribuit, ut hic videlicet unus libellus extat in fine primi Conciliorum Tomi. Studio tunc florebat Fl. Boëthius, qui Consul fuerat anno Christi 489. Et quem Rex ille Barbarus exilio multárat.
units.tr: Gratian. The bishop also ought to be adorned. By the episcopal ornaments we must understand virtues, which the Lord promises to them when he says, "Her priests shall be clothed with salvation." Hence in the Old Testament priests are read of as adorned with various garments by the Lord's command, because the life of a bishop ought to shine with many kinds of virtue, so that he may bring to his rank a dignity that he did not receive from it: for it is not places but life and morals that make a priest holy. Hence they should know that by taking up the office they have obtained not a licence to sin but a necessity of living well. Hence Pope Symmachus says: Pope Symmachus, in the five hundredth year of salvation, while the Gothic king Theodoric ruled Italy through the sloth of the Greeks, was attacked by his rivals more than once, four times in council, during the nearly fifteen years of his rule, when he made his own defence; writing then was most dangerous. He held six synods at Rome; in the fourth he was acquitted, in the year 504, and for that reason it was then called the Palmaris synod. Yet a part of the clergy hostile to Symmachus criticised it as not canonically made. Ennodius, a certain deacon of Symmachus, then composed for his defence a not inelegant little book, which was later confirmed by the fifth synod and ordered to have the force of synodal decrees as well. The present canon is taken from it, and not a few others, which Gratian nevertheless attributes in his work to Symmachus himself; so that this one little book survives at the end of the first volume of the Councils. At that time Boethius, who had been consul in the year of Christ 489, flourished in learning, and that barbarian king had punished him with exile.

units.la: Pontificia dignitas omnem quoquomodo delinquendi licentiam Pontificibus adimit.
units.tr: The papal dignity takes away from popes every licence to sin in any way whatever.

units.la: N Oon nos beatum Petrum (sicut dicitis) à Domino, cum sedis privilegio, vel successores eius, peccandi indicamus licentiam suscepisse. Ille quippe perennem meritorum dotem cum haereditate innocentiae transmisit ad posteros. Quod illi concessum est per actuum lucem, ad illos pertinet, quos par conversationis splendor illuminat. Quis enim sanctum dubitet esse, quem apex tantae dignitatis attollit? In quo si desint bona acquisita per merita, sufficiunt, quae à loci decessore praestantur: Aut enim claros ad haec fastigia erigit: aut qui eriguntur, illustrat.
units.tr: Not that we say that blessed Peter (as you say) received from the Lord, together with the privilege of his see, or that his successors received, a licence to sin. For he handed down to posterity a perpetual dowry of merits together with the inheritance of innocence. What was granted to him by the light of his deeds pertains to those whom an equal brilliance of conduct illuminates. For who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up? If in him the good works acquired by merit are lacking, those supplied by the predecessor of the place suffice: for either he raises the illustrious to these heights, or he illuminates those who are raised.

units.la: Item. Hieronymus ad Heliodorum To.1. Epist.1 circa finem. Veri sunt Apostolorum successores, quicunque servant Apostolorum mores.
units.tr: Likewise. Jerome, to Heliodorus, Epistle 1, near the end. They are the true successors of the Apostles who keep the manners of the Apostles.

units.la: N On est facile stare loco Pauli: tenere gradum Petri, iam cum Christo regnantium. (Quibus ex verbis subinfert Gratianus.) Hinc dicitur.
units.tr: It is not easy to stand in the place of Paul, to hold the rank of Peter, now reigning with Christ. (From these words Gratian adds:) Hence it is said:

units.la: Non Sanctorum filii sunt, qui tenent loca Sanctorum: sed qui exercent opera eorum. Item. Gregorius. Digna Gregorio sententia, licet ista mihi verba non sint in codicibus lecta, sed multùs illam confirmat scribens in superbiam Ioannu, & aliorum quorundam Episcoporum Constantinopo. qui se cognominabant oecumenicos, hoc est, universales terrae sive mundi Patriarchas. Epist. 32.34.36.38.39. lib. 4. plurimisque locis aliis.
units.tr: They are not the sons of the saints who hold the places of the saints, but those who perform their works. Likewise Gregory. A sentence worthy of Gregory, although these words are not read in the manuscripts for me; but he strongly confirms it, writing against the pride of John and certain other bishops of Constantinople who called themselves oecumenical, that is, patriarchs of the universal earth or world. Epistles 32, 34, 36, 38, 39, book 4, and in very many other places.

units.la: Virtute solâ, non opibus, non loco, non sanguine niti Sacerdotes oportet.
units.tr: Priests ought to rest on virtue alone, not on wealth, nor on place, nor on blood.

units.la: N Os qui praesumus, non ex locorum, vel generis dignitate, sed morum nobilitate innotescere debemus: nec urbium claritate, sed fidei puritate. Item Gregorius Anastasio Presbytero. In Epist. 29. lib. 6.
units.tr: We who preside ought to be made known not by the dignity of places or of birth, but by the nobility of our morals; nor by the splendour of cities, but by the purity of our faith. Likewise Gregory to the presbyter Anastasius, Epistle 29, book 6.

units.la: Vitâ Sanctâ, non loco, vel ordine Sancto, appropinquamus Deo.
units.tr: By a holy life, not by a holy place or a holy order, do we draw near to God.

units.la: NOn loca, vel ordines creatori nostro nos proximos faciunt: Sed nos aut merita bona ei coniungunt, aut mala disiungunt.
units.tr: Places or orders do not make us near to our Creator; but good merits join us to him, and evil ones separate us.

units.la: Graviter ruit, quod altum, vel ponderosum ruit.
units.tr: That falls heavily which falls from a height or with weight.

units.la: HOmo Christianus fortiter cadit in peccato, propter duas causas: Aut propter magnitudinem peccati: Aut propter altitudinem dignitatis.
units.tr: A Christian man falls heavily into sin for two reasons: either because of the greatness of the sin, or because of the height of his dignity.

units.la: Universitas fidelium pro malo Papa debet instanter orare: Inemendabilem tolerare non debet.
units.tr: The whole body of the faithful ought to pray earnestly for a bad Pope; it ought not to tolerate one who cannot be corrected.

units.la: SI Papa, suæ & fraternæ salutis negligens deprehenditur, inutilis & remissus in suis operibus, & insuper à bono taciturnus (quod magis officit sibi, & omnibus nihilominus) in numerabiles populos cateratim secum ducit mancipio gehennæ, cum ipso plagis multis in æternum vapulaturus. Huius culpas istic redarguere præsumit mot talium nullus: quia cunctos ipse iudicaturus, à nemine est iudicandus: nisi deprehendatur à fide deuius. pro cuius perpetuo statu universitas fidelium tanto instantius orat, quanto suam salutem, post Deum, ex illius incolumitate animaduertit propensius pendere.
units.tr: If a Pope is found negligent of his own salvation and that of his brothers, useless and slack in his works, and moreover silent about the good (which harms himself the more, and all the same), he leads countless peoples headlong with him, to be slaves of Gehenna, and he himself is about to be beaten with many blows for ever. No one of such a kind presumes to rebuke his faults here, because he himself is to judge all and is to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have strayed from the faith. For whose perpetual state the whole body of the faithful prays all the more earnestly, as it perceives that its own salvation, after God, depends the more on his well-being.

units.la: Non ordines, sed vitæ merita nos Deo commend-
units.tr: Not ranks, but the merits of life commend us to God.

units.la: ANte omnia peto, ut cogitet religiosa prudentia tua, nihil esse in hac vita, & maximè hoc tempore, facilius, & latius, & hominibus acceptabilius, Episcopi, aut Presbyteri, aut Diaconi officio, si perfunctorie, atq; adulatorie res agatur: sed nihil apud Deum miserabilius, & tristius, & damnabilius. Item, Nihil esse in hac vita, & maximè hoc tempore, difficilius, & laboriosius, & periculosius, Episcopi, & Presbyteri, aut Diaconi officio: sed apud Deum nihil beatius, si eo modo militetur quo nolster Imperator iubet. Quis autem sit iste modus, nec à pueritia, nec ab adolescentia mea didici: & eo tempore quo discere coeperam, vis mihi facta est, merito peccatorum meorum (nam quid aliud existimem, nescio) Ut secundus locus gubernaculorum mihi traderetur, qui remum tenere non noueram.
units.tr: Above all I ask that your religious prudence consider that there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time, easier, broader, and more acceptable to men than the office of bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, if the business is done carelessly and with flattery; but nothing before God more wretched, sad, and damnable. Likewise, there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time, more difficult, laborious, and perilous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing more blessed, if one serves in the way our Emperor commands. What that way is, I learned neither from my boyhood nor from my youth; and at the time when I had begun to learn, force was done to me, by the merit of my sins (for what else I should think, I do not know), so that the second place at the helm was handed to me, though I did not know how to hold the oar.

units.la: Terrenus est, non Ecclesiasticus, Episcopatus, in quo iuste ac legitime non viuitur.
units.tr: That episcopate is earthly, not ecclesiastical, in which one does not live justly and lawfully.

units.la: SIcut viri & mulieris digna coniunctio unum facit matrimonium, & sicut duorum copulatio unum perficit corpus: ita Clericatus & Sacerdotium unum faciunt Presbyterum: & electio & consecratio unum facit Episcopum: quae omnia unum faciunt corpus: quod citius corrumpitur, & ad terram trahitur, nisi legaliter conseruetur, nisi iuste viuendo laudetur.
units.tr: As the worthy union of a man and a woman makes one marriage, and as the joining of two makes one body, so clerical status and the priesthood make one presbyter, and election and consecration make one bishop; all these make one body, which is quickly corrupted and dragged to the ground unless it is lawfully preserved, unless it is praised by living justly.

units.la: Non loci, vel generis excellentia, sed mores, & virtutes nobilitant hominem.
units.tr: It is not the excellence of place or of birth, but morals and virtues, that ennoble a man.

units.la: ILlud autem animaduerte, Quod extra Paradisum vir factus est: Intra Paradisum mulier. ut aduertas, quod non loci, non generis nobilitate, sed virtute unusquisque que gratiam sibi comparat. Denique, extra Paradisum (hoc est in inferiori loco) vir factus, melior inuenitur: & illa quae in meliori loco (hoc est in Paradiso) facta est, inferior reperitur. Item. Gregorius Epist. 5. lib. 6. ad Cyriacum Episcopum Constantinopopum Constantinopolitanum.
units.tr: Notice, moreover, that outside Paradise man was made, inside Paradise woman; so that you may see that each one acquires grace for himself not by the nobility of place or of birth, but by virtue. Finally, a man made outside Paradise (that is, in a lower place) is found the better; and she who was made in the better place (that is, in Paradise) is found the inferior. Likewise Gregory, Epistle 5, book 6, to Cyriacus, Bishop of Constantinople.

units.la: Si Christus non adesset, nusquam sine periculo consistere valemus.
units.tr: If Christ were not present, we could nowhere stand without danger.

units.la: QValibet occulta loca, sine gratia, animam saluare non possunt: quod aliquando in ipsis quoque conspicimus erratis electorum: Nam Loth in ipsa peruersa Ciuitate fuit iustus, In monte peccauit. Sed ista cur dicimus, quum maiora nouerimus? Quid enim Paradiso iucundius? quid caelo securius? & tamen Homo ex Paradiso, & Angelus de caelo, peccando cecidit. Idem Gregorius. Non sunt haec ipsa Gregorij verba, sed ex Gregorio collecta per Gratianum: quorum sensus habetur in cap 1. libri 9. & in fine cap. 12. libri 26. & cap. 12. lib. 35. super Iob.
units.tr: Hidden places of any kind cannot save the soul without grace; we sometimes see this even in the errors of the elect. For Lot was righteous in that wicked city, and he sinned on the mountain. But why do we say these things, when we know greater ones? For what is more pleasant than Paradise? What is safer than heaven? And yet man from Paradise and an angel from heaven fell by sinning. Likewise Gregory. These are not Gregory's own words, but collected from Gregory by Gratian; their sense is found in the first chapter of book 9, at the end of chapter 12 of book 26, and chapter 12 of book 35 on Job.

units.la: Nobili deiiciendus est loco, qui moribus ignobilis est.
units.tr: One must be cast down from a noble place who is ignoble in morals.

units.la: ADam primus homo pro peccato de Paradiso eiectus est. Hoc est, Quia Dei nobilitatem a se deiecit, nobilitate loci priuatus est. Item. Chrysostomus Homil. 43. ad cap. 23. Matthaei. In Homiliae principio. Exponens illud——Super Cathedram Moysi, &c.
units.tr: Adam, the first man, was cast out of Paradise because of sin. That is, because he cast the nobility of God out of himself, he was deprived of the nobility of place. Likewise Chrysostom, Homily 43 on Matthew chapter 23, at the beginning of the homily, expounding that passage: "Upon the seat of Moses," etc.

units.la: Non est verus Sacerdos, quisquis nominatur Sacerdos.
units.tr: He is not a true priest who is merely named priest.

units.la: MVlti Sacerdotes, & pauci Sacerdotes. Multi nomine, Pauci opere. Videte ergo, quomodo sedeatis super Cathedram: quia non Cathedra facit Sacerdotem, sed Sacerdos Cathedram. Nō locus sanctificat hominem, sed homo locum. Non omnis Sacerdos, Sanctus est. Sed omnis Sanctus, Sacerdos. Qui bene sederit super Cathedram, honorem accipiet ab illa: Qui male sederit, iniuriam facit Cathedræ. Ideóque malus Sacerdos de Sacerdotio suo crimen acquirit, non dignitatem. In iudicio enim sedens, Si quidem bene dixeris, & bene docueris, omnium iudex es: si autem bene docueris, & malè vixeris, tui solius condemnator es: Nam bene viuendo, & bene docendo, populum instruis, quomodo viuere debeat. Bene autem docendo, & malè viuendo, Deum instruis, quomodo te debeat condemnare. Idem Chrysostomus. Homilia.35. Exponens illud Matthæi: Scitis,quòd Principes Gentium,&c.cap.10.
units.tr: Many are priests, and few are priests: many in name, few in deed. See therefore how you sit upon the chair, for it is not the chair that makes the priest, but the priest who makes the chair. Place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place. Not every priest is holy, but every holy man is a priest. He who sits well upon the chair will receive honour from it; he who sits badly does injury to the chair. Therefore a bad priest acquires guilt from his priesthood, not dignity. For sitting in judgement: if indeed you speak well and teach well, you are judge of all; but if you teach well and live badly, you are the condemner of yourself alone. For by living well and teaching well you instruct the people how they ought to live; but by teaching well and living badly you instruct God how he ought to condemn you. Likewise Chrysostom, Homily 35, expounding that of Matthew: "You know that the princes of the Gentiles," etc., chapter 10.

units.la: Non Ecclesiæ gradus, sed quæ gradum decent, ab Ecclesiasticis quæri debent.
units.tr: Church ranks are not to be sought from churchmen; rather, what befits each rank should be sought from them.

units.la: QVicunque desiderat primatum cœlestem, sequatur humilitatem terrestrem. Quicunque autem desiderat Primatum in terra, inueniet confusionem in cœlo: Vt iam inter seruos Christi non sit de primatu certamen. (Unde, infert Gratianus) Nec inter seruos Christi computabitur, qui de primatu tractauerit. (Exinde Chrysostomus) Nec vnusquisque eorum festinet, quomodo aliis maior appareat, sed quomodo omnibus inferior videatur: quoniam, non qui maior fuerit in honore, ille est iustior: sed qui fuerit iustior, ille maior. Conuersatio ergo melior est desideranda, non dignior gradus. Quæ Gratianus in hanc totam distinctionem congessit, ad interiora duntaxat mentis ornamenta pertinent, vti videtis. Illa quidem plus omnibus necessaria: Verùm, nulla ne cura Clericis habenda est, de cultu corporis exteriore? Et habendam certè docet ipsius Apostoli verbum, κόσμεῖ. Hominem modestum, bene moratum, moribus, videlicet, bene compositis, honestum, moderatum significans. Denotat etiam cultum, cultum, bene paratum: refertúrque ad habitum, sine amictum corporis. 1. Timoth. cap.2. ὡσαύτως καὶ τὰς γυναῖκας ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ. Similiter & mulieres in habitu ornato Sic enim vetus interpres. Interius ergo maximè curandum, sed exterius minimè negligendum. Iam de Gratiano.
units.tr: Whoever desires the heavenly primacy, let him follow earthly humility. But whoever desires primacy on earth will find confusion in heaven, so that among the servants of Christ there should be no contest about primacy. (Hence Gratian infers:) Nor shall he be counted among the servants of Christ who has treated of primacy. (Then Chrysostom:) Let none of them hasten to appear greater than the rest, but to seem inferior to all; for it is not the one who is greater in honour who is more just, but the one who is more just who is greater. A better way of life, therefore, is to be desired, not a more worthy rank. What Gratian has gathered into this whole distinction, as you see, pertains only to the inner adornments of the mind. Those are indeed more necessary than all else. But should clerics have no concern at all for the outward appearance of the body? The Apostle's own word teaches that they certainly should, κόσμεῖ [kosmei, "in an orderly way"]. It signifies a man who is modest, well-mannered, honourable and restrained, that is, of well-ordered conduct. It also denotes adornment, being well prepared, and it refers to dress or the clothing of the body. 1 Timothy 2: ὡσαύτως καὶ τὰς γυναῖκας ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ [hōsautōs kai tas gynaikas en katastolē kosmiōi, "likewise also the women in modest apparel"]. Thus the old translator renders it: "Likewise also women in ornate habit." Therefore the inner life is above all to be cared for, but the outer is by no means to be neglected. So much for Gratian.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLI.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XLI.

units.la: Gratianus. ECCE, Quibus oporteat Sacerdotem esse ornatum moribus.
units.tr: Gratian. Behold, with what morals a priest ought to be adorned.

units.la: Sed præterea, Oportet illum esse ornatum in exterioribus, habitu, videlicet, & incessu. Habitu, ut nec fulgidis, nec sordidis se vestibus ornet. Ut enim ait Hieronymus. Ad Nepotianum, De vita Clericorum. Et ad Eustochium. De custo. Virg.
units.tr: Moreover, he ought to be adorned in outward things, namely in dress and in bearing. As to dress, he should adorn himself neither with showy nor with squalid garments, as Jerome says. To Nepotianus, On the Life of Clerics; and to Eustochium, On Keeping Virginity.

units.la: NEc affectatæ sordes, nec exquisitæ delitiæ laudes pa- riunt.
units.tr: Neither affected squalor nor sought-after luxury wins praise.

units.la: Quod tam de vestibus, quàm de cibis intelligendum est. Vnde Augustinus ait in libro 3. cap. 12. De doctrina Christiana. To. 3.
units.tr: This must be understood of clothing as much as of food. Hence Augustine says in book 3, chapter 12 of On Christian Doctrine, vol. 3:

units.la: In omni vsu rerum oportet abesse libidinem, hoc est, Effrenatam cupiditatem, voluntatemque, aduersa ratione suscepta. Sic enim Cicero definit Libidinem. Tusc. 4. Quæ (ut ait) in omnibus stultis inuenitur.
units.tr: In every use of things, lust must be absent, that is, unbridled desire and will taken up against right reason. For thus Cicero defines lust, in the Tusculan Disputations, book 4, where (as he says) it is found in all fools.

units.la: Quisquis rebus prætereuntibus restrictius vtitur, quàm sese habent mores eorum, cum quibus viuit: aut Temperans, aut Superstitiosus est. Quisquis verò sic eis vtitur, vt metas consuetudinis bonorum, inter quos versatur, excedat: aut aliquid significat: aut flagitiosus est. In omnibus enim talibus non vsus rerum, sed vtentis libido in culpa est. Quod igitur locis, & temporibus, & personis conueniat, diligenter attendendum est, ne temerè flagitia reprehendamus. Fieri enim potest, vt sine aliquo vitio cupidinis, vel voracitatis, preciosissimo cibo Sapiens vtatur: insipiens autem fœdissimâ gulæ flammâ in vilissimum ardescat. Et sanus quisque malluerit, more domini, pisce vesci, quàm lenticulâ, more Esau nepotis Abrahæ: Aut ordeo, more iumentorum. Non enim propterea continentiores nobis sunt pleraque bestiæ, quia vilioribus aluntur escis. Nam in omnibus huiuscemodi rebus, non ex earum rerum natura, quibus vtimur, sed ex causa utendi, & modo appetendi, vel probandum est, vel improbandum, quod facimus.
units.tr: Whoever uses passing things more strictly than the customs of those among whom he lives require is either temperate or superstitious. Whoever uses them so as to go beyond the bounds of custom among the good people with whom he dwells either makes a display or is wicked. For in all such cases the fault lies not in the use of things but in the desire of the one using them. Therefore one must attend carefully to what agrees with places, times and persons, lest we rashly censure faults. For it can happen that a wise man, without any vice of desire or greed, uses very costly food, while a fool burns with the most foul flame of gluttony for the cheapest. And any sane person would rather eat fish, like the Lord, than lentil stew, like Esau the grandson of Abraham, or barley, like beasts of burden. For many beasts are not on that account more self-controlled than we, because they are fed on coarser food. Indeed, in all things of this kind, what we do is to be approved or disapproved not by the nature of the things we use but by the purpose of using them and the manner of desiring them.

units.la: Item. Augustinus super Epistolam Ioannis. Augustini quidem sententia est, ab eo non semel scripta. Sed quo in loco sint hæc verba, non inueni. Certè non sunt in commentariis à Gratiano citatis, in Epistolam Ioannis Tom. 9. Præcipuè legas Augustinum cap. 31. libri 10. confess. Et de moribus Manichæorum cap. 11. libri 2. Tomo. 1.
units.tr: Likewise. Augustine, on his Epistle of John. The sentiment is indeed Augustine's, and he wrote it more than once, but I have not found in what place these words stand. Certainly they are not in the commentaries on the Epistle of John cited by Gratian, vol. 9. Chiefly you should read Augustine, On the Confessions book 10, chapter 31, and On the Morals of the Manichaeans, book 2, chapter 11, vol. 1.

units.la: Non est cibus in vituperatione, sed luxus.
units.tr: The fault lies not in food but in luxury.

units.la: DElicia quaelibet, si absque desiderio percipiantur, non officiunt. Et viles cibi appetenter accepti impediunt profectum abstinentiae. Dauid enim aquam male concupitam effudit: & Helias carnes comedit.
units.tr: Any delicacies, if they are received without desire, do no harm; and cheap foods, if taken greedily, hinder progress in abstinence. For David poured out water that he had desired wrongly, and Elijah ate flesh.

units.la: Idem. Augustinus in libro De verbis Domini, sermone 5. secundum Matthaeum, ad finem sermonis. To.10. More suo & immutat, & transmutat authoris verba.
units.tr: Again. Augustine, in his book On the Words of the Lord, sermon 5 on Matthew, at the end of the sermon, vol. 10. In his usual way he both alters and transposes the author's words.

units.la: Ad cuiusuis abstinentiam cibi, nemo contra valetudinis suae rationem cogitur.
units.tr: No one is compelled, against the reasoning of his own health, to abstain from any food.

units.la: NOn cogantur divites pauperum cibis vesci, ut tantur consuetudine infirmitatis suae, sed doleant aliter se non posse. Si consuetudinem mutant, aegrotant. Vtantur superfluis, dent inopibus necessaria. Vtantur preciosis, dent pauperibus vilia. Idem. In lib. 2. quaestionum Euangeliorum, quaest. 11. Tomo 4.
units.tr: Let not the rich be compelled to eat the food of the poor, so that they lose the habit of their own weakness; rather let them grieve that they cannot do otherwise. If they change their habit, they fall ill. Let them use what is superfluous and give the needy what is necessary. Let them use costly things and give the poor cheap things. Same author, in book 2 of the Questions on the Gospels, question 11, vol. 4.

units.la: Abstinentia vera est, Non cibis & potu carere, sed aequanimiter posse carere.
units.tr: True abstinence is not to be without food and drink, but to be able to go without them with an equable mind.

units.la: QVod dicit Dominus in Euangelio, Iustificata est Sapientia ab omnibus filiis suis. Ostendit filios Sapientiae intelligere, nec in abstinendo, nec in manducando esse iustitiam, sed in aequanimitate tolerandi inopiam: & in temperantia, per abundantiam non se corrumpendi: atque opportune sumendi, vel non sumedi ea, quorum non usus, sed concupiscentia reprehendenda est. Non enim interest omnino, quid alimentorum sumas, ut succurras necessitati corporis: dummodo congruas in generibus alimentorum, his, cum quibus tibi viuendum est. Neque quantum sumas, interest multum: cum videamus aliorum stomachum citius satiari: & eos tamen illi ipsi parvo, quo satiantur, ardenter & intolerabiliter, & omnino turpiter inhiare: Alios autem, plusculo quidem satiari, sed tolerabilius inopiam perpeti: vel ante ora positas epulas (si id in tempore, aut opus sit, aut necesse sit) cum tranquillitate aspicere, neque tangere. Magis ergo interest, non quid, vel quantum alimentorum, pro congruentia hominum, atque personae suae, & pro suae valetudinis necessitate, quis capiat: sed quanta facilitate & serenitate animi careat, cum his vel oportet, vel etiam necesse est carere: ut illud in animo Christiani compleat, quod Apostolus dicit: Scio & minus habere: scio & abundare in omnibus: & in omnibus imbutus sum, & satiari, & esurire, & abundare, & penuriam pati. Omnia possum in eo, qui me confortat.
units.tr: What the Lord says in the Gospel, "Wisdom is justified by all her children," shows that the children of Wisdom understand that righteousness lies neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in bearing want with an equable mind, and in temperance, not being corrupted by abundance, and in taking or not taking at the right time those things whose mere use, rather than desire, is to be censured. For it makes no great difference what kind of food you take to supply the needs of the body, provided that it agrees with the kinds of food of those among whom you must live. Nor does it matter greatly how much you take, since we see that the stomachs of others are satisfied more quickly, and yet those same people gape eagerly, intolerably and utterly shamefully at the little with which they are satisfied; while others, satisfied with a somewhat larger amount, bear want more patiently, or look calmly at a feast set before them, and do not touch it, when it is timely or necessary to do so. Therefore it matters more not what or how much food a person takes, in keeping with his own fitness, his person and the needs of his health, but with how much ease and serenity of mind he goes without those things with which he must, or even necessarily must, do without. Thus the Christian fulfils in his heart what the Apostle says: "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me."

units.la: Item. Ex Concilio Gangrensi. Ista fuit adversus Armeniae quendam Monachum Eustachium Synodi conclusio: non annumerata 20. Canonibus illius Synodi, quam totam prolixioribus commentariolis nuper explicavimus. Non satis appositè reddita mihi Graeca videntur huius initio Canonis. In quo sic legitur.
units.tr: Likewise. From the Council of Gangra. This was the conclusion of the Synod against a certain monk of Armenia, Eustathius; it is not counted among the twenty canons of that Synod, which I have recently explained in full in fairly lengthy little commentaries. The Greek of the opening of this canon seems to me not rendered quite aptly. In it one reads thus:

units.la: Ἀπότηα, ὁ δὲ πέλεαν ἀμφιασμάτων, ... τὰς δὲ ἐκ λύτους, ἡ πεφυμηλίας ἐν τῇ ἑαυτῶν ποιόδος, οὐκ ἀχρεῖ χόμεθα.
units.tr: Ἀπότηα, ὁ δὲ πέλεαν ἀμφιασμάτων, ... τὰς δὲ ἐκ λύτους, ἡ πεφυμηλίας ἐν τῇ ἑαυτῶν ποιόδος, οὐκ ἀχρεῖ χόμεθα. [Greek text as printed, corrupted in the scan]

units.la: Id est.
units.tr: That is:

units.la: Simplicitatem, vilitatémque vestimentorum, ad curam solùm corporis, non accuratam nec exquisitā, comprobamus. Sed absumptas & attritas in vestibus progressiones (id est, ut autumo, in publicum prodire, velut ad ostentationem, cum vestibus laceris atque dissutis) non recipimus.
units.tr: We approve simplicity and cheapness of clothing, directed only to care for the body, not careful or elaborate. But we do not admit garments worn out and threadbare, or ostentatious display (that is, as I suppose, appearing in public, as if for show, in torn and ragged clothes).

units.la: In qualicunque veste, vel victu non est virtus, aut religio constituenda.
units.tr: Virtue or piety is not to be placed in any clothing or food whatever.

units.la: PArsimoniam, cum veste humili, non reprobamus: sicut etiam ornatum praeter corporis diligentiam infucatum laudamus: dissolutos autem & fractos vestibus & incessu non recipimus. Quae postea sequuntur in Canone, sunt à proposito diversa, nec satis fideliter versa.
units.tr: We do not condemn frugality with humble clothing, just as we also praise adornment that, apart from care for the body, is unpainted; but we do not admit those who are slack and feeble in their dress and bearing. What follows in the canon is different from the purpose here and not rendered quite faithfully.

units.la: Apostolicas, Ecclesiasticúsque Paradoseis, in templis extrucndu, in precibus vbiuis locorum fundendis, in populi con uentibus habendis, in pauperibus fratribus subleuandis, in omnibus denique rebus obseruare iubemus.
units.tr: We order that the Apostolic and Ecclesiastical traditions be observed in building churches, in pouring out prayers in every place, in holding the assemblies of the people, in relieving poor brothers, and in short in all things.

units.la: § Pietatem in priuatis domibus non includentes, omnem locum in nomine Dei aedificatum honoramus. Et congregationem in Ecclesia Dei factam ad utilitatem communem recipimus. Et bona opera, quae supra vires in fratres pauperes exercentur, secundum Ecclesiasticas traditiones beatificamus: & omnia quae conueniunt traditionibus Apostolicis, & Sanctarum scripturarum praeceptis, in Ecclesia fieri exoptamus. Item. Gregorius, Epist. 24. lib. 1.
units.tr: § Not confining piety to private houses, we honour every place built in the name of God, and we receive the gathering made in the Church of God for the common good. And good works that are performed for poor brothers beyond their strength we commend according to the ecclesiastical traditions; and we desire that everything which agrees with the apostolic traditions and the precepts of the holy Scriptures be done in the Church. Likewise. Gregory, Epistle 24, book 1.

units.la: Decipimur specie recti. Vitiis enim suis, & erroribus homines imponunt frequenter nomen honestum, sicut est in quodam Poeta.
units.tr: We are deceived by the appearance of right. For men often impose an honourable name on their vices and errors, as is found in a certain poet.

units.la: SÆpe se vitia ingerunt, & se virtutes esse mentiuntur: ut Tenacitas, Parsimonia. Effusio, Largitas. Crudelitas, Zelus iustitiae. Remissio, Pietas velit videri. Item. Ex Concilio Cartha. 4. cap 14. & 15.
units.tr: Vices often thrust themselves in and pretend to be virtues: as tenacity passes for thrift; effusion for generosity; cruelty for zeal for justice; slackness wishes to be seen as piety. Likewise. From the Council of Carthage, book 4, chapters 14 and 15.

units.la: Non aulico fastu, sed Euangelico ritu: Non vana regum sublimitate, sed vera Christi humilitate viuere simpliciter Christi Sacerdotes oportet.
units.tr: Christ's priests ought to live simply, not with courtly pomp but with the Gospel manner, not with the empty loftiness of kings but with the true humility of Christ.

units.la: EPiscopus vilem suppellectilem, & mensam, ac victum pauperem habeat: & dignitatis suae authoritatem, fidei & vitae meritis quaerat. Hospitium quoque non longe ab Ecclesia habeat. Item. Ex eodem cap. 45.
units.tr: A bishop should have humble furnishings, a table and a poor fare, and he should seek the authority of his dignity from the merits of his faith and life. He should also have a lodging not far from the Church. Likewise. From the same, chapter 45.

units.la: CLericus professionem suam, & habitu, & incessu probet: & ideo nec vestibus, nec calciamentis decore quaerat.
units.tr: A cleric should show his profession both in his dress and in his bearing, and therefore should seek decorum neither in his clothes nor in his shoes.

units.la: Ex praedictis colligit, Gratianus SICVT ergo in cibis mores eorum, cum quibus viuimus, obseruare monemur: sic & de indumentis intelligendum est. vt enim alibi dicitur.
units.tr: From the foregoing, Gratian gathers: Just as we are advised to observe the customs of those among whom we live in regard to food, so it must be understood of clothing too. For as is said elsewhere:

units.la: QVisquis contemptis his cum quibus viuit, lautiora sibi, vel austeriora prae caeteris indumenta, vel alimenta quærit: aut Intemperans est: aut Superstitiosus est.
units.tr: Whoever, despising those with whom he lives, seeks for himself more elegant or more austere clothing or food than others are ? Is either intemperate or superstitious.

units.la: Gratianus. IN incessu autem debet esse Sacerdos ornatus: Vt gravitate itineris, mētis maturitatem ostendat. Incompositio enim corporis (vt Augustinus ait) inæqualitatem indicat mentis. Vnde historiographus ille. (Salustius in principio Catilinarij belli.) QVVM eius mutabilitatem describeret, cuius conscientia excitata curis mentem vastabat: inter cætera hoc etiā notabile indicauit dicens.
units.tr: Gratian. Moreover, a priest ought to be dignified in his gait, so that the seriousness of his walk shows the maturity of his mind. For bodily disorder (as Augustine says) indicates unevenness of mind. Hence that historian, Sallust, at the beginning of the Catilinarian War, when he was describing the changeableness of a man whose conscience, roused by anxieties, was laying waste his mind, noted among other things this also, saying:

units.la: Incessus eius modò citus, modò tardus.
units.tr: His gait was now quick, now slow.

units.la: Ad aliud (quod Sextum est) Episcopale schema progreditur Gratianus, in quo sic est.
units.tr: Gratian next proceeds to the sixth episcopal dress, in which he says as follows.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLII.
units.tr: Distinction 42.

units.la: ΔΕΙ ΤΟΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΞΕΝΟΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ.
units.tr: The bishop must be a lover of strangers [Φιλόξενον εἶναι δεῖ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον].

units.la: ξένος appellatur quiuis aduena, peregrinus, & externus. Φιλόξενος Amator hospitum, aduenarum, & quorumque peregrinorum. Latinis appellatur, Hospitalis, ptus & liberalis est ad omnium susceptionem & tractationem, qui peregrē veniunt. Sultaxat erga suos, aut indigenas, & amicos hospitalis esset Episcopus, affectu laborat: ut esset (quod esse iubetur) Philoxenus. Ignotis & alienis egentibus debet Hospitalitatis officium. quod ita Gratianus probat.
units.tr: Xenos is the name for any stranger, foreigner, or outsider. Philoxenos means a lover of guests, of strangers, and of any foreigners whatever [Φιλόξενος]. In Latin it is called hospitable, and it means generous and open in receiving and entertaining all who come as strangers. If a bishop were hospitable only toward his own people, or natives and friends, he would labour under partiality. So he should be (as he is commanded to be) a philoxenos. He owes the duty of hospitality to strangers and to needy outsiders. Gratian proves this as follows.

units.la: Benignitas, id est, Liberalitas & beneficentia, præstandique facilitas (Haec est Hospitalitas) imperatur Sacerdotibus. Hoc rationibus aliquot, & exemplis Gratianus probat, inquiens. HOSPITALEM verò Sacerdotem esse oportet: ne sit de numero eorum, quibus in iudicio dicetur: Hospes fui, & non suscepistis me. In certos Canones redegimus sequentia, quæ Gratianus ex incertis authoribus compilauit.
units.tr: Kindness, that is, liberality and beneficence, and readiness to give (this is hospitality), is enjoined on priests. Gratian proves this by several reasons and examples, saying: A priest ought to be hospitable, lest he be of the number of those to whom it will be said at judgment: I was a guest and you did not receive me. We have reduced the following, which Gratian compiled from uncertain authors, into definite canons.

units.la: Euangelicus vir, primus faciat, quod aliis faciendum præ dicat.
units.tr: Let the evangelical man first do what he preaches that others should do.

units.la: QVi secutus Apostolum fuerit, Alios ad Hospitalitatem debet inuitare. Quomodo autem Hospitalitatis exhortator esse poterit, qui domum propriam Hospitibus claudit? Si enim Sacerdos, primùm àseipso, & à domestica sua Ecclesia debet exigere, quod postea populis imperet: Si primùm, imitando Christum, debet ipse facere, quæ postea populum doceat: necesse est, vt pauperes Hospitio primus recipiat, quò ad Hospitalitatem facilius suo exemplo subditos attrahat.
units.tr: He who has followed the Apostle ought to invite others to hospitality. But how can he be an exhorter to hospitality who shuts his own house against guests? For if a priest must first demand of himself and of his own household what he afterwards commands the people, and if he must first do himself, imitating Christ, what he afterwards teaches the people, then it is necessary that he first receive the poor into his hospitality, so that by his own example he may more easily draw his subjects to hospitality.

units.la: Sacerdos esse debet imitator eorum, qui fide, patientia, (nunc addo) benignitate promissiones haereditaverunt. ad Heb. 6. vbi proponitur, vt hic, Abraham in exemplum.
units.tr: A priest ought to be an imitator of those who through faith and patience, and (I now add) through kindness, have inherited the promises. Heb. 6, where Abraham is set forth as the example, as here.

units.la: ORdinandus itaque Sacerdos ad memoriam revocet, quomodo Abraham, & Loth per Hospitalitatis opera, Deo placere, & Angelos hospitio meruerunt recipere: & quomodo Angeli Sodomis hospitalem domum ingressi, Loth cum familia sua liberaverunt: Et clausas domos hospitibus, ignis ingressus perdiderit.
units.tr: Therefore the man being ordained should call to mind how Abraham and Lot, by works of hospitality, merited to please God and to receive angels as guests; and how the angels, entering the hospitable house at Sodom, delivered Lot with his family, while fire destroyed the houses that were closed to guests.

units.la: Sacerdotem non largiri Eleemosynas, perinde est, ac aliena rapere, & impium profite esse: quisquis vero talis est, reiiciendus est, vt αποβλης. de quo Paulus hic.
units.tr: For a priest not to bestow alms is just the same as seizing what belongs to others and professing impiety. Whoever is such is to be rejected as an outcast [ἀπόβλητος], which is what Paul speaks of here.

units.la: QVomodo etiam (secundum Hieronymum) Aliena rapere convincitur, qui ultra necessaria sibi retinere probatur. Ac sic, per omnia pietatis opera se instituat, ut praesentis vitae subsidia, & aeternae claritatis praemia, à Deo percipiat. utrumque enim pietati promittitur. Unde Apostolus scribens ad Timotheum ait: Exerce teipsum ad pietatem. Nam corporalis quidem exercitatio ad modicum utilis est. Pietas autem est utilis ad omnia, habens promissionem vitae, quae nunc est, & futurae. Ab hac quisquis alienus fuerit, in Sacerdotem ordinari non poterit. Si enim vidua ab Ecclesia recipi prohibetur, quae pauperes non recepit hospitio, quae pedes sanctorum non lauit, quae omne opus bonum non est executa: multo magis sunt prohibendi à Sacerdotio, qui ab opere pietatis probantur alieni. Vnde. Quidam Hospitalitatis opera despicientes, in Gangrenensi concilio excommunicantur. sic enim in eo statutum est. cap. 11.
units.tr: Likewise (according to Jerome), he is convicted of seizing what belongs to others who is shown to keep for himself more than he needs. And so let him train himself in all the works of piety, that he may receive from God the supports of the present life and the rewards of eternal glory, for both are promised to piety. Hence the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: Exercise yourself unto godliness; for bodily exercise profits little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. Whoever is a stranger to this cannot be ordained a priest. For if a widow is forbidden to be received by the Church if she has not received the poor in hospitality, has not washed the feet of the saints, and has not carried out every good work, then much more are those to be kept from the priesthood who are proved strangers to the works of piety. Hence: some who despised the works of hospitality were excommunicated at the Council of Gangra; for so it was decreed there, canon 11.

units.la: Anathema contemnenti fraternae charitatis Symbola.
units.tr: Anathema against one who despises the symbols of fraternal charity.

units.la: SI quis despicit eos, qui * fideliter Agapas [id est coniuvia pauperum] exhibent: & propter honorem Domini conuocant Fratres: & noluerit communicare huiusmodi conuocationibus, † parui pendens quod geritur, Anathema sit.
units.tr: If anyone despises those who faithfully hold agapes [that is, feasts for the poor], and who for the honour of the Lord summon the brethren, and refuses to take part in such gatherings, esteeming lightly what is done, let him be anathema.

units.la: φιλαπτωτικών διστεφης non est ordinandus. Nec enim solent eius generis homines esse φιλόξενοι Gratianus.
units.tr: A man who is a lover of gain [φιλαπτωτικός] and double-minded [διστεφής] must not be ordained. For men of that kind are not usually lovers of strangers [φιλόξενοι]. Gratian.

units.la: HInc etiam Ioannes Euangelista in Epistola sua tertia, quendam Diotrephen excommunicauit: qui nec pauperes recipiebat, & recipientes, de Ecclesia deiiciebat.
units.tr: Here also the Evangelist John, in his third Epistle, excommunicated a certain Diotrephes, who did not receive the poor, and who cast out of the Church those who did receive them.

units.la: Gratianus. I N Hospitalitate autem non est habendus delectus personarum: sed indifferenter, quibuscunque sufficimus, Hospitales nos exhibere debemus. Vnde Ioannes Chrysostomus, Homil. 11. ad cap. 6. Epist ad Hebraeos.
units.tr: Gratian. In hospitality, however, there should be no selection of persons; rather we ought to show ourselves hospitable indifferently to whomever we are able. Hence John Chrysostom, Homily 11 on Hebrews, on chapter 6.

units.la: Vtinam Diotrephen quempiam (quando iam soli tales opima rodunt Ecclesiae Christus excitet, qui Graecis omnibus aedendis Episcopi tanti scriptis agat Philoxenum. Nam magno talium dedecore (sed erubescere nescinnt) maximo studiosorum damno peregrinantur apud nos.
units.tr: Would that God would raise up some Diotrephes (since now only such men devour the rich revenues of the Church), who, with all the Greek writings to be published, would act as such a bishop, a Philoxenus! For with great shame to such men (but they do not know how to blush), and to the great loss of scholars, strangers wander among us.

units.la: Nullis transeuntibus peregrinis Eleemosyna denegari debet.
units.tr: No alms should be denied to any passing strangers.

units.la: QViescamus ab hac absurda curiositate, & diabolica, & perniciosa. Si enim in Clero se electum esse dicat, si Sacerdotem se nominet, Scrutare: non enim sine periculo in talibus indiscussa communicatio est. Circa maiora periculum vertitur: non enim das, sed accipis. Si vero pro nutrimento postulat, nihil examines: Inquire quomodo Abraham Hospitalitate, circa omnes transeuntes ostendebat: si scrutator fuisset circa refugientes ad se, nunquam Angelos Hospitio recepisset: fortasis enim, non putans eos Angelos esse, cum reliquis repulisset: sed quoniam omnes recipiebat, suscepit & angelos. Non enim ex vita eorum, quos accipis, mercedem tibi retributurus est Deus: sed ex voluntate tua, & liberalitate multa, ex misericordia, ex bonitate. Gratianus. S E D, Licet ipsa conuiuia despicienda non sint, tamen non in Ecclesiis celebrari, nec Clericos ad ea conuocatos, partes ex eis sibi tollere oportet. Vnde in Laodicensi Concilio, cap. 17. & cap. 18.
units.tr: Let us abstain from this absurd, diabolical and pernicious curiosity. For if a man says that he has been chosen into the clergy, if he calls himself a priest, do not examine him, for in such matters communication without inquiry is not free from danger. The greater danger lies with the one who gives, for you are not giving but receiving. But if he asks for sustenance, examine nothing. Consider how Abraham showed hospitality to all who passed by. Had he been an inquisitor about those who fled to him, he would never have received the angels as guests; perhaps, not thinking them to be angels, he would have repulsed them with the rest. But since he received all, he also welcomed the angels. For God will reward you not according to the lives of those you receive, but according to your will and generosity, your mercy and goodness. Gratian. BUT, although the feasts themselves are not to be despised, yet they should not be celebrated in churches, nor should clerics invited to them take portions of them for themselves. Hence in the Council of Laodicea, canons 17 and 18.

units.la: Ex Agape nullus accumbentium partem praesumat. Sed nec in aede sacra prabeatur ἀγάπη.
units.tr: No one reclining at an agape should presume to take a portion. Nor should an agape be offered in the sacred building [ἀγάπη].

units.la: NOn oportet †altaris Ministros, vel Clericos, aut Laicos, ad Agápen vocatos, partes tollere: propter iniuriam quae ex hac occasione Ecclesiastico ordini poterit †deputari.
units.tr: Ministers of the altar, or clerics, or laymen invited to an agape, ought not to take portions, because of the injury which may be imputed to the ecclesiastical order on this occasion.

units.la: Item. Mox ibidem.
units.tr: Likewise. Immediately afterwards in the same place.

units.la: NOn oportet † in Basilicis, vel in Ecclesiis, Agápen facere: & † intus manducare † vel accubitus sternere. Item. Ex Concilio Carthaginensi. Conciliorum Carthaginensium Graecorum conscriptorum, Canon praesens est quadragesimus secundus. In editis Latine Concilii est trigesimus Concilij tertij Carthag. habiti Casario, & Attico Coss. Hoc est. Anno salutis 398.
units.tr: Agapes ought not to be held in basilicas or in churches, nor should people eat within them or spread couches there. Likewise, from the Council of Carthage. The present canon is the forty-second of the Greek Carthaginian councils as written down; in the Latin edition it is the thirtieth of the third Council of Carthage, held in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus. That is, in the year of salvation 398.

units.la: Qui domos habent, in templo Dei nec edere nec bibere debent. 1. ad Corinth. 7.
units.tr: Those who have houses ought not to eat or drink in the temple of God. 1 Cor. 7.

units.la: NVlli Episcopi, vel clerici in Ecclesia conuiuentur: nisi forte transeuntes, hospitiorum necessitate, † illic reficientur. Populi etiam ab huiusmodi conuiuijs (quantum potest fieri) prohibeantur. Item. Ex dictis beati Benedicti Abbatis. Ex cap. 19. De disciplina psallendi. Et ex cap. 20. De reverentia orationis. In regula S. Benedicti. Canon praesens elici potest.
units.tr: No bishops or clerics should be entertained in the church, unless perhaps passing travellers, from necessity of lodging, are refreshed there. The people too should be kept, as far as can be done, from such feasts. Likewise, from the sayings of the blessed Abbot Benedict, chapter 19 (On the discipline of psalmody) and chapter 20 (On reverence in prayer), in the Rule of St Benedict. The present canon may be drawn from these.

units.la: Domus Dei, domus est orationis, non alterius cuiusuis actionis. Io. 2.
units.tr: The house of God is a house of prayer, not of any other activity. John 2.

units.la: ORatorium, hoc sit, quod dicitur: nec ibi quicquam aliud geratur, vel tradatur, quàm quod diuinis laudibus conueniat. Item. Augustinus Epist. 109. ad Monachas.
units.tr: An oratory, that is what it is called: nothing else should be done or handed on there except what befits divine praises. Likewise, Augustine, Letter 109, to the nuns.

units.la: Quamquam non sic legatur in Augustino, sed est.
units.tr: Although this is not so read in Augustine, yet it is his meaning.

units.la: In Oratorio nemo aliquid agat, nisi ad quod est factum: unde & nomen accepit.
units.tr: In an oratory let no one do anything except that for which it was made; hence it also took its name.

units.la: IN oratorio, praeter orandi & psallendi cultum, penitus nihil agatur: Vt huic nomini & opera iugiter impensa concordent. Dictum satis de Hospitalitate, Gentilium quoque literis commendata virtute. Iam se Gratianus alibi vertit, explicans Apostolum, qui septimo loco inbet Episcopum esse.
units.tr: In the oratory, apart from the worship of prayer and psalmody, absolutely nothing is to be done, so that the works constantly carried on there agree with the name. Enough has been said about hospitality, a virtue commended also in the writings of the Gentiles. Now Gratian turns to another matter, explaining the Apostle, who in the seventh place bids that a bishop be...

units.la: ΔΙΔΑΚΤΙΚΟΝ.
units.tr: Didaktikon [διδακτικόν]

units.la: Huius loci versio duplex erat annis Hieronymi, quaedam, Docilem transferebat. Hanc ipse taxat, & Latinam simplicitatem vocat, id est, non satis aptam Latinitatem, libro contra Pelagianos primo. Quo in loco διδακτικὸν idem vertit, Qui docere possit, quae vera est significatio vocis. Nam διδακτικὸς est appositus, paratus, aptus ad docendum. Docibilem dixerunt 2. ad Timoth. cap. 2. Secunda versio διδακτικὸν, Doctorem dicebat. Hanc ille sequitur primo contra Iovinianum libro. Et in fine Epistolae ad Oceanum, quae nostra quoque vulgaris est, atque recepta. Qualitas una Christianis Episcopis maxime propria. De qua Sanctus ille Doctor Episcoporum legatur in locis modo citatis. Alios quosdam citantem Gratianum videamus.
units.tr: In Jerome's time this passage had two Latin versions. One, which rendered it "docile" [docilem], Jerome himself criticises and calls "plain Latin" [Latinam simplicitatem], that is, a Latin that is not quite apt, in his first book against the Pelagians. In that place he renders διδακτικόν as "able to teach" [Qui docere possit], which is the true meaning of the word, for διδακτικός means fit, ready and apt for teaching. The Latin "docile" [docibilem] is used in 2 Timothy, chapter 2. The second version rendered διδακτικόν as "teacher" [Doctorem]. Jerome follows this in the first book against Jovinian, and at the end of his letter to Oceanus, which is also in our common and accepted edition. It is a quality especially proper to Christian bishops. That holy doctor's views on bishops may be read in the passages just cited. Let us see what Gratian cites from other authors.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XXXXIII.
units.tr: Distinction 43.

units.la: Gratianus. PVDICVS quoque debet esse Sacerdos, Ut & moribus, & verbis pudorem indesinenter exhibeat. Unde in Canticis Canticorum, Genas sponsae, id est, Praedicatores, Turturi comparantur. Quod in principio De Sacerdotali pudicitia, hoc est, de religiosa quadam puritate atque munditia repetit hic Gratianus, pertinet ad sex primas Eucrinias abunde superius elucidatas. Quare modo non aliud afferam, quam quod, Dei Sacerdotes oportet σώφρονα, id est, quacunque pudica, non solum facere, sed etiam cogitare. ad Philip. cap. 4. Nedum manibus, sed oculis quoque, vittu, vestitu continentes esse. Qua fuit Atheniensis cuiusdam Praetoris (Periclis, ut puto) de quibuscunque Magistratibus sententia. Iam de Presbyterorum doctrina.
units.tr: Gratian. The priest too ought to be chaste, so that he constantly shows modesty both in his conduct and in his words. Hence in the Song of Songs the cheeks of the bride, that is, the preachers, are compared to a turtledove. What Gratian here repeats at the beginning of the section on priestly chastity, that is, a certain religious purity and cleanness, relates to the six first Eucrinias, which were explained at length above. So I will add only this: the priests of God ought to be σώφρονες [sōphrones], that is, modest in every way, not only in action but also in thought (Philippians 4). They should be self-controlled not only in their hands but also in their eyes, their speech and their dress. This was the opinion of a certain Athenian praetor (Pericles, I think) about all magistrates. Now on the teaching of elders.

units.la: Episcopo nihil prodest, conscientia virtutum frui, si non & creditum sibi populum possit instruere. Gratianus.
units.tr: It profits a bishop nothing to enjoy the consciousness of his virtues if he cannot also instruct the people entrusted to him. Gratian.

units.la: DEbet Episcopus Gratiam docendi habere: quia (ut Hieronymus ait, ad Oceanum) Innocentis, absque sermone, conversatio, quantum exemplo prodest, tantum silentio nocet. nam latratu canis, & baculo Pastorum, lupi sunt arcendi.
units.tr: A bishop ought to have the gift of teaching, because (as Jerome says, to Oceanus) the blameless life of a man, apart from preaching, benefits others as much by example as it harms them by silence. For, as with the barking of a dog and the shepherd's staff, wolves must be kept off.

units.la: Gratianus. IN ipsa autem doctrina Discretum oportet esse Rectorem: ne aut tacenda proferat, aut dicenda taceat. Unde Gregorius in 4. cap. sui Pastoralis parte 2. ait. Huc integrum transcripsit illud quartum caput.
units.tr: Gratian. In teaching itself the ruler ought to be discerning, so that he neither utters what should be kept silent nor keeps silent about what should be said. Hence Gregory, in the fourth chapter of the second part of his Pastoral Care, says: [here Gratian copied that whole fourth chapter].

units.la: Nec omnia, nec omnibus, nec passim, Doctor Evangelicus de Evangelio dicere debet. Matt. 7. Act. cap. 16.
units.tr: The Gospel teacher ought to speak neither everything, nor to everyone, nor at random about the Gospel (Matthew 7; Acts 16).

units.la: SIt Rector discretus in silentio: utilis in verbo: ne aut tacenda proferat, aut proferenda reticescat. Nam sicut incauta locutio in errorem pertrahit: ita indiscretum silentium eos, qui erudiri poterant, in errore derelinquit. Saepe namque Rectores improvidi humanam amittere gratiam formidâtes, loqui libere recta pertimescunt: & iuxta Veritatis vocem, Nequaquam gregis custodis, Pastorum studio, sed Mercenariorum vice, deseruiunt: quia veniente Lupo, fugiunt, dum se sub silentio abscondunt.
units.tr: Let the ruler be discerning in silence and useful in speech, so that he neither utters what ought to be kept back nor keeps silent about what ought to be uttered. For just as careless speech draws people into error, so indiscreet silence leaves in error those who could have been taught. Indeed, negligent rulers often, fearing to lose human favour, dread to speak the truth freely; and, in the words of Truth, they serve not with the care of a shepherd of the flock but like hirelings, because when the wolf comes they flee, hiding themselves in silence.

units.la: Silentium Rectoribus & Episcopis populorum pernitiosum est. (August. Epist. 203.) Ut alia non agamus (ait Hieronymus, lib. contra Pelag. 2.) Ut abstineamus nos ab omni specie peccatorum, certè, Verum tacuisse peccatum est.
units.tr: Silence is harmful to the rulers and bishops of the peoples (Augustine, Letter 203). To say nothing of other things (says Jerome, against Pelagius, book 2): if we abstain from every kind of sin, yet to keep silent about the truth is itself a sin.

units.la: § Hinc namque eos per prophetam Dominus increpat, dicens: Canes muti, non valentes latrare. Hinc rursus queritur, dicens: Non ascendistis ex adverso, neque oppositis murum pro domo Israël, ut staretis in prælio, in die Domini. Ex adverso quippe ascendere, est pro defensione gregis, voce liberâ, huius mundi potestatibus contraire. Et, In die Domini in prælio stare, Est prauis decertantibus ex iustitiæ amore resistere. Pastori enim recta timuisse dicere, quid est aliud, quàm tacendo terga præbuisse? qui nimirum si pro grege se obiicit: murum pro domo Israel hostibus opponit. Hinc rursus delinquenti populo dicitur: Prophetæ tui viderunt tibi falsa & stulta: nec aperiebant tibi iniquitatem tuam, ut te ad pœnitentiam provocarent.Prophetæ quippe in Sacro eloquio nonnunquam Doctores vocantur: qui dum fugitiua esse præsentia indicant, quæ futura sunt manifestant: quos Divinus sermo falsa videre redarguit: quia dum culpas corripere metuunt, incassum delinquentibus, promissâ securitate, blandiuntur: qui iniquitatem peccantium nequaquam aperiunt, quia ab increpationis voce conticescunt. Clavis quippe apertionis, est sermo correptionis: quia increpatio, culpam detegit, quam sæpe nescit ipse etiam, qui perpetrauit. Hinc Paulus ait: Vt potens sit in Doctrina sana exhortari, & eos, qui contradicunt, redarguere. Hinc per Malachiam dicitur: Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt Scientiam, & Legem requirunt ex ore eius: quia Angelus Domini exercitum est. Hinc per Esaiam Dominus admonet, dicens: Clama, ne cesses, quasi tuba exalta vocem tuam. Praeconis quippe officium suscipit, quisquis ad sacerdotium accedit: ut ante aduentum iudicis, qui terribiliter sequitur, ipse, scilicet, clamando gradiatur.
units.tr: § Hence the Lord rebukes them through the prophet, saying: "Dumb dogs, not able to bark." Again he complains: "You have not gone up against the enemy, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord." To go up against the enemy is to resist the powers of this world with a free voice in defence of the flock. And to stand in battle on the day of the Lord is to resist the wicked, contending out of love of righteousness. For what else is it for a shepherd to fear to say what is right, than by silence to turn his back? Indeed, if he sets himself before the flock, he sets a wall for the house of Israel against its enemies. Again the sinning people is told: "Your prophets have seen for you false and foolish things; they did not uncover your iniquity, to call you to repentance." For in Holy Scripture prophets are sometimes called teachers: while they show that present things are fleeting, they make clear what is to come. Divine speech rebukes those who see falsely, because, while they fear to reprove faults, they flatter sinners in vain with promised security, and do not uncover the iniquity of those who sin, since they fall silent from the voice of rebuke. For the key to opening is the word of correction, since rebuke uncovers a fault which often the very one who committed it does not know. Hence Paul says: "That he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict." Hence it is said through Malachi: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and men seek the law at his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts." Hence the Lord admonishes through Isaiah, saying: "Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet." For whoever comes to the priesthood takes up the office of a herald, so that before the coming of the judge, who follows terribly, he himself may go before, crying aloud.

units.la: Non est a Spiritu Dei factus Episcopus, qui verba Spiritus assiduè non praedicat.
units.tr: He is not made bishop by the Spirit of God who does not constantly preach the words of the Spirit.

units.la: § Sacerdos ergo si praedicationis est nescius, quam clamoris vocem daturus est praeco mutus? Hinc est enim quod in actibus Apostolorum legitur: Super pastores primos, in linguarum specie, Spiritus Sanctus insedit, quia nimirum quos repleuerit, de se protinus loquentes facit.
units.tr: § If then the priest is ignorant of preaching, what cry will a mute herald give? For this is why it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit sat upon the first shepherds in the form of tongues: because, of course, those whom he fills he at once makes speak of him.

units.la: Sacerdos absque tintinnabulis nō impune domum Domini vel ingreditur, vel egreditur. Aposcopi regij discant hinc, quaenam sint ista Sacerdotalia Tintinnabula.
units.tr: A priest who enters or leaves the house of the Lord without bells does not do so unpunished. Let the royal overseers learn from this what these priestly bells are.

units.la: § Hinc Moysi praecipitur in Exodo, Vt tabernaculum Sacerdos ingrediens tintinnabulis ambiatur: ut videlicet, Praedicatoris voces habeat, ne superni spectatoris iudicium ex silentio offendat. Scriptum quippe est: Audiatur sonitus, quando ingreditur & egreditur sanctuarium in conspectu Domini: & non moriatur. Sacerdos namque ingrediens vel egrediens moritur, si deo sonitus non auditur: quia iram contra se occulti iudicis exigit, si sine praedicationis sonitu incedit.
units.tr: § Hence Moses is commanded in Exodus that the priest, entering the tabernacle, be surrounded by bells, that is, that he have the voice of a preacher, so as not to offend the judgment of the Watcher above by silence. For it is written: "Let the sound be heard when he enters and goes out of the sanctuary before the Lord, and he will not die." The priest who enters or goes out dies if no sound is heard by God, because he brings on himself the anger of the hidden judge if he goes in without the sound of preaching.

units.la: Coram Domino nudus est Sacerdos, qui non est Iustitiâ vestitus, id est, Vniuersa virtu- te. Vestes enim Sacerdotis opera bona, id est, Iustitiam designant.
units.tr: The priest who is not clothed in righteousness, that is, in the whole of virtue, is naked before the Lord. For the priest's garments signify good works, that is, righteousness.

units.la: § Aptè autem tintinnabula vestimentis illius describuntur inserta. Vestimenta enim Sacerdotis quid aliud, quàm recta opera debemus accipere? Prophetâ testantes qui ait: Sacerdotes tui induantur iustitiam. Vestimentis itaque illius tintinnabula inhærent, si vitæ vitam cum linguæ sonitu ipsa quoque bona opera Sacerdotis clament.
units.tr: § Fittingly, however, bells are described as sewn into his garments. For what else should we understand the priest's garments to be but right works, as the prophet bears witness when he says: "Let your priests be clothed with righteousness." So the bells are attached to his garments when the good works of the priest, joined with the sound of his tongue, cry out the life of his life.

units.la: Doctoris Christiani sermo, non in doctis humanæ Sapientiæ verbis, Sed in gratia debet esse sale conditus. Ut sciat, quomodo cuique loqui, quomodoque respondere debeat, 1. Corinth. 2. & ad Coloss. 4.
units.tr: The speech of a Christian teacher ought to be seasoned with salt, not in the learned words of human wisdom but in grace, so that he knows how he ought to speak to each person and how he ought to answer (1 Corinthians 2; Colossians 4).

units.la: § Sed quum Rector se ad loquendum præparat, sub quanto cautelæ studio loquatur, attendat: ne si inordinatè ad loquendum rapitur, erroris vulnere corda audientium feriantur: & quum fortasse Sapiens videri desiderat, unitatis compagem insipienter abscindat. Hinc nanque Veritas dicit: Habete Sal in vobis. &, Pacem habete inter vos. per Sal quippe verbi Sapientia designatur. Qui loqui igitur sapienter nititur, magnopere metuat, ne eius eloquio audientium unitas confundatur. Hinc Paulus ait: Non plus sapere, quàm oportet sapere: sed sapere ad sobrietatem.
units.tr: § But when the ruler prepares himself to speak, let him pay attention to how carefully he speaks, lest, if he is hurried into speech without order, the hearts of his hearers be struck with the wound of error; and lest, while perhaps wishing to seem wise, he foolishly cut apart the bond of unity. For Truth says: "Have salt in yourselves," and "Have peace among yourselves." For by salt the wisdom of the word is signified. So whoever strives to speak wisely should greatly fear lest by his speech the unity of his hearers be confounded. Hence Paul says: "Not to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto soberness."
