units.la: Mali Punici (quod aliý Malum Granatum vocant) species intexta Sacerdotali vesti duo significat: Et Ecclesiæ grenium, quæ omnem credentium turbam suo cortice tegit: Et Veritate consonantiámque virtutum, iuxta illud, multitudinis credentium cor erat unum, & anima una. Sic enim singuli sunt in Ecclesia diuisi gradus, ut omnes eádem compage teneantur. Hæc Hieronymus in opusculo, de quadragintaduab. Mansionib. loquens de Mansione decima sexta. To.3.
units.tr: The form of the pomegranate (which some call the malum granatum), woven into the priestly vestment, signifies two things: the grain of the Church, which covers the whole crowd of believers with its rind, and the agreement and harmony of the virtues, according to that saying: "The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul." For in the Church the separate ranks are so divided that all are held together by one bond. Jerome says this in his little work on the forty-two stations, speaking of the sixteenth station, in volume 3.

units.la: § Hinc in Sacerdotis veste, iuxta Diuinam vocem, tintinnabulis mala Punica coniunguntur. Quid enim per mala Punica, nisi fidei unitas designatur? Nam sicut in malo Punico, uno exterius cortice, multa interius grana muniuntur: sic innumetos sanctæ Ecclesiæ populos unitas fidei contegit, quos intus diuersitas meritorum tenet. Ne igitur Rector incautus ad loquendum proruat: hoc, quod iam praemisimus, per semetipsam Veritas discipulis clamat: Habete Sal in vobis &, Pacem habete inter vos. ac si figuratè per habitum Sacerdotis dicat: Mala Punica Tintinabulis iungite: vt per omne, quod dicitis, Vnitate fidei, cautâ obseruatione, teneatis.
units.tr: § Hence in the priest's vestment, according to the divine word, pomegranates are joined with bells. For what do pomegranates signify but the unity of faith? For as in a pomegranate many grains are protected within under one outer rind, so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, whom the diversity of merits holds within. So let the ruler who is not careful not rush into speech. Truth itself cries to the disciples what we have already set forth: "Have salt in yourselves," and "Have peace among yourselves." As if by the priest's garment he were saying figuratively: join the pomegranates to the bells, so that by all that you say you may hold fast to the unity of faith with careful observance.

units.la: Doctoris Christiani, tanquam prudentis viri, sermo, statera ponderari debet. Ecclesiastici cap. 21. Id est, Vt neque longus, neque breuis existat, Vterque noxius est.
units.tr: The sermon of a Christian teacher, like that of a prudent man, ought to be weighed in a balance. Ecclesiasticus, chapter 21. That is, it should be neither too long nor too short, since either extreme is harmful.

units.la: § Prouidendum quoque est, folicitâ intentione, Rectoribus, vt ab eis, non solùm prava nullo modo, sed nec recta quidem nimiè & inordinatè proferantur: quia sape dictorum virtus perditur, quum apud corda audientium, loquacitatis incautâ importunitate leuigatur. & authorem suum hæc eadem loquacitas inquinat, quæ seruire auditoribus ad vsum profectus ignorat. Vnde bene per Moysen dicitur: Vir qui fluxum seminis patitur, immundus erit. In mente quippe audientium semen sequuturæ cogitationis, est qualitas audita locutionis: quia dum per aurem sermo concipitur, cogitatio in mente generatur. Vnde & ab huius mundi Sapientibus, Prædicator egregius, Seminiuerbius est vocatus. Qui ergo fluxum seminis patitur, immundus asseritur: quia multiloquio subditus, ex eo sese inquinat, quod si ordinatè promeret, prolem rectæ cogitationis ædere in audientium corda potuisset: dúmque incautus per loquacitatem defluit, non ad vsum generis, sed ad immunditiam, semen effundit. Vnde Paulus quoque quum discipulum de instantia prædicationis admoneret, dixit: Testificor coram Deo & Christo Iesu, qui iudicaturus
units.tr: § Rulers must also take care, with anxious attention, that they do not utter things that are right in themselves, but in an unrestrained and disorderly way. For the power of what is said is often lost when it is worn away in the hearers' hearts by the careless importunity of talkativeness. And that same talkativeness defiles its own author, since it does not know how to serve the hearers for their advancement. Hence Moses rightly says: "A man who suffers a flux of seed shall be unclean." For in the minds of the hearers, the heard speech is the seed of the thought that will follow, since while the word is conceived through the ear, the thought is generated in the mind. Hence also the outstanding preacher was called "Seminiverbius" (word-sower) by the wise men of this world. Therefore he who suffers a flux of seed is declared unclean, because, given over to much speaking, he defiles himself by pouring out, without order, the seed that could have brought forth, in the hearers' hearts, the offspring of right thought. While he carelessly runs off through his talkativeness, he spills his seed not for the purpose of generation but into uncleanness. Hence Paul too, when he admonished his disciple about urgency in preaching, said: "I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge

units.la: Ioan. 3. turus est vivos & mortuos, & per adventum ipsius, & regnum eius: Praedica verbum: Insta opportunè, importunè. Dicturus Importunè, praemisit, Opportunè: quia, scilicet, apud auditoris mentem ipsa suâ utilitate se destruit, si habere Importunitas Opportunitatem nescit. Item. Clemens Petri Paulique discipulus ac successor, in Epistola sua tertia Christianis omnibus descripta, sic habet ad illius Epistolae finem.
units.tr: Ioan. 3. the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season." In saying "out of season," he first put "in season," because, plainly, importunity destroys itself by its own uselessness in the hearer's mind, if importunity does not know how to wait for opportunity. Likewise Clement, the disciple and successor of Peter and Paul, in his third Epistle addressed to all Christians, says this at the end of that Epistle:

units.la: Secreta doctrinae Caelestis, non sunt hominibus deplorata malitiae communicanda: S ed auidis duntaxat, aut certè sanabilibus aperienda.
units.tr: The secrets of heavenly teaching are not to be handed over to men of malice, but are to be opened only to the eager, or at least to those who can be healed.

units.la: IN mandatis habemus, Ut venientes ad civitatem, discamus prius, quis in ea dignus sit, ut apud eum, cibum sumamus: quantò magis noscere convenit, quis, qualisve sit is, cui immortalitatis verba credenda sunt: Solicíti enim debemus esse, Ne margaritas nostras mittamus ante porcos. Sed & ob alias causas utile est viri huius habere notitiam. Si enim sciam, quia in his, de quibus non potest dubitari quòd bona sint, emendatus est & inculpabilis, Hoc est, Si sobrius, si misericors, si iustus, si mitis & humanus est (quae utique bona esse nullus ambigit) tunc consequens videbitur, ut ei, qui obtinet bona virtutum, etiam quod deest fidei & scientiae conferatur: & in quibus maculari eius vita videbatur, quae est in reliquis probabilis, emendetur. Si verò in his, quae palam sunt, peccatis inuolutus, permanet inquinatus: non me oportet aliquid de secretioribus & remotis divinae Scientiae proloqui: sed magis protestari & convenire illum, ut peccare desinat, & actus suos à vitiis emendet.
units.tr: We are commanded that, when coming to a city, we should first learn who in it is worthy that we should eat with him; how much more, then, is it fitting to know who and what sort of man he is, whose words of immortality are to be believed? For we ought to be careful not to cast our pearls before swine. But it is also useful to have knowledge of this man for other reasons. For if I know that in those matters about which there can be no doubt that they are good, he is blameless and free from fault, that is, if he is sober, merciful, just, gentle and humane (which everyone admits are certainly good things), then it will seem to follow that what is lacking in faith and knowledge should also be bestowed upon one who possesses the good things of the virtues, and that in those respects in which his life seemed stained, while in the rest it is commendable, it should be corrected. But if he remains defiled, involved in sins that are openly evident, I must not speak anything about the more hidden and remote matters of divine knowledge, but rather must bear witness to him and admonish him to cease sinning and to correct his deeds from their vices.

units.la: Ita malis hominibus est respondendum, ut peiores non fiant: & boni tamen sibi non videantur.
units.tr: Evil men are to be answered in such a way that they do not become worse, and yet good men do not think that they themselves are being wronged.

units.la: § Quòd si ingesserit se, & prouocauerit nos dicere, quæ eum minus recte agentem non oporteat audire: prudenter eum debemus eludere. Nam nihil omnino respondere, auditorum causâ, vtile non videtur: ne forte existiment nos responsionis penuriâ declinare certamen: & sic fides eorū lædatur, non intelligentiū propositum nostrum.
units.tr: § But if he thrusts himself forward and provokes us to say things which, since he is acting wrongly, he ought not to hear, we should wisely evade him. For to make no answer at all for the sake of the hearers does not seem useful, lest they perhaps suppose that we are avoiding the contest for want of a reply, and so their faith is harmed, not the purpose of those who understand our intention.

units.la: Item. Anacletus, De oppressione Præl atorum. Epist.1. Hic Romæ sedebat temporibus Domitiani.
units.tr: Likewise. Anacletus, On the Oppression of Prelates, Epistle 1. He sat at Rome in the time of Domitian.

units.la: Vt ab oratione pro persequutoribus nostris, sic ab eorumdem admonitione, desistendum non est.
units.tr: Just as we must not cease praying for our persecutors, so we must not cease admonishing them.

units.la: S Cimus autem multos ob id infestare Doctores suos, vt eos perdant, & placita propriæ voluntatis adimpleant. Non propterea tamen Doctores (inquantum vires suppetunt) à recta emulatione, & bona institutione, recedere debent: scientes, quia, Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam.
units.tr: § We know, however, that many attack their teachers for this very reason, that they may destroy them and fulfil the wishes of their own will. Nevertheless, teachers ought not, so far as their strength allows, to withdraw from right emulation and good instruction, knowing that "blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake."

units.la: Item. Gregorius Venantio Episcopo. Epistola est 33. lib.1.
units.tr: Likewise. Gregory to Bishop Venantius. It is Epistle 33 of book 1.

units.la: Sanguinem subiectorum pereuntium requirit Deus è manibus negligentium præfectorum. Exech.3.
units.tr: God requires the blood of perishing subjects at the hands of negligent rulers. Ezekiel 3.

units.la: E Phesiis Paulus dicit: Mundæ sunt hodie manus meæ à sanguine omnium vestrûm. Nó enim subterfugi quò minùs annuntiarem omne consilium Dei vobis. Mundus ergo à sanguine eorum non esset, si eis Dei consilium annuntiare noluisset. quia, quum increpare delinquentes noluerit, eos proculdubiò tacendo Pastor occidit.
units.tr: In his speech to the Ephesians Paul says: "I am innocent today of the blood of all of you, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God." Therefore he would not have been clear of their blood if he had been unwilling to declare to them the counsel of God. For since the pastor who refuses to rebuke wrongdoers undoubtedly kills them by his silence.

units.la: Item. Nicolaus Papa.1. circa finem Epistolæ prolixæ ad Michaelem Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum.
units.tr: Likewise. Pope Nicholas I, near the end of a long Epistle to Michael, Emperor of Constantinople.

units.la: Æterna pœnam damnationis incurrit Episcopus, qui semen verbi Dei non spargit. Eadémque pœnà tenetur, quisquis dispersum fideliter non excipit.
units.tr: The bishop who does not scatter the seed of the word of God incurs the eternal penalty of damnation. And the same penalty binds whoever does not faithfully receive what has been scattered.

units.la: Dispensatio
units.tr: Stewardship

units.la: DIspesatio est nobis cœlestis seminis iniuncta: vę si nō sparserimus: væ si tacuerimus. Quod quum electionis vas formidet, & clamet, quāto magis cuilibet exiguo metuendū est? Proinde, sicut nō leue discrimen incumbit Pontificibus siluisse pro Diuinitatis cultu, & Ecclesiæ correctione, quod congruit: ita his (quod absit) non mediocre periculum est, qui quum debeant parere, despiciunt. PARITER quoque obseruare debet Sacerdos, Ne indignis & non intelligentibus, Secreta mysteria, suâ prædicatione, referre incipiat. Qui enim ea docet, quæ ab auditoribus non valent intelligi: non ad eorum vtilitatem, sed sui ostentationem facit. Vnde in expositione Beati immaculati dicitur. Hoc initiū est Psalmi centesimi decimiotlaui. Nomen authoris apposuisset Gratianus: Indicassemus locum. Nam prolixus est ille Psalmus: in quem prolixè multi quoque scripsere: præ ceteris, diuus Ambrosius duos & viginti Sermones in illum composuit. Digna Canone sententia, cuiuscunque sit.
units.tr: Stewardship of the heavenly seed is laid upon us: woe if we do not sow, woe if we keep silent. Since the chosen vessel fears this and cries out, how much more must every humble man fear it? Therefore, just as no slight peril rests on bishops who keep silent about the worship of the Godhead and the correction of the Church, which is fitting, so those who despise what they ought to obey face no small danger (God forbid). Likewise the priest must also take care not to begin, in his preaching, to disclose the secret mysteries to the unworthy and the uncomprehending. For he who teaches things that his hearers cannot understand does it not for their benefit but for his own display. Hence in the exposition of "Blessed are the undefiled" it is said: "This is the beginning of the hundred and eighteenth Psalm." Gratian would have added the author's name; we would have pointed out the passage. For that Psalm is lengthy, and many have written on it at length; above all, the blessed Ambrose composed twenty-two sermons on it. A sentence worthy of the Canon, whoever it is by.

units.la: Garrulus est, Adulator, aut Gloriosus, qui non dicenda diuulgat.
units.tr: He is a gossip, a flatterer, or a boaster, who spreads abroad what should not be spoken.

units.la: VItium animi est indignis secreta vulgare: quod fit vel loquacitate incautâ, dum sine iudicio volat irrevocabile verbum: vel adulatione, vt ei placeat, cui secreta revelat: vel iactatione scientiæ, vt plura scire videatur. Gratianus. Ex quibus omnibus profecto datur intelligi, Quanta debet esse discretio in prædicatione Sacerdotis: quâ si forte caruerit, tanquam torto naso, Sacerdotalis officij iudicatur indignus.
units.tr: It is a fault of mind to make secrets common among the unworthy. This happens either through careless talkativeness, when an irrevocable word flies out without judgement; or through flattery, so as to please the one to whom one reveals the secrets; or through boasting of knowledge, so as to seem to know more. Gratian. From all of which it can certainly be understood how great discretion must be in the preaching of a priest; if he happens to lack it, he is judged unfit for the priestly office, like one with a crooked nose.

units.la: Doctos esse debere Sacerdotes ostendimus integris tribus distinctionibus 36. 37. 38. superius. In hac autem 43. distinct. monstratur, quòd ipsos non tantummodò Doctos, sed etiam Doctores decet esse. Doctores quidem, Non qui Laurea, Pileolis, & Annulis insigniantur (quandoquidem plures iam sumus tales Doctores, quam Docti) Sed Doctores, qui docent: qui nomini, quod vsurpant, actu respondeant. Iam dos octava Sacrorum ministrorum sequitur. Apostolus Episcopum iubet esse,
units.tr: We have shown that priests ought to be learned in the three whole distinctions 36, 37 and 38 above. In this 43rd distinction, however, it is shown that they ought to be not only learned but also teachers. Teachers indeed: not those who are adorned with laurels, caps and rings (since we already have more such teachers than learned men), but those who actually teach, who in deed answer to the name they claim. Now follows the eighth point concerning sacred ministers. The Apostle orders that a bishop be

units.la: MH ΠΑΡΟΙΝΟΝ.
units.tr: Not given to wine [μὴ πάροινον]

units.la: Quod Hieronymus, omnésque Latini traducunt Non vinolentum, Vino non obnoxium, seu non vinosum, non ebriosum. Solus Chrysostomus (ex consequenti Theophylactus) ait, πα̂ροινον, οὐχ ὑμέθυσον ὑπταῦθα quoiv ἀλλὰ ὑβρισήν, ἐν αὐτάλη. Paræum hic ebriosum non dicit Apostolus: Sed iniuriosum, morosum, superbum, sibi placentem, in alios debacchantem: qualibus vitiis ebrij maderē solent: Nostram cum Gratiano sequemur editionem vulgatam. Præsertim, quum Paulus ipse de Diaconis paulò post loquens, hanc velut exponat vocem. μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ πεποιχέντες. Id est, Non vino multo deditos: quod est, non vinolentos. De Clericali sobrietate plura iam diximus in Diorismo 35.
units.tr: Jerome and all the Latins render it "not violent," "not given to wine," or "not winebibbing," "not drunken." Only Chrysostom (and consequently Theophylact) says [πάροινον, οὐχ ὡς μεθύσον, ἀλλὰ ὑβριστήν, ἐν αὐθαδείᾳ] "not as a drunkard, but insolent, in self-will." Here the Apostle does not call him drunken, but injurious, morose, proud, self-pleasing, raging against others, the kind of vices drunkards usually have. We shall follow, with Gratian, our edition, the Vulgate. Especially since Paul himself, speaking a little later of deacons, explains this very word: [μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ προσέχοντας], that is, not devoted to much wine, which means not drunkards. We have said more about clerical sobriety already in distinction 35.

units.la: DISTINCTIO. XLIIII.
units.tr: Distinction 44.

units.la: Gratianus. QVVM autem Vinolentus esse prohibetur, Gulæ intemperantiam nequaquam habere permittitur. neque enim Ebrietas prohibetur, & Voracitas permittitur: utrunque enim inter opera tenebrarum Apostolus commemorat scribens Romanis: Non in Comessationibus, & Ebrietatibus. Ventris namque ingluvies ad luxuriam provocat facile, & omne opus bonum dissoluit.
units.tr: Gratian. But when drunkenness is forbidden, gluttony is by no means to be allowed. For drunkenness is not forbidden while greed is permitted; the Apostle lists both among the works of darkness when he writes to the Romans: "Not in revelling and drunkenness." Indeed, excess of the belly easily leads to lust and dissolves every good work.

units.la: Unde Hieronymus Amandi Presbyteri Quæstioni secundæ respondens. Epistol. Breuis Epistola. To.3. Gratianus mutauit verba: sensum retinuit. Ibi sic habetur.
units.tr: Hence Jerome, answering the second question of Amandus the Presbyter, in his Letter, "A Brief Epistle," vol. 3. Gratian changed the words but kept the sense. There it reads as follows.

units.la: VEntrem distentum cibo, & potionibus irrigatum, voluptas Genitalium sequitur. Et pro membrorum ordine, ordo est vitiorum. Rursus idem primum caput exponens ad Titum.
units.tr: When the belly is stuffed with food and watered with drink, the pleasure of the genitals follows. And as the order of the limbs goes, so goes the order of the vices. Again, the same writer, expounding the first chapter to Titus.

units.la: SPecta Ventre, & Genitalia. Pro qualitate vitiorum, ordo membrorum. Quæ verò Gratianus hic retulit, verba sunt Augustini Sermonum De tempore 65. To. 10. His aliunde sumptam Nabuzardam archimagiri tropologiam subdidit. Aliud ex hinc Hieronymi verbum adiecit, quod est in fine cap.3. Commentariorum in Micheam. To.6.
units.tr: Look to the belly and the genitals. The order of the limbs corresponds to the nature of the vices. What Gratian has cited here are the words of Augustine, in Sermon 65 On the Time, vol. 10. To these, taken from elsewhere, he has added the allegory of Nabuzaradan, the chief of the cooks. He has added another saying of Jerome, which is at the end of chapter 3 of the Commentary on Micah, vol. 6.

units.la: VEnter, & Genitalia sibimetipsis vicina sunt: ut ex vicinitate membrorum, confœderatio intelligatur vitiorum. Gratianus. HINC Nabuzardam Princeps cocorum muros Hierusalem destruxisse legitur: quia venter, cui multitudo cocorum deseruit, ædificia virtutum ad solum redigit. Sacerdos itaque de altari viuere, non luxuriari quaerat. Unde ait Hieronymus.
units.tr: The belly and the genitals are close neighbours to each other, so that from the closeness of the members a league of the vices is understood. Gratian. Hence we read that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the cooks, broke down the walls of Jerusalem, because the belly, which the multitude of cooks serves, reduces the buildings of virtues to the ground. Therefore a priest should seek to live from the altar, not to indulge in luxury. Hence Jerome says:

units.la: TIbi, ô Sacerdos, de altari viuere, non luxuriari permittitur. Gratianus. SVNT autem Comessationes, non solùm Sacerdotibus, sed etiam Laicis noxiæ: qui festiuos & solennes dies non aliter se digne celebrare putant, nisi comessationibus deseruiant. Unde Augustinus scribit ad Aurelium Episcopum. Epist.64. Quam Gratianus non magno cum iudicio discidit.
units.tr: You, O priest, are permitted to live from the altar, not to indulge in luxury. Gratian. Revelries, however, are harmful not only to priests but also to laymen, who think that they cannot properly celebrate festive and solemn days unless they give themselves to revelry. Hence Augustine writes to Aurelius the bishop, Letter 64. Which Gratian cut up without much judgement.

units.la: Comessationes & Compotationes fœdæ quidem sunt, & omnibus flagitiosæ: Sed Ecclesiæ prætextu factæ, sunt etiam sacrilegæ. Augusti.
units.tr: Revelries and drinking parties are indeed foul and disgraceful to all; but when they are held under the pretext of the Church, they are also sacrilegious. Augustine.

units.la: COmessationes, & Ebrietates ita concessæ & licitæ putantur, ut in honorem etiam beatissimorum martyrum, non solùm per dies solennes (quod ipsum, quis non lugendū videat, qui hæc non carnis oculis inspicit?) sed etiam quotidie celebrentur.
units.tr: Revelries and drunken feasts are thought to be so permitted and lawful that they are celebrated in honour of the most blessed martyrs, not only on solemn days (which is itself to be lamented, by anyone who looks at these things with more than fleshly eyes), but even every day.

units.la: Mala populi consuetudo sensim diuinis minis & monitionibus, non hominum statim pœnis & terroribus est tollenda.
units.tr: The bad custom of the people is to be removed gradually by divine threats and warnings, not at once by human punishments and terrors.

units.la: § Non ergo asperè (quantùm existimo) non duriter, non modo imperioso ista tolluntur: sed magis docendo, quàm iubendo: magis monendo, quàm minando. Sic enim agendum est cum multitudine peccantiū. Seueritas autem exercenda est in peccata paucorum. Et si quid minamur, cum dolore fiat, de scripturis comminando vindictam suturam: ne nosipsi in nostra potestate, sed Deus in nostro sermone timeatur. Itaque prius monebuntur spiritales, aut spiritalibus proximi: quorum authoritate, & lenissimis quidem, sed instantissimis admonitionibus, cætera multitudo frangatur. Item. Ex concilio Laodicensi. cap. 24.
units.tr: § So these things are not removed, I think, harshly, roughly, or merely by command, but rather by teaching than by ordering, and by admonishing rather than threatening. For this is how one must deal with the multitude of sinners. Severity, however, is to be applied to the sins of a few. And if we threaten anything, let it be done with grief, warning from the Scriptures that vengeance will follow, so that God is feared not in our power but in our speech. Thus the spiritual men will be warned first, or those nearest to the spiritual; by whose authority, and by the gentlest yet most insistent admonitions, the rest of the multitude will be broken. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, canon 24.

units.la: Clerico, nisi peregrinanti, nefas est cauponari: vel, ad edendum, potandumve, cauponam ingredi.
units.tr: For a cleric, unless he is travelling abroad, it is wrong to keep a tavern, or to enter a tavern to eat or drink.

units.la: NOn oportet Clericos, à Presbyteris usque ad Diaconos, & deinceps ordinis Ecclesiastici omnes, usque ad ministros, aut Lectores, aut Exorcistas, aut Ostiarios, aut Psalmistas, aut etiam eos qui in proposito continentiæ sunt, tabernas intrare. Item. Ex sexta Synodo. Nonus est Synodi Canon.
units.tr: Clerics, from the presbyters down to the deacons, and all of the ecclesiastical order onwards, down to the ministers, or readers, or exorcists, or doorkeepers, or psalm-singers, or even those who are under a vow of continence, must not enter taverns. Likewise, from the sixth Synod. It is the ninth canon of the Synod.

units.la: NVlli Clerico licet tabernam aut ergasterium habere. Si enim huiusmodi tabernam ingredi prohibetur: quantò magis aliis ministrare in ea? Si quis verò tale quid fecerit: aut cesset, aut deponatur. Item. Ex Concilio Carthaginensi. Conciliorum Carthaginensium Græcè conscriptorum
units.tr: No cleric is allowed to have a tavern or a workshop. For if he is forbidden to enter such a tavern, how much more to serve others in it? If anyone, however, does such a thing, let him either desist or be deposed. Likewise, from the Council of Carthage. Of the Carthaginian councils written in Greek.

units.la: * ἐμπορικούς. * ὑπηρετῶν. * ἢ τὰ παγματα τῶν ασκητῶν. * κερπηλικὸν ἐργαστήριον. * τῷ τοιούτῳ. * ὀυκ ἐπὶ τὰ πράγματα. * καὶ ἀ μὴ ἐμπίμως αὐτῷ ἐγχείειν.
units.tr: * [ἐμπορικούς] trading. * [ὑπηρετῶν] serving. * [ἢ τὰ παγματα τῶν ασκητῶν] or the wares of the hucksters. * [κερπηλικὸν ἐργαστήριον] a retail shop. * [τῷ τοιούτῳ] to such a one. * [ὀυκ ἐπὶ τὰ πράγματα] not to business. * [καὶ ἀ μὴ ἐμπίμως αὐτῷ ἐγχείειν] and not to busy himself with it.

units.la: Canon praesens est quadragesimus. In editis Latini Conciliis est vigesimus septimus, Concilij certy Carthaginensis : perperam quarto tribuunt.
units.tr: This canon is the fortieth. In the printed Latin councils it is the twenty-seventh, of an uncertain Carthaginian council; they wrongly assign it to the fourth.

units.la: CLerici, edendi vel bibendi causâ, tabernas non ingrediantur: nisi peregrinationis necessitate compulsi. Item. Gregorius Natali Episcopo Salonitano Epist. 14. lib. 2.
units.tr: Clerics are not to enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel. Likewise, Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona, Letter 14, book 2.

units.la: Conuiuatoris Episcopi culpa non leuis est: & eius etiam, qui maiores non reueretur.
units.tr: The fault of a bishop who is a feaster is not slight, and so is the fault of one who does not show respect to his elders.

units.la: MVltis ab urbe tua venientibus (frater charissime) didici, Pastorali curâ derelictâ, solis te conuiuiis occupatum: quae audita non crederem, nisi haec actionum tuarum experimentis probarem. Nam, quia nequaquam lectioni studeas, nequaquam exhortationi inuigiles, sed ipsum quoque vsum Ecclesiastici ordinis ignores: hoc est in testimonium, quòd his, sub quibus es positus, seruare reuerentiam nescis. Idem. Ad eundem Epist.37.codem lib.2.
units.tr: Many who came from your city (dearest brother) have told me that, having neglected your pastoral care, you are occupied only with banquets. I would not believe what I have heard unless I proved it by the evidence of your actions. For since you are not at all devoted to reading, and do not keep watch over exhortation, but are even ignorant of the very practice of the ecclesiastical order, this is the testimony that you do not know how to show respect to those over whom you are placed. The same writer, to the same, Letter 37, in the same book 2.

units.la: Ea demum Clericis conuiuia licet inire, per quae nihil ingeniorum impeditur, nec temperantia modus amittitur. Augustinus, alioqui fugitans conuiuiorum, sic se tamen natali suo die conuiuatum, sed & quotidie conuiuari solitum scribit, initio libelli de beata vita. To.1.
units.tr: Clerics may take part in only those banquets by which nothing of their talents is hindered, and by which the measure of temperance is not lost. Augustine, who otherwise shuns banquets, nonetheless writes that on his birthday he was feasted, and that he was accustomed to be feasted every day as well, at the beginning of his book On the Happy Life, vol. 1.

units.la: COnuiuia communia, quae ex intentione impendendae charitatis fiunt, rectè vestra fraternitas in suis epulis laudat: sed tamen sciendum est, quia tunc ex charitate veraciter prodeunt, quum in eis nulla absentium vita mordetur: nullus ex irrisione reprehenditur: nec in eis inanes saecularium negociorum fabulae, sed verba sacrae lectionis audiuntur: quum non plus, quàm necesse sit, corpori seruitur, sed sola eius infirmitas reficitur, vt ad vsus exercendae virtutis habeatur. Haec itaque si vos in vestris conuiuiis agitis, Abstinentium (fateor) magistri estis. Item. Nannetes (quos & Nannitas Ptolemaeus appellauit) Celticae Galliae populus est, ad hostia Ligeris. Vrbs ibi celebris, gentis fere nomen retinens. Nantes, Episcopi sedes. Vbi quondam celebratum Concilium, saepe Gratianus hoc in opere citat. citat. Illius autem neque tempus habebatur, nec aliud quippiam (quod ego sciam) praeter ista Gratiani fragmenta, superesset. Per antiquum fuisse convenit, nam Palaeis annumerant.
units.tr: Common banquets, which are held with the intention of exercising charity, your brotherhood rightly praises in your feasts. But it must be known that they truly arise from charity only when in them no absent person's life is bitten at, no one is rebuked in mockery, and no empty tales of worldly business are heard in them, but words of sacred reading; when the body is served no more than necessity requires, and only its weakness is refreshed, so that it is kept fit for the practice of exercising virtue. If therefore you conduct your banquets in this way, you are (I confess) masters of abstainers. Likewise. The Nannetes (whom Ptolemy also called the Nannitae) are a people of Celtic Gaul, at the mouths of the Loire. There is a famous city there, which keeps nearly the name of the people: Nantes, the seat of a bishop. A council was once held there, which Gratian often cites in this work. Neither its date is recorded, nor anything else (so far as I know) survives except these fragments of Gratian. It is agreed that it was ancient, for they count it among the Palaea.

units.la: Nequaquam turpibus & obscoenis Canticis, aut iocis obstrepere, Multoque Vino decet hilarescere convivia clericorum.
units.tr: By no means should banquets of clerics be disturbed by shameful and obscene songs or jokes; and it is proper that the banquets of clerics grow merry with much wine.

units.la: NUllus Presbyterorum, quando ad anniversarium diem XXX, aut VII, vel III, alicuius defuncti, aut quācunque vocatione ad Collectam convenerit, se inebriare vllatenus praesumat: nec precatus, amore Sanctorum, vel ipsius animae, bibere, aut alios ad bibendum cogere, vel se alienâ precatione ingurgitare, nec plausus & risus inconditos, & fabulas inanes ibi referre, aut cantare praesumat: aut turpia ioca, vel vrso, vel tornatricibus ante se fieri patiatur: nec laruas daemonum ante se ferri consentiat: quia hoc diabolicum est, & Sacris Canonibus prohibitum. Rursus in eodem.
units.tr: No presbyter, when he has come together to the Collect on the anniversary day of the thirtieth, seventh, or third day of any deceased person, or for any other summons, may in any way presume to get drunk; nor, having prayed out of love for the saints or for the soul itself, may he presume to drink, or compel others to drink, or to gorge himself on another's prayer; nor may he presume there to report or sing uncouth applause and laughter and empty tales; nor permit foul jokes to be made before him, whether by a bear, or by female dancers; nor consent to have the masks of demons carried before him, because this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons. Again, in the same.

units.la: Presbyterorum convivium à precatione coeptum, in precationem desinat: Sacra verò lectio medium teneat. Homiliam Chrysostomi legas, De fide Annae Sanctelis. To.1.
units.tr: Let the banquet of the presbyters, begun with prayer, end in prayer; and let sacred reading hold the middle. You may read the homily of Chrysostom On the Faith of Saint Anna, vol. 1.

units.la: QVando autem conueniunt Presbyteri ad aliquod convivium, aliquis prior illorum versum ante mensam incipiat, & cibum benedicat: & tunc secundum ordinem sedeant, alter alteri honorem praebentes: & per vices cibum & potum benedicant: & aliquis de illorum Clericis aliquid de Sancta scriptura legat. Post refectionem similiter hymum dicant, ad exemplum Domini, sicut in Caena fecisse legitur: & se contineant omnes Presbyteri, maximè in talibus locis: Vt non vituperetur ministerium eorum. Rursus in eodem.
units.tr: When the presbyters come together for some banquet, let the first of them begin the verse before the table and bless the food; and then let them sit in order, giving honour to one another; and in turn let them bless food and drink; and let one of their clerics read something from holy Scripture. After the meal, let them likewise sing a hymn, after the example of the Lord, as is read to have been done at the Supper; and let all the presbyters restrain themselves, especially in such places, so that their ministry is not blamed. Again, in the same.

units.la: Sic sua convivia Presbyteri celebrare debent, vt à mensa mox oraturi surgere valeant.
units.tr: Presbyters ought so to celebrate their banquets that they can rise from the table and soon be able to pray.

units.la: QVando Presbyteri, per Calendas simul conueniunt, post peractum Diuinum ministerium, ad necessariam collectionem, non quasi ad plenam refectionem, sed quasi ad prandium, ibi ad tabulas resideant: ne per talia inhonesta conuiuia se inuicem grauent: quia indecens est & onerosum: sæpe etiam tarde ad Ecclesiam redeuntes, maius damnum de reprehensione consequuntur (quod de grauedine mutua contrahunt) quàm lucrum ibi faciant: nam de huiusmodi conuentu Paulus Corinthios reprehendit: quia inconuenienter Cœnam Dominicam manducare conueniebant. Sic & qui ad Cœnam Dominicam, id est ad collationem verbi, sub occasione conueniunt, & ex ingluuie, ventris causâ, coniunguntur, reprehensibiles coram Deo, & hominibus habentur. Et ideo peractis omnibus, Qui volunt, panem cum charitate in domo fratris sui simul cum fratribus frangant: & singuli singulum bibere faciant: & maximè ultra tertiam vicem, poculum non contingant: & sic ad Ecclesias redeant. Item. Ex Concilio Laodicensi. Græcè est. 54. In additione Latina. 55.
units.tr: When the presbyters meet together on the Calends, after the divine service has been completed, for the necessary collection, not as for a full meal but as for a lunch, let them sit down there at the tables, so that they do not burden one another by such dishonourable banquets, for it is unseemly and burdensome. Often too, returning late to the Church, they incur greater loss through rebuke (which they contract from their mutual heaviness) than they gain there; for it was on account of a gathering of this kind that Paul rebuked the Corinthians, because they came together to eat the Lord's Supper unworthily. So too those who gather under the pretext of the Lord's Supper, that is, of the reading of the Word, and are joined together by gluttony for the sake of the belly, are held to be blameworthy before God and men. And therefore, when all things are finished, let those who wish break bread with love in the house of their brother together with the brethren; and let each cause each to drink; and above all let them not touch the cup beyond the third round; and so let them return to the churches. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea. In Greek it is canon 54; in the Latin addition, 55.

units.la: Clericis ad Symposia vetatur Symbola dare. Laicis quoque.
units.tr: Clerics are forbidden to give contributions for feasts. Laymen too.

units.la: NOn oportet† altaris Ministros, aut Clericos, ex Symbolis † conuiuia celebrare. Sed nec Laicos. Item. Ex Concilio Toletano, cap.7. Quum per Hispaniam damnata plenè fuisset hæresis Ariana, circa tempora Pelagij Papæ. 2. Hoc est, anno Christi 508. vel eò circa, fuit habitum præsens Concilium.
units.tr: Ministers of the altar or clerics ought not to hold banquets paid for by contributions. Nor should laymen. Likewise, from the Council of Toledo, chapter 7. When the Arian heresy had been thoroughly condemned throughout Spain, around the time of Pope Pelagius, that is, in the year of Christ 508 or thereabouts, the present council was held.

units.la: A Pontificalibus, & Sacerdotalibus cœnis, Sacrarum scripturarum ferculum remoueri nunquam debet.
units.tr: The course of the holy Scriptures must never be removed from pontifical and priestly banquets.

units.la: PRo reuerentia Dei, & Sacerdotum, id vniuersa constituit Synodus, ut (quia solent crebrò mensis otiosæ fabulæ interponi) in omni Sacerdotali conuiuio lectio Diuinarum scripturarum misceatur. Per hoc enim & animæ ædificantur ad bonum, & fabulæ non necessariæ prohibentur.
units.tr: For the reverence of God and of the priests, the whole synod has decided that, since idle tales often creep into the table talk, the reading of the divine Scriptures should be mixed into every priestly banquet. In this way souls are built up in goodness, and unnecessary talk is kept out.

units.la: Item. Ex Concilio Martini Papæ, cap. 61.
units.tr: Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 61.

units.la: Symbolorum collatores improbantur.
units.tr: Those who collect contributions for feasts are condemned.

units.la: NON liceat Sacerdotes, vel Clericos, sed nec religiosos Laicos, convivia facere de Confertis. Ex eodem, in cap. 66.
units.tr: Clerics or priests, and also religious laymen, are not permitted to hold feasts from collected contributions. From the same source, in chapter 66.

units.la: Hora cibi sumendi præscripta Clericis est Hora tertia (modò nobis accedit ad decimā) qui non nisi multa cum gratiarum actione sumendus est.
units.tr: The hour prescribed for clerics to take food is the third hour (though for us it now falls at the tenth), and it must be taken with much thanksgiving.

units.la: NON oportet Clericos, vel Laicos religiosos ante Sa- cram horam diei tertiā inire convivia: nec aliquando Clericos, nisi Hymno dicto, comedere panem: & post cibos, gratiam authori Deo referre. Gratianus ita concludit.
units.tr: Clerics and religious laymen ought not to enter banquets before the sacred third hour of the day, nor ever for clerics to eat bread unless a hymn has been sung, and after eating to give thanks to God the author. Gratian concludes thus.

units.la: SI ergo Laicis Comessationes damnabiles sunt, multò magis Sacerdotibus imputantur ad gehennam. Venter enim pinguis (ut Hieronymus ait ad Nepotianum) crassum sensum generat, quum Sacerdotalis sensus econtrario vigil esse debeat & tenuis. Atque ideo, Edacitatis vitio obnoxii, in Sacerdotes vngi non debent. Hi enim (ut ait Gregorius in Morali.) qui adhuc vitiorum bello subiacet, nequaquam per prædicationis vsum præesse magisterio cæterorum debent. Hæc Gregorius in principio, cap. 12. lib. 23. moralis expositionis in Iob.
units.tr: If, then, drinking bouts are condemned in laymen, they are charged to priests all the more heavily, unto Gehenna. For a fat belly (as Jerome says to Nepotianus) produces a dull mind, whereas the priestly mind ought to be alert and lean on the contrary. And therefore those subject to the vice of gluttony ought not to be anointed as priests. For (as Gregory says in the Moralia) one who is still under the warfare of vices must by no means, through the practice of preaching, preside over the teaching of others. These are Gregory's words at the beginning of chapter 12 of book 23 of his Moral Exposition on Job.

units.la: Nona iam sequitur Episcopi virtus, Eaque perneccessaria. Vetat illum Paulus esse.
units.tr: The ninth virtue of the bishop now follows, and it is very necessary. Paul forbids him to be

units.la: ΠΛΗΚΤΗΝ.
units.tr: NOT A STRIKER [ΠΛΗΚΤΗΝ].

units.la: Plactes dicitur percussor & verberator manu. Violenti, non castigantis nomen est. Attamen translatè quoque Plactes obiurgator, & improbus conuiciator appellatur. Aut qui sermone conscientiæ vulnerat aliorum. Gratianus hic utrumque designat, Inquiens.
units.tr: A plactes is called one who strikes and beats with the hand. It is the name of a violent man, not of one who chastises. Yet figuratively a plactes is also called a reviler and a shameless insulter, or one who wounds others with words that pierce the conscience. Gratian here designates both, saying

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLV.
units.tr: DISTINCTION 45.

units.la: Sequitur ___ Non percussorem.
units.tr: It follows: ___ Not a striker.

units.la: Gratianus. NON enim oportet Episcopum ita esse irascibilem & perturbati sensus, ut percutiat: qui debet esse patiens: sed sequatur eum, qui dorsum posuit ad flagella. Unde Gregorius scribit Ioanni Episcopo Constantinopolitano. Epist. 52. libro secundo.
units.tr: Gratian. For a bishop ought not to be so irascible and disturbed in mind that he strikes. He ought to be patient, and to follow the one who offered his back to the scourges. Hence Gregory writes to John, Bishop of Constantinople, Letter 52, book 2.

units.la: Non verberum, sed verborum vi coërcere suos debet Episcopus.
units.tr: A bishop ought to restrain his people by the force of words, not of blows.

units.la: QVid autem de Episcopis, qui verberibus timeri volunt, Canones dicant: bene Fraternitas vestra novit. Pastores enim facti sumus, non Percussores, egregius Predicator dicit: Argue, obsecra, increpa, In omni patientia & doctrina. Noua vero atque inaudita est ista praedicatio, quae verberibus exigit fidem. Inscribedis & aduersariis suis oblitus Gratianus Concilij nomen adscribere, nos quoque reliquit incertos. Hoc editi Conciliorum libri non habent. Succurrit, quod dicere nostri solent. Allegationem generalem sufficere.
units.tr: As for what the canons say about bishops who want to be feared with blows, your Brotherhood knows well. For we have been made ministers, not strikers, as the outstanding preacher says: "Reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine." But this teaching, which demands faith by means of blows, is new and unheard of. Gratian, forgetting to add the name of the Council to his opponents' writings, has also left us uncertain. The printed books of the Councils do not contain this. What our people are accustomed to say comes to mind: a general citation is enough.

units.la: Caedere ministros Ecclesiae verberibus, deforme ac seruile est, Ideo vetitum est. Homicidio abrogatio triduana pro durissimis flagellis habetur.
units.tr: To beat the ministers of the Church with blows is shameful and servile, and therefore it is forbidden. For a murder, a three-day suspension is considered a very severe scourging.

units.la: NEminem quisquam peccantem Clericum caedeattingat. Non Presbyter Diaconum, non Episcopus Clericum, vel seruitorem Ecclesiae ad caedem perducat. quod si ita causa exigit, id est, Si incorrigibilis extiterit Clericus, triduo privetur honore, ut poenitens redeat ad matrem Ecclesiam. Item. Gregorius Paschasio Episcopo Neapoli. In Epist. 15. lib. 11.
units.tr: Let no one strike a cleric who sins. Let no presbyter bring a deacon, nor a bishop a cleric or a servant of the Church, to a beating. But if the case so requires, that is, if the cleric proves incorrigible, let him be deprived of his honour for three days, so that he may return as a penitent to mother Church. Likewise, Gregory to Paschasius, Bishop of Naples, Letter 15, book 11.

units.la: Ducere, non Trahere decet infideles ad fidem.
units.tr: It is fitting to lead unbelievers to the faith, not to drag them.

units.la: QVi syncera intentione, extraneos a Christiana religione, ad fidem cupiunt rectam perducere: blandimentis debent, non asperitatibus studere: ne, quorum mentem reddita ad planum ratio poterat revocare, pellat procul aduersitas. Nam quicunque aliter agunt, & eos sub hoc velamine a consueta ritus sui volunt cultura removere: suas illi magis, quam Dei causas probantur attendere.
units.tr: Those who desire with sincere intention to bring outsiders from the Christian religion to the right faith ought to strive by gentle persuasion, not by harshness, lest adversity drive far away those whose minds reason could have brought back to the plain way. For whoever acts otherwise, and wants to remove them under this pretext from the customary worship of their rite, is shown to be looking to his own causes rather than God's.

units.la: Legalibus suis inter Christianos ceremoniis Iudaeos absque vi relinqui Gregorius mandauit.
units.tr: Gregory ordered that the Jews be left, without force, to their legal ceremonies among Christians.

units.la: § Iudaei siquidem Neapolim habitantes questi sunt nobis, asserentes, quod quidam eos a quibusdam feriarum suarum solennibus irrationabiliter nitantur arcere: ne illis sit licitum festiuitatum suarum solennia colere, sicut eis nunc vsque, & parentibus eorum, longis retro temporibus licuit obseruare. quòd si ita se veritas habet, superuacuae rei videntur operam dare. Nam quid utilitatis est, quando (etsi contra longum vsum fuerint vetiti) ad fidem illis, & conuersionem nihil proficit? Aut cur Iudaeis, qualiter caerimonias suas colere debeant, regulas ponimus, si per hoc eos lucrari non possumus? Agendum est ergo, ut potiùs ratione & mansuetudine provocati sequi nos velint, non sugere: ut eos, ex eorum codicibus ostendentes quae dicimus, ad sinum matris Ecclesiae Deo possimus auxilianteconuertere. Itaque fraternitas tua eos monitis, prout poterit, Deo adiuuante, ad convertendum accendat: & de suis illos solennibus inquietari denuò non permittat: sed omnes festiuitates feriasque suas (sicut hactenus tam ipsi, quàm parentes eorum per longa colentes retro tempora tenuerunt) liberam habeant observandi, celebrandique licentiam.
units.tr: § Indeed, the Jews living at Naples have complained to us, asserting that certain people unreasonably try to keep them from the solemn observances of their festivals, so that it is not allowed for them to celebrate the solemnities of their feasts, as they and their forebears were permitted to observe for long ages past. But if the matter stands as they say, these people seem to be taking pains over a useless thing. For what advantage is there, when (even if they were forbidden against long custom) nothing is gained for their faith and conversion? Or why do we lay down rules for the Jews as to how they ought to keep their ceremonies, if we cannot win them over by this means? It must therefore be done that, provoked rather by reason and gentleness, they may wish to follow us, not flee from us, so that, showing them from their own books what we say, we may by God's help convert them to the bosom of mother Church. Therefore let your Fraternity, as far as you are able, with God helping, stir them by admonitions to conversion, and do not allow them to be disturbed again in their solemn observances, but let them have freedom to keep and celebrate all their festivals and feast days, as they and their forebears have kept them through long ages until now.

units.la: Item. Vniuersis Episcopis per Galliam, & Germaniam constitutis. Neque diuinare queo quis Pontificum scripserit haec ad alios.
units.tr: Likewise, to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and Germany. I cannot divine which of the Pontiffs wrote these things to others.

units.la: In Ecclesia, Delinquentem non statim sequitur de patrato delicto Iudicium.
units.tr: In the Church, judgment for a wrong once committed does not immediately follow the offender.

units.la: LIcet accidant pleráque Sacerdotibus, quae sunt reprehendenda, plus tamen erga corrigendos agat beneuolentia, quàm seueritas, plus cohortatio, quàm comminatio, plus charitas, quàm potestas: quum nemo nostrum sine reprehensione, aut sine peccato viuat. Nam si Dominus statim post trinam negationem, beatum Petrum Apostolum, praeceptorem nostrum iudicasset, non tantum ex eo fructum, sicut fecit, recepisset. Expectandi ergo, atque corrigendi magis sunt rectores Ecclesiæ, quàm statim iudicandi. Vnde necesse est, quæque negocia Ecclesiastica, post multarum experimenta causarum, solicitius perspici, & diligentius præcaueri: quatenus per Spiritum Charitatis & pacis, omnis materies scandalorum, & præsumptio inuidorum, atque oppressio simplicium fratrum de Ecclesiis Domini auferantur. Et sicut non vult quisquam fratrum se aliorum iudicio prægrauari: ita non audeat alij inferre, quod sibi non vult fieri. Gratianus. Iudæi non sunt cogendi ad fidem: quam tamen si inuiti susceperint, cogendi sunt retinere. Vnde. In Toletano Concilio. 4. statutum est, cap. 56. circiter an. Do. 645.
units.tr: Although many things that deserve rebuke happen among priests, goodwill should work more with those to be corrected than severity, exhortation more than threat, charity more than power, since none of us lives without reproach or without sin. For if the Lord had immediately judged the blessed Apostle Peter, our teacher, after his threefold denial, he would not have received so much fruit from it as he did. The rulers of the Church are therefore to be waited for and corrected rather than judged at once. Hence it is necessary that all ecclesiastical affairs be examined more carefully and guarded against more diligently, after the experience of many cases, so that through the Spirit of charity and peace every matter of scandal, the presumption of the envious, and the oppression of simple brothers may be removed from the churches of the Lord. And just as none of the brothers wants to be burdened by the judgment of others, so let no one dare to inflict on others what he does not want done to himself. Gratian. Jews are not to be compelled to the faith; yet if they have received it unwillingly, they are to be compelled to keep it. Hence, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, it was decreed in chapter 56, about the year of the Lord 645.

units.la: Salus inuito ac reluctanti non confertur. Quod autem Salutem velit aliquis, aut nilo inscrutabilis est illa Dei voluntas.
units.tr: Salvation is not conferred on one who is unwilling and resisting. As for whether anyone wants salvation, that will of God is indeed unsearchable.

units.la: DE Iudæis autem præcepit sancta Synodus, Nemini deinceps ad credendum, vim inferri: cuius enim vult, Deus miseretur, & quem vult, indurat. Non enim tales inuiti saluandi sunt, sed volentes, vt integra sit forma iustitiæ. Sicut enim homo, propriâ arbitrij voluntate, serpenti obediens periit: sic, vocante se gratiâ Dei, propriâ mentis conuersione, quisque credendo saluatur. Ergo non vi, sed liberâ arbitrij voluntate & facultate, vt conuertantur, suadendi sunt, non impellendi.
units.tr: Concerning the Jews, the holy Synod has further commanded that no one be forced to believe, for "he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens." For such people are not to be saved unwillingly, but willingly, so that the form of justice may remain whole. For just as man, by the free choice of his own will, perished by obeying the serpent, so each one is saved by believing, by his own conversion of mind, when the grace of God calls him. Therefore they are to be persuaded, not driven, to be converted by free will and power of choice, not by force.

units.la: Heraclius Imperator ab Ariolis monitus imperio Christianorum magnum tunc imminere periculum à circuncisio populo, Iudæorum gentem ratus denotari, Quicunque toto suo regno Iudæi fuere, Christianos fieri coegit. Idemque vt facerent, Dagobertum Francorum, & Sisebutum Visigothorum, Reges, (qui dudum Gallias & Hispanias occuparant) literis admonuit: quod & fecêre. circiter annum Do. 639. De talibus hic agitur.
units.tr: Emperor Heraclius, warned by soothsayers that a great danger then threatened the empire of the Christians from the circumcised people, thinking that the nation of the Jews was meant, compelled all those who had been Jews throughout his whole realm to become Christians. He also admonished by letter Dagobert, King of the Franks, and Sisebut, King of the Visigoths (who had long before occupied Gaul and Spain), to do the same, and they did so, about the year of the Lord 639. It is of such matters that this passage treats.

units.la: Qui semel Christi fidem volens nolens professus est, Hanc perpetuò seruare compellitur.
units.tr: Whoever has once professed the faith of Christ, willingly or unwillingly, is compelled to keep it always.

units.la: § Qui autem iampridem ad Christianitatem venire coacti sunt, (sicut factum est temporibus religiosissimi principis Zizebuti) quia iam constat eos Sacramentis Divinis sociatos, & Baptismi gratiam suscepisse, & chrismate unctos esse, & corporis sanguinisque Domini extitisse participes: oportet ut fidem etiam quam vi, vel necessitate susceperunt, tenere cogantur, ne nomen Domini blasphemetur, & fides, quam susceperunt, vilis ac contemptibilis habeatur. Item. Leo Papa. 1. Anastasio Episcopo Thessalonicensi. In Epistol. 82.
units.tr: § But those who were long ago forced to come to Christianity (as happened in the times of the most religious prince Sisebut), since it is now established that they have been joined to the divine sacraments, have received the grace of baptism, have been anointed with chrism, and have become partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, it is right that they be compelled to hold the faith, even though they received it by force or necessity, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith they have received be held cheap and contemptible. Likewise, Pope Leo I, to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, Letter 82.

units.la: Sic nostris delinquentibus fratribus ahibenda est correctio, ut salua semper maneat inter nos fraterna dilectio. Non enim dixit Apostolus, Increpa: Sed, obsecra, ut fratres. 1. Timoth. 5. Rursus, Argue (dixit) Increpa, verumtamen, cum omni patientia. 2. ad Timoth. 4.
units.tr: Thus correction is to be applied to our brothers when they offend, so that brotherly love may always remain safe among us. For the Apostle did not say "rebuke," but "entreat, as brothers." 1 Tim. 5. Again, he said "reprove, rebuke, yet with all patience." 2 Tim. 4.

units.la: Licet nonnunquam accidant, quae in Sacerdotalibus sunt reprehendenda personis: plus tamen erga corrigendos agat benevolentia, quam severitas, plus exhortatio quam comminatio, plus charitas quam potestas. Sed ab his, qui, quae sua sunt, quaerunt, non quae Iesu Christi, facile ab hac lege disceditur: & dum dominari magis, quam consulere subditis quaerunt, Honor placet, Inflat superbia, & quod prouisum est ad concordiam, tendit ad noxam. Item. Ex Canone Apostolorum, 27.
units.tr: Although it sometimes happens that things are found in priests' persons that deserve rebuke, goodwill should work more with those to be corrected than severity, exhortation more than threat, charity more than power. But those who seek what is their own, not what is of Jesus Christ, easily depart from this law; and while they seek to rule rather than to advise their subjects, honour pleases them, pride puffs them up, and what was provided for concord tends to harm. Likewise, from the Canon of the Apostles, 27.

units.la: Ille qui dorsum suum posuit ad flagella, quique maledictus non remaledixit, Episcopum percussorem damnauit, Haec Hieronymus ad Oceanum.
units.tr: He who offered his back to the scourges, and who, when cursed, did not curse back, condemned the bishop who strikes. These are the words of Jerome to Oceanus.

units.la: EPiscopum, aut Presbyterum, aut Diaconum percutientem fideles delinquentes, aut infideles iniquè agentes, & per huiusmodi volentem timeri, deiici ab ossicio suo praecipimus: quia nunquam nos docuit hoc Dominus: sed econtrario, Ipse quum percuteretur, non repercutiebat: quùm malediceretur, nō maledicebat: quùm pateretur, non comminabatur. Item. Ex Concilio Bracharensi. 3. cap. 6. circiter an. 670.
units.tr: We command that a bishop, a presbyter, or a deacon who strikes faithful offenders, or unbelievers who act unjustly, and who wishes to be feared through such means, be deposed from his office, because the Lord never taught us this; rather, when he was struck, he did not strike back; when he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten. Likewise, from the Third Council of Braga, chapter 6, about the year 670.

units.la: Non abest a specie tyrannidis Episcopus, qui flagellorum crudelitate suam nititur authoritatem defendere. Quod qui fecerit, Excommunicatus alio relegatur.
units.tr: The bishop who strives to defend his authority by the cruelty of scourges is not far from the appearance of tyranny. Whoever does this is to be excommunicated and sent away to another place.

units.la: QVum beatus Apostolus, arguere & obsecrare, vel increpare in omni bonitate & patientia praecipiat, extra hanc Doctrinam nouimus quosdam ex fratribus, tantis caedibus in Honoratos efferuescere, quantas poterant latrocinantium promereri personae. Et ideo, qui gradus iam Ecclesiasticos meruerunt, id est, Presbyteri, Abbates, & Leuitae, qui (exceptis grauioribus & mortalibus culpis) nullis debent verberibus subiacere: non est dignum, ut passim unusquisque Praelatus honorabiliora membra sua, prout voluerit, & ei placuerit, verberibus subiiciat, & dolori: ne dum incaute subdita percutit membra, ipse quoque debitam sibi subditorum reverentiam subtrahat. Iuxta illud, quod quidam Sapiens dicit: Leniter castigatus reverentiam exhibet castiganti. Asperitatis autem nimiae increpatio, nec increpationem recipit, nec salutem. Et ideo si quis aliter, quam dictum est, praedictos honorabiles subditos, licentia perceptae potestatis elatus, malitia animi tantum crediderit verberandos, iuxta modum verberum, quae intulerit, Excommunicationis pariter & Exilij sententiam sustinebit.
units.tr: Since the blessed Apostle commands us to rebuke, entreat, and reprove with all goodness and patience, we know that outside this teaching some brethren have flared up against their superiors with such slaughter as the characters of brigands might deserve. Therefore those who have already earned ecclesiastical grades, that is, presbyters, abbots, and Levites, should (except for graver and mortal faults) be subject to no beatings. It is not fitting that every prelate should at random subject his more honourable members to blows and pain, as he pleases and as it suits him, lest, while he carelessly strikes the members under him, he himself lose the reverence due to him from his subordinates. This accords with what a certain wise man says: one who is gently corrected shows respect to the corrector, but the reproof of excessive harshness receives neither reproof nor salvation. Therefore, if anyone otherwise than has been said, puffed up by the license of power received, has believed in his wickedness that the aforesaid honourable subordinates should be beaten, he shall undergo, in proportion to the blows he inflicted, a sentence of excommunication and exile alike.

units.la: Virga & Correptio tribuit sapientiam. παιδευσει, και ελεγχος. Prouerb. 29.
units.tr: The rod and correction give wisdom. [παιδευσει, και ελεγχος]. Prov. 29.

units.la: SAlomon vero contra monet, dicens: Percute filium tuum virga, & liberabis animam eius a morte. Hinc etiam beatus Gregorius scribit in Dialogorum libro 2. cap. 4. Beatum Benedictum, quendam monachum, virga percutiendo, sanasse, quem crebrâ admonitione curare non poterat. Hinc etiam Dominus, flagello facto de funiculis, male versantes in templo flagellauit, & de orationis domo eiecit. Hinc etiam Apostolus Fornicatorem illum Satanæ corporaliter vexãdum tradidit: & magnum Elymam corporali cæcitate damnauit. Hinc etiam in Canonibus, Pueri, qui ante rationales annos irrationabiliter versantur, verberibus castigati iubentur. Virgines quoque, si religionis veste depositâ, aliis se copulauerint, ergastulis retrudi præcipiuntur. Hinc etiam Gregorius in Moralibus.20.lib.cap.6. Hic refertur integrum cap.
units.tr: Solomon, on the other hand, advises against this, saying: Beat your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death. Hence also the blessed Gregory writes in the second book of the Dialogues, chapter 4, that the blessed Benedict healed a certain monk by striking him with a rod, whom he could not cure by frequent admonition. Hence also the Lord, having made a whip of cords, scourged those who trafficked in the temple and drove them out of the house of prayer. Hence also the Apostle handed over that fornicator to Satan to be physically afflicted, and condemned the great Elymas to bodily blindness. Hence also in the Canons, boys who behave irrationally before the age of reason are ordered to be chastised with blows. Virgins too, if they put aside the veil of religion and join themselves to others, are ordered to be thrust into prisons. Hence also Gregory in the twentieth book of the Moralia, chapter 6. The whole chapter is cited here.

units.la: Vino, simul & Oleo (scilicet) Monentis asperitate, pariter & Lenitate curandi sunt delinquentes.
units.tr: Wine and oil together are to be applied to offenders: the harshness of the admonisher and also the gentleness of the healer.

units.la: DIsciplina vel Misericordia multùm destituitur, si vna sine altera teneatur. Sed circa subditos, inesse debet Rectoribus & iustè consolans Misericordia, & piè saeuies Disciplina. Hinc est quòd semiuiui illius vulneribus, qui à Samaritano in stabulum ductus est, & Vinum adhibetur, & Oleum: ut per Vinum mordeantur vulnera, per Oleum foueantur: quatenus vnusquisque, qui sanandis vulneribus præest, in Vino, morsum distinctionis adhibeat, in Oleo, mollitiem pietatis. Per vinum mundentur putrida. Per Oleum sananda foueantur. Miscenda est ergo lenitas cum seueritate, faciendúmque quoddam ex vtraque temperamentum: ut neque multâ asperitate exulcerentur subditi, neque nimiâ benignitate soluantur.
units.tr: Discipline or mercy is greatly lacking if one is held without the other. But towards subordinates, rulers ought to have both a mercy that justly consoles and a discipline that severely but dutifully punishes. Hence it is that the wounds of that half-dead man, whom the Samaritan led to an inn, were treated with both wine and oil: so that the wounds are bitten by the wine and cherished by the oil. In the same way, everyone who presides over the healing of wounds should apply, in the wine, the bite of correction, and in the oil, the softness of compassion. Putrid things are cleansed by wine; things to be healed are cherished by oil. Gentleness must therefore be mixed with severity, and a certain temperament made from both, so that subordinates are neither ulcerated by too much harshness nor loosened by excessive kindness.

units.la: Virga & manna pariter in Arca, Dulcia notât simul & amara boni Rectoris verbera.
units.tr: The rod and the manna together in the ark signify that the blows of a good ruler are both sweet and bitter.

units.la: § Hoc nimirum illa tabernaculi Arca significat, in qua cum tabulis Virga simul & Manna est: quia, quum scripturæ Sacræ Scientia est in boni Rectoris pectore, Si est Virga districtionis, sit & Manna dulcedinis.
units.tr: § Indeed, that ark of the tabernacle signifies this, in which the rod and the manna were placed together with the tablets, because, since knowledge of Holy Scripture is in the breast of a good ruler, if there is the rod of strictness, let there also be the manna of sweetness.

units.la: Rector bonus vnà cum Baculo Virgam gestet. Hàc deiiciat: Illo subleuet.
units.tr: A good ruler should carry a rod together with a staff. With the one he should strike down; with the other he should support.

units.la: § Hinc etiam Dauid ait: Virga tua, & Baculus tuus, ipsa me consolata sunt. Virgâ enim percutimur, & Baculo sustentamur. Si ergo est districtio Iustitiæ, quæ feriat: sit & consolatio baculi, quæ sustentet. Sit itáque amor, sed non emolliens. sit rigor, sed non exasperans: sit Zelus, sed non immoderatè sæuiens: sit pietas, sed non plus, quàm expediat, parcens.
units.tr: § Hence David also says: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me. For we are struck with the rod and sustained by the staff. If, then, there is the severity of justice, which strikes, let there also be the comfort of the staff, which sustains. Let there be love, but not softening; let there be rigour, but not embittering; let there be zeal, but not raging immoderately; let there be piety, but not sparing more than is expedient.

units.la: Rector bonus, exemplo Mosis, Pœnam suis & inferat, & auferat: mortem precetur, atque deprecetur.
units.tr: A good ruler, after the example of Moses, should both inflict and remove punishment upon his own, and should both pray for death and beseech it.

units.la: § Intueri libet in Moysi pectore Misericordiam cum Seueritate sociatam. Videamus amantem piè, & districtè sæuientem. Certè, quum Israeliticus populus ante Dei oculos penè inueniabilem contraxisset offensam, ita vt eius rector audisset: Descende, peccauit populus tuus: ac si diuina vox diceret: Qui in tali peccato lapsus est, meus non est. atque subiungeret: Dimitte me, vt irascatur suror meus contra eos, & deleam eos: faciámque te in gentem magnam. Ille semel, & iterum pro populo, cui præerat, obicem se ad impetum Dei irascentis opponens, ait: Aut dimitte eis hanc noxam: aut si non facis, dele me de libro tuo, quem scripsisti. Pensemus ergo, quibus visceribus eundem populum amauit, pro cuius vita de libro vitæ deleri se petiit: Sed tamen iste, qui tanto amore eius populi constringitur, contra eius culpas pensemus quanto zelo rectitudinis accendatur. Mox enim vt culpæ veniam, ne delerentur, obtinuit, zelo rectitudinis succensus, inquit: Ponat vir gladium super femur suum, ite & redite de porta vsque ad portam per medium castrorum, & occidat vnusquisque fratrem, vxorem, & amicum, & proximum suum: ceciderúntque in illo die quasi viginti tria millia hominum. Ecce, Qui vitā omnium, etiam cum sua morte, petiit, paucorum vitam gladio extinxit. Intus arsit ignibus amoris: foris accensus est zelo seueritatis. Tanta fuit pietas, vt se pro illis coram Domino morti offerre non dubitaret: tanta seueritas, vt eos, quos diuinitus feriri timuerat, ipse iudicii gladio feriret. Sic amauit eos, quibus praefuit, vt pro eis nec sibi parceret: & tamen delinquentes sic persecutus est, quos amauit, vt eos, etiam Domino parcente prosterneret. Vtrobique legatus fortis, vtrobique admirabilis mediator, causam populi apud Deū precibus, causam Dei apud populum gladiis allegauit. Intus amans, diuinae irae, supplicando, obstitit. Foris saeuiens, culpam feriendo consumpsit. In regimine ergo populi vtrunque Moyses miscuit: Vt nec disciplinae deesset misericordia, nec misericordiae disciplina.
units.tr: § It is pleasing to gaze on the breast of Moses, where mercy is joined with severity. Let us see him loving dutifully and raging strictly. Certainly, when the people of Israel had incurred an offence almost beyond remedy before the eyes of God, so that their ruler had heard: Go down, your people have sinned, as if the divine voice were saying: he who has fallen into such a sin is not mine; and then it would add: Leave me alone, that my wrath may burn against them and I may destroy them, and make you a great nation. He, once and again, on behalf of the people over whom he presided, set himself as a barrier against the onslaught of the angry God, and said: Either forgive them this wrong, or if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written. Let us consider, then, with what bowels of love he loved that people, for whose life he sought to be blotted out of the book of life. But yet this man, who was bound by such love for that people, let us consider how fervently he was kindled with zeal for righteousness against their sins. For as soon as he had obtained pardon for their guilt, lest they be blotted out, he, inflamed with zeal for righteousness, said: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh, go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each slay his brother, wife, friend, and neighbour; and there fell on that day about twenty-three thousand men. Behold: he who sought the life of all, even at the cost of his own death, extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fires of love; without, he was kindled with the zeal of severity. So great was his piety that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord for them; so great was his severity that he himself struck with the sword of judgment those whom he had feared would be struck by God. Thus he loved those over whom he presided, that he did not spare himself on their behalf; and yet he so pursued the sinners whom he loved that he laid them low even when the Lord was sparing them. On both sides a brave envoy, on both sides an admirable mediator, he pleaded the people's cause before God with prayers, and God's cause before the people with swords. Within, loving, he withstood the divine wrath by supplicating; without, raging, he consumed the guilt by striking. In governing the people, therefore, Moses mixed both: so that mercy was not lacking to discipline, nor discipline to mercy.

units.la: In bonis rectoribus mixta sit & regendi potestas, & consolandi benignitas.
units.tr: In good rulers, the power to govern and the kindness to console should be mixed.

units.la: § Vnde in Iob, iuxta vtrânque virtutem, dicitur: Quúmque sederem, quasi rex, circunstante exercitu, eram tamen mœrentium consolator. Sedere quippe, circunstante exercitu, vigor est ac disciplina regiminis. Mœrentium verò corda consolari, est ministerium pietatis. cap.54.lib.5.De summo bono.
units.tr: § Hence in Job, according to each virtue, it is said: When I sat as a king, with an army standing around, I was nevertheless a comforter of those who mourn. For to sit, with an army standing around, is the vigour and discipline of rule. But to console the hearts of the mourning is the ministry of piety. Chapter 54, book 5, On the Highest Good.

units.la: Iustus, atque Misericors debet esse Iudex: quae duo sunt Epitheta Dei, iudicis omnium supremi.
units.tr: A judge ought to be both just and merciful: which are two epithets of God, the supreme judge of all.

units.la: OMnis, qui iustè iudicat, stateram in manu gestat. In utróque penso Iustitiam & Misericordiam portat: sed per Iustitiam reddit peccati sententiam, per Misericordiam, peccati temperat poenâ. Vt iusto libramine quædam per æquitatem corrigat: quædam vero per miserationem indulgeat. Qui Dei iudicia oculis suis proponit, semper timens & tremens in omni negocio formidat, ne de Iustitiæ tramite deuians cadat:& unde non iustificatur, inde potiùs condemnetur. Item. Augustinus in Enchiridio, cap.71. Tomo.3.
units.tr: Everyone who judges justly carries a balance in his hand. In each pan he carries justice and mercy: but through justice he pronounces the sentence of sin, and through mercy he tempers the punishment of sin, so that by a just balance he may correct some things with equity, and indulge others with compassion. He who sets the judgments of God before his eyes, always fearing and trembling, dreads in every matter lest, straying from the path of justice, he fall; and where he is not justified, there he may rather be condemned. Likewise Augustine in the Enchiridion, chapter 71, Tome 3.

units.la: Etiam pœnis atque verberibus infligendis in commeritos, Iudex esse dicitur Misericors. Et, Qui veniam dat petenti, Dat eleemosynam.
units.tr: Even in inflicting punishments and blows upon those who deserve them, a judge is said to be merciful. And he who gives pardon to one who asks gives alms.

units.la: ET qui emendat verbere, in quem potestas datur, vel coërcet aliquâ disciplinâ (& tamen peccatum eius, quo ab illo læsus, aut offensus est, dimittit ex corde, vel orat ut ei dimittatur) non solùm in eo quòd dimittit ex corde atque orat, verumetiam in eo quòd corripit, & aliquâ emendatoriâ pœnâ plectit, Eleemosynam dat, quia misericordiam præstat. Multa enim bona præstatur inuitis, quando eorum consulitur utilitati, non voluntati, quia ipsi inueniuntur sibi inimici. Gratianus. SVNT enim multa genera Eleemosynarum, de quibus Albinus ait. Hic Albinus dictus est & Alcuinus, Monachus Abb. S. Martini Turonensis, auditor Bedæ. In Rhetoricis quibusdã disputationibus appellatur venerandus Magister, à Carolo Magno Rege, qui fertur illius fuisse discipulus. Anno 770. Multa scriptitauit. Iuo Carnotensis (ex quo sumpsit hoc Gratianus) in titulo de Eleemosyna, lib.2, locum non indicauit.
units.tr: AND he who corrects with blows, over whom power is given, or restrains with some discipline (and yet forgives from the heart the sin by which he has been harmed or offended, or prays that it be forgiven him), gives alms not only in that he forgives from the heart and prays, but also in that he corrects and punishes with some corrective penalty, because he shows mercy. For many good things are done for those who are unwilling, when their advantage is consulted rather than their will, since they themselves are found to be their own enemies. Gratian. For there are many kinds of alms, of which Albinus says. This Albinus is also called Alcuin, a monk and abbot of St Martin of Tours, a pupil of Bede. In certain rhetorical disputations he is called the venerable Master, by King Charlemagne, who is said to have been his pupil. In the year 770 he wrote many works. Ivo of Chartres (from whom Gratian took this) did not indicate the place in the title on alms, book 2.

units.la: Eleemosyna, quædam Corporalis est, quædam est Spiritalis: & Utrumque mixta quædam est. Exempla videas in citato nunc Augustini, cap.72.
units.tr: Almsgiving is of two kinds: some is bodily and some is spiritual, and some is a mixture of both. See the examples in Augustine, cited just now, chapter 72.

units.la: TRia sunt genera Eleemosynarum, una, Corporalis, egenti dare quicquid poteris: altera, Spiritualis, dimittere à quo læsus fueris: Tertia, Delinquentes corrigere, & errantes, in viam reducere veritatis. Item. Augustinus in lib. 50. Homiliarum, ad finem Homil. 6. To. 10.
units.tr: There are three kinds of almsgiving. The first is bodily: to give the needy whatever you can. The second is spiritual: to forgive the one by whom you have been wronged. The third is to correct offenders and to lead the erring back to the way of truth. Likewise Augustine, in the fiftieth book of Homilies, at the end of Homily 6, volume 10.

units.la: De penu quidem, vel pecunis sit Eleemosyna: Sed illa maior est, quæ procedit à cordis thesauro.
units.tr: Almsgiving may indeed consist of food or money, but that which comes from the treasury of the heart is greater.

units.la: Duæ sunt Eleemosynæ, Vna Cordis, Alia Pecuniæ. Eleemosyna Cordis, est dimittere ei à quo læsus es. Nam dare aliquid indigenti aliquando quaris, & non habes. Indulge peccanti, quantum volueris, redundabit tibi. Eleemosyna Cordis multò maior est, quàm Eleemosyna Corporis. Charitatis Eleemosyna sine substantia terrena sufficit sibi: Illa verò quæ corporaliter datur, si sine benigno corde tribuitur, omnino non sufficit. Iam Gratianus ex antecedentibus concludit, omnia concilians. Non percutiat, & percutiat, Episcopus.
units.tr: There are two almsgivings: one of the heart, the other of money. Almsgiving of the heart is to forgive the one by whom you have been wronged. For sometimes you wish to give something to the needy and you have nothing to give. Pardon the sinner as much as you wish, and it will return to you. Almsgiving of the heart is far greater than almsgiving of the body. Charitable almsgiving without earthly substance is sufficient in itself; but that which is given bodily, if it is bestowed without a kindly heart, is by no means sufficient. Now Gratian concludes from what goes before, reconciling the apparent contradiction: "Let the bishop not strike, and yet let him strike."

units.la: Gratianus. Ex his omnibus apparet, Quòd, nec lenitas mansuetudinis sine rectitudine severitatis, nec zelus rectitudinis sine mansuetudine, in Prælatis debet inueniri. Percussores ergo (qui, præmissis authoritatibus, ab Episcopali officio remouentur) non quilibet corporaliter flagellantes, sed, prætermissa mansuetudine, ad verbera semper parati, intelligendi sunt: qui per flagella, nō vitia corrigere, sed timeri appetunt: quibus Petrus scripsit.
units.tr: Gratian. From all this it appears that neither the gentleness of mildness without the rectitude of severity, nor the zeal of rectitude without mildness, ought to be found in prelates. Therefore the strikers (who, by the authorities cited above, are removed from the episcopal office) are to be understood not as all who beat the body with blows, but as those who, setting mildness aside, are always ready for blows, and who seek to be feared through scourges rather than to correct vices. To such people Peter wrote:

units.la: § Nesitis Dominantes in clero, sed forma facti gregis ex animo. Hinc etiam Gregorius scribit in Moralibus, lib. 19. cap. 16. in 19. cap. Iob.
units.tr: "Not as lords over those in the clergy, but as examples to the flock from the heart." Hence Gregory also writes in the Moralia, book 19, chapter 16, on chapter 19 of Job.

units.la: Neque misericordia mœstus sit Prælatus: neque crudelitate sævus: sed modestia temperatus. Hæc est Lenitas & Mansuetudo.
units.tr: The prelate should be neither saddened by pity nor savage through cruelty, but tempered by moderation. This is gentleness and mildness.

units.la: Sunt nanque nonnulli ita districti, ut etiam omnem mansuetudinem benignitatis amittant: & sunt nonnulli ita mansueti, ut perdant districti iura regiminis. Unde cunctis Rectoribus utráque summopere sunt tenenda. Ut nec in disciplinæ vigore, benignitatem mansuetudinis, nec rursus in mansuetudine, districtionem deseriant disciplinæ: quatenus nec à compassione pietatis obdurescant, quum contumacem corrigunt: Nec disciplinæ vigorem molliant, quum infirmorum animos consolantur. Regat ergo vigor disciplinæ mansuetudinem: & mansuetudo ornet vigorem: & sic alterum commendetur ex altero, ut nec Vigor sit rigidus, nec Masuetudo dissoluta.
units.tr: For there are some so strict that they lose all the mildness of kindness, and there are some so mild that they lose the firm rights of government. Therefore both qualities must be held in the highest regard by all rulers: so that they do not abandon the kindness of mildness in the vigour of discipline, nor again abandon the strictness of discipline in mildness; so that they do not harden through the compassion of piety when they correct the stubborn, nor soften the vigour of discipline when they console the weak in spirit. Let the vigour of discipline therefore govern the mildness, and let mildness adorn the vigour, and so let each be commended by the other: that the vigour not be harsh, nor the mildness loose.

units.la: Idem. Homilia 34. Euangeliorum. In cap. 15. Lucæ. Initio statim Homiliæ.
units.tr: The same, Homily 34 on the Gospels, on chapter 15 of Luke, at the very beginning of the homily.
