units.la: Peccata, non peccantes, insectetur Iudex. Et vbique præ se ferat, Quicquid agit, iu-uandi studio agere se, non odio.
units.tr: The judge should pursue sins, not sinners, and should show in everything he does that he acts out of a desire to help, not out of hatred.

units.la: VEra iustitia compassionem habet: falsa vero dedignationem, quanuis & iusti soleant recte peccatoribus dedignari. Sed aliud est, quod agitur typho superbiæ: aliud quod zelo disciplinæ. Dedignantur etenim, sed non dedignantes: Persequutionem commouent, sed amantes. At contrà, Hi qui de falsa iustitia superbire solent, cæteros quosque despiciunt, nullâ infirmantibus misericordiâ condescendunt: & quò se peccatores esse non credunt, eò deterius peccatores siunt. Item. Hieronymus ad cap. 4. lamentationum Hiere.
units.tr: True justice has compassion; false justice has disdain, although even the just are accustomed rightly to disdain sinners. But what is done in the pride of arrogance is one thing, and what is done in the zeal of discipline is another. For they disdain, yet do not disdain; they stir up persecution, yet they love. On the contrary, those who are accustomed to take pride in false justice despise all others and do not stoop with mercy to the weak; and the less they believe themselves to be sinners, the worse sinners they become. Likewise Jerome, on chapter 4 of Lamentations of Jeremiah.

units.la: Si qui dulcedine sanari possunt, Austeritate non expedit eos percellere.
units.tr: If people can be healed by sweetness, it is not expedient to strike them down with severity.

units.la: RE cedite (inquiunt) polluti. Recedite, abite, nolite nos tangere, nobiscum nolite cōmunicare. Talis loquela non illuminat cæcum, non sanat ægrotum, non curat infirmum: sed magis occîdit, atque in desperationem, periclitantem mittit. Boni etenim rectores ex sua infirmitate aliorum infirmitates pensantes, magis per humanitatis & mansuetudinis lenimentum student peccantes ab erroris laqueo eruere, quàm per austeritatem in foueam perditionis nutantes propellere. Vnde Doctor Gentium: Factus sum, inquit, infirmus infirmis, Vt infirmos lucrifacerē.
units.tr: "Withdraw," they say, "you who are defiled! Go away, do not touch us, do not have fellowship with us." Such speech does not enlighten the blind, does not heal the sick, does not cure the weak, but rather kills and sends the one in peril into despair. Good rulers, weighing the weaknesses of others by their own weakness, strive rather to rescue sinners from the snare of error by the softening of humanity and mildness, than to drive those who are wavering into the pit of perdition by austerity. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles: "I have become weak to the weak," he says, "that I might gain the weak."

units.la: Irem. Origenes Homilia 7. in Iosue. Cur ista nostri Hieronymo solent adscribere, superius dicebamus.
units.tr: Likewise Origen, Homily 7 on Joshua. Why these words are usually ascribed to our Jerome, we said above.

units.la: Vnius etiam peccato polluitur atque punitur vniuersus populus, praesertim, quum sciês ipscopus dissimulat illud.
units.tr: Even by the sin of one person the whole people is defiled and punished, especially when the bishop knowingly overlooks it.

units.la: SEd illud non ociose transcurrendum est, Quòd, vno peccante, Ira Dei super omnem populum venit. Hôc modo accidit. Quando Sacerdotes, qui populo praesunt, erga delinquentes benevoli videri volunt: & verentes peccantium linguas, ne forte malè de eis loquantur, Sacerdotalis seueritatis immemores nolunt complere, quod scriptum est: Peccantem coram omnibus argue: ut caeteri metum habeant. Et iterum: Auferte malum à vobis ipsis. Nec zelo Dei succensi imitantur Apostolorum dicentem: Tradidi huiusmodi hominem Satanae in interitum carnis, ut spiritus salvus fiat. Neque illud Euangelij implere studENT, Vt si viderint peccantem, primò secretè conueniant: post etiam duobus, vel tribus arbitris. Quod si contempserit, & post haec, Ecclesiae correctione non fuerit emendatus, De Ecclesia expulsum, velut gentilem habeant, ac publicanum. Et dum uni parcunt, uniuersae Ecclesiae moliuntur interitum. Quae est ista misericordia, quae ista bonitas, uni parcere, & omnes in discrimen adducere? Polluitur enim ex uno peccatore Populus. Sicut ex una oue morbida uniuersus grex inficitur, sic & uno fornicante, vel aliud quodcunque scelus committente, plebs universa polluitur. Hinc etiam dicitur alibi:______
units.tr: But this must not be passed over lightly: that when one person sins, the wrath of God comes upon the whole people. This happens in the following way: when priests, who preside over the people, wish to appear kind towards offenders, and fearing the tongues of sinners, lest they perhaps speak ill of them, forget their priestly severity and are unwilling to fulfil what is written: "Rebuke the sinner before all, that the others may have fear." And again: "Remove the evil from among yourselves." Nor, burning with zeal for God, do they imitate the Apostle who said: "I have delivered such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved." Nor do they strive to fulfil that precept of the Gospel: that if they see a sinner, they should first meet him privately; afterwards, with two or three witnesses. But if he despises these, and after these is not amended by the correction of the Church, they should regard him as expelled from the Church, like a Gentile and a tax collector. And while they spare one, they bring about the destruction of the whole Church. What mercy is this, what goodness, to spare one and to bring all into peril? For the people is defiled by one sinner. Just as the whole flock is infected by one diseased sheep, so too the whole community is polluted by one fornicator, or by anyone else who commits some other crime. Hence it is also said elsewhere:

units.la: REctorem subditis pietas, Matrem: Disciplina vero, Patrem exhibeat. Proponit Gratianus nouum percussorum genus, οὐ κερδὰ χεῖρα πλήκτας, sed qui lingua verberant, obiurgationibus probrosis & conuitiis amarulentis: vel qui turpes, aut otiosos sermones in alienas ingerunt aures.
units.tr: Let piety show the ruler as a mother to his subjects, but discipline as a father. Gratian proposes a new kind of striker: not one who strikes with the hand (οὐ κερδὰ χεῖρα πλήκτας), but one who strikes with the tongue, with shameful rebukes and bitter reproaches, or who pours base or idle talk into the ears of others.

units.la: Dist.46. 140 SPECVLVM
units.tr: Dist. 46. 140 THE MIRROR

units.la: Gratianus. Percussor quoque dicitur, qui sermone inutili infirmorum conscientiâ vulnerat. Unde Anacletus Papa, Epist.2. De Anacleto diximus, explicantes vocabulum, Presbyter.
units.tr: Gratian. A striker is also called one who wounds the consciences of the weak with useless speech. Hence Pope Anacletus, Epistle 2: "We have spoken of Anacletus, explaining the word presbyter."

units.la: Sicut gladio corpora, sic & anima verbo malo percutiuntur.
units.tr: Just as bodies are struck with the sword, so souls are struck with an evil word.

units.la: S Anè Percussor ille doctor dicitur, qui sermone inutili conscientiam percutit infirmorum. Ideo tenere vos, & omnes fideles oportet eum, qui secundùm doctrinam fidelis est, sermonem, Vt potens sit consolari in doctrina Sancta, & contradicentes redarguere, & recte viuentes atque etiam rectam fidem tuentes consolidare. Anacleto succinunt Hieronymus & Chrysostomus, hoc Apostoli mandatum declarantes. Post quod in eodem sequitur. Non litigiosum. Quod uno verbo dixit Apostolus.
units.tr: That teacher is called a striker who strikes the consciences of the weak with useless speech. Therefore you and all the faithful ought to hold to the word that is faithful according to doctrine, so that he may be able to console in sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict, and to strengthen those who live rightly and also guard the right faith. Jerome and Chrysostom agree with Anacletus, declaring this command of the Apostle. After which, in the same place, there follows: "not quarrelsome." This the Apostle said in one word.

units.la: AMAXON.
units.tr: Not quarrelsome [ἄμαχον]

units.la: Hoc est: Absque iurgio. Alienum à pugna, fori, scilicet, ac verborum. Non enim vetat esse Lanistas, vel Pugiles (quod in quovis de populo reprehensibile foret) sed Apostolus instituit Ecclesiae ministros, quid facere non debeant: quod secundo sequentis Epistolae capite verbum repetit, inquiens. ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥ ΟΥ ΔΕΙ ΜΑΧΕΣΘΑΙ. Seruum autem Domini non oportet pugnare, id est, litigare, quemadmodum transtulit antiquus interpres. Et ad Titum cap. 3. ΑΜΑΧΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Decimum Sacerdotis ornamentum.
units.tr: This means: without wrangling, far removed from strife of the courts and of words. For he does not forbid there to be gladiators or boxers (which would be blameworthy in any ordinary person); rather, the Apostle lays down what ministers of the Church ought not to do. He repeats this word in the second chapter of the following Epistle, saying: "But the servant of the Lord must not fight" [ΔΟΥΛΟΝ ΔΕ ΚΥΡΙΟΥ ΟΥ ΔΕΙ ΜΑΧΕΣΘΑΙ]. That is, the servant of the Lord must not strive, that is, quarrel, as the old translator rendered it. And in Ad Titum cap. 3: "to be not quarrelsome" [ΑΜΑΧΟΥΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ]. The tenth ornament of the priest.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLVI.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XLVI.

units.la: Gratianus. SEQVITVR in Epistola ad Timotheum. Non litigiosum.
units.tr: Gratian. It follows in the Epistle to Timothy: Not contentious.

units.la: Nihil est impudentius arrogantiâ Rusticorum, qui garrulitatem, authoritate putant: & Parati semper ad lites, in subiectû sibi gregè tumidis sermonibus tonât. Haec Hieronymus ad Oceanum. Vbi pro Rusticorum, lego, Rabulorum. Nam sic idem Sanctus ad Nepotianum de vita Clericorum scribit: loquens ibi de cõcionibus Episcoporum. Gratianus. Quod ex arrogantia superbiæ prouenire manifestû est. Unde Gregorius scribit in moralibus, libro vigesimo tertio, parte quintâ: in fine cap.12. & in principio. 13. Exponens caput.33. Iob.
units.tr: Nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of the rustics, who think that garrulity is authority, and who, always ready for lawsuits, thunder with bombastic words over the flock placed under them. Thus Jerome to Oceanus. Here, for "of the rustics," I read "of the wranglers." For the same Saint writes thus to Nepotian about the life of clergy, speaking there about the sermons of bishops. Gratian. That this arises plainly from the arrogance of pride. Whence Gregory writes in the Moralia, book 23, part 5, at the end of chapter 12 and the beginning of 13, expounding chapter 33 of Job.

units.la: Verbum Dei non debet cum fastu & arrogantia praedicari.
units.tr: The word of God must not be preached with haughtiness and arrogance.

units.la: H Oc habet proprium Doctrina arrogantium, vt humiliter nesciant inferre, quae docent: & recta, quae sapiunt, etiam recte ministrare non possunt. In verbis enim eorum proditur, quod quum docent, quasi in quodam sibi videntur sublimitatis culmine residere: eosque, quos docent, ut longe infra se positos, velut in imo, despiciunt: quibus non consulendo, sed vix dominando, loqui dignantur. Recte autem his per prophetam Dominus dicit: Vos autem cum austeritate imperabatis eis, & cum potentia. Cum austeritate enim & potentia imperant, qui subditos suos, non cum tranquilitate ratiocinando corrigere, sed asperè inflectere dominando festinant. At contrà, vera doctrina tanto vehementius hoc elationis vitium fugit per cognitionem, quanto ardentius verborum suorum iaculis ipsum magistrum elationis insequitur. Cauet enim, ne eum elatis moribus praedicet, quem in cordibus audientium Sacris sermonibus insectatur. Gratianus. ECCE. Quare litigiosi prohibentur in Episcopos ordinari. Est & alia causa huius prohibitionis. Litigiosi nanque vel adulationibus animos principum sibi conciliant: Vel fratribus suis detrahendo, infamiae notam ingerunt. Vel inter fratres discordiam seminando, seditionem nunquam facere cessant. Quae omnia in Praelatis damnabilia esse probantur. Unde. Gregorius scribit in moralibus. lib. 18. parte. 4. cap. 3. In 17. cap. Iob.
units.tr: This is the particular mark of arrogant teaching: that it cannot humbly admit what it teaches, and cannot properly administer the right things it knows. For in their words it is revealed that, when they teach, they seem to themselves to sit as on a height of lofty eminence, and they look down on those whom they teach as placed far beneath them, as if in the depths; they deign to speak to them not by consulting them but by barely lording it over them. Rightly the Lord says of such people through the prophet: "But you ruled over them with harshness and with power." For those rule with harshness and power who hasten to correct their subjects not by reasoning with calm, but by harshly bending them through domination. On the contrary, true doctrine flees this vice of pride all the more vehemently through knowledge, the more ardently it pursues the very master of pride with the darts of its words. For it takes care not to preach him as one of haughty manners, whom it assails in the hearts of its hearers with holy sermons. Gratian. Behold. Hence litigious men are forbidden to be ordained as bishops. There is also another reason for this prohibition. For litigious men either win over the minds of princes by flattery, or by slandering their brothers they bring upon them the stain of infamy, or by sowing discord among the brothers they never cease to stir up sedition. All of which are proved to be damnable in prelates. Whence Gregory writes in the Moralia, book 18, part 4, chapter 3, on chapter 17 of Job.

units.la: Mysteriorum Dei concionator non debet esse palpo nec adulator. Horrenda est enim blasphemia coram domino, quando laudatur peccator in desideriis animae suae: & iniquus benedicitur. Psal. 9.
units.tr: A preacher of the mysteries of God ought not to be a flatterer or a sycophant. For it is a horrible blasphemy before the Lord when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed. Ps. 9.

units.la: SVnt nonnulli, qui dum malefacta hominum laudibus efferunt, augent, quae increpare debuerunt. Hinc enim per Prophetam dicitur: Vae his qui consuunt pulvillos sub omni cubito manus, & faciunt cervicalia sub capite universae aetatis. Ad hoc quippe pulvillus ponitur, ut mollius quiescatur. Quisquis ergo male agentibus adulatur, pulvillum sub cubito, vel capite iacentis ponit: ut qui corripi ex culpa debuerat, in ea fultus laudibus molliter quiescat.
units.tr: There are some who, while they extol the evil deeds of men with praises, increase what they ought to have rebuked. For thus it is said through the prophet: "Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and make pillows under the head of every age." For a cushion is placed for this purpose, that one may rest more softly. Whoever therefore flatters those who act badly places a cushion under the elbow or head of the one lying down, so that he who ought to have been corrected for his fault, being propped up by praises, may rest softly in it.

units.la: Hinc rursus scriptum est: Ipse ædificabat parietem, illi autem liniebant eum. Parietis quippe nomine, peccati duritia designatur. Ædificare ergo parietem, est contra se quempiam obstacula peccati construere. Sed parietem liniunt, qui peccata perpetrantibus adulantur ut quod illi peruerse agentes ædificant, ipsi adulantes quasi nitidum reddant. Sed Sanctus vir, sicut mala de bonis nō æstimat, ita iudicare bona de malis recusat, dicens: Absit hoc à me, ut iustos vos iudicem: donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea. Hinc etiam in Concilio Chartaginen. 4. cap. 54.
units.tr: Hence it is written again: "He himself was building the wall, but they were plastering it." For by the name of the wall the hardness of sin is designated. To build a wall, therefore, is for someone to construct obstacles of sin against himself. But they plaster the wall who flatter those committing sins, so that what those acting perversely build, the flatterers, as it were, make shining. But the holy man, just as he does not judge evils from goods, so he refuses to judge goods from evils, saying: "Far be it from me that I should judge you righteous; until I die I will not depart from my innocence." Hence also in the Council of Carthage 4, chapter 54.

units.la: Inuidi, fratrum Delatores & Accusatores, Adulatores, atque Proditores, Maledici, Scurriles, Seditiosi non sunt in Clerum recipiendi: Receptique sunt amonendi.
units.tr: Envious men, informers and accusers of brothers, flatterers, betrayers, slanderers, buffoons and seditious men are not to be received into the clergy; and those who have been received are to be admonished.

units.la: CLericus inuidens fratrum profectibus, donec in vitio est, non promoueatur. Item. cap. 55. eiusdem.
units.tr: A cleric who envies the progress of his brothers is not to be promoted, for as long as he is in this vice. Likewise chapter 55 of the same.

units.la: ACcusatores fratrum, Episcopus excommunicet, qui non probanda fratribus obiiciunt: & si emendauerint vitium, recipiat eos ad communionem, non ad Clerum. Item. Cap. 56. eiusdem Concilii Cartha. 4.
units.tr: A bishop is to excommunicate accusers of brothers who bring against them charges that cannot be proved; and if they amend their vice, he is to receive them into communion, but not into the clergy. Likewise chapter 56 of the same Council of Carthage 4.

units.la: CLericus qui adulationibus, & proditionibus vacare deprehenditur, degradetur ab officio. Itē. Cap. 57. eiusdē.
units.tr: A cleric who is found to be devoted to flattery and betrayal is to be degraded from his office. Likewise chapter 57 of the same.

units.la: CLericus maledicus (maximè in Sacerdotibus) cogatur ad postulandam veniam: si noluerit, Degradetur: nec vnquam absque satisfactione ad officium reuocetur. Item. Cap. 60. eiusdem.
units.tr: A slanderous cleric (especially among priests) is to be compelled to ask pardon; if he is unwilling, he is to be degraded, and he is never to be restored to office without satisfaction. Likewise chapter 60 of the same.

units.la: CLericum scurrilem, & verbis turpibus ioculatorē, ab officio esse retrahendum censemus. Item. Cap. 67.
units.tr: We judge that a buffoon cleric, a jester with shameful words, is to be removed from office. Likewise chapter 67.

units.la: SEditionarios statuimus nunquam ordinandos Clericos sicut nec vsurarios, vel iniuriarum suarum vltores.
units.tr: We decree that seditious men are never to be ordained as clerics, nor usurers, nor avengers of their own injuries.

units.la: Duo de prohibito fœnore Canones inconsideranter hic adsuti fuēre. Nam Diorismi sequētis argumento congruunt: quò nos transtulimus. Liter & iurgia solent, vt plurimùm, ex aliena cupiditate nasci: Propterea iubet Apostolus Ecclesiæ ministros esse, ______
units.tr: Two canons on forbidden usury have been inconsiderately stitched in here. For they agree with the argument of the following Dictum, to which we have transferred them. Moreover, strife and quarrels usually arise from the greed of others; therefore the Apostle orders the ministers of the Church to be ______

units.la: ἈΦΙΛΑΡΓΥΡΟΥΣ.
units.tr: NOT LOVERS OF MONEY, [ἈΦΙΛΑΡΓΥΡΟΥΣ].

units.la: Id est. Non amantes pecuniæ, Non auaros, Non cupidos, vt est, in vetere interprete: qui & φιλαργυρίαν traduxit in Cupiditatè. 1 .Timoth. 6. ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία. Duo simul hic proponuntur insignia Sacerdotum____ Ne sint Auari: Ne sint Turpis lucri cupidi. Qua de re Gratianus ab hoc extremo Canone (qui meminit Vsurariorum) velut occasione datâ, progrediens ad subsequentem disputationem, sic ait.
units.tr: That is: Not lovers of money, not greedy, not covetous, as the old translator has it, who also rendered φιλαργυρίαν as cupidity. 1 Timothy 6: For the love of money is the root of all evils [ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία]. Two notable marks of priests are proposed here at once: that they should not be greedy, and that they should not be eager for shameful gain. On this matter Gratian, taking occasion from this last canon (which mentions usurers), proceeds to the following discussion and says thus.

units.la: DISTINCTIO. XLVII.
units.tr: Distinction 47.

units.la: Gratianus. QVOD autem in huius capituli fine Vsurarij prohibentur ordinari, inde est, Quòd Vsuram exercentes, Cupiditati deseruire probantur. Cupidi autem ab Apostolo ordinari prohibentur: quia tales facilè à Iusto deuiarent. Vnde in Canonibus Apostolorum.cap.44.legitur.
units.tr: Gratian. That usurers are forbidden to be ordained at the end of this chapter follows from this: those who practise usury are shown to be slaves to greed. The Apostle also forbids greedy men to be ordained, because such men would easily turn aside from what is just. Hence it is read in the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 44.

units.la: In Ecclesiæ ministris vsura omnino damnatur.
units.tr: Usury is utterly condemned in ministers of the Church.

units.la: EPiscopus, aut Presbyter, aut Diaconus vsuras à debitoribus exigens, Aut desinat, Aut deponatur.
units.tr: A bishop, a presbyter, or a deacon who exacts usury from his debtors shall either stop, or be deposed.

units.la: Item. Ex Concilio Niceno,can.17.
units.tr: Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, canon 17.

units.la: Vsuras exigens, siue Clericus, siue Regulæ quiuis alius subiectus, deiiciatur.
units.tr: Whoever exacts usury, whether a cleric or any other man bound by a rule, shall be cast down.

units.la: QVoniam multi sub regula constituti, Auaritiam, & turpia lucra sectantur, obliti diuinæ scripturæ dicentis: Qui pecuniam suam non dedit ad vsurâ: Et mutuum dates, centesimas exigunt: Iustè censuit magna & Sancta Synodus, Vt si quis inuentus fuerit post hanc diffinitionem, Vsuras accipiens, aut aliquam adinuentionem faciens, vel quolibet modo negocia transigens. aut hemiolia, [id est sescupla] exigens, vel aliquod tale prorsus excogitans, turpis lucri gratiâ: deiiciatur à Clero, & alienus existat à Regula. Ex concilio Laodicensi,cap.4.
units.tr: Since many who are bound by a rule pursue avarice and shameful gain, forgetting what Holy Scripture says, "He who has not lent his money at usury, and has not taken interest," they exact a hundred per cent. Therefore the great and holy Synod has justly decreed that if anyone is found after this definition to accept usury, or to devise some contrivance, or to conduct business in any way, or to exact a hemiolia [that is, sescupla], or to think up anything of the kind, for the sake of shameful gain, he shall be cast out of the clergy and cease to belong to the rule. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 4.

units.la: NOn licet fœnerari ministris altaris, vel in Sacerdotali ordine constitutis: Et Vsuras, & lucra [quæ sescupla dicuntur] accipere. Item. Leo Papa.1.Epistola.1.omnibus Episcopis scripta. Maximo, & Paterio Coss.id est,anno Christ.445.cap.4.Epist.
units.tr: It is not lawful for ministers of the altar, or those established in the priestly order, to lend at interest, or to take usury and gains [which are called sescupla]. Likewise, Pope Leo, first letter, written to all bishops, in the consulship of Maximus and Paterius, that is, in the year of Christ 445, chapter 4 of the letters.

units.la: Alieno, suo͞ue nomine, Clerici ne fœnerantor.
units.tr: A cleric must not lend at interest, either in his own name or in another's.

units.la: SIcut non suo, ita nec alieno nomine, aliquis Clericorum exercere fœnus attentet. Indecens est enim crimen suum commodis alienis impedere. Fœnus autem hoc solum aspicere & exercere debemus, ut quod hic misericorditer tribuimus, à Domino (qui multipliciter & in perpetuũ mansura retribuit) recipere valeamus.Hinc etiam Gregorius, In 19. lib. Moralium. cap. 25. ad cap. 28. Iob. scribit dicens:
units.tr: Just as no one of the clergy should attempt to carry on moneylending in his own name, so neither should he do so in another's name. For it is unseemly to put one's own crime at the service of another's advantage. We ought to look upon and practise lending at interest only in this way: that what we here give in mercy we may receive back from the Lord, who repays many times over and for ever. Hence also Gregory, in the nineteenth book of the Morals, chapter 25, on chapter 28 of Job, writes, saying:

units.la: Deo simul & sæculo seruire: Terrenis pariter & Cœlestibus animum rebus intendere, Vel impossibile est, vel sanè quàm difficile.
units.tr: To serve God and the world at once, to direct the mind both to earthly and to heavenly things, is either impossible or, surely, very difficult.

units.la: OMnes huius sæculi dilectores in Terrenis rebus fortes sunt, in Cœlestibus debiles. Nam pro temporali gloria vsque ad mortem desudare appetunt: & pro spe perpetua ne parum quidem in labore subsistunt. pro Terrenis lucris quaslibet iniurias tolerant: & pro Cœlesti mercede, vel tenuissimi verbi ferre contumelias recusant. Terreno iudici toto etiam die assistere fortes sunt. In oratione verò coram Domino, vel vnius horæ momento lassantur. Sæpe nuditatem, deiectionem, famam pro acquirendis diuitiis, atque honoribus tolerant, & earum rerum se abstinentiâ cruciant, ad quas adipiscendas festinant: Superna autem laboriosè quærere tanto magis dissimulant, quantò ea retribui tardiùs putant.
units.tr: All lovers of this world are strong in earthly things and weak in heavenly ones. For they are eager to labour even to death for temporal glory, yet they hardly hold out for a moment in labour for the hope of eternity. For earthly gain they endure any injury, but for a heavenly reward they refuse to bear even the slightest word of reproach. They are strong enough to stand before an earthly judge the whole day. But in prayer before the Lord they grow weary in a single moment of an hour. Often they endure nakedness, disgrace and loss of reputation to acquire riches and honours, and they torment themselves by abstaining from the very things they hasten to obtain. But to seek heavenly things with labour they neglect all the more, the more slowly they think these will be repaid.

units.la: Aliis alij conferuntur arboribus. Soli Palmæ solus Iustus æquiparatur.
units.tr: Different trees are compared with different people. Only the palm is likened to the just man alone.

units.la: § Hi itaque, quasi aliarum arborum more, deorsum vasti sunt, sursum angusti: quia fortes in Inferiora subsistunt, sed ad Superiora deficiunt. At contrà, ex qualitate Palmarum designatur proficiens vita Iustorum, qui nequaquam sunt in Terrenis desideriis fortes, & in Cœlestibus debiles: sed longiùs atque distantiùs studiosos magis Deo se exhibent, quàm Seculo fuisse meminerint.
units.tr: § Such men, then, like other trees, are broad below and narrow above: for they are strong in lower things but fail in higher ones. On the other hand, the character of palms signifies the advancing life of the just, who are by no means strong in earthly desires and weak in heavenly ones, but who show themselves far more eager for God, by a longer and wider stretch, than they remember having been for the world.

units.la: Quàm fortes fuimus in Malis patrandis, Tam fortes nos esse iubet Apostolus in Bonis agendis.
units.tr: As strong as we were in doing evil, so strong does the Apostle bid us be in doing good.

units.la: § Nam cùm quibusdam per prædicatorem nostrum dicitur: Humanum dico propter infirmitatem carnis vestræ. sicut enim exhibuistis membra vestra seruire immunditiæ & iniquitati ad iniquitatem: ita nunc exhibete membra vestra seruire Iustitiæ in sanctificationem: eorum proculdubio infirmitati condescenditur. Ac si eis apertius diceretur: Si nequaquam amplius potestis, saltem tales estote in fructu bonorum operum, quales fuistis dudum in actione vitiorum: nec debiliores vos habeat sancta libertas Charitatis, quàm vos in carne validos habuit vsus terrenæ voluptatis. Idem Gregorius ciuibus Neapol. Epist. 40. lib. 8.
units.tr: § For when our preacher says to some: "I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For as you once presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification," surely he is stooping to their weakness. It is as if it were said to them more plainly: "If you can no longer do so much, at least be such in the fruit of good works as you once were in the practice of vices. And let not the holy freedom of charity find you weaker than the use of earthly pleasure found you strong in the flesh." The same Gregory, to the citizens of Naples, letter 40, book 8.

units.la: Fœnerator in Clerum nunquam recipiatur.
units.tr: A moneylender must never be received into the clergy.

units.la: DE Petro insuper ad nos peruenisse cognoscite, quia solidos dedit ad vsuras. quod vos oportet cum omni subtilitate perquirere. & si ita constiterit, alium eligite, & ab huiusmodi vos persona sine mora suspendite. Nam nos amatoribus vsurarum nullâ ratione manus imponimus.
units.tr: Know also that it has come to us concerning Peter that he lent money at usury. You must enquire into this with all care; and if it is confirmed, choose another, and suspend such a person from office without delay. For we never lay hands on lovers of usury on any ground.

units.la: Absenti non est, nisi parcissimè, facienda gratia, seu conferendum Beneficium: sed tantùm præsentibus, & bene probatis. In Exegesi. cap. de multa. Exponens hoc verbum, per sedem Apostolicam. Istud declarabam.
units.tr: A favour is not to be granted, nor a benefice conferred, to one who is absent, except very sparingly, but only to those who are present and well proved. In the commentary on the chapter "De multa," explaining this phrase, "through the Apostolic See." I was declaring this.

units.la: § Si verò subtili habitâ inquisitione, hoc falsum esse putaueritis, quia persona eius nobis ignota est, & vtrùm ita sit de simplicitate eius, quod ad nos perlatum est, ignoramus: cum decreto à vobis facto, ad nos eum venire necesse est, vt vitam morésque illius solicitiùs inquirentes, sen sum quoque pariter cognoscamus: Vt si iudicio huic aptus exiterit, vestra in eo (adiuuante Domino) desideria compleamus. Item. Ex Concilio Elibertano, cap. 10. Vbique legendum (namsepe citatur) Ex Concilio Iliberino. Ulterioris Hispaniæ ciuitas est Iliberis, quam modò Granadam dicì putant. Eò patres Hispani, circa Nicænæ Synodi tempus, conuenerunt.
units.tr: But if, after a careful enquiry, you judge this to be false, because his person is unknown to us, and we do not know whether what has been reported to us about his simplicity is true, then he must come to us with a decree made by you, so that we may enquire more carefully into his life and character and likewise come to know his mind; so that, if he proves fit for this office, we may fulfil your wishes in him, with the Lord's help. Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, chapter 10. Everywhere it should be read (for it is often cited so) "From the Council of Iliberis." Iliberis is a city in Further Spain, which they now think is called Granada. To it the Spanish fathers, around the time of the Nicene Synod, came together.

units.la: Tam gradu, quàm communione priuandus est fœnerator Clericus.
units.tr: A clerical moneylender must be deprived of both rank and communion.

units.la: SI quis Clericorum detectus fuerit vsuras accipere, placuit hunc degradari, & abstinere. Item. Leo Papa 1. Anatholio Episcopo Constantinopo. Epist. 51.
units.tr: If any of the clergy is found to take usury, it is decided that he be degraded and abstain. Likewise, Pope Leo, first, to Bishop Anatolius of Constantinople, letter 51.

units.la: Error, & Cupiditas violát Sacerdotij maiestatē. Sine sit ea Philargyria, Sine sit ἀπληστία.
units.tr: Error and greed violate the majesty of the priesthood. Let it be philargyria, let it be insatiability.

units.la: VIrum Catholicum, & præcipuè Domini Sacerdotem, sicut nullo errore implicari, ita nullâ oportet cupiditate violari, dicente Sanctâ scripturâ: Post concupiscentias tuas ne eas. Mens enim potetię auida, nec abstinere nouit à vetitis, nec gaudere cœcesiis, nec pietati adhibere consensum.
units.tr: A Catholic man, and above all a priest of the Lord, ought to be entangled by no error, just as he ought to be violated by no greed, Holy Scripture saying: "Do not go after your lusts." For a mind greedy for power neither knows how to abstain from forbidden things, nor to rejoice in what is right, nor to give its assent to piety.

units.la: Item. Gregorius Epist.110.lib.7.ad Syagrium, Hæduorum Episcopum.
units.tr: Likewise, Gregory, letter 110, book 7, to Syagrius, bishop of the Aedui.

units.la: Sacerdotem coërcere decet omnes suas Cupiditates
units.tr: It befits a priest to restrain all his desires.

units.la: BOnorum authori inhærere aliter non valemus, nisi Cupiditatem à nobis (quæ omnium malorum radix est) abscindamus. Item. Ambrosius, de eo quod scriptum est in Euangelio: Hominis cuiusdam diuitis fructus uberes ager attulit. Luc. cap. 12. c. Sermone 81. To. 5.
units.tr: We cannot cling to the author of good things unless we cut off from ourselves greed, which is the root of all evils. Likewise, Ambrose, on what is written in the Gospel: "The fields of a certain rich man brought forth abundant fruit," Luke chapter 12, in sermon 81, volume 5.

units.la: Expletur nunquam, neque satiatur Cupiditatis sitis.
units.tr: The thirst of greed is never filled, nor is it satisfied.

units.la: SIcut hi, qui per insaniam mente translati sunt, non iam res ipsas, sed phantasias passionis suæ vident: ita etiam mens auari semel vinculis cupiditatis auri astricta, semper Aurum, semper Argentum videt, semper reditus computat, gratiùs Aurum, quàm solem intuetur. Ipsa eius oratio & supplicatio ad Deum, Aurum quærit. Et vellet, atque optaret, ut omnia ei in Aurum conuerterentur. Denique, quod potest, Frumentum in aurum conuertere conatur. Vinum mutat in Aurum. Eidem Lana efficitur aurum. Omnes fructus eius, Omne negocium, Omne, quod mouetur, in Aurum vertitur. Interdum etiam, vsuræ arte nequissimâ, ex ipso Auro Aurum nascitur. Sed quid agis? Nec satietas unquâ, nec finis aderit Cupiditati.
units.tr: Just as those who have been carried out of their minds by madness no longer see the things themselves, but the phantasies of their own passion, so too the mind of a miser, once bound by the chains of the lust for gold, always sees gold and silver, always reckons his income, and gazes at gold more fondly than at the sun. Even his prayer and supplication to God seeks gold. And he would wish and desire that everything be turned into gold for him. Finally, whatever he can, he tries to turn grain into gold. He changes wine into gold. For him wool too becomes gold. All his produce, all his business, everything that is moved, is turned into gold. Sometimes, too, by the most wicked art of usury, gold is born from gold itself. But what are you doing? Greed will never have satiety nor an end.

units.la: Quae sibi superfluunt bona, sibi propria dicere nemo debet.
units.tr: No one ought to call his own those goods which are left over and above what he needs.

units.la: Sed ais, quid iniustum est, si, quum aliena non invadam, propria diligentius servo? O impudens dictum? Propria dicis? Quae? Quid ex reconditis in hunc mundum detulisti? Quando ingressus es in hanc lucem, quando de matris ventre existi, quibus facultatibus, quaeso, quibus subsidiis stipatus ingressus es? Et paulò post.
units.tr: But you say: what is wrong if, since I do not seize what belongs to others, I guard what is mine more carefully? O shameless saying! Do you call them yours? Which ones? What have you brought into this world out of the storehouse? When you entered this light, when you came out of your mother's womb, with what resources, I ask, with what supplies, did you enter, attended by them? And a little later.

units.la: Terra communiter omnibus hominibus data est. Proprium nemo dicat, quod è communi, plusquam sufficeret, sumptum, & violenter obtentum est. Paulò inferius.
units.tr: The earth has been given in common to all men. No one should call his own what has been taken from the common stock, and seized by force, beyond what would suffice. A little further below.

units.la: Inuasor est Alienorum, qui de sua copia non succurrit inopiae Proximorum.
units.tr: He is a plunderer of other people's goods who does not come to the aid of his neighbours' need from his own abundance.

units.la: Nunquid iniquus est Deus, ut nobis non aequaliter distribuat vitae subsidia? ut tu quidem esses affluens & abundans: aliis verò deesset, & egerent? An idcirco magis, quia & tibi voluit benignitatis suae experimenta conferre, & alium per virtutem Patientiae coronare? Tu verò, susceptis Dei muneribus, & in sinum tuum redactis, nihil te putas agere iniquum, si tam multorum vitae subsidia solus obtineas? Quis enim tam iniustus, tam avidus, tam avarus, quàm qui multorum alimenta, suum non usum, sed abundantiam & delicias facit? Neque enim minùs est criminis, habenti tollere, quàm quum possis & abundas, indigentibus denegare. Esurientium panis est, quem tu detines. nudorum indumentum est, quod tu recludis. & miserorum redemptio est, & absolutio, Pecunia, quam tu interram defodis. Ergo, Tantorum te scias invadere bona, quantis ipse possis praestare, si velis. Itaque, praedictu esto conclusum, quod Philargyria Sacerdotalibus institutis est omnium maxime contraria: qua nullum quoque crimen in Canone damnatius.
units.tr: Is God unjust, that He does not distribute the means of life equally among us, so that you should be rich and abounding while others lack and go in want? Or is it rather because He wished to give you tokens of His kindness, and to crown another through the virtue of patience? But you, having received God's gifts and gathered them into your bosom, do you think you do nothing wrong in keeping for yourself alone the means of life of so many? For who is so unjust, so greedy, so avaricious, as the man who turns the food of many not to use but to abundance and luxury? For it is no less a crime to take from one who has, than, when you are able and abounding, to deny it to the needy. The bread you hold back belongs to the hungry; the clothing you lock away belongs to the naked; the money you bury in the ground is the ransom and release of the wretched. Therefore know that you are seizing goods as great as those with which you could help, if you chose. Hence let it be concluded, as said above, that covetousness is utterly opposed to the priestly institutions, and that no crime is more condemned in the Canon.

units.la: Post haec ad aliam transit Apostoli sententiam Gratianus, quae sic habet.
units.tr: After this, Gratian passes to another saying of the Apostle, which reads thus.

units.la: ΤΟΝ ΙΔΙΟΥ ΟΙΚΟΥ ΚΑΛΩΣ ΠΡΟΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΝ: ΤΕΚΝΑ ΕΧΟΝΤΑ ΕΝ ΥΠΟΤΑΓΗ ΜΕΤΑ ΠΑΣΗΣ ΣΕΜΝΟΤΗΤΟΣ.
units.tr: ΤΟΝ ΙΔΙΟΥ ΟΙΚΟΝ ΚΑΛΩΣ ΠΡΟΙΣΤΑΜΕΝΟΝ: ΤΕΚΝΑ ΕΧΟΝΤΑ ΕΝ ΥΠΟΤΑΓΗ ΜΕΤΑ ΠΑΣΗΣ ΣΕΜΝΟΤΗΤΟΣ [ton idiou oikon kalōs proistamenon: tekna echonta en hypotagē meta pasēs semnotētos]

units.la: Hoc insigne proprium ac peculiare est a coniugio, vel post coniugium venientibus ad Sacerdotium.
units.tr: This is a distinctive and special mark of those who come to the priesthood from marriage, or after marriage.

units.la: SVae domui bene praepositum. Filios habentem subdi- tos cum omni castitate, sine accusatione Luxuriae. Vide
units.tr: Well set over his own house, having children subject to him with all chastity, without accusation of lechery. See

units.la: (ait Hieronymus) quanta pudicitia exigatur in Episcopo: Vt si filij eius impudici fuerint, ipse Episcopus esse non possit.
units.tr: (says Jerome) how great purity is required in a bishop: so that if his sons are unchaste, he himself cannot be a bishop.

units.la: Eligebantur ab Ecclesia quondam Mariti Patresque familias in Sacerdotium. Nec enim tunc temporis, tot erant, Virgines, aut Casti, mundique Caelibes, quot erant necessarij Sacerdotes: ut Hieronymus in Iouinianum scripsit. Ab his tria, quae non ab aliis, exigebantur. Ut unius uxoris essent. Ut domum suam bene regerent. Vt (si quos genuissent) filios sine accusatione Luxuria subditos haberent. Hieronymi verbum subiungam, libro contra Pelagianos primo. Post ad Gratianum veniemus.
units.tr: Formerly husbands and heads of families were chosen by the Church for the priesthood. For at that time there were not as many virgins, or chaste and pure celibates, as there were priests needed, as Jerome wrote in his work against Jovinian. From these men three things were required that were not required of others: that they be husbands of one wife; that they rule their own house well; and that they have their children (if they had begotten any) subject to them without accusation of lechery. I will add Jerome's own words, from the first book against the Pelagians. Afterwards we shall come to Gratian.

units.la: Episcopo propriam non sufficit habere pudicitiam: nisi ea filiorum, & comitum, ac ministrorum pudore decoretur, dicente Dauid. Ambulans in via immaculata, Hic mihi ministrabat. Apostolum iam Gratianus exponat.
units.tr: It is not enough for a bishop to have chastity of his own, unless it is adorned also by the modesty of his sons, companions and ministers, as David says: "He who walks in the unspotted way, he ministered to me." Now let Gratian expound the Apostle.

units.la: Gratianus. NECESSE est etiam ut ille qui ordinandus est, Suae domui sit bene praepositus, id est, Si in Laicali habitu uxorem habuit, vel Filios, a vitiis ad virtutum studia & verbo & exemplo prouocet. Vt quod postea praecepturis est populis, prius exigat a domesticis. Unde Apostolus Ephesiis scribit, ut filios suos non ad iracundiam prouocent: sed enutriant illos in omni disciplina & correctione Domini. Unde quum Paulus ad Timotheum scribens dixisset: Suae Domui bene praepositu. statim subiunxit: Habentem filios sibi subditos in omni castitate, & non in accusatione luxuriae. non enim talium cohabitator frontem habet alios redarguendi.
units.tr: Gratian. It is necessary also that the man who is to be ordained be set well over his own house; that is, if in lay condition he has a wife or children, he should urge them from vices to the pursuit of virtues, both by word and by example, so that he first requires from his household what he is afterwards to command of the people. Hence the Apostle writes to the Ephesians that they should not provoke their sons to anger, but bring them up in all discipline and correction of the Lord. Hence, when Paul, writing to Timothy, had said, "set well over his own house," he immediately added, "having children subject to him in all chastity, and not under accusation of lechery." For one who lives with such people does not have the face to rebuke others.

units.la: Pater de salute ac disciplina filiorum soliitus. Gratianus.
units.tr: The father, free from care for the salvation and discipline of his sons. Gratian.

units.la: VNde, De beato Iob legitur, Quod pro filiis suis quo- tidiana offerebat Deo sacrificia, offerens holocausta per singulos: quos tanta Charitatis perfectio in unum co- nstrinxerat, ut quisque eorum in suo die conuiuium fratribus bus
units.tr: Hence it is read of blessed Job that he offered daily sacrifices to God for his sons, offering burnt offerings for each of them, since such perfection of love had bound them together that each of them, on his own day, would prepare a feast for his brothers

units.la: bus præpararet, & ad epulandum secum tres sorores suas pariter inuitaret.
units.tr: and would invite his three sisters to dine with him together.

units.la: Patres indulgentes.
units.tr: The Fathers, on indulgence.

units.la: § Quod quia Hely facere dissimulauit, ac falsa pietate superatus, delinquentes filios ferire noluit, (sicut in libro Regum legitur) apud districtum iudicem semetipsum cum filiis crudeli damnatione percussit. unde ei diuinā voce dicitur: Honorasti filios tuos magis quàm me.
units.tr: Because Eli neglected to do this, and, overcome by a false piety, was unwilling to strike his sinning sons (as is read in the book of Kings), he condemned himself and his sons before the strict judge with a cruel damnation. Hence the divine voice says to him: "You have honoured your sons more than me."

units.la: Hinc etiam Dauid erga filios, bonitatem, non disciplinæ seueritatem exercens, eorum iuuentutē experimento didicit esse perniciosam, quorum pueritiam vagâ licentiâ permisit esse voluptuosam. Vnus quippe eorum sororem suam stupro corrumpens, à fratre eius. Absalone, videlicet inter epulas, quas fratribus suis fraudulenter parauerat, obtruncatus est. Absalon verò postquam veniam à patre obtinuit, de regno illum expulit, & ad concubinas eius ingressus est: demum per inuia deserti patrem persequens, quercui inhæsit, atque ita suspensus interiit. Hinc etiā Paulus ad Timotheum scribit dicens.
units.tr: Likewise David, showing kindness rather than severity of discipline towards his sons, learned by experience how harmful their youth was, since he had allowed their boyhood to be pleasure-seeking through a wandering licence. For one of them, who defiled his sister by rape, was slain by her brother Absalom at a feast that he had fraudulently prepared for his brothers. Absalom, however, after obtaining pardon from his father, drove him from the kingdom and went in to his concubines. Finally, pursuing his father through the trackless desert, he clung to an oak and, hanging there, perished. Hence Paul also writes to Timothy, saying:

units.la: Qui Priuata nescit, longe minus administrare Publica nouit.
units.tr: "He who does not know how to manage his own affairs will know even less how to administer public ones."

units.la: Qui suorum, & maximè domesticorum, curam non habet, Fidem negauit: & est infideli deterior. Iure ergo qui domui suæ nescit præesse, in Episcopum ordinari prohibetur: quia, qui in re minima, de qua sibi familiarior debet inesse cura, fidelis non est: quomodo in Ecclesia Dei, vbi tot sunt alieni, solicitam diligentiam exhibebit? Vnde Hieronymus in Comment.cap.1.Epistol.ad Titum.
units.tr: He who has no care for his own, and above all for his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Rightly, therefore, one who does not know how to rule his own house is forbidden to be ordained bishop; for one who is not faithful in the smallest matter, in which he ought to feel a closer concern, how will he show diligent care in the Church of God, where there are so many strangers? Hence Jerome, in his commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus:

units.la: Tam sanctū est Sacerdotij nomen, Vt, & ea, quæ sunt extra nos posita, nobis imputentur.
units.tr: So holy is the name of priesthood that even those things which are placed outside us are imputed to us.

units.la: NON enim iustus polluitur ex vitiis filiorum: sed libertas ab Apostolo, Ecclesiæ principi reseruatur: Vt talis fiat, qui non timeat propter vitia liberorum, extraneos reprehendere. Gratianus. Quod tunc fiet, si non erit, quod sibi imputetur. quum enim gressus hominis à Domino dirigantur: Nec sint in homine, eius viæ: Corripere quidem potest, Corrigere autem non valet. Pulsare potest, non Aperire: Manus comprimere, non animum mutare. Vnde Augustinus Hipponis Clero, Senioribus, & vniuersę plebi. Epistol.137. scribēs.
units.tr: For the righteous man is not defiled by the vices of his sons. But the freedom to rebuke is reserved by the Apostle, the prince of the Church, so that a man may be one who does not fear to reprove outsiders on account of his children's vices. Gratian. This will happen when there is nothing that can be imputed to him, since a man's steps are directed by the Lord, and it is not in man to direct his own ways. He can reprove, but he cannot correct; he can knock, but he cannot open; he can restrain the hands, but he cannot change the heart. Hence Augustine, writing to the clergy, the elders and the whole people of Hippo, in Epistle 137:

units.la: In magna domo, sine aliquo patris familias vituperio, possunt esse, ac semper fuerunt, Vasa quidem, in Honorem quaedam, & alia in Ignominiam. Sed ignominiosa, quis mundari nequeunt, abiicienda veniunt. 2. ad Timoth. 2. c.
units.tr: In a great house, without any reproach to the father of the family, there can be, and always have been, vessels some for honour and others for dishonour. But those that are dishonourable and cannot be cleansed must be cast away. 2 Tim. 2.

units.la: QVantumlibet vigilet disciplina domus meæ Homo sum: & inter homines viuo. Nec mihi arrogare audeo, ut domus mea melior sit, quàm arca Noe, vbi tamen inter octo homines unus reprobus inventus est. Aut melior sit, quàm domus Abrahæ, cui dictum est: Eiice ancillam, & filium eius. Aut melior sit quàm domus Isaac, cui de duobus geminis dictum est: Iacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui. Simpliciter autem fateor charitati vestræ coram Domino Deo nostro, qui testis est super animam meam, ex quo Deo servire coepi: quoniam, sicut difficile sum expertus meliores, quàm qui in Monasteriis profecerunt: ita non sum deteriores expertus, quàm qui in Monasteriis ceciderunt. Ita, ut hinc arbitrer dictum in Apocalipsi: Iustus iustificetur adhuc. & qui in sordibus est, sordescat adhuc. Item. Cypriano Cornelius Papa. Cornelius Romæ, Carthagine Cyprianus, ambo fide, virtute, pietate, denique martyrio præstantes, eodem gerebant Episcopatū tempore circiter annum Do.260. Mutuas vtrinque legimus alias nonnullas Epistolas. Huiusce tantummodò superest hoc in Gratiano fragmentum.
units.tr: However carefully the discipline of my house is watched, I am a man and I live among men. Nor do I dare to claim that my house is better than Noah's ark, where nevertheless one reprobate was found among eight men; or better than Abraham's house, to which it was said, "Cast out the maidservant and her son"; or better than Isaac's house, of which, concerning the twin sons, it was said, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." Yet I simply confess to your charity, before the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul from the time I began to serve God: just as I have found it hard to find better men than those who have advanced in monasteries, so I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. Thus I judge that what is said in the Apocalypse applies: "Let the righteous be justified still, and let him who is filthy be filthy still." Likewise, Cornelius the Pope to Cyprian. Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage, both excelling in faith, virtue, piety and finally martyrdom, held the episcopate at the same time, about the year of the Lord 260. We read several other letters exchanged between them on both sides; of this one only this fragment survives in Gratian.

units.la: Sponte Malorum casus non debet auertere Bonos, quominus bi continuò recti perstent. Sponte verò malus est, qui recta monenti obediens non est.
units.tr: The fall of the wicked by their own will ought not to turn the good aside, so that they should not continue to remain upright. He is wicked by his own will who does not obey one who admonishes him rightly.

units.la: QVod ad nos attinet, Conscientiæ nostræ convenit semper dare operam, ne quis culpâ nostrâ de Ecclesia pereat. Si quis autem vltrò, & crimine suo perierit, & Pœnitentiam agere, atque ad Ecclesiam redire noluerit: nos in die iudicij inculpatos futuros credimus, qui eorum consulimus sanitati: Illos solos in poenis remansuros, qui noluerint consilij nostri salubritate sanari. Nec mouere nos debent conuitia perditorum, quò minùs à via recta & à terta regula non recedamus, quam Apostolus instituit dicens: Si hominibus placere, Christi seruus nõ essem.
units.tr: As far as concerns us, it is always fitting for our conscience to take care that no one perishes from the Church through our fault. But if anyone of his own accord and by his own crime has perished, and is unwilling to do repentance and return to the Church, we believe that we shall be blameless on the day of judgement, who have looked to their health; those alone will remain in punishments who would not be healed by the wholesome effect of our counsel. Nor should the reproaches of the lost move us, so that we do not depart from the right way and from the rule which the Apostle laid down, saying: "If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ."

units.la: In Apostolo sequitur & aliud omnibus Sacerdotibus futuris apprimè necessariû puta.
units.tr: In the Apostle there follows also another thing most necessary for all future priests, namely:

units.la: Non Neophytum. Hoc est. Non nuper natum, siue non nuper plantatum. Metaphora Paulo familiaris. Id est, Non recèns Baptizatum, & Christianum factum quasi diceres, Non Nouitium: qui non est in Ecclesiastico ministerio deuotissimè versatus. Iã quærebatur Hieronymus hoc præceptum suo tempore non obseruari. Libro contra Pelagianos primo. & ad Oceanum. Cuius verba Gratianus initio mox subsequentis Distinctionis retulit; more tamen suo, trunca & immutata quadam.
units.tr: Not a neophyte. That is, not recently born, or not recently planted, a metaphor familiar to Paul: not newly baptised and made a Christian, as you might say, not a novice, who has not been most devotedly engaged in the ecclesiastical ministry. Jerome already complained that this precept was not observed in his own time, in the first book against the Pelagians and in his letter to Oceanus. Gratian, in his usual manner, quoted the words of this at the beginning of the following Distinction, somewhat truncated and altered.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLVIII.
units.tr: DISTINCTION 48.

units.la: Gratianus. PROHIBENTVR autem Neophyti in Episcopos ordinari. Hieronymus in fine Epistolæ ad Oceanum. To. 1.
units.tr: Gratian. Novices, however, are forbidden to be ordained as bishops. Jerome, at the end of the letter to Oceanus, vol. 1.

units.la: Tyrones in belli duces non sunt creandi. Hoc est, Nouitij non sunt in Antistites assumendi.
units.tr: Recruits are not to be made commanders in war. That is, novices are not to be taken up as heads of the Church.

units.la: QVi catechumenus heri fuit, hodie non sit Episcopus. qui heri erat in Theatro, hodie non sedeat in Ecclesia. qui vespere erat in circo, hodie non ministret altario. qui dudum fuerat fautor histrionum, hodie non sit consecrator virginum. Causa autem huius prohibitionis est secundùm Apostolum, Ne elatus in superbiam, tanquam religio Christiana plurimùm eo egeret, incidat in ruinam Diaboli. Momentaneus enim Sacerdos ignorat humilitatem & mansuetudinem rusticorum: sese contemnere nescit: non ieiunauit, non fleuit, non se correxit, non pauperibus erogauit. In arrogantiam (quæ est ruina Diaboli) incidit, qui in puncto horæ, necdum Discipuli, fiunt Magistri.
units.tr: Whoever was a catechumen yesterday should not be a bishop today. Whoever was in the theatre yesterday should not sit in the church today. Whoever was in the circus in the evening should not minister at the altar today. Whoever was lately a patron of actors should not be a consecrator of virgins today. The reason for this prohibition, according to the Apostle, is that a man puffed up with pride, as if the Christian religion needed him very much, may fall into the ruin of the devil. For the priest made in a moment does not know the humility and gentleness of country folk; he does not know how to despise himself; he has not fasted, has not wept, has not corrected himself, has not given to the poor. He falls into arrogance, which is the ruin of the devil, he who in the space of an hour, not yet disciples, becomes masters.

units.la: Innocentius Papa primus, ait in Epistol 12. Aurelio in Aphrica Episcopo scripta, Palladio Consule, videlicet, anno Do.419.
units.tr: Innocent I, Pope, says in Epistle 12, written to Aurelius, bishop in Africa, in the consulship of Palladius, that is, in the year of the Lord 419:

units.la: MIserum est eum fieri magistrum, qui nunquam fuit discipulus. Eumque summum Sacerdotem fieri, qui nullo vnquam in gradu fuerit obsequutus Sacerdoti.
units.tr: It is a wretched thing for someone to become a teacher who was never a disciple, and for someone to become chief priest who has never in any rank obeyed a priest.

units.la: De Neophytis in Nicæni quoque Concilij Canone.2.legitur. Nonnihil secus habet hæc antiqua traductio, quàm Græca sonant, vt annotauimus in margine.
units.tr: The Neophytes are also mentioned in canon 2 of the Council of Nicaea. This old translation differs somewhat from what the Greek says, as we noted in the margin.

units.la: ¶ Catechismus præscriptum tempus erat ante Baptismum: Neque mox à Baptismo licebat adsequi Sacerdotium.
units.tr: ¶ A catechumenate was the time prescribed before baptism, and it was not allowed to attain the priesthood immediately after baptism.

units.la: QVoniam multa sunt, siue per necessitatem: * siue ex quacunque causa, contra regulam gesta: Ita vt homines ex vita Gentilium * nuper adhuc catechizati, vel instructi statim ad spirituale Baptisma venissent: & continuo quum Baptizati sunt, etiam ad Episcopatū vel Presbyterium promoti sunt: recte igitur visum est de cætero nihil tale fieri. nam & tempore opus est, vt sit catechumenus: & post Baptisma multâ probatione indiget: euidens nanque est Apostolicum præceptum, dicens: Non Neophytum: ne forte elatus in superbiam, in iudicium incidat, & in laqueum Diaboli. Si verò, procedente tempore, aliquod * mortale peccatum admiserit: & conuictus duobus, vel tribus testibus fuerit: cessabit à clero, qui huiusmodi est. Si quis verò præter hoc fecerit, tanquam contraria statutis Sancti Concilij * gerens, etiam ipse præcipitabitur de statu Cleri. Gratianus. NEOPHYTI verò hodie appellantur, propositum Sacrae religionis nouiter assumentes. Vnde beatus Gregorius scribit Syagrio Hæduorum Episcopo: Epist.iio.lib.7.
units.tr: Since many things have been done contrary to the rule, whether through necessity or for whatever other cause, so that men coming from the life of the Gentiles, only recently catechized or instructed, came at once to spiritual baptism, and as soon as they were baptized were also promoted to the episcopate or the presbyterate, it has therefore rightly seemed good that nothing of the kind be done in future. For time is needed for the catechumen to be a catechumen, and after baptism he needs much testing; the apostolic precept is plain, saying: not a neophyte, lest perhaps puffed up with pride he fall into judgment and into the snare of the devil. But if, as time goes on, he commits some mortal sin and is convicted by two or three witnesses, he shall cease from the clergy, being of this kind. If anyone however does otherwise, acting contrary to the decrees of the holy Council, he too shall be cast down from the rank of the clergy. Gratian. Neophytes, however, are called today those who newly take up the profession of the sacred religion. Whence blessed Gregory writes to Syagrius, bishop of the Aedui, Epistle 2, book 7.

units.la: Ecclesiam ruere facit ordinatio Nouitiorum.
units.tr: The ordination of novices makes the Church fall.

units.la: S Icut Neophytus dicebatur, qui in initio sanctæ fidei erat eruditione plantatus: sic modò Neophytus habendus est, qui repente in religionis habitu plantatus ad ambiendos Sacros ordines irrepserit. Ordinatè ergo ad ordines ascendendum est: nam casum appetit, qui ad summi loci fastigia, postpositis gradibus, per abrupta quærit ascensum. Scimus autem, quòd ædificati parietes nō priùs tignorum pondus accipiunt, nisi à nouitatis suæ humore siccentur: ne si ante pondera, quàm solidentur, accipiant, cunctam, simul ad terram, fabricam deponent.
units.tr: Just as a Neophyte was called one who had been planted in the knowledge of the holy faith at its beginning, so now he is to be regarded as a Neophyte who has suddenly been planted in the habit of religion and has crept in to seek the holy orders. Therefore one must ascend to orders in due order; for he who seeks an ascent by steep paths, leaving the steps behind, to the summit of the highest place, seeks his fall. We know, moreover, that walls built do not receive the weight of the beams until they have been dried by the moisture of their newness; for if they received the weight before they were made firm, the whole structure would collapse to the ground together.

units.la: In vltima Sermonis istius adeò fidelis periodo sic habetur.
units.tr: The last sentence of this so faithful sermon reads thus.

units.la: ΔΕΙ ΔΕ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΚΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΝ ΚΑΛΗΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΩΝ ΕΞΩΘΕΝ· ΙΝΑ ΜΗ ΕΙΣ ΟΝΕΙΔΙΣΜΟΝ ΕΜΠΕΣΗ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΓΙΔΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΒΟΛΟΥ.
units.tr: It is necessary that he also have a good testimony from those outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. [ΔΕΙ ΔΕ ΑΥΤΟΝ ΚΑΙ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΝ ΚΑΛΗΝ ΕΧΕΙΝ ΑΠΟ ΤΩΝ ΕΞΩΘΕΝ· ΙΝΑ ΜΗ ΕΙΣ ΟΝΕΙΔΙΣΜΟΝ ΕΜΠΕΣΗ, ΚΑΙ ΠΑΓΙΔΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΑΒΟΛΟΥ.]

units.la: Oportet autem illum, & testimonium habere bonum ab iis, qui foris sunt: vt non in opprobrium incidat, & in laqueum diaboli.
units.tr: He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and into the snare of the devil.

units.la: VIII. q. i. Can. Licet.
units.tr: Causa VIII, q. i, Can. Licet.

units.la: Referuntur & Enarrantur ista Pauli verba, ex Origenis authoritate, sic in octauum caput Leuitici scribentis.
units.tr: These words of Paul are cited and expounded on the authority of Origen, who writes thus on the eighth chapter of Leviticus.

units.la: Videamus ergo, quali ordine Pontifex instituitur. Convocauit Moyses synagogam, & dixit ad eos. Hoc est verbum, quod præcepit Dominus.
units.tr: Let us see, then, in what order the high priest is instituted. Moses called the synagogue together and said to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded.

units.la: Non alius Ecclesiæ regendæ præficiendus est, quàm qui vitæ sanctitate, moribus, doctrinâ, virtutibus alios in Ecclesia præcellit. Hoc est, Optimus, & Ecclesiæ commodissimus semper est eligendus. Hæc periocha sex librorum Chrysostomi de Sacerdotio.
units.tr: No one is to be placed over the governance of the Church except one who surpasses others in the Church in holiness of life, in morals, in learning and in virtues. That is, the best and most useful for the Church is always to be chosen. This is the summary of the six books of Chrysostom on the Priesthood.

units.la: Licet ergo Dominus de constituendo Pontifice præcepisset, & iam Dominus elegisset: attamen conuocatur & Synagoga. Requiritur enim in ordinando Sacerdote & præsentia populi. Vt sciant omnes & certi sint: quia, Qui præstantior est ex omni populo, Qui doctior, Qui sanctior, Qui in omni virtute eminentior, Ille eligitur ad Sacerdotium. Et hoc, attestante populo. Ne qua postmodum retractatio cuiquam, Ne quis scrupulus resideret. Hoc est autem, quod & Apostolus praecipit in ordinatione Sacerdotis, dicens—— Oportet autem illum & testimonium habere bonum ab iis, qui foris sunt. Hæc in dicto Can. Licet. ex Rufini translatione, quam perperam tribuunt Hieronymo, quod superius admonui. dist. 36.
units.tr: Therefore, although the Lord had commanded about the appointment of the high priest, and had already chosen him, nevertheless the synagogue is also convened. For the presence of the people is required in the ordination of a priest, so that all may know and be certain that whoever is more outstanding than all the people, more learned, more holy, more eminent in every virtue, is chosen for the priesthood. And this with the people bearing witness, so that no later challenge may be raised by anyone, and no doubt may remain. This, moreover, is what the Apostle also prescribes in the ordination of a priest, saying: He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside. These things are in the said canon Licet, taken from Rufinus's translation, which they wrongly attribute to Jerome, as I warned above, dist. 36.

units.la: Demum, Gratianus Epilogum faciens omnium, quæ De clericorum moribus antedicta fuerunt, In sequenti quadragesima nona distinctione, Leviticorum conditionem corporum, qualem per Moysen Deus primo descripserat, ad animorum transfert in nobis qualitatem, divi Gregorij, præ cæteris, authoritate nitens: qui sanè rem perelegantèr tractavit, atque loci tropos indicavit. Hæc Ethologiæ nostræ finem dabit,
units.tr: Finally, Gratian, making an epilogue of all that was said above about the morals of clergy, in the following forty-ninth distinction, transfers the condition of the Levites' bodies, as God first described it through Moses, to the quality of our souls, relying especially on the authority of divine Gregory, who treated the matter most elegantly and pointed out the tropes of the passage. This will bring our Ethology to an end.

units.la: DISTINCTIO XLIX.
units.tr: DISTINCTION XLIX.

units.la: Gratianus. E C C E, A quibus vitiis debeant esse immunes, qui sunt in Presbyteros ordinandi, apparet. Qui enim intercessores pro populo ad Deum parantur, necesse est ut eius gratiam bene viuendo mereantur. Unde Hieronymus super Malachiam. Non sunt ista Hieronymi verba: sed ex eius commentariis in Malachiæ prophetiam (præcipuè in cap. 1.) coaceruauit ea Gratianus, Hieronymoque tribuit: quia sensus inibi, multisque locis aliis, est ipsius Hieronymi. Sic authorum sæpius abutitur nomine.
units.tr: Gratian. Here it appears from what vices those who are to be ordained priests ought to be free. For those who are appointed as intercessors for the people before God must necessarily earn his grace by living well. Hence Jerome on Malachi. These are not Jerome's words. Gratian gathered them from Jerome's commentaries on the prophecy of Malachi (especially on chapter 1), and attributed them to Jerome, since the sense is his own there and in many other places. In this way he often abuses an author's name.

units.la: Nomen Dei despicit, & Sacrificium polluit, quisquis ad altare, vel munere seu precio, vel aliàs indignè accedit. Ac etiam, qui verbum, non ad salutem, sed in gratiam, populo dispergit.
units.tr: He who approaches the altar unworthily, whether with a gift or a fee or otherwise, despises the name of God and pollutes the sacrifice. So too does he who scatters the word among the people not for their salvation but for favour.

units.la: S Acerdotes nomen Domini despiciunt: & Panem polluitum offerunt, qui ad altare indignè accedunt, quique, dato munere, Sacerdotium præsumunt. Panem quoque polluit, qui Doctrinâ Domini in populo malè dispergit: & qui honorat potentem, & despicit pauperem. Et infrà.
units.tr: Priests despise the name of the Lord and offer polluted bread when they approach the altar unworthily, and when they presume upon the priesthood by giving a gift. He also pollutes the bread who badly scatters the teaching of the Lord among the people, and who honours the powerful and despises the poor. And below.

units.la: Indoctos, & Quæstuarios, & Vitiosos admonens Altari, polluit Altare.
units.tr: Admonishing the untaught, the mercenary and the vicious, he pollutes the altar.

units.la: § Si offeratis cæcum animal ad immolandum, nonne malum est? Superiùs accusati de Panibus, nunc accusantur de Victimis. Cæcum animal offert, qui ordinat indoctum in loco docti: magistrúmque facit, qui vix discipulus esse poterat. Claudum offert, qui lucra terrena quærentem locat: vtpote pedem in diuersa ponentem: vnum in Diuinis: alterum in Carnalibus: cui potest inferri illud de libro Regum: Vsquequo claudicatis in duas partes? Languidum offert, qui Vitiosum habet pro Religioso: quíque Tardum & Pigrum probat Patientem: dicens illum negligentiæ non redarguendum. Indignum est enim dare Deo, quod dedignatur homo.
units.tr: § "If you offer a blind animal for sacrifice, is it not evil?" Above, they were accused about the bread; now they are accused about the victims. He offers a blind animal who appoints an untaught man in the place of a teacher, and makes a master of one who could scarcely be a disciple. He offers a lame animal who places a man who seeks earthly gain, one who puts one foot in divine things and the other in carnal ones; to him can be applied that passage from the book of Kings: "How long will you halt between two opinions?" He offers a sick animal who holds a vicious man to be religious, and who approves a slow and lazy man as patient, saying that he is not to be rebuked for negligence. For it is unworthy to give to God what a man would disdain to give.

units.la: Item. Gregorius, ait in Pastorali cap.11. primæ partis illius libri. Quod integrum fere transcripsit huc Gratianus. In paragraphos distinximus.
units.tr: Likewise. Gregory says in the Pastoral Care, chapter 11 of the first part of that book, which Gratian transcribed here almost entire. We have divided it into paragraphs.

units.la: Aliis veniam, gratiamque non petat, qui ipse veniæ gratiaque indignus existit.
units.tr: Let him not seek pardon and grace for others who is himself unworthy of pardon and grace.

units.la: SOlicitè formidadum est, ne qui placare posse iram Dei creditur, hanc ipse ex proprio reatu mereatur. cunctì enim liquidò novimus: quia quum is, qui displicet, ad intercedendum mittitur, irati animus ad deteriora provocatur. Qui ergo desideriis terrenis adstringitur, caveat ne di stricti iram iudicis graviùs accendens, dum loco delectatur gloriæ, fiat subditis author ruinæ. Solerter ergo se quisque metiatur: nec locum regiminis assumere audeat, si adhuc in se vitium damnabiliter regnat: ne is quem crimen depravat proprium, intercessor fieri appetat pro culpis aliorum.
units.tr: One must be very careful lest he who is believed able to appease the anger of God should himself merit that anger through his own guilt. For we all clearly know that when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angered party is provoked to worse. Therefore he who is bound by earthly desires should take care lest, by kindling more heavily the anger of the strict judge while he delights in the place of glory, he become the author of ruin to his subjects. Let each therefore measure himself carefully, and not dare to assume a place of rule if vice still reigns damnably within him, lest one whom his own crime corrupts should seek to become an intercessor for the sins of others.

units.la: Continuò sequitur in eodem capite.
units.tr: Immediately it follows in the same chapter.

units.la: Quibus morbi, vitiúve quid inest, Hos ab Altari Domini reiecit Moses.
units.tr: Moses rejected from the altar of the Lord those who have any diseases or defects.

units.la: HInc etenim supernâ voce ad Moysen dicitur in Leuitico: Loquere ad Aaron: Homo de semine tuo per familias, qui habuerit maculam, non offerat panes Deo suo: nec accedat ad ministerium eius. ubi repente subiungitur: Si cæcus fuerit, Si claudus, Si vel parvo, vel grandi vel torto naso, Si fracto pede, Si mancus, Si lippus, Si gibbosus, Si albuginem habes in oculo, Si iugem scabiem, Si impetiginem in corpore, Vel ponderosus.
units.tr: For thus it is said by a voice from heaven to Moses in Leviticus: "Speak to Aaron: A man of your seed throughout their families who has a blemish shall not offer the bread of his God, nor approach to his ministry." Where it is suddenly added: "If he is blind, if he is lame, if he has a small or large or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot, if he is maimed, if he is purblind, if he is hunchbacked, if he has a white film in his eye, if he has a continual scab, or an itch in the body, or is ruptured."

units.la: Cæcus est, Qui suæ salutis viam non videt, nec in scripturarum lucem prospicit.
units.tr: The blind is he who does not see the way of his salvation, nor look toward the light of the Scriptures.

units.la: CÆcus quippe est, qui supernæ lucem contemplationis ignorat: qui præsentis vitæ tenebris pressus, dum lucem venturam nequaquam diligendo conspicit, quo gressus operis porrigat, nescit. Hinc etenim, prophetate Anna, dicitur: Pedes sanctorum suorum seruabit: & impij in tenebris conticescent.
units.tr: For he is blind who is ignorant of the light of heavenly contemplation: who, pressed by the darkness of the present life, while he does not look upon the coming light with love, does not know whither to direct the steps of his work. Hence, indeed, the prophetess Hannah says: "He will keep the feet of his saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness."

units.la: Claudus est, qui non recta pergit in via Domini: Nec in ea firmus, pede graditur utroque.
units.tr: The lame is he who does not walk straight in the way of the Lord, nor is he firm in it, walking on both feet.

units.la: C Laudus vero est, qui quidem, quo pergere debeat, aspicit: sed per infirmitatem mentis, vitae viam persectae non valet tenere, quam videt: quia videlicet, Dum quis ad virtutis statum fluxa consuetudine non erigitur: quo desiderium eius nititur, illuc gressus operis efficaciter non sequuntur. Hinc etenim Paulus dicit: Remissas manus, & dissoluta genua erigite: & gressus rectos facite pedibus vestris: ut non claudicans quis erret: magis autem sanetur.
units.tr: But the lame is he who indeed sees where he ought to go, but through weakness of mind is not able to keep to the way of perfect life which he sees. That is to say, while someone is not raised to the state of virtue by a fluid habit, the steps of his work do not effectively follow where his desire strives. Hence Paul says: "Lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight steps for your feet, so that no one who is limping may go astray, but rather be healed."

units.la: Deformi sunt naso, qui bonum scripturarum sensum vel non odorantur: vel male perfrictis naribus odorantur.
units.tr: Those are deformed in the nose who either do not smell the good sense of the Scriptures, or smell it with nostrils badly stopped up.

units.la: P Aruo autem naso est, qui ad tenendam mensuram discretionis idoneus non est. Naso quippe odores, foetoresque discernimus: Recte ergo per nasum Discretio exprimitur: per quam virtutes eligimus: delicta reprobamus. Vnde & in laudibus sponsae dicitur: Nasus tuus, sicut turris quae est in Libano: quia nimirum sancta Ecclesia, quae ex causis singulis tentamenta prodeant, per discretionem conspicit: & ventura vitiorum bella ex alto deprehendit.
units.tr: He is flat-nosed who is not fit to hold the measure of discernment. For by the nose we distinguish odours and stenches; rightly, then, discernment is signified by the nose, by which we choose virtues and reject faults. Whence also in the praise of the bride it is said: "Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon," because holy Church, no doubt, sees through discernment from what individual causes temptations come forth, and from on high detects the coming wars of vices.

units.la: Quemadmodum, qui nihil sentit (hoc est, indoctus & Hebes) Paruo dictus est nunc esse naso: Sic etiam Qui male sentit, aut superbe sapit, Hic nasum grandem vel obtortum dicitur habere.
units.tr: Just as he who perceives nothing (that is, the untaught and dull) is now said to have a small nose, so also he who thinks badly, or savours of pride, is said to have a large or crooked nose.

units.la: § Sed sunt nonnulli, qui dum nolunt hebetes existimari, saepe se quibusdam exquisitionibus, plusquam necesse est, exercentes, & nimia subtilitate falluntur. Vnde hic quoque subditur, vel Grandi, vel Torto naso. Nasus quippe grandis & tortus, est discretionis subtilitas immoderata: quae dum, plusquam decet, excreuerit, actionis suae rectitudinem ipsa confundit.
units.tr: § But there are some who, while they do not wish to be thought dull, often exercise themselves in certain subtleties more than is necessary, and are deceived by excessive refinement. Hence here also is added "or large, or crooked nose." For a large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment, which, when it has grown more than is fitting, itself confounds the rectitude of its action.

units.la: Bonis omnino vacuus operibus, neque se movens in via Domini, neque iusta contrectans, dicitur & manus & pedes nullos habere. ὁ αὐτῷ σύντετριμμα χεῖρες, καὶ σύντετριμμα ποδὸς. vt est in septuaginta.
units.tr: Wholly empty of good works, neither moving in the way of the Lord nor handling what is just, he is said to have neither hands nor feet: ὁ αὐτῷ σύντετριμμα χεῖρες, καὶ σύντετριμμα ποδὸς, as in the Septuagint.

units.la: FRacto autem pede, vel manu est, qui viam Domini pergere omnino non valet: atque à bonis actibus funditus exors vacat. quatenus haec, nō vt claudus salte, cum infirmitate teneat, sed ab his omnimodo alienus existat.
units.tr: But one with a broken foot or hand is he who is altogether unable to walk the way of the Lord, and who lies utterly cut off from good deeds; in that he does not hold on, like the lame, with weakness, but stands wholly alien to them.

units.la: Regni terreni curae, in Regno Caelorum, id est, In Ecclesia, reddunt hominem gibbosum.
units.tr: The cares of the earthly kingdom, in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the Church, make a man hunchbacked.

units.la: GIbbosus vero est, quem terrenae solicitudinis pondus deprimit, ne vnquam ad superna respiciat: sed solis his, quae in infimis calcantur, intendit. qui, & siquando aliquid ex bono patriae caelestis audierit, ad hoc, nimirum peruersae consuetudinis pondere praegrauatus, cordis faciē non attollit: quia cogitationis statum erigere non valet, quem terrenę solicitudinis vsus curuū tenet. Ex eorū quippe specie, Psalmista dicit: Incuruatus, & humiliatus sum vsquequaque. quorum culpam per semetipsam veritas reprobans ait: Semen autem, quod in spinas cecidit, hi sunt qui audierunt verbum, & à sollicitudinibus, & diuitiis, & voluptatibus huius vitae euntes suffocantur, & non referunt fructum.
units.tr: But he is hunchbacked whom the weight of earthly anxiety presses down, so that he never looks up to things above, but attends only to those things which are trodden underfoot below. Even if he should hear something of the good of the heavenly fatherland, he does not lift up the face of his heart to it, weighed down by the burden of a perverse habit; for he cannot raise the state of his thought, which the practice of earthly anxiety keeps bent. Of such people the Psalmist indeed says: "I am bowed down and humbled on every side." Truth itself, condemning their fault, says: "The seed that fell among thorns, these are they who have heard the word, and as they go are choked by the cares, riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit."

units.la: Lippiunt in Ecclesia, qui mentis aciem, quam perspicacē nacti sunt, in carnis opera figūt.
units.tr: In the Church, those who fix upon the works of the flesh the keenness of mind which they have acquired become purblind.

units.la: LIppus vero est, cuius quidem ingenium ad cognitionem veritatis emicat: sed tamē hoc carnalia opera obscurāt. In lippis quippe oculis pupillae sanae sunt: sed humore defluente, infirmantes palpebrae crassescunt: quae, quia infusione crebrâ atteruntur, etiam acies pupillae vitiatur. Et sunt nonnulli, quorum sensum carnalis vitæ operatio sauciat: qui videre recta subtiliter per ingenium poterant, sed vsu prauorum actuum caligant. Lipppus itaque est, cuius sensum natura exacuit, sed conuersationis prauitas confundit: cui bene per Angelum dicitur: Collyrio inunge oculos tuos, vt videas. Collyrio quippe oculos, vt videamus, inungimus, quum ad cognoscendam veri luminis claritatem, intellectus nostri aciem medicamine operationis bonæ adiuuamus.
units.tr: He is purblind whose talent shines forth toward the knowledge of the truth, but whose carnal works nevertheless darken it.
