For in purblind eyes the pupils are sound, but with the humour flowing down, the weakened eyelids thicken; and because they are worn away by frequent discharge, the sharpness of the pupil too is impaired. And there are some whose sense the activity of carnal life wounds: they could see straight clearly by their natural ability, but by the practice of depraved acts they grow dim. He therefore is purblind whose nature has sharpened his sense, but the perversity of his conduct confounds it; to him the Angel rightly says: "Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see." For we anoint our eyes with eye-salve that we may see when, to recognise the clarity of the true light, we help the keenness of our understanding by the remedy of good works.

units.la: Magna est oculorum mentis Albugo, quæ nostram non sinit nos videre vilitatem.
units.tr: The cataract of the mind's eyes is great; it does not let us see our own worthlessness.

units.la: ALbuginem vero habet in oculo, qui veritatis lucem videre non sinitur: quia arrogantiâ Sapientiæ seu Iustitiæ excæcatur. Pupilla nanque oculi nigra videt: albuginem tolerâs nihil videt: quia, videlicet, sensus humanæ cogitationis, si stultum se, peccatoremque intelligit, cognitionem intimæ claritatis apprehendit. Si autem sibi candore Iustitiæ siue Sapientiæ tribuit, à luce se superna cognitionis excludit: & eò claritate veri luminis nequaquam penetrat, quò se apud se per arrogantiâ exaltat: sicut de quibusdam dicitur: Dicentes enim se esse Sapientes, stulti facti sunt.
units.tr: A cataract is in the eye of the one who is not allowed to see the light of truth, because he is blinded by the arrogance of wisdom or righteousness. The pupil of the eye is black and sees; the white film sees nothing. So when the mind's perception understands itself to be foolish and sinful, it grasps the knowledge of inner clarity. But if it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it shuts itself off from the supernal light of knowledge. The more it exalts itself through arrogance, the less it penetrates the clarity of the true light, as is said of certain people: "Claiming to be wise, they became fools" [Rom. 1:22].

units.la: Mala illum scabies vrget, qui malum mente conceptum deducit in actum. Λόγος vel Ἀγρία, velut est in Septuaginta.
units.tr: The mange of the scab torments the one who carries out in action the evil he has conceived in his mind: logos or agria, as in the Septuagint [Λόγος vel Ἀγρία].

units.la: IVgem vero scabiem habet, cui carnis petulantia sine cessatione dominatur. In scabie etenim feruor viscerum ad cutem trahitur: per quam recte luxuria designatur: quia si cordis tentatio vsque ad operationem prosilit, nimirum feruor intimus vsque ad cutis scabiem prorupit, & foris iam corpus sauciat: quia dum in cogitatione voluptas non reprimitur, etiam in actione dominatur. Quasi enim cutis pruriginem Paulus curabat abstergere, quum dicebat: Tentatio vos non apprehendat, nisi humana. ac si apertè diceret. Humanū quidē est in corde tentatione perpeti: Demoniacū vero est in tentationis certamine & operatione superari.
units.tr: He has a red scab who is constantly ruled by the wantonness of the flesh. For in scab the heat of the inner parts is drawn out to the skin, and by this luxury is rightly signified: if the temptation of the heart leaps forward into action, the inner heat certainly breaks out to the scab of the skin and now wounds the body outwardly, because when pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also rules in deed. Paul, as it were, was trying to wipe away the itching of the skin when he said: "Let not temptation take hold of you except what is human" [1 Cor. 10:13], as if he were plainly saying: it is human to suffer temptation in the heart; but it is demonic to be overcome in the struggle and act of temptation.

units.la: Sordidis Lichenibus infestatur, quisquis Avaritiae impetigine foedatur.
units.tr: Whoever is defiled by the scab of avarice is afflicted with foul lichens.

units.la: IMpetiginem quóque habet in corpore, quisquis avaritiâ vastatur in mente: quæ si in parvis non compescitur, nimirū sine mensura dilatatur. Impetigo quippe sine dolore corpus occupat: & absque occupati tædio excrescens, membrorum decorem fœdat: quia & avaritia captivam animam, dum quasi delectat, exulcerat: dum adipiscenda quæque cogitationi obiicit, ad inimicitias accendit: & dolorem in vulnere non facit, quia æstuanti animo ex culpa abundantiam promittit. Sed decor membrorum perditur, quia aliarum quóque virtutum per hanc pulchritudo depravatur: & quasi totū corpus exasperat, quia per universa vitia animum supplantat: Paulo attestante, qui ait. Radix omnium malorum est cupiditas.
units.tr: He also has the impetigo in his body who is laid waste by avarice in his mind. If it is not restrained in small things, it certainly spreads without measure. Impetigo indeed occupies the body without pain, and growing without troubling its victim, it disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So avarice too, while it seems to delight the captive soul, ulcerates it; while it presents every desirable thing to thought, it kindles enmities; and it causes no pain in the wound, because it promises abundance to the heated mind from sin. But the beauty of the limbs is lost, because through this vice the beauty of the other virtues is corrupted too, and it roughens the whole body, as it were, because it supplants the soul through all vices, as Paul bears witness, who says: "The love of money is the root of all evils" [1 Tim. 6:10].

units.la: Μανίᾳ εἰς, infamisque Laboratu Hernia, qui, quod potestate nequit, attamen voluntate peragit.
units.tr: Into madness [Μανίᾳ εἰς], and infamous, the hernia of the labourer, who accomplishes by will what he cannot accomplish by power.

units.la: POnderosus verò est, qui turpitudinem opere non exercet: sed tamen ab hac, cogitatione continuâ sine moderamine grauatur in mente: qui nequaquam quidem usque ad opus nefarium rapitur, sed eius animus voluptate luxuriæ, sine vllo repugnationis obstaculo, delectatur. Vitium quippe est ponderis, cùm humor viscerum ad virilia labitur: quæ profectò cum molestia dedecoris intumescunt. Ponderosus ergo est, qui totis cogitationibus ad lasciuiam defluens, pondus turpitudinis gestat in corde: & quanuis prava non exerceat opere: ab his tamen non auellitur mente: nec ad vsum boni operis in aperto valet assurgere, quia grauat hunc in abditis pondus turpe.
units.tr: He is weighed down who does not carry out the shameful deed in action, but is nevertheless burdened by it in mind through continual thought without restraint: he is not indeed carried away to the wicked deed, but his mind takes pleasure in the lust of wantonness, with no obstacle of resistance. For it is a fault of weight when the humour of the bowels slides down to the genitals, which indeed swell with the discomfort of disgrace. He is therefore weighed down who, flowing through all his thoughts into lasciviousness, carries the weight of baseness in his heart; and although he does not practise the wicked things in action, he is nevertheless not torn away from them in mind: nor can he rise up to the practice of good work openly, because the shameful weight burdens him in hidden places.

units.la: Quisquis ergo quolibet horum vitio subigitur, Panes Domino offerre prohibetur: nec profecto diluere aliena delicta non valeat is, quem adhuc propria deuastant. Quia igitur paucis, ad Pastorale magisterium dignus qualiter veniat: atque hoc indignus, qualiter pertimescat, ostendimus: nunc is qui ad illud digne peruenerit, in eo qualiter viuere debeat, demonstremus.
units.tr: Therefore whoever is subdued by any one of these vices is forbidden to offer the bread to the Lord, nor indeed can he who is still laid waste by his own sins wipe away the sins of others. Therefore, having shown briefly how one who is worthy comes to the pastoral office, and how the unworthy should fear it, we will now show how he who has worthily attained it ought to live in it.

units.la: AVDITORI CHRISTIANO QVINTINVS
units.tr: TO THE CHRISTIAN HEARER, QUINTINUS

units.la: Hactenus Apostolum nobis exposuit Gratianus, omnia strictim breuique complexus, quaecunque religiosum ac fidelem Iesu Christi ministrum, ex animo puréque Diuinis inseruientem, decet. Quae latius (ipso nos docente atque ducente Christo) pergemus, vt poterimus, quotidianis nostris ad vos sermonibus & praelectionibus explicare. Caeterum, velut a Hieronymo coepi, sic etiam desinere visum. Et (quaeso) quo melius, ac tutius? Ille, doctrina quidem maximus, maior autem sanctitate, Doctor Ecclesiae, dum suus Atticus aduersus Critobulum de verbis his ipsis Paulinis non pauca disseruisset, ita demum disputationem clausit in primo contra Pelagianos libro.
units.tr: Gratian has explained the Apostle to us up to this point, touching briefly and in summary on everything that befits a religious and faithful minister of Jesus Christ, one who serves the divine things with a sincere and pure heart. With Christ himself teaching and leading us, we shall go on to explain these matters more fully, as we can, in our daily sermons and lectures to you. Otherwise, I thought it best to end as I began, following Jerome. And (I ask) what could be better or safer? He, indeed the greatest in learning and greater still in holiness, the Doctor of the Church, when his Atticus had disputed at length against Critobulus about these very Pauline words, finally closed the discussion in the first book against the Pelagians.

units.la: PVTO, quod non facile sit reperire, qualem praecepit Apostolus, Episcopum: Maxime illud, vt potens sit aduersarius resistere, & peruersas opprimere ac superare doctrinas. Aut nullus, inquam, aut rarus est, qui omnia habeat, quae habere debet Episcopus. Et tamen, si vnum vel duo de catalogo virtutum, Episcopo cuiquam defuerint, non tamen, iusti carebit vocabulo. Nec ex eo damnabitur, quod non habet: sed ex eo coronabitur, quod possidet. Omnia enim habere, & nullo indigere, Virtutis eius est, qui peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inuentus est in ore eius, & in quo princeps huius mundi non habet quicquam.
units.tr: "It is not easy to find the kind of bishop the Apostle prescribes, above all one who is able to withstand an adversary and to refute and overcome perverse teachings. I say that either no one, or very few, have all the qualities a bishop ought to have. And yet, if one or two of the catalogue of virtues are lacking in any bishop, he will not lose the name of bishop. Nor will he be condemned for what he lacks, but crowned for what he possesses. For to have all things and to lack nothing belongs to the virtue of him who committed no sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found, and in whom the prince of this world has nothing."

units.la: Haec ille.
units.tr: Thus he.

units.la: A nobis perpetuo laudetur Animarum nostrarum summus Episcopus, qui sua, prout vult, cuique dispertitur.
units.tr: Let our supreme Bishop of our souls, who distributes his own gifts to each as he wills, be praised by us forever.

units.la: Sacerdotalis Ethologia.
units.tr: Sacerdotal Ethology.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
